Introduction
A Note on the English Edition
This book is the English translation of the volume: Colom, Enrique, and An-
gel Rodríguez Luño, Scelti in Cristo per essere santi. I. Morale fondamentale.
1st reprint of the 3rd edition, Rome: Edizioni Università della Santa Croce,
2008. It is the first volume of four which make up the moral theology man-
ual developed by the professors of the Department of Moral Theology of the
Pontifical University of the Holy Cross (Rome).
The translation into English of the Introduction and Chapter I was done by
Gerald Malsbary. The rest of the book and the final revision of the entire
text is the work of our collaborator Thomas Daniel Howes. To him goes our
recognition for the dedication and competence with which he accomplished
his task.
The Authors
A Note on the Italian Edition
This book is designed as a manual for the study of fundamental moral theol-
ogy. It is addressed primarily to those who are undertaking a required course
of study in Catholic theology at seminaries or ecclesiastical colleges.
The
editorial and typographical style, the choice of topics, and the extent of mate-
rial covered are intended to meet the needs of such students. Nevertheless, we
trust that the book will likewise be of interest for those who pursue theological
and moral studies at a non specialist, though nonetheless serious level.
The didactic purpose of our work calls for a clear presentation of the princi-
ples provided by Revelation and Catholic doctrine for the understanding of
Christian life, distinguishing such principles from our own precise philosoph-
ical and theological formulation of them. Theologians are well aware that
the distinction between doctrine and theological reflection is not always kept,
since at times it is not easy to formulate doctrine in terminology that is not
to some degree already theological or even philosophical. Such a distinction


Introduction
nonetheless exists, and is necessary in order to adequately reflect both the
necessary fidelity to Catholic doctrinal identity and the desired freedom of
theological research. This interest in clearly tracing the boundary between
Catholic doctrine and our personal reflection is what motivates our frequent
references to biblical foundations, to the teachings of the Second Vatican
Council—especially its doctrine of the universal call to holiness—as well as to
more recent interventions of the magisterium with regard to moral questions,
such as Veritatis Splendor, and the Catechism of the Catholic Church.
The reader will soon discover that although this book is founded on Catholic
doctrine, it is not simply a kind of “theologically neutral” exposition of that
doctrine.
In fact, our intention has been to carry out for the first time an
exposition of Catholic moral theology on the basis of the most recent develop-
ments in what is referred to today as “virtue ethics,” following a line of moral
research that has been strongly represented in English speaking countries as
well as in Italy and Germany for the past fifteen to twenty years.
In the
course of reading this book, the reader will come to understand its nature
and motivations, but for now we would like to offer the following provisional
sketch.
Virtue ethics, as we understand it, is not simply a method for articulating
a special moral theology; on the contrary, just how moral theology should
be articulated remains an unsolved problem, that we hope to confront as we
go along. Nor do we conceive of it as a “weak” or “light” version of a non-
cognitivist ethics which (accepting the impossibility of any true moral theory)
retreats to the study of character, or to a psychology of the virtues. To put
it in simpler terms, we do not conceive of virtue ethics as “an ethics without
norms” that will only remain at the level of vague exhortations. Virtue ethics,
as we understand it is a line of research that takes up the quandaries (aporiai,
in Greek philosophical language) of modern normative ethics, that is to say,
of an ethics that is completely focused on obligation, on norms, and on acts
as analyzed from the point of view of an external observer (i.e., an “ethics of
the third person”), and proposes instead an ethics that in its structure recalls
classical ethics and presents itself as an alternative (in structure, at least,
if not necessarily in content) to an ethics of obligation or “casuistic” ethics.
This line of research provides, among other advantages, for a rediscovery of the
scientific validity of what was the mature moral theory of Thomas Aquinas—
namely that contained in the Summa Theologiae—which nevertheless needs
to be brought up to date on some particular points.
The fundamental characteristic of our approach is that the center of ethical
theory consists in the practical (and not merely theoretical) consideration of
the good of human life considered in its totality, the good that had tradi-
tionally been referred to as the finis ultimus. The most basic task of moral


Introduction
philosophy would consequently consist in helping persons locate themselves
on a plane of reflection that contemplates human life as a whole, and, starting
from this perspective, might then be in a position to distinguish the priorities
to be assigned to the various activities that make up one's life as a whole
and to clarify the criteria according to which one should govern the use and
actualization of human goods; this ordering of priorities and these criteria
of rational governance form the essential content of the moral virtues. To
enter into the concrete problems of normative ethics without having first un-
dertaken this preliminary clarification about the type of life we wish to lead
would be equivalent to building the second floor of a building before building
its foundations and first floor. Our approach therefore presupposes that the
human good can be rationally investigated and a fortiori theologically inves-
tigated. Theological research, on the basis of Revelation, can avail itself of
a more precise and complete answer to the question about what is the ulti-
mate meaning of human life, in whose light fundamental concepts of morality
acquire a sharper image and a more exact contextualization.
The pedagogical purpose of this book has encouraged us to proceed cautiously
(for some perhaps too cautiously, for others, not cautiously enough). Before
the new building is completed, it is better not to demolish the old one and then
say we should not have torn it down completely after all. In other words, many
concepts and distinctions of casuistic morality are still very useful for students
and theologians, and perhaps always will be, provided they be updated and
duly placed into a new framework. We are aware that some passages of this
book will strike the reader as being rather eclectic. This is a risk that we
consider worth taking for the reason that, as just explained, this is a first
attempt that is necessarily imperfect, which puts a priority on the didactic
purpose as well as the radical development of the theological approach we
have assumed, but without giving up on a significantly coherent methodology
and thematization which seems to us to be adequate, at least in terms of the
current state of research.
We would like to conclude by explaining our ordering of the material. The first
chapter constitutes our introduction to moral theology, explaining its object
and its sources. In this chapter is conveyed our precise position on the epis-
temological status of moral theology as a practical wisdom. The First Part
studies the universal call to holiness, the ultimate end of Christian morality,
consisting in the fullness of divine filiation and which is realized in the follow-
ing of Christ (Chapter II); next, the discussion moves to a panoramic vision of
the fundamental lines of conduct whereby the believer seeks union with Christ
through his own actions and according to his conditions and circumstances
(Chapter III). This part is articulated according to the biblical notion of “call
and response,” which in any case cannot be absolutized if the nature of the


Chapter 0
moral life is to be described precisely as a human and moral phenomenon.
It is true that the Christian discovers a definite divine call behind ethical
imperatives, but it is also true that the Christian moral life does not consist
in replying “yes” or “no” to a question expressed in terms of a definite and
unambiguous context. If the moral life is not to be reduced to a struggle to
avoid serious sins, it is also, and above all, an active seeking, the power of
individually determining one's mode of living with imagination and courage,
such that all our actions become a means of attaining union with Christ.
The Second Part, more analytical in character, treats of moral anthropology,
that is, the sum total of natural structures and active principles infused by
God that make it possible for the human being—as the image of God—to be
an acting moral subject who works out a plan of life that is coherent with
his own well-being as a human being and a Christian. In this third edition
we have modified both the structure and contents of this part. The themes
we study are the following: the freedom of the children of God (Ch. IV),
the inclinations, feelings, and emotions (Ch. V), the nature and evaluation
of moral action (Ch. VI), and the moral virtues and gifts of the Holy Spirit
(Ch. VII).
The Third Part analyzes the normative dimension of the moral activity of
the human being. Both the internal cognitive principles and the external aids
come under consideration, permitting the believer to identify and refine the
conduct suitable for realizing the end to which he is destined. Also to be
examined are: the moral law (Ch. VIII), human laws that make it explicit
and more ultimately determine its context (Ch. IX), and conscience (Ch. X).
Finally, detailed consideration is given to sin, the act by which the human
being distances himself from Christ, and conversion, which entails a return to
Him (Ch. XI).
We hope that our labors will prove to be of some utility for the reader, and
that the suggestions and just criticisms of
our colleagues have helped us
improve the quality of the service we hope to render in this work: it is thanks
to them, in fact, that we have introduced notable changes in this third edition.
The Authors


## CHAPTER 1 {#colom-scelti.1}
The Nature, Object, and
Sources of Moral Theology
The Christian moral life is itself the presupposition and point of departure for
any reflection upon it. In order to understand the nature of moral theology it is
therefore necessary to set forth at the very beginning a few brief considerations
about Christian living ( 1); then, taking account of this reality, we will
examine the epistemology of moral theology ( 2) and its sources ( 3).
1.1
The Christian Moral Life
The Christian moral life is the life of man in Christ, or, more exactly, the
life of the human being as a child of God through the Holy Spirit. This is,
in substance, a gift of God, received at first with faith and baptism, which
however requires the free acceptance and collaboration of the human person
1.1.1
Children of God through the Holy Spirit
With faith and baptism, a person is truly incorporated into the crucified and
glorified Christ, and reborn to a sharing of the divine life, as the Apostle says:
“You were buried together with Him in Baptism, and in Him also rose again-
through faith in the working of God, who raised Him from the dead” (Col.
2, 12).1 The human being is freed from sin and receives the first sanctifying
grace, a true participation in the divine nature2 which configures the person
1 Conc. Vat. II, Decree Unitatis redintegratio, no. 22. Cf. also Lumen Gentium, no. 7,
and Council of Florence, Bull Exsultate Deo,
22 Nov. 1439–the origin of the celebrated
formula of baptism as “Gate of the spiritual life” (DS 1314).
2 Cf. 2 Pet 1:4.


Chapter 1
ontologically with Christ and makes her truly become a child of God.3 Faith
in Christ, along with baptism, brings about a complete change of the person;
and provides the gift of a new life, a real participation in the very life of the
Son of God. With faith and baptism is received, definitively, the grace of divine
filiation, which is the foundation of Christian life. Divine filiation implies, in
fact, the reception of the supernatural principles of the new life: sanctifying
grace as the remote vital principle, and the theological virtues, infused moral
virtues, and gifts of the Holy Spirit as the immediately operative principles.
The grace of divine filiation received in baptism is in reality only a beginning,
the seed of a new life animated by an intrinsic dynamism toward development
and growth until the attainment of “mature manhood, to the extent of the
full stature of Christ.”4 The followers of Christ “by God's gift . . . must hold
on to and complete in their lives this holiness they have received.” 5 This
`completing' or `perfecting' is a moral undertaking that strives for an ever
greater identification with Christ, with his sentiments 6 and his words, 7with
his mode of living and thinking, while observing his commandments and his
teachings,8 with the same obedience and the same love shown by Jesus before
the will of His Father.9 The principal agent of such moral progress is the Holy
Spirit—the Sanctifier—with whom we are free collaborators, and the final goal
of our growth in Christ is the eschatological consummation of participation
in the Trinitarian life, to which we were destined in Christ before the creation
of the world.10
We are saying, then, that along our path in this world, we Christians are called
to develop and express by and in our works the divine life, from the moment
that this is communicated to us in baptism with the grace of the Holy Spirit.
It should be made clear, the Christian life does not consist in external works,
as considered isolated in their material factualness. Rather, the Christian life
is a life—a life that Christ lives in us,11 completed by the principles of justice,
love and action that inspire the life of Christ (the imitation of Christ) and
which constitute the Christian virtues, and principally charity, that is, the
love of Christ, the bond of Christian perfection that is to be sought above all
other things.12

The Nature, Object, and Sources of Moral Theology
1.1.2
The Sacramental and Ecclesiastical Character
of the Christian Moral Life
It is necessary to reflect, even if somewhat briefly, on the sacramental and
ecclesiastical basis of the Christian moral life.
We can take our point of
departure with a twofold consideration: on the one hand, God wants salvation
to reach all men of all times13; on the other hand, the means chosen by God
to do this is the Incarnation of His Son, and this implies that the saving
words and actions of Christ happened in a concrete place and time.
The
sacramental character of the whole plan of salvation proceeds from the divine
design to extend the effect of salvation through a sensibly-grasped mediation
instituted by Christ Himself, by virtue of which spatio-temporal distances are
overcome. Such human mediation is constituted of the Church, the “universal
sacrament of salvation”14, and the sacraments, the sensible and efficacious
signs of grace, instituted by Christ and safeguarded and administered by the
Church.
We have already mentioned the role of baptism in the Christian life. This
makes us at once members of Christ and members of the Church15: all those
baptized in Christ are one in Christ Jesus.16 The other sacraments are no less
important. Confirmation, among other things, introduces us more profoundly
into divine filiation, works the full outpouring of the Holy Spirit and His gifts,
and at the same time renders our bond with the Church more perfect.17 The
eucharist is the “fount and apex of the whole Christian life” 18 or the “center
and root of the spiritual life of the Christian”.19 This brings about a deep
and intimate union with Christ, makes present the sacrifice on Mount Calvary
and applies its benefits, increases grace and keeps one from sin, restores lost
powers, reinforces the unity of the Church, and gives a pledge of future glory.20
Extremely important for the moral life is the sacrament of penance, which
permits the recovery of grace and the merits lost on account of sin, renews
the soul and makes for a new beginning of the moral life, constituting in
addition an efficacious means for the formation of the moral conscience. It
frequenting of the sacraments, still others in alms giving; but they are mistaken: perfection
consists in loving God with all your heart.” (Saint Alphonsus Liguori, Pratica di amar Gesù

Chapter 1
is not possible here to emphasize the important role of the other sacraments,
or the more recent studies on the role that they play in the Christian moral
life.21It should suffice for now to keep in mind that the Christian life has a
sacramental basis, without which it would either not be possible or would
disappear.22
But the saving mediation of the Church is not limited to the administration
of the sacraments. The teachings and moral examples of the Lord are meant
as well to overcome spatio-temporal distances and cultural barriers, becoming
contemporaneous and relevant for each of us, even to the point of involving
us completely.
This takes place by way of preaching and the living moral
tradition of the Church, the “necessary mediation by which the individual
believer learns the Way of the Lord transmitted by apostolic exhortation.”23
The life of the Church, understood as the road traveled by the Christian
community through history under the magisterial authority of the legitimate
pastors and with the stimulus represented by the saints recognized as such
by her, is the privileged hermeneutical space of Christian moral experience.
The life and moral tradition of the Church also respond to the human need
to undertake an understanding of morality on the basis of an ethos rooted
in and shared by a community,24 but it is not only this. The apostles and
their successors received from Christ the command to transmit His moral
instruction faithfully,25 making it concrete and applying it to the particular
circumstances of each society and epoch, and Christ Himself promised the
assistance of the Holy Spirit in order to keep the identity of the transmitted
message intact.26 There exists in the Church, therefore, a magisterium, and
also a moral magisterium, which by the will of Christ is truly normative for the
conscience of the believer.27We shall later concentrate on the nature, modality

The Nature, Object, and Sources of Moral Theology
and significance of the Church's moral magisterium and on other questions
related to that theme.28
For the present it is sufficient to note that the
relationship between the human person and Christ in which the Christian
moral life consists “is not considered and established by the believer himself
in an individualistic solitude”,29 but is established within the Church and in
communion with her.
We must add that the Church is not only the ambit or “means” whereby the
Christian message normally came to meet us on one day or another. The
ecclesial community is its permanent abode, inseparable from life in Christ.
Saint Paul sets up a strict parallelism between being children of God through
faith in Christ Jesus and baptism,30 and all being “one in Christ Jesus”.31 “To
be one” does not only mean having a common faith, but being all united as the
Body of Christ: “so we, though many, are one body in Christ and individually
parts of one another”.32 The Pauline analogy between the human body and
Christ/the Church is meant to clarify how union with Christ is not possible
without all being formed into the Body of Christ together. This opens up a
perspective of deep participation and communion of a mystical character that
involves all Christians. In Christian life, ecclesial communion is not only a
form of respect or an element to keep in mind. It belongs to its very essence.
Christ cannot be divided. Lack of awareness of ecclesial belonging, and still
more, division as such, would constitute an attack against the very essence of
our being and living in Christ.
1.1.3
Christian Morality and Human Morality
If the Christian moral life begins with baptism, the same cannot be said
about life or moral experience in general. There is an ethical experience and
an ethical reflection that exists prior to Christianity and also independently
from the Old Testament revelation (such as Aristotelian ethics for example),
because the human being, by his natural condition, is a moral being, and
is therefore capable of understanding the distinction between good and evil
as such. Human moral competence is not objectively exterior to the divine
plan of salvation, because man was created through Christ and in view of
Christ.33 Nevertheless, being predestined to communion with God in Christ
presupposes that man is not God, but a non-divine being having its own
Instruction Donum Veritatis, as well as Veritatis Splendor 110–117 and the CCC 85–87
and 888–892 and (more specifically on the moral magisterium) 2032–2040.
28 See below, subsection 1.3.2.
29 C. Caffarra, Viventi in Cristo (1986) 63.
30 Cf. Gal 3:26–27.
31 Gal 3:28.
32 Rom 12:5.

Chapter 1
creaturely integrity which has to be known and understood. Consequently it
seems legitimate to ponder the relationship between Christian morality and
the human moral structure, or if you will, about the specific moral structure of
the Christian, who is a moral subject for two reasons: insofar as he is human
and insofar as he is Christian. This is a question which has received a variety
of answers throughout the history of moral theology, and which has given rise
to a debate in recent years about the specific nature of Christian morality,
and subsequently, regarding “moral autonomy in a Christian context”;34 with
which we shall occupy ourselves shortly. In the meantime, we shall take up
only the simplest and most immediate aspects of the question, which will
form the basis for a more adequate treatment of more specific points in a
subsequent discussion.
We find a first strong indication in the summary of Jesus' message found
in Mark 1: 15: “This is the time of fulfillment.
The kingdom of God is
at hand. Repent, and believe in the gospel.”
With the Savior's preaching
the time of waiting is over, and a new time begins in which the fulfillment
of the Messianic prophecies will take place. A profound transformation of
the human being is being called for (“repent”: metanoeîte, paenitemini) as
well as a living and operative reception of all that the words of the Savior
are teaching, announcing, communicating. Two concepts are relevant to our
point: newness and fulfillment.
This first indication is made complete with another message conveyed in the

the Prophets. I have come not to abolish but to fulfill I tell you, unless your
righteousness surpasses that of the scribes and Pharisees, you will not enter
into the kingdom of heaven.”35 The reference to the Law of Moses (which
also contains the necessary foundations of the natural moral law, especially
the Decalogue) and the Prophets is a double one: the intention is not to
abolish them, but to bring them to fulfillment (pl	erôsai: to complete, to
perfect, or to complete by way of action36). This is taken to mean that with

The Nature, Object, and Sources of Moral Theology
regard to the Law of Moses (and implicitly also with regard to the natural
moral law37) the Christian message is yes something new, but something
new without rupture, a newness that is also a fulfillment. Christian morality
exceeds human morality and the law of Moses, but at the same time brings
them to their fulfillment.
If the good of man is retained and brought to its fullness when it is elevated
to the level of divine filiation, then, in one respect, the Christian message in-
trinsically possesses a universal significance, and is recognizable by all—with
the help of grace—as the most complete expression of the truth about man:
“Only in the mystery of the incarnate word does the mystery of man take
on light”.38
In another respect, Christianity implies a very deep apprecia-
tion of the realities of human moral virtues, including them as a necessary
presupposition of the Christian moral life.
However, the human moral virtues are not just presuppositions. If by human
virtues we mean the moral habits that constitute the perfection of man as
such, even of non-believers,39 we will certainly have to think that the devel-
opment of such human qualities precedes on the logical plane the development
of the Christian virtues;40 in practice, however, the two developments work
together and are interrelated in various ways. On the one hand, the ethical
virtues are not only a means for the exercise of Christian virtues, but they are
at the same time a consequence and fruit of charity for the Christian person;41
on the other hand, faith in Christ, being woven into the dynamism of human
action, “also requires a reformulation of the meaning and hierarchy of the
virtues.
They are not any longer simply the result of human practices, but
are infused by God. The active primacy of charity and the other theological
virtues changes the meaning of the whole complex of the virtues, crowned as
they are by the gifts of the Holy Spirit. With reference to Christ, new virtues
come into play, unknown to classical philosophy: humility, obedience, and
service (cf. Phil. 2 and John 13).”42 It is significant in this connection that

Chapter 1
Saint Paul considers patience, fidelity, gentleness, and self-control as fruits of
the action of the Holy Spirit in the Christian.43
If the Christian life is founded in Christ, perfectus Deus, perfectus homo44,
God and Man without confusion or separation, then we must avoid all opposi-
tion between the human element and the divine element of Christian morality;
between reason and faith, between free will and grace. A dialectic that can
find no way to affirm the divine element but by a negation or devaluation of
the human element or which, vice versa, can only affirm the human element
by limiting or devaluing the divine element, would not be compatible with
the reality and logic of the Incarnation. The devaluation of the human eth-
ical virtues would make Christian morality less credible, and would not be
theologically justifiable even in the perspective of the theologia Crucis. If it
is true that in the human being there are things which must die beneath the
sign of the Cross, it is also true that in the sign of the Cross all that is good
and virtuous in man reaches its most complete development.45 In the Cross of
Christ the old man—the animalis homo referred to by St. Paul—must die,46
but not what is true virtue in man: “Whatever is true, whatever is honorable,
whatever is just, whatever is pure, whatever is lovely, whatever is gracious, if
there is anything worthy of praise, think about these things.” 47
It is true that the normative requirements of the supernatural virtues and
those of the human moral virtues are dissimilar when we confront them with
the cognitive possibilities of human practical reasoning; this is something that
must be kept in mind. But if the differentiation generated by this particu-
lar viewpoint is not conceived in a dialectical way, it in no way compromises
the unitary character of the Christian moral life, where Christian and human
ethical virtues are interwoven at several levels and with rather complex artic-
ulations.
Such interweaving corresponds in the final analysis to the divine
plan of salvation.48 The whole man is renewed by the grace of divine filiation.
In the moral life of the believer there are no purely “human” strata. “Nothing
can be foreign to Christ's care. If we enter into the theology of it instead
of limiting ourselves to functional categories, we cannot say that there are
things—good, noble, or indifferent—which are exclusively worldly. This can-
not be after the Word of God has lived among the children of men, felt hunger

The Nature, Object, and Sources of Moral Theology
and thirst, worked with his hands, experienced friendship and obedience and
suffering and death. `For in him all the fullness of God was pleased to dwell,
and through him to reconcile all things, whether in earth or in heaven, making
peace by the blood of the cross.'(Col. 1, 19–20).”49
In this book we will be using the expression `Christian life' or `Christian moral
life', whether we are referring to the area of the infused virtues (theological
or moral) or to the area of the human moral virtues, and consequently also to
that which has traditionally been called natural law. This latter, in distinction
from the infused virtues and their object, does not in principle exceed human
possibilities, but it is integrated into Christian life, giving rise to a moral
perspective that is something more than the simple sum of one human part
plus another divine part, and in which the ethical virtues acquire a salvific
meaning. Therefore the Letters of the New Testament cite explicitly as being
among the actions that exclude one from the Kingdom of God, the behaviors
that are offensive to the human ethical virtues,50 and the Church considers as
contrary to Catholic doctrine the distinction “between an ethical order which
would be human in origin and of value for this world alone, and an order of
salvation, for which only certain intentions and interior attitudes regarding
God and neighbor would be significant.”51 In other words, not only are faith,
hope, and charity relevant for salvation: also relevant are the moral virtues, or
the “second tablet” of the Ten Commandments.52 The integration of the eth-
ical virtues in Christian life does not mean, however, that they are normative
exclusively for Christians, or that their requirements lose their natural com-
municability by way of rational discourse. Nevertheless, we think that their
deepest meaning for human life, while remaining rationally comprehensible,
cannot be exhausted by the rational level.
A corollary of what has just been said is that it does not seem right to under-
stand the relation between faith and moral reasoning as divided them into two
mutually exclusive functions, as if faith could only say something about the
interior life (intentions, motivations, will, feelings, etc.), while correct behav-
ior would be the area where reason had an exclusive competency. Faith too
can be the ground of good reasoning in the order both of ethical argumen-
tation and of the material content of actions. The rigid distinction between
paraenesis and normative ethics, so widely diffused today, should be seriously
called into question.

Chapter 1
1.2
Moral Theology
as the “Science” of Christian Living
1.2.1
Object and Functions of Moral Theology
We have already mentioned that the nature of moral theology can be explained
and understood only with reference to Christian moral life—an historical re-
sult following upon God's communication of himself in Christ, which never-
theless requires the free collaboration of man. The life of the faithful in Christ
within the ecclesial community, under the authoritative guide of its pastors,
comes first;53 moral theology comes later, and constitutes the scientific un-
derstanding and systematic exposition of that life. Moral theology is thus a
reflective knowledge. In more concrete terms, it can be understood among
the diverse forms of moral reflection working in the light of Christ within the
Church,54 “its specific nature as a scientific reflection on the Gospel as the gift
and commandment of new life, a reflection on the life which 'professes the
truth in love' (cf. Eph 4:15) and on the Church's life of holiness, in which
there shines forth the truth about the good brought to its perfection.” 55
We are saying, then, that moral theology is the part of theology that has for its
proper object the understanding of the life of the faithful in Christ. In a now
celebrated passage, the Second Vatican Council affirms that moral theology
ought to illustrate in a scientific way “the loftiness of the calling of the faithful
in Christ and the obligation that is theirs of bearing fruit in charity for the life
of the world”.56 Moral theology is intended to bring to “conscious reflection
the life that is born of our being in Christ through the Holy Spirit, constantly
verifying that life with reference to its principle, which is divine Revelation
as witnessed by Holy Scripture and Tradition”.57
Both the beginning and the growth of moral theological reflection arise in
response to needs that are partly common to all theology and partly specific.
Man was created in order to understand truth, and this involves a need to
think about what he is and what he does. To this need is added the “dy-
53 We are speaking here of the life of the faithful in Christ within the ecclesial community
under the guidance of pastors to make clear that we are concerned here with a theological
and normative concept, corresponding to the divine plan, and not a purely sociological one.
Behaviors and attitudes that are known to have occurred among Christians, even among
the earliest Christians, but which were condemned by the pastors, do not belong to the
life of the faithful in Christ. Cf. for example 1 Cor 5 (incest); 1 Cor 11, 17–34 (abuses in
the celebration of the Eucharist); Romans 14 (misunderstanding and mutual condemnation
between the strong and weak in faith).
54 Cf. Veritatis Splendor 29.
55 Ibid. 110.
56Optatam Totius 16.
57 C. Caffarra, Viventi in Cristo (1986), 72.


The Nature, Object, and Sources of Moral Theology
namism found in the faith itself”,58 which, by revealing to the human being
the ultimate truth about his destiny and the way to reach it,59 seeks to be
understood—fides quaerens intellectum—and to be communicated, whether
to believers, that they acquire a more profound comprehension, or to non-
believers, that they too attain to a knowledge of Christ. Theological reflection
thereby serves to reinforce the life of the faithful and contributes to the de-
velopment of the Church's apostolic activity. It responds as well, in a more
profound sense, to the need “of Christian life to speak of itself in coherent
and reflective human discourse: because in that way, too, the grace of God in
Christ might be glorified.”60
If it is true for the Christian event as a whole that it is realized in
history, then that fact is particularly significant for Christian moral re-
ality. Christian moral action—but this can also be said about human
action in general—is a sphere affected to the greatest degree by contin-
gency and by historical, cultural, and scientific/technological changes.
Actions are always particular, and their circumstances are always many-
sided and variable. Old problems are posed in a new way, and entirely
new problems are posed for the first time by the evolution of society and
scientific progress. The capacity and the ecclesial responsibility of guar-
anteeing the substantial identity of Christian life through the centuries
was entrusted by Christ to his pastors—the episcopal college cum Petro
et sub Petro—and only they can teach with authority in the dogmatic
and moral field. Nevertheless, the complexity of moral questions makes
particularly important the reflective verification of new solutions in the
primordial light of Revelation, as well as the projection of that same
light upon new problems, ever emerging and still in need of solution.
All this is the task of moral theology, which takes shape as a service to
the faithful and as an ecclesial vocation to be actualized in collaboration
with the pastors and as subject to their ultimate judgment.
1.2.2
The Epistemological Status of Moral Theology
The concept of moral theology as the understanding of the life of the faithful
in Christ must be clarified more specifically. We need to explain in particular
the specific mode of understanding the Christian life that moral theology
aims to attain.
The Encyclical Veritatis Splendor alludes to the complexity
of the question when it says that moral theology is “a science which accepts
and examines Divine Revelation while at the same time responding to the
demands of human reason.”61 Moral theology is concerned “with the good
and the evil of human acts and of the person who performs them; in this
58Donum Veritatis 7.
59 Ibid.
60 C. Caffarra, Viventi in Cristo (1986), 73.
61 Veritatis Splendor 29.


Chapter 1
sense it is accessible to all people,” but it is also theology, the science of God
“inasmuch as it acknowledges that the origin and end of moral action are
found in the One who `alone is good' and who, by giving himself to man in
Christ, offers him the happiness of divine life.”62
From the description of the Christian moral life proposed in the first sec-
tion of this chapter it emerges that moral theology must have a Christological
foundation. The Christian moral life is adhesion to Christ, and a vital com-
munion with Him, the search for the fullness of divine filiation, and therefore
a life lived according to faith. This thesis, which admits of various concrete
theological interpretations, has become since Veritatis Splendor a doctrinal
indication that cannot be abandoned. It is correct to point out that many
theologians were working in this direction before the appearance of Veritatis
Splendor,63 and in a certain sense the encyclical conveys from such research
results which had already obtained broad consensus.
The first chapter of Veritatis Splendor only proposes a path to follow, accom-
panied by some general indications. There is an epistemological problem that
remains open to further theological elaboration: namely, how to integrate the
rational aspect (natural moral law) with the inner, foundational Christologi-
cal perspective, and how to elaborate the latter so that it could constitute a
point of view that inspires the entire field of ethics and not just one section of
it. To be precise, what remains open is the problem of instituting an adequate
mediation by means of ethical categories that are at once well-founded and
coherent with the Christological perspective. Without such mediation, the
foundational discourse easily runs the risk of being entirely inconclusive in
practice.64

practical reason, by governing and modifying, when necessary, its first practical principles.


The Nature, Object, and Sources of Moral Theology
In our view it is necessary to reflect upon the rational analytical categories
to use, since not all are able to be adequately inserted into the theological
perspective we described above.
One must note in particular that in the
moral reflection of the twentieth century a tendency has become widespread
of conceiving moral life as a fact—the moral fact—that moral theology would
have to explain in a mode analogous to the way the natural sciences explain
natural facts.65 Since the moral fact consists—for the writers who share in
this tendency—in the consciousness of values and moral obligations derived
therefrom, the task of the moral theologian would be that of grounding moral
obligation and of identifying its essential meanings. Moral theology is con-
stituted in this case as knowledge about norms to be observed—that is, as a
morality of obligation.
This conception of moral theology strives to approach the modern sci-
entific mentality, with the good intention of becoming more easily un-
derstandable for the men of our time, and simultaneously wants to
maintain that moral reflection is a normative science, and not simply
a description of human custom. But it is conditioned by the idea that
the natural sciences are the model against which all scientific knowledge
ought to measure itself, an idea that encourages the understanding of
moral praxis through a method that distorts its nature and specificity.
In fact, the moral life is not a fact that can be understood from the per-
spective of an outside observer. This perspective constrains the study
and evaluation of human action as the action of a third person (Roger
has carried out the action x; is such an action licit or illicit? What
norm does action x fall under? How can the validity of such a norm
be established, as well as the obligation to obey it?). We are speaking
then of an ethics pursued from the “perspective of the third person”.66
This perspective brings about an ethics of obligation, which, among
other things, studies from the outside a reality such as human action,
which originates and acquires its moral character within the heart of
This does not mean, however, that one can always deduce what to do here and now from
the ontological condition of being a child of God. A mediation
is needed to arrive at a
moral judgment, in which the natural moral law plays an important role. The extreme
opposite position does not in any way seem acceptable to us, that is to say, the position of
all those who think that faith in Christ, or our condition of being sons of God in Christ,
says absolutely nothing about the content of concrete ethical action, which would instead
be the exclusive camp of the autonomous reason. The Christological foundation rightly
understood would have to sweep aside these opposing positions. The alternative between
“reason or faith” is not admissible in morality at any level. Rather, we must say “both
reason and faith”, not as a sum or juxtaposition, but as an effective integration. The inte-
gration is attained neither by those who maintain autonomous reason alone nor by those
who reduce moral theology to Christology.

man.67 This contradiction gives rise to noticeable ambiguities, even at

We hold, by contrast, that the moral problem, “is not so much about rules
to be followed, but about the full meaning of life.”69The analytical categories
required by moral theology ought to be congruent with a vision of the moral
life precisely as a life, as a way of acting that is understood and evaluated
primarily with reference to an end towards which the moral subject guides
himself, and only secondarily with reference to a rule. Christian moral life is
an activity through which the Christian works out, on the basis of faith and
the other Christian and human virtues, an order or plan of life which deter-
mines the mode and the measure according to which various goods are sought,
used or realized, in order for Christian sanctity to be capable of concrete ac-
tualization; in other words, such an order permits the believer to identify the
actions and behaviors that execute here and now, and in a concrete way, life
in Christ.
This is all an existential reality, lived out in a conscious way, but not ordi-
narily with reflection. Moral theology grasps this order, which is immanent in
Christian living, and brings it to conscious and scientific reflection, 70 making
explicit its principles and internal logic, verifying its agreement with Revela-
tion, and promoting its communicability. Attention is therefore concentrated
on its end, which is the good of human life understood as a whole, and which
the moral subject exhibits daily with her concrete behavior. In this way, moral
theology takes on the internal perspective of the moral subject who is the au-
thor of her own conduct, which is to say, the “perspective of the first person”,
and of the internal intentional dynamism that informs human actions. This
perspective is rich in implications for work in moral theology, as the reader
will be able to see throughout this book.
What we have been saying means that moral theology is elaborated as an “op-
erative science”,71 a practical theological science or at least a knowledge that

The Nature, Object, and Sources of Moral Theology
possesses some of the methodological characteristics of the practical sciences.
This poses the question as to how a practical science can be part of theology,
traditionally considered a speculative or theoretical science about God. Saint
Thomas himself poses this question, and in the works that express his most
mature synthesis of his theological thought he offers a satisfying solution to
the problem, even if it has not always been very well understood. When he
studies the scientific status of theology in general, Thomas notes that moral
philosophy is a practical science. Nevertheless he maintains that theology,
occupying itself principally with God, is a theoretical science that can study
at one and the same time the object of the theoretical philosophical sciences
as well as the object of the practical philosophical sciences, because theology
studies both from a formally superior and common perspective: insofar as
they are the contents of divine Revelation.72
But the Thomistic solution has an internal articulation that needs to
be clarified with some precision. For St. Thomas the object of theology
is God, certainly, but not just God in Himself but also insofar as He
is the principle and end of created things, and especially man.73 Now,
the particular relationship between God and man explains how within
theology there is room for a moralis consideratio. 74 As St. Thomas
explains in the important prologue to the Secunda pars, man is the
image of God, so that, like God his exemplar, man is also the principle
of his own actions, and like God, is free and the master of his own
actions. Moral theology studies the structures and the aids that God
gives to man, so that man can be the true originator of the conduct
that will lead him to his end. And thus Abbà notes that “the practical
knowledge that we have as authors of our own good works, that is, our
phronesis or prudentia, and the practical science that we build upon
that, is a participation in that ratio whereby God governs creatures and
man in particular, that is, the eternal law. In just this way, practical
wisdom or prudence, and moral science become our mode of knowing
the eternal law. There can be a true and proper moral and practical
science about man as the author of his own actions in a theology about
God. The unique divine knowledge, participated in by our intellects, by
remaining substantially one because of the pronouncements of divine
Revelation upon which it depends as upon its own principles, becomes
articulated in a speculative or theoretical science about God and his
works (Prima pars75), and about Christ, the incarnate Son of God and
his theandric works, (Tertia pars), and in a practical science about man
and his human works (Secunda pars) . . . in this way, the Aristotelian
perspective of the first person can be adopted in theology”.76
72 Cf. S. Th. I, q. 1, a. 3, ad 2 and ad 4.
73 Cf. S. Th. I, q. 2, prol.
74 S. Th. I-II, q. 6, prol.
75 The author is referring here to the parts of the Summa Theologiae.
76 G. Abbà, Quale impostazione per la filosofia morale?
(1996) 60–61 [italics have


Chapter 1
In our judgment, the ethical approach known today by the name of “ethics
of the first person” or “virtue ethics”77 is one that is better able to develop
the mediation that is needed for the epistemological status of moral theology.
We are in agreement with Melina when he writes that the category of virtue
“offers the rational and human presupposition for a christocentric morality of
caritas, which permits us to overcome a morality of pure obligation and to
unite the natural dimension to the supernatural. The perspective of the first
person, proper to a morality of the virtues, is the only one that allows us to
grasp adequately the moral point of view as praxis, through which the subject
is called to actualize himself as a person. The organic unity of the Christian
moral life does not nullify the difference between the natural human order of
the virtues and the supernatural order of charity. The rational dimension of
the virtues, assumed in the superior logic of charity, is respected in accordance
with its proper demands. In the christocentric perspective, the human and the
divine are united “without confusion and without separation.” 78 The category
of virtue furthermore permits us to understand how faith in Christ enters into
and transforms the principles of the practical reason, such that Christ becomes
concretely the true internal principle of moral action.79The virtues practiced
and taught by Christ become the practical principles of moral action.

The Nature, Object, and Sources of Moral Theology
which theology studies the theoretical truths to believe and the practical truths
that permit the personalizing of the behaviors that agree with the truths of
faith. The unity of theological wisdom is complex and intrincate, but is al-
ways a true and real unity.
One cannot speak or write about everything
at the same time.
For pedagogical reasons—reasons connected, that is, to
study and teaching—theology has been divided into various parts (dogmatic
theology, moral theology, biblical theology, etc.), and these parts in turn are
divided into various “treatises”. But the same pedagogical experience teaches
us that the comprehension of any theological theme requires frequent refer-
ence to questions that belong to other parts or other treatises. This need is
especially evident in moral theology. It is not possible to approach the study
of moral theology without keeping in mind its Christological, ecclesiological,
and sacramental foundations.
Typically dogmatic questions such as creation and predestination in Christ,
original sin and concupiscence, redemption and justification, the last things,
the action of the Holy Spirit in the Church and in the individual believer,
etc. are essential points of reference for the moral theologian. Equally nec-
essary is recourse to the Old and New Testaments
and spiritual theology,
also intimately connected to moral theology. By definition, in fact, however
insuperable the pedagogical difficulties might be, it cannot be denied that
the study of moral theology requires the profession and the consideration of
the entire Christian faith, “which is not simply a set of propositions to be
accepted with intellectual assent. Rather, faith is a lived knowledge of Christ,
a living remembrance of His commandments, and a truth to be lived out. A
word, in any event, is not truly received until it passes into action, until it is
put into practice. Faith is a decision involving ones whole existence. It is an
encounter, a dialogue, a communion of love and of life between the believer
and Jesus Christ, the Way, the Truth, and the Life (cf. Jn 14:6). It entails
an act of trusting abandonment to Christ, which enables us to live as he lived
(cf. Gal 2:20), in profound love of God and of our brothers and sisters.” 80
1.3
The Sources of Moral Theology
The sources of moral theology are substantially the same as for theology in
general. They are also the object of study for a specific theological treatise,
known as fundamental theology.81 We can limit ourselves here to recalling

1.3.1
Divine Revelation
Sacred Scripture and Tradition — The specific source and the perennial
foundation of moral theology, as of all theology, is divine Revelation. In the
words of the Second Vatican Council, “Sacred theology rests on the written
word of God, together with sacred tradition, as its primary and perpetual
foundation. By scrutinizing in the light of faith all truth stored up in the
mystery of Christ, theology is most powerfully strengthened and constantly
rejuvenated by that word”.82 Theological knowledge is the human effort of
understanding and scientifically delving deep into the content of Revelation
as acquired by faith.
Theology is the science of faith.
In faith, theology
finds both its own proper principles of content (fides quae) as well as the
light which inspires it (fides qua) and renders possible its deeper rational
understanding. The theological object of study cannot beome an “object of
reason except on the condition that reason believes and to the measure in
which reason remains under the influence of faith.”83 The inner dynamism
of theological knowledge was expressed by Saint Augustine in the celebrated
formula, “credo ut intelligam et intelligo ut melius credam”[“I believe in order
to understand and I understand in order better to believe”].84 From this it
can be seen that faith is both the end of theology and its intrinsic governing
principle.
Divine Revelation finds its complement in Christ Jesus, who commanded the
Apostles to preach to all persons the Gospel, which is the source of all saving
truth and moral teaching”.85
These Apostles, “and the men of their circle”
did this by word of mouth or in writing.86 Revelation was transmitted from
an apostolic origin therefore, both by sacred Scripture and sacred Tradition.
“Hence there exists a close connection and communication between sacred
Tradition and sacred Scripture.
For both of them, flowing from the same
divine wellspring, in a certain way merge into a unity and tend toward the
same end. . . .therefore both [sacred Tradition and sacred Scripture] are to be
accepted and venerated with the same sense of loyalty and reverence.” 87 It
is important to realize that Tradition is a living reality, which “develop[s] in
the Church with the help of the Holy Spirit. . . For there is a growth in the
understanding of the realities and the words which have been handed down.

83 J. H. Nicholas, Sintesi dogmatica, (Vatican City: LEV, 1991). Vol. I, 22.
84 St. Augustine, Sermo, 43, 7 -9; NBA 29, 757–761.
85 Dei Verbum 7.

The Nature, Object, and Sources of Moral Theology
This happens through the contemplation and study made by believers, who
treasure these things in their hearts (see Luke, 2:19, 51) through a penetrating
understanding of the spiritual realities which they experience, and through the
preaching of those who have received through Episcopal succession the sure
gift of truth.”88 This means, among other things, that the sacred Scripture,
written by way of divine inspiration and entrusted to the Church, is read
and understood as it has been read and interpreted by the Church.89 In this
sense, sacred Scripture without Tradition is formally insufficient, which is to
say, without Tradition, the canon of Scripture could not be recognized as such
nor would its correct interpretation be guaranteed. But as to whether it is
materially insufficient, that is, insufficient also from the point of view of its
content, is a debated question which it is not in our purview to resolve here.90
What is certain is that both are interconnected to such a degree that each
cannot exist without the other.91
The Magisterium of the Church — Christ promised the assistance of the
Holy Spirit so that the Church could preserve the deposit of divine Revelation
intact, both in believing and in teaching, that is to say, in faith both professed
and exemplified.
The task of authentically interpreting and preserving the
Word of God in the name of Christ, was entrusted uniquely to the living Mag-
isterium of the Church. The magisterium is not above the Word of God, “but
serves it, teaching only what has been handed on”,92 always in reliance on the
Holy Spirit. The Second Vatican Council has underlined the intimate bond
between Scripture, Tradition, and the Magisterium. “Sacred tradition, Sacred
Scripture and the teaching authority of the Church, in accord with God's most
wise design, are so linked and joined together that one cannot stand without
the others, and that all together and each in its own way under the action of
the one Holy Spirit contribute effectively to the salvation of souls.” 93
The office of teaching in matters of faith and morals belongs to the bish-
ops in communion with the Roman Pontiff, and to the Roman Pontiff
by himself. These authorities “are to be respected by all as witnesses to
divine and Catholic truth”,94 even when they do not intend to define a
teaching dogmatically.95

The Nature, Object, and Sources of Moral Theology
The Magisterium and Theology — It pertains to the nature of theology,
as a rational exploration of the revealed mystery, to have an adequate under-
standing of the existing relationship between the magisterium and the Church
that is free from distortions and dialectical oppositions; this is a task for the-
ologians as well as the people of God. In the strict sense, the magisterium
does not constitute an autonomous source of theology. The source and norm
of theology is divine Revelation, and the role of the magisterium must be con-
sidered in relation to that. In its intimate connection with Sacred Scripture
and Sacred Tradition,102 which reflects the plan of the Creator, the magis-
terium precedes and governs theological work in the same way as it does so for
the faith. For theology, the magisterium is not a non-scientific authority in
opposition to rational research, but constitutes, rather, the necessary presup-
position for it. At the same time, it is true that “theology is not simply and
exclusively an auxiliary function of the magisterium”.103 It is not limited to
repeating or summarizing doctrine to the extent that they are taught by the
magisterium. Theology has its own dynamism, rooted in the striving toward
truth and the rational understanding that is proper to man and to the faith
as such, in such a way that theology is concerned both with reinforcing the
Christian life of the faithful and with the necessary task of `giving account of
the hope that lies within it' for those who still do not know Christ.
Moreover, “the unity of faith, in function of which the Magisterium has
the authority and ultimate deliberative power to interpret the Word
of God as written and transmitted, is the primary value, which, if re-
spected, does not lead to the suffocation of theological investigation,
but rather provides it with a stable foundation”.104 It is also impor-
tant to keep in mind the ecclesial character of theology: for it to attain
its goal, “theology can never be reduced to the 'private' reflection of a
theologian or group of theologians. The living environment of the the-
ologian is the Church, and to remain true to its identity, theology can
do no less than participate intimately in the context of the life of the
Church, in its teaching, in its holiness, in its prayer.”105 The sense of
belonging responsibly to the Church always allows for an adequate res-
olution of tensions that occasionally arise between theological research
and the teaching of pastors,and resolves them in a way that will not be
traumatic for the faithful;106 such tensions are, up to a point, inevitable
in all the realities that involve human beings, but if they go beyond a
certain size or character they are nothing but manifestations of a lack

of faith and love toward the ecclesial mediation that Christ willed and

On the other hand, the functions of pastors and theologians are dis-
tinct.107 Pastors do not enter into scientific-theological debates, unless
it is necessary on occasion for the benefit of the faithful, and then only,
as it were, indirectly; likewise, it is not the business of theology to gov-
ern the community of the faithful.
What is demanded of theology is
that it be good theology, that is, that it fulfills its mission with scientific
rigor, a mission that is founded in the faith and regulated by the faith,
and seeks a more profound understanding of faith, but without being
in any way false to its pastoral destination.108
By definition, then, the magisterium and theology, while having diverse roles,
have ultimately the same end: to preserve the People of God in the truth
which sets them free. This common service to the community of the faithful,
and to all humanity as well, both grounds and inspires a relationship of mutual
collaboration between the two.109
1.3.2
The Content of Revelation and the Competence
of the Magisterium in Moral Matters
Revelation, the Magisterium, and Morality — The gospel was preached
by the Apostles and their successors as “the source of all saving truth and
moral teaching”.110 This affirmation of the Dogmatic Constitution on Divine
Revelation of the Second Vatican Council expresses in general terms what has
always been the mind of the Church: the Gospel is also the source of “all moral
teaching”; and the use of the formula in rebus fidei et morum (“in matters
of faith and morals”) has become traditional, with reference either to the
content of Revelation or to the area in which the Magisterium of the Church
is doctrinally and authoritatively competent.111Furthermore, the existence of
a moral teaching of revealed content and of a specific doctrinal competence on
the part of the ecclesiastical Magisterium has been universally and peacefully
affirmed by moral theology up to the first half of the twentieth century.

108 Cf. Ibidem.

and Dei Verbum of the Second Vatican Council, by the Declarations Mysterium Ecclesiae
and Professio Fidei, by the Instruction Donum Veritatis, and by the Encyclical Veritatis
Splendor. The expression has also been used in dogmatic definitions (cf. DS 3074).


The Nature, Object, and Sources of Moral Theology
The specific competence of the magisterium in the field of morality is, above
all, a reality of the two millenia long history of the life of the Church.112From
the theological point of view, such a reality is fundamentally explained by
two considerations. The Magisterium of the Church is competent in the eth-
ical realm a) as the guardian and interpreter of Revelation (and therefore of
the ethical content of that Revelation), and b) insofar as Christ directed the
Apostles and their successors to preach his message of salvation: and the ob-
servance of the entire moral law is necessary for salvation. 113 On the basis
of this second reason, the Church has also affirmed its competency in matters
of the natural moral law,114 without, nonetheless, having to invalidate the
theoretical question as to whether there also exist true ethical requirements
of the natural moral law which are not in any way revealed or which are not
bound to the guardianship and exposition of the deposit of faith.
“Autonomous Morality” — In the years following the Second Vatican
Council, a theological orientation began to emerge, known as “autonomous
morality” or “autonomous morality in a Christian context”,115 which pro-
posed a re-thinking of the relationship between human morality and Christian
morality. The solution to the problem was a tendency to deny the compe-
tence of the Church's Magisterium in the realm of concrete moral norms of
the natural moral law, which in turn presupposed the refutation of the basis
of such competence, that is, the relevance of such norms to the deposit of rev-
elation and their relevance for salvation. An important debate resulted from
this,116and some proponents of this orientation came to sustain some mani-

The encyclical Veritatis Splendor clearly affirmed that we must speak of
a “rightful autonomy of the practical reason”,117 but at the same time
affirmed in a manner equally convincing that some Catholic moralists
were proposing an interpretation of the autonomy of the human moral
reason which contained “positions incompatible with Catholic teach-
ing”.118 These positions are explained in nos. 36 and 37 of the encycli-
cal, although in reality the connection between faith and morality is a
theme that recurs throughout. The essential teaching of nos. 36 and
37 can be collected under five points:
1. It is made clear at the very beginning—and it is a very important clarification—
that the criticized orientation “has certainly never attempted to set human
freedom against the divine law or to question the existence of an ultimate
religious foundation for moral norms.” 119
2. The criticized orientation, has, nonetheless, introduced a profound change in
the mode of understanding the relationship between the human reason and
God, by denying the two principal ways by which this relationship has been
established in traditional Catholic morality: “disregarding the dependence of
human reason on Divine Wisdom and the need, given the present state of
fallen nature, for Divine Revelation as an effective means for knowing moral
truths, even those of the natural order, [some] have actually posited a com-
plete sovereignty of reason in the domain of moral norms regarding the right
ordering of life in this world.”120 In other words, the concept of a creative
reason has been proposed that would establish what is right or wrong in the
field of worldly action according to the ever-changing requirements of partic-
ular historical situations. From this follows the affirmation that “such norms
would constitute the boundaries for a merely 'human' morality; they would
be the expression of a law which man in an autonomous manner lays down for
himself and which has its source exclusively in human reason. In no way could
God be considered the Author of this law, except in the sense that human
reason exercises its autonomy in setting down laws by virtue of a primordial
and total mandate given to man by God.” 121

The Nature, Object, and Sources of Moral Theology
3. This position was then employed as a fundamental criterion for Biblical
hermeneutics, since their concept of reason is incompatible with the possi-
bility of a Revelation, on God's part, of moral precepts respecting concrete
moral norms.122 “This has then led to an actual denial that there exists, in
Divine Revelation, a specific and determined moral content, universally valid
and permanent.”123
4. The Christian authors who are coming under criticism maintain that this new
concept of autonomy ought to be restricted to the plane of moral normativity,
and for this purpose it is to be carefully separated from the normative plane
of religion and salvation. There is consequently a distinction between ethi-
cal truths and the truths of salvation, a distinction which Veritatis Splendor
considers contrary to Catholic doctrine.124
5. From the positions indicated in points 3) and 4) there is derived in a logically
coherent way “the denial of a specific doctrinal competence on the part of the
Church and her magisterium with regard to particular moral norms which
deal with the so-called “human good”,125 since such an interpretation rejects
the two reasons which ground such competence in principle: it is denied that
the depositum fidei contains a specific and concrete moral teaching, and it is
denied that the concrete norms of the natural moral law are an integral part
of the message of salvation that the Church brings to all persons in virtue of
Christ's own mandate.
After the publication of the encyclical, the authors who believed that they
were being called to correction affirmed that no Catholic moral theologian
had ever maintained such positions.126
But this defense does not hold up
in the face of a critical comparison of the encyclical with the major works
written by these authors127 both before and after its publication.128

Chapter 1
Faith and Morality — The basic problem is the mode of understanding hu-
man morality in relationship to God and to Christian morality, or, according
to the language employed in Veritatis Splendor, the relation between faith
and morals. This is a fairly complex issue, and although we have already
expressed in general terms the position which seems to us to be the most
adequate,129 there are still other more specific aspects which still need to be
clarified. The problem can admit of a variety of concrete solutions that are
all doctrinally acceptable.
The position of “autonomous morality”, on the
other hand, has some notable values which, according to Veritatis Splendor,
“belong to the best tradition of Catholic thought.” 130 In fact, it was intended
to favor dialogue with modern culture, by underlining the rational charac-
ter131—and consequently the universally comprehensible and communicable
character132—of the natural moral law, as it has also emphasized its interior
character,133 which could not be understood as a heteronomy.134 But Veri-
tatis Splendor also indicates the definite boundaries beyond which Catholic
doctrine is left behind.
These are principally the following:
1. It is not permitted to pass from the autonomous epistemological principle of
the human reason with regard to the natural moral law (the “rightful auton-
omy of the human reason”) to the affirmation of the ontological autonomy of
human morality, and thus to the denial that the natural moral law is a divine
law.
2. It is not permitted to pass from a specifically “Christian” horizon (in the
sense of something “exclusive” or “special”) on the plane of faith and grace
(sometimes referred to as the “transcendental level”) to the affirmation of the
irrelevance for salvation of certain kinds of behavior related to the natural
ethical virtues (justice, temperance, etc.).
3. It is not permitted to pass from the cognitive autonomy of human reason,
which is relative in practice, to the denial of the presence in divine Revelation
of ethical demands of the natural moral law.
In other words, the concept
way, a theologically and ecclesiastically incorrect attitude is encouraged (cf. Lumen
gentium 25, 1), and at the same time, the exactness of the diagnosis and doctrinal
discernment employed in Veritatis Splendor are only confirmed by the facts.
The
exorbitant criticism of this book expresses a conviction that moral questions cannot
be the object of the Church's magisterium by the very nature of their matter (ratione
materiae).”

The Nature, Object, and Sources of Moral Theology
of autonomy cannot be stressed to the point that God, in order to respect
the freedom of His creature, would have no choice but to withdraw from the
life and the world of human beings in such a way that there were an empty
space in God that corresponded to the legislative autonomy of man, a space
in which “nothing is written.”135And now—according to the supporters of
an “autonomous morality”–what appear to be concrete moral instructions in
Sacred Scripture, must be explained in another way: as norms shared in by
the cultural environment of the sacred writers and which would therefore be
changeable norms, etc.136 This is not the sense in which God has entrusted
the world to man, in order to govern and shape it.137
4. As a corollary, there is no foundation for denying the competence of the mag-
isterium of pastors in the moral realm. This does not mean, however, that
we should not also keep in view the relative epistemological autonomy of the
human reason as regards the natural moral law (“the rightful autonomy of the
practical reason,” according to Veritatis Splendor). In fact, the magisterium
of the Church customarily limits itself to teaching the doctrinal content that
the pastoral circumstances of every age show as advisable to emphasize, to
counter the doubts and misunderstandings that can harm the faithful, and
to encourage them to take up positions, but without proposing authoritative
arguments in the concrete. In the majority of cases, it is the business of moral
theology to identify and deepen the arguments that are suitable for making
doctrinal instruction more readily comprehensible.138
135 Cf. the correct observations of M. Rhonheimer, “Autonomia e teonomia moral
según la encíclica Veritatis Splendor”, in G. del Pozo Abejón (ed.), Commentarios
a la `Veritatis Splendor`, 543–578.
What Revelation teaches us is that God not
only does not, in fact, withdraw from the moral life and history of humanity, but
enters into the world to the extent of sharing—in Christ—our human condition and
becoming an example for living.
136 Distinct from this is another very real problem that has been raised by some
writers: in the Sacred Scriptures—including the letters of the Apostles but espe-
cially the Old Testament—we find apparently situated at the same level normative
affirmations that have only a transitory meaning alongside other affirmations of
perennial validity. Rational discernment and good sense is always necessary. But
above all, the teachings of Christ are what furnish the criteria for an adequate dis-
cernment. This is why it is crucial to read the Old Testament in the light of the
New, and to read the difficult passages of the New Testament as they have been
read in the Church since the time of the Apostles; in the last analysis, an adequate
understanding of the role of Tradition is decisive.
137 The Biblical question, furthermore, is especially confused since, on the one side,
the supporters of autonomous morality say that their position only takes seriously
the difficulties that the exegetes have had in finding a revealed ethos, and thus Fuchs
writes: “Modern exegesis affirms that, in general, the more concrete moral affirma-
tions contained in Scripture cannot be considered to be moral norms revealed by
God, and cannot be proposed by the Church as infallible.” (J. Fuchs, Responsabilità
personale e norma morale [Bologna: Dehoniane, 1978] 202). On the other hand,
many competent exegetes affirm that the difficulties in this sense proceed rather
from the moralists: Cf. G. Segalla, Introduzione all' etica biblica del Nuovo Testa-
mento (Brescia: Queriniana, 1989), 21, and R. Schnackenburg, Il messagio morale
del Nuovo Testamento (1989), vol. 1, 17–30.
138 Cf. for example the encouragements in this sense offered by John-Paul II in his


Chapter 1
In this connection it is necessary to add two final considerations. In the first
place, it appears crucial, in considering all the material of this nature, to have
the ability to conceive of the relations between faith and reason and between
natural knowledge and Revelation in a non-dialectical manner. It is not true
that this world is only related to reason and the other world to faith, anymore
than the idea that the arena of argumentation is only to be identified with
reason while the realm of faith pertains only to the will or emotions. God has
revealed certain things regarding our moral action which the reason would also
arrive at per se.139 Scheeben's way of explaining the interrelationship between
faith and reason seems to us particularly suggestive: such a relationship is not
dialectical but “spousal”, so that Christ can be considered as “the Man-God
that results from two principles of activity, that of the divine nature and
that of human nature, as a type of the relationship between reason and faith
as two principles of knowing”.140
In the final analysis, it is a question of
taking seriously the logic of the Incarnation. Secondarily, we think that the
problem has been remarkably complicated by the excessively normativistic
approach assumed in “autonomous morality”. The study of the ethical content
of Revelation from the point of view of the end of the moral life and of the
virtues would have been much easier.
1.3.3
Natural Reason and the Philosophical
and Human Sciences
Human Reason and Moral Theology — We now know that “true the-
ology proceeds from the faith and aims at leading to the faith”.141 Between
the very beginning point of faith and the more profound understanding of
faith that one strives to reach, lies the application of reason to the content of
revelation, or the rational exploration of faith—and this is the work of theol-
ogy, properly speaking. The ordered and systematic exercise of reason is an
essential part of theology. But this is true, not in the sense of a simple juxta-
position of two cognitive powers, but in the sense in which both of them give
way to what is known as theology, a human wisdom, but founded on princi-
ples that have been divinely revealed. Scheeben correctly wrote that “the one

Encyclical Evangelium Vitae 98, 3.
