140 M.J. Scheeben, I misteri del Cristianesimo (Brescia: Morcelliana,1960, 3rd ed.) 797.
On the relationship between faith and reason, cf. A. Rodríguez Luño, “La risposta del pen-
siero metafisico alla crisi dell'etica contemporanea: l'essere come libertà”, in G. Chalmeta
(ed.), Crisi di senso e pensiero metafisico (Roma: Armando, 1993) 73–89; A. Rodríguez
Luño, “Pensiero filosofico e fede cristiana. A proposito delll' enciclica Fides et ratio”, Acta
Philosophica 9 (2000) 33–57.
141 Pastores Dabo Vobis 53.


The Nature, Object, and Sources of Moral Theology
saying, fides quaerit intellectum, is not fully intelligible without the addition
of the other saying: intellectus quaerit fidem; fides and intellectus mutually
require and complement one another to form the organic unity of a wisdom
that proceeds from God and centers on the truths revealed by Him. Through
fides I accept the word of God; through intellectus I understand it: but only
through both at the same time do I acquire for myself the wisdom of God
expressed in the word of God, and become one who knows that wisdom.” 142
The unity and the harmony between reason and faith thus becomes the distin-
guishing characteristic of good theology, and on the basis of this criterion the
Church has expressed its preference for using Thomas Aquinas' philosophy of
being.143 This is a preference that certainly does not entail an exclusiveness
that is closed to the advances that have since been made in the history of
philosophical thinking.
In the course of this work, we have already referred twice to the relationship
between faith and reason.
The theme is so important for theology that a
few more clarifications are necessary.
A fruitful formulation of the relation-
ship between faith and reason must include two further fundamental aspects.
1) Christian revelation transcends and at the same time includes the entire
historical-philosophical horizon of man. It is true that in revelation the most
important questions of man are answered, but it is also true that revelation
greatly exceeds such questions in such a way that it cannot be conditioned, an-
ticipated, limited, or interpreted on the basis of human questions. This is how
any “philosophism” is avoided—that is to say, a subordination of the word of
God to the criterion of a entirely philosophical hermeneutics. 2) On the other
hand, the vindication of the freedom (or love) and absoluteness of a God Who
reveals Himself cannot be accomplished by denying to reason the power of ex-
ploring the essential consistency of created realities. This means avoiding the
nominalist error of seeing things as if they were a pure singular fact and fully
contingent in their existence as mere objects of the will of God, in which there
is little to be known, since they do not contain any necessary truth, or still
less, any universal truth.144 Existence would then be a contingent fact with
no explanation beside the will of God, who puts them in existence outside of
Himself. This would lead to the destruction of truth—enabling an indefinite
plurality according to the variety of hermeneutical perspectives assumed—and
the fundamental principle of philosophical realism would be denied: that is,

143 Cf.
Optatam totius, no.
16.
For a commentary on the principal teachings of the
Church on this point, cf. L. Clavell, Metafisica e libertà (Rome: Armando, 1996) 93–112
and 123–137. The profound and unbreakable bond between the consciousness of faith and
the consciousness of reason and the perennial freshness of Aquinas' thought in this area
were strongly emphasized in the encyclical Fides et ratio.

Chapter 1
the principle that veritas supra ens fundatur (“truth is founded on being”).
In other words, we must avoid the contradiction of wanting to emphasize the
absoluteness of God through a philosophical procedure that ultimately limits
that absoluteness profoundly, since in practice a limit is imposed—the limit
of God not being able to cause any effects that have their own proper con-
sistency. Nominalism reasons in this way: just as every universal consists in
its own properties, then the universal cannot be real, because it cannot be
created, which is to say, there could not be a simple effect of a total cause,
since it also possesses its own consistency. For the nominalist, the absolute-
ness of God is preserved only if existence signifies uniqueness and contingency.
History is witness of the great losses that this perspective—though seemingly
a very “theological” perspective—has caused theology, and moral theology in
particular (consider, for example, the voluntaristic understanding of the di-
vine law).
In conclusion, much attention needs to be paid to this matter,
since the balance between reason and faith is a very delicate one;
easy to
accept in theory, but difficult to realize concretely in the theologian's praxis.
Philosophical Ethics and Moral Theology — In order to apply these
general considerations to moral theology, it is necessary that we recall once
more the principle of newness without a rupture,145 in virtue of which it is
true that the knowledge of our moral being cannot be exhausted in any ra-
tional exploration, since the ultimate significance of the moral life only comes
to be known in the perspective of Christ.146
But it is also true that the
grace of divine filiation, although exceeding the human condition, does not
alter it (grace perfects nature without destroying it); similarly, without the
unchanging subsistence of the human condition, grace could not be received
or understood in its specific reality as a gratuitous gift.147
We must con-
clude therefore that an exact knowledge of the natural moral condition of the
human being, which is the object of philosophical ethics, is indispensable for
moral theology. In the words of John Paul II: “ Moral theology has perhaps
an even greater need [with regard to fundamental theology] of philosophy's
contribution. In the New Testament, human life is much less governed by
prescriptions than in the Old Testament. Life in the Spirit leads believers to
a freedom and responsibility which surpass the Law. Yet the Gospel and the
Apostolic writings still set forth both general principles of Christian conduct
and specific teachings and precepts. In order to apply these to the particular
circumstances of individual and communal life, Christians must be able fully
to engage their conscience and the power of their reason. In other words,
145 See above, section 1.1.3.
146 Cf. Col 1:16–17.
147 On the ontological foundation of moral action (both natural and supernatural), with
particular reference to Thomas Aquinas, see E. Colom, Dios y el obrar humano, (Pamplona:
Eunsa, 1976), esp. pp. 13–31.


The Nature, Object, and Sources of Moral Theology
moral theology requires a sound philosophical vision of human nature and
society, as well as of the general principles of ethical decision-making.” 148
While philosophical ethics will never constitute the ultimate hermeneutical
principle for understanding Christian living, it should supply the foundations
that make possible and facilitate theological comprehension. A philosophical
ethics, for example, that looks at moral reality from a positivistic angle, as
a kind of normative restriction coming from outside the human being, would
not permit the understanding of Christian life as a development of the divine
grace that exists in our hearts through baptism. There are at least four great
themes for which philosophical ethics is of fundamental importance: moral
epistemology, the concept of the moral subject, the theory of action, and the
theory of normative principles.149
Moral epistemology. Man can be identified with Christ in his way of
seeing, valuing and feeling,150 and therefore of acting to the measure
in which faith, hope and charity, as well as the ethical virtues, become
principles of his practical reasoning. To understand how this reality
functions it is necessary to grasp the role of the virtues as vital prin-
ciples of moral knowledge attainable by the practical reason, and not
merely as habits that facilitate the putting-into-practice of what the rea-
son or conscience has decided on its own, independently of the virtues.
It is a matter, then, of making explicit a moral epistemology that is not
rationalistic or normativistic, but centered around the knowledge of the
good of human life as a whole and around the virtues; not abstract,
but anchored in the real, salvation-historical situation of the human
person.151
The concept of the moral subject. This entails the concept of the person
as a moral agent. In Veritatis Splendor, for example, the moral subject,
represented by the figure of the rich young man, possesses characteris-
tics that make him incompatible with the familiar figures of the modern
studies of moral subjectivity, such as the “utilitarian subject” or the “au-
tonomous subject”,152 in whom consciousness of the truth is either not
attainable or does not play a dominant role. The rich young man has a
fairly precise idea of what would be the complete good for man (eternal
life), which he seeks with interest, and he understands that particular
behaviors are judged by the extent to which they agree with that type
of life. His lack of generosity puts him into a contradiction with what he
bears within himself, and consequently he goes away sad. By contrast, it

149 For a complete exposition of our way of looking at these ethical problems we refer the
reader to A. Rodríguez Luño, Ética General (2001) (the text of the fourth Spanish ed. is
substantially different from the first ed., which alone has been translated into Italian, and
which has been cited previously).
150 Cf. Phil 2:5.
151 Cf. Veritatis Splendor 64.
152 Cf. G. Abbà, Quale impostazione per la filosofia morale? (1996) 239–274.


Chapter 1
is particularly important to attend carefully to the characteristics of the
autonomous subject, since such attention to the subject is presupposed
by moral theological theories that are centered on the dialectic between
law and freedom or between law and conscience, and more generally
by ethical theories that revolve around the concept of duty or obliga-
tion. Such theories conceive of the subject as a freely-deciding agent
whose inner constitution has rendered him radically indifferent, and in
such a way that ethical demands are necessarily understood as being
extrinsic and imposed; it is not understood how in a mistaken choice
the subject's intimate practical nature and intimate aspirations—as a
human being and as a child of God in Christ—are contradicted. An
anthropological foundation needs to show in detail how the practical
nature of the human subject is really constituted.
The theory of action is viewed in conjunction with the concept of the
acting subject.
The concepts of the utilitarian subject and the au-
tonomous subject already imply a certain theory of moral action. With-
out an adequate analytical description of action that renders clear just
what one's moral identity depends upon, the degree of responsibility
one has for the subsequent effects, etc., there cannot be any solution
to the various problems relating to moral cooperation, indirect action,
praeter-intentional causality of effects, etc.
Finally, we come to the question of normative principles. Beyond any
doubt, practical requirements of the Christian life can be spoken of in
terms of norms, and there need to be such norms for catechesis and ped-
agogical purposes. But the problem is whether such language as this
was originally the most suitable language for expressing the Christian
life, the lex gratiae, the development in action of the theological virtues
and gifts received by a child of God in Christ. Our answer is that norms
are only a derived mode of expressing the requirements of Christian life,
which in origin are requirements of virtue—of the theological and the
moral virtues—and not simply considered as an alternative mode of
ethical classification or categorization (these are not what the virtues
are), but as the real principles that underlie the entire mode of func-
tioning and perceiving of the moral reason illuminated by faith, that
is, of the moral reasoning of a child of God. The virtues are, thus, the
true normative principles of the Christian life. This fact has notable
consequences, even for an adequate mode of describing moral actions,
which, in terms of the virtues, cannot be described in merely phys-
ical, pre-moral ways.
This avoids a minimalist conception of ethics,
and guarantees a connection with spirituality.
It is also the manner
of speaking presupposed in the Letters of the New Testament, in the
works of the Fathers, of the great saints and many important spiritual
authors.
The Use of the Human Sciences — Finally, we consider the auxiliary,
but still important role played by the human or social sciences (psychology,


The Nature, Object, and Sources of Moral Theology
sociology, etc). Nobody is unaware of the importance they have for permit-
ting a better understanding of the actual conditions in which the Christian
moral life develops.153 With regard to these sciences it must be kept in mind
that “because the Church's morality necessarily involves a normative dimen-
sion, moral theology cannot be reduced to a body of knowledge worked out
purely in the context of the so-called behavioral sciences. The latter are con-
cerned with the phenomenon of morality as a historical and social fact; moral
theology, however, while needing to make use of the behavioral and natural
sciences, does not rely on the results of formal empirical observation or phe-
nomenological understanding alone”.154 Their use, nevertheless, is governed
by the criteria of theological epistemology.

## CHAPTER 2 {#colom-scelti.2}
Chosen in Christ before
the Creation of the World:
The Universal Call to
Holiness
2.1
Dogmatic Theology and Moral Theology
in the Face of the Question
of the Meaning of Human Existence
2.1.1
The Dogmatic Doctrine on the Final End
of Human Life
The question of the ultimate meaning of human existence (from where
do I come, to where will I go?) has always stimulated philosophical and
theological reflection. It can be investigated both from a speculative and
a practical point of view. Metaphysics and theology confront it from
a speculative point of view, that is, from a perspective of reflection in
which man becomes fundamentally driven by the desire for things to
present themselves as they actually are, while at the same time putting
temporarily in brackets other existentially relevant considerations.
A speculative investigation, of a prevalently metaphysical nature, into
the ultimate meaning of human life was done by Saint Thomas Aquinas
in the First Part of the Summa Theologiae. Considering the creative
action of God, he asks what could be the end or goal of creation and
therefore of the things created, including humans. Saint Thomas rightly


Chapter 2
notes that imperfect agents tend always, with their acts, toward the
acquisition of some thing. But this is not the case with God. “To the
First Agent, Who is agent only, to act for the acquisition of some end;
He intends only to communicate His perfection, which is His goodness;
while every creature intends to acquire its own perfection, which is the
likeness of the divine perfection and goodness.
Therefore the divine
goodness is the end of all things.”1
Natural reason can reach the conclusion that God creates in order to manifest
His glory and to communicate His perfection. The glory of God is also the
end of created things, which they nonetheless reach in different ways. The
intelligent creatures, like man, “attain it in a more special way, that is, through
their proper operation of understanding Him. Hence, this must be the end of
the intellectual creature, namely, to understand God.” 2
Such rational truth is confirmed by Revelation, and constitutes the Catholic
dogmatic doctrine concerning the final end of creation. “Scripture and Tra-
dition never cease to teach and celebrate this fundamental truth: `The world
was made for the glory of God' (Cf. Dei Filius, can. # 5: DS 3025), for God
has no other reason for creating than his love and goodness: `Creatures came
into existence when the key of love opened his hand' (St. Thomas Aquinas,
Sent. II, prol.).”3
The dogmatic doctrines on the elevation of man to the supernatural order,
on original sin, and on redemption complete the theological response to the
question concerning the meaning of human existence. “God, in his infinite
goodness, has ordained man to a supernatural end,” 4 directing him to the
vision of His essence. With his fall from grace, man lost the original holiness
and justice in which he was established5 and also disrupted his due order in
relation to his last end.6 God in His mercy, when the fullness of time had
come,7 sent to humankind Jesus Christ, His Son, “that He might both redeem
the Jews, who were under the Law, and the `gentiles, who did not follow after
justice, might attain to justice' [Rom. 9:30], and that all men `might receive
the adoption of sons' [Gal. 4:5]. `Him God has proposed as a propitiator
through faith in his blood, for our sins' [Rom. 3:25], and not for our sins only,
but also for those of the whole world [I John 2:2].” 8
All men, therefore are destined to acquire in Christ communion of knowledge
and love with God through the work of the Holy Spirit. With beautiful and

is that only in the mystery of the incarnate Word does the mystery of man
take on light [ Christ, the final Adam, by the revelation of the mystery of the
Father and His love, fully reveals man to man himself and makes his supreme
calling clear [ All this holds true not only for Christians, but for all men of
good will in whose hearts grace works in an unseen way. For, since Christ

divine, we ought to believe that the Holy Spirit in a manner known only to
God offers to every man the possibility of being associated with this paschal

2.1.2
The Moral Consideration of the Final End
of Human Existence
The preceding considerations of a dogmatic character are undeniable to any
Catholic moralist. It may be a surprise then that St. Thomas Aquinas, in
the first questions of the moral part of the Summa Theologiae,10 takes up
this problem of the final end almost starting from scratch, with a dialectic-
inductive methodology that does not seem to suppose the above-mentioned
dogmatic basis. This problem has led to varying interpretations.
A very balanced interpretation is that proposed by Günthör.11 Accord-
ing to this author, the reader of the first questions of the moral part
of the Summa Theologiae “is immediately struck by the great distance
which separates it from the response of Sacred Scripture to the ques-
tion of fundamental morality. The latter, in fact, is a response to the
history of salvation, i.e. it brings attention to the call that God has
revealed and still reveals to men. Its perspective is therefore concrete
and theocentric, because it speaks first of all of the saving action of
God in our regard, and only afterward makes a call to right action as a
response of man to God's initiative. The line of thought of St. Thomas
is instead abstract, philosophical, and in a certain measure, anthro-
pocentric, inasmuch as he sets off from an analysis of the structures
of man who is separated from his final end.”12 The formulation of St.
Thomas invites itself to different objections: for one, it runs the risk of
remaining a philosophical theory of happiness rather than a theology of
God's salvation; furthermore, the eudaemonistic system can lend itself
to a hedonistic—or at least egoistic—vision, in which man seeks “his”
happiness instead of loving God in Himself and for Himself; in the end
this is anthroprocentric: “The end of all is man, who arrives at his own
9 GS 22.
10 Cf. S Th I-II, q. 1–5.
11 Cf. A. Günthör, Chiamata e risposta. Una nuova teologia morale, 4th ed. vol. I
(Rome: Paoline, 1982), 173–186, our translation.
12Ibid., 174.


Chapter 2
beatitude, something which is man's thing and not God's.”13
After having brought out the fundamental lines of the Thomistic study
of the final end of man,14 Günthör observes rightly that these objections
are based on a misunderstanding of the true thought of St. Thomas,
who rather possesses the merit of bringing to light “the correspondence
between the final end alloted to us by the fact of grace, and the deep
structural attraction of man for its attainment. If the Scriptures speak
of communion with God which he has already given to us as a gift [
Thomas comes to tell us that this vocation does not seize men who are
not already predisposed. In fact, it carries them toward the satisfaction
of their most intimate yearning. The great contribution of St. Thomas
to the foundation of the Christian moral life consists specifically in the
fact that he shows in what way such a vocation corresponds to the inti-
mate structure of man.”15 Günthör concludes his valid study affirming
that there exists nevertheless a diversity of perspectives regarding what
has been outlined. One treats here, however, of two perspectives that
do not exclude, but rather complete each other. “In effect, whenever
one limits himself exclusively to the biblical perspective, they are not
properly doing theology, which is a scientific penetration of Revelation.
Likewise, whenever one attends only to the vision of St. Thomas, he
runs the risk of developing the philosophical-speculative aspect of the-
ology in a unilateral manner.”16
It would seem to us that to begin moral theology with a study of the final
end of human life that is not simply a reproduction of the results reached by
dogmatic theology—since the study is being done with a different method and
viewpoint—is an indispensable demand of the perspective “of the first person”
proper to moral theology as a practical science.17 The study of the final end
must be fit into and re-elaborated by the perspective of man who, as image
of God, is a true subject, agent, and author of his own conduct,18 and whose
actions lead himself toward his complete and definitive good.19 The ultimate
meaning of existence is a reality that, in the Thomistic moral perspective
of the “first person”, remains intrinsically linked to all other moral realities
and structures (e.g. virtues, norms, conscience, sin, etc.), which could not be

chen Themas'. Anmerkungen zu W. Pannenbergs Aristoteleskritik, Anthropotes 13 (1997)
211–223, with the reply of Pannenberg, Eine Antwort, Anthropotes 13 (1997) 485–492.

Chosen in Christ before the Creation of the World: The Universal Call to Holiness
adequately understood without considering their essential relation with the
final end.20
The history of moral theology demonstrates in an irrefutable way that
if the above-mentioned dogmatic foundations do not become inserted
into and re-elaborated in the “perspective of the first person”, even if
remaining as undesputed dogmatic data, they will end up performing no
role in moral theology. A negative consequence of such a project is that
the treatment of the final end disappears completely or, at least, almost
completely.
This carries with itself a change in the meaning of the
principal moral concepts. In an “ethics of obligation”, in fact, men come
to be conceived as subjects who do not feel themselves attracted to any
ultimate good. They are autonomous decision makers whose freedom
of indifference has no other motive to respect the moral law than the
authority of God who imposes it.21 The role of the practical reason is
then to take note of the commandments and to decide to obey them,
once the conscience has determined that the commandments are truly
binding here and now, after having evaluated all of the circumstances.22
Between ethical demands and the final end, in this perspective, there
does not exist an intrinsic relation, this is the reason the commandments
eventually become a positive and extrinsic datum for man, concerning
which there is little to understand and from which he is to liberate
himself as soon as possible. The practical reason, however, is no longer
competent to elaborate an order in the acts of the will in view of the
known final end,
a final end which is both desired by man and at
the same time binding.23 The virtues, then, become superfluous, and
superfluous becomes also the active role of the practical reason which
needs to be prepared and facilitated on the intellectual, affective, and
dispositional level by the virtues.24
It is necessary, therefore, to start off with a consideration of the role that
the end plays in the moral life, beginning with natural ethical experience, in
order to re-present under such a light the Christian teaching concerning the
ultimate meaning of human life.

Chapter 2
2.2
The Good of Human Life Taken as a Whole
in Natural Ethical Experience
It often happens that a person will come to see his life with a sense of deep
dissatisfaction and even frustration. Perhaps in the past this person did not
make condemnable choices from the point of view of moral norms (did not
kill or steal, was always faithful to his spouse, etc.), but still this person has a
clear perception of his life as something he would like to do over. This person
may feel the bitterness of loneliness and feel that perhaps his choice to have
privileged work rather than the family was deeply mistaken. His greater ener-
gies were given to professional work, which tended especially toward economic
sufficiency, and the passing of time demonstrated that such busy activity had
done little for him, and in the end, if the person could go back, he would not
take the same path.
Classical morality maintained that its principal work consisted in avoiding
these comprehensive and irremediable failures and this, in a more positive or
general way, through the orientation of personal choices in view of the full
success of human life. The human aspiration to the good is an aspiration
that follows the reason, and is marked by the same transcendental, and one
may wish to say, infinite breadth that is characteristic of the reason. There-
fore, it is an aspiration which starts the reason moving in search of the truth
about the Good. The human good, in all of its breadth, can be an object of
investigation and of rational foundation. Such an investigation can be accom-
plished, leading a person to a level of reflection in which—elevating himself
above immediate and perhaps pressing demands of the present moment—he
may comprehensively contemplate his own life taken as a whole. Here we deal
with a reflection of the good of human life in its entirety. Only in light of this
reflection can one's own priorities and choices be reconsidered and, if need be
the case, modified.25 This is the motivation that leads us to embark on an
analysis of the purpose of action, which we will run through briefly.
”Every art and every investigation, and likewise every practical pursuit or
undertaking, seems to aim at some good: hence it has been well said that
the Good is That at which all things aim.”26 This consideration, with which
Aristotle opens the Nicomachean Ethics, brings to light that every action, and
every operative human project, tends to an end or aim considered to be good
or suitable. Investigation in this line makes known that single human actions
structure themselves according to sequences that are more or less unitary,
in which certain actions or certain goods are ordained to others. Rational
25 For a formulation of classical ethics c.f. J. Annas, The Morality of Happiness (New
York: Oxford University Press, 1993).
26 Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics, I, 1: 1094 1–3.


Chosen in Christ before the Creation of the World: The Universal Call to Holiness
reflection makes apparent that in this series of actions or of goods (ends)
ordained toward others, one cannot proceed to infinity. There must exist a
perfect good, a good that is desired and sought for itself and not for the sake
of something else, and this is generically called happiness.
St. Thomas explains it as such: “Now there is to be observed a twofold
order in ends: the order of intention and the order of execution: and in
either of these orders there must be something first. For that which is
first in the order of intention, is the principle, as it were, moving the ap-
petite; consequently, if you remove this principle, there will be nothing
to move the appetite. On the other hand, the principle in execution is
that wherein operation has its beginning; and if this principle be taken
away, no one will begin to work. Now the principle in the intention is
the last end; while the principle in execution is the first of the things
which are ordained to the end. Consequently, on neither side is it pos-
sible to go to infinity since if there were no last end, nothing would be
desired, nor would any action have its term, nor would the intention of
the agent be at rest; while if there is no first thing among those that
are ordained to the end, none would begin to work at anything, and
counsel would have no term, but would continue indefinitely.”27
This classical explanation could be the object of an important objection. Ex-
perience seems to teach that there does not exist a unique final end or supreme
good, but there exist rather diverse activities and spheres of human activities,
each of which has its own final end. For example, the totality of actions that
a doctor sets himself to do as a doctor, have as their end to procure the health
of the sick. Certain actions done by the doctor on Sunday have instead as
their ends rest, leisure, and so on. Could it not be that the different final
ends of different activities are also the diverse ends of man as capital goods
of particular spheres of life?
This objection appears weaker after continued reflection. On the one hand,
it is to be noted that some human activities have a role which is merely
instrumental; whereas others may cause deep satisfaction, but even in these,
still not every aspiration will be satisfied, because there are other things that
people desire and for this reason they will still continue to act. It does not
seem that the ends of such an activity can be considered as goods willed
absolutely for themselves. But it remains above all the fact that throughout
life the final ends of different activities enter into conflict with one another:
the demands of work, which are also economic demands, can conflict with the
demands of rest and of health, or perhaps the care due to one's own family,
or still yet with certain moral or religious convictions. In the face of such a
conflict, it is necessary to choose, that is, it is necessary to limit some activities
to take better care of others, etc. According to which criteria, i.e. in view
27 S. Th. I-II, q. 1, a. 4.


Chapter 2
of which good, should the different activities be ordained?
The criteria for
ordering these choices presuppose that one has an idea of the contribution
that each activity (work, family, moral or religious convictions, health, etc.)
can give to the full success of his own life, i.e. to his own happiness. This is
a true problem, for the sense of failure or of frustration, of which we spoke
at the beginning of this section, proceeds precisely from not having known to
establish the due order and the due priorities for the different activities that
make up human life.
Therefore, the question is inevitably asked: what is the final end or perfect
good of human life taken as a whole, the good that renders life worthy of being
loved, without lacking anything?28 It is a question about human happiness,
of what is truly good for man. This question does not necessarily presuppose
that human happiness must consist in a single good or a single activity to
the exclusion of others.
But it is believed that the response that will be
given to such a question will define a way of life that is better than the
others, understanding as a way of life the program or criterion that defines
which goods—and according to which priorities, measures and types—must
be desired and carried out. It is thought, ultimately, that moral reflection
will help us to understand how a happy life can be achieved, the satisfying
life which we long for ourselves and for all the people we love; and also to
understand how we can avoid the types of life which render us unhappy,
disgraced, and hopeless, the types of life we would not want for ourselves or
for those dear to us.
Though rational inquiry cannot always rationally justify all the possible pref-
erences between different goods,29 it is still able to justify that, in the light of
what truly constitutes the final good of human life, a certain order and pro-
portion must be established between the different human activities,30 and it
can, above all, identify certain modes of rational regulation for all activities,
which then must be respected in all circumstances.31 In this way, one can
determine which are the proper virtues for man in order to live a better life.
Previously we presented and evaluated the response philosophy has given
throughout the centuries to the question of the final end of man.32 The fore-
going reflections intended to uniquely define the perspective of investigation
in which moral theology is inserted, a perspective that finds in divine Revela-
tion the response that completely brings to light the problem of the ultimate
28 Cf. Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics, I, 7: 1096 a 12 - 1098 b 9.
29 For example, it would not be possible to justify in the abstract that it is better to
dedicate one's life to the study and teaching of mathematics, or to the practice of a sport
or musical instrument.
30 That is, between professional work, family life, health, religious practices, etc.
31 Justice, for example, is a criterion to be respected in continuity with every interest and
good.
32 Cf. A. Rodríguez Luño, Ética General (2001), 115–154.


Chosen in Christ before the Creation of the World: The Universal Call to Holiness
meaning of human life, and that also provides a criterion for establishing its
own priorities, as well as for directing in a concrete way life's most important
choices.
2.3
Holiness: the Fullness of Divine Filiation
for the Christian, as the Final End
of Human Life
The question which must now be given a response is the following: according
to Christian faith, does there exist some human activity or at least some
program or type of life that is desirable in itself and not for the sake of
something else? It is not enough to repropose the already mentioned dogmatic
data. It would serve little to reiterate that the world and man were created
for the glory of God, or that man is called to the vision of God, if it is not said
in such a way that man—who is an active agent who reflects on his own life
considered as a whole—can draw from it operative guidance. Does speaking of
the vision of God as the final end of man mean that Christians must abandon
all their daily activities to retire in the desert for the work of contemplation?
Or does it mean that the present life is like a child's game in anticipation of
the arrival of the moment when we reach, in the Great Beyond, the vision of
God? Or is it that our end, while being fully achievable only in the next life,
can also be imperfectly—and in a less developed way—reached in this life,
provided our earthly activities are ordered and organized in a certain way
and with a certain spirit?
Among the diverse responses found in Sacred Scripture and the Catholic moral
tradition, it seems to us that it is the concept of holiness that can best establish
an articulate response to our question. We can take our starting point from
the Letter to the Ephesians, which contains one of the most complete summary
formulas. God the Father “chose us in him [Christ], before the foundation of
the world, to be holy and without blemish before him. In love he destined us
for adoption to himself through Jesus Christ, in accord with the favor of his
will, for the praise of the glory of his grace that he granted us in the beloved.” 33
From these words, holding our consideration to their significance in the plane
of morals, we can draw the conclusion that the aspiration to absolute good is
categorized and lived by the Christian as an aspiration to holiness, understood
as the fullness of divine filiation, that begins in the earthly following and
imitation of Christ.
As a child of God, the Christian is called already in
this world to be “alter Christus, ipse Christus,”34 in perfect obedience to the
33Eph 1:4–6.
34 Holiness as the fullness of divine filiation and the subsequent call to be “alter Christus,


Chapter 2
Father's will, living according to the virtues that Christ has taught with his
life and words and that are gratuitously given to us with baptismal grace as
a seed that is destined to grow.
The concept of Christian holiness—or its synonym sanctity—contains a rich
and complex semantic analogy.35
In any case, holiness is appropriate for
signifying the goal of Christian aspirations; though, while in its full realization
it represents a unique unitary activity (the direct vision of God in glory), in its
earthy realization it implies a comprehensive program of life and therefore a
set of criteria for regulating human activities (the virtues). However, this does
not mean that just from the concept of Christian holiness one can analytically
deduce all the moral rules.
Rather, it is necessary to remember that the
concept of holiness is to be inserted into an investigation spurring from the
question concerning the good of human life in its entirety, and not into research
of a normative character provoked by a concrete and difficult situation to
resolve. Holiness is the end that gives meaning to the Christian life. The
problem of rules comes afterwards, and we shall deal with it further on.36
We shall thus commence a detailed study of the meanings of Christian holi-
ness.
2.3.1
Teachings Concerning Holiness in the Bible
Old Testament — Holiness in the Old Testament is centered around
the holiness of God: “There is no Holy One like the Lord”;37 in fact, ho-
liness constitutes the characteristic proper to the divine Being.38 The
Hebrew word qadosh that expresses the concept of holiness comes from
a root word which means to cut or to separate: for God is Holy on
account of His radical separation and transcendence.39 But this does
not mean that divine holiness is static or inimitable: it manifests it-
self dynamically in all His works, and people must live according to

in the same volume is the far-reaching study of A. Aranda, “Il cristiano, `alter Christus',

its model: “Be holy, for I, the Lord your God, am holy.”40 Moreover,
the Old Testament shows different aspects of holiness: the prophets
especially underline its soteriological character inasmuch as it reveals
God's love and makes known to men their sins from which they are to
be liberated.41 In the priestly literature, but not only in it, holiness
comes to be considered in relation to cult or worship: the place where
the Lord manifests Himself is holy, as well as the temple, the priests,
the sabbath, and the feast days.42 Israel, as the elect people, separated
from other people for the fact of being of God, is a holy people,43 and
the insistence on Israel being a people consecrated to the Lord is em-
phasized even more in Deuteronomy.44 From another perspective, the
wisdom books link holiness to wisdom which is as a light that comes
from the Lord to guide the Holy Ones.45 Nonetheless, the holiness of
the creature, which is participation in the divine holiness, is not purely
passive but rather requires the repudiation of impurity and the dispo-
sition to act with consistent moral conduct,46 even though it remains
God's task to sanctify men.47
New Testament — In the New Testament, the concept of holiness has a
very wide range of meaning.48 For now we can point out that there are some
passages in which the term is used with a sense that reflects its prevalent use
in the Old Testament. So the name of God,49 His covenant,50 His follower,51
the angels,52 the prophets,53 the Scriptures,54 and the Law55 are called holy,
among other things. But what seems more characteristic of the New Testa-
ment is that holiness appears linked to the Holy Spirit who, while being a gift
of the Messianic age, carries the believer to a participation in the holiness of
God which up to that time was unthinkable. Following this direction—leaving
aside lexical investigations and assuming the perspective of systematic moral
theology—we can distinguish: 1) the initial ontological holiness or sanctity;
2) Eternal Life as the eschatological fulfillment of Christian holiness, which

2.3.2
The Divine Gift of Initial Holiness
Just as in the Old Testament where holiness was a participation in the holiness
of the Lord, so in the New Testament Jesus, as the Holy One of God, renders
the Church and the Christians to be participants in His holiness, that is,
they become sanctified in Christ Jesus through identification with Him and
by the cleansing of the Spirit.56 The Christians even came to call themselves
“saints” or “holy ones”. St. Paul refers to the faithful of Corinth as
those
“who have been sanctified in Christ Jesus.”57 This meaning of sanctity, at least
in a direct sense, does not have a moral meaning, but comes to be used in
a sense analogous to other expressions such as “the perfectly mature,” 58 “the
called,”59 “the chosen,”60 or ”those who believe.”61 This brings to the light, in
fact, the gift of initial holiness received by those who have accepted the faith
and have received baptism. The Christians were purified and sanctified by
grace—the formal ontological principle of the life of the faithful—and enriched
with Christian virtue. Guided by the Holy Spirit,62 they have received their
first configuration with Christ, becoming children of God63 and participants
in the divine nature.64
In this sense (but not only in this sense) the Church is called “holy”.
“The Church This is because Christ, the Son of God, who with the
Father and the Spirit is hailed as `alone holy,' loved the Church as his
Bride, giving himself up for her so as to sanctify her; he joined her to
himself as his body and endowed her with the gift of the Holy Spirit for
the glory of God.” (LG 39). The Church, then, is `the holy People of
God,' (ibid., 12) and her members are called “saints.” (cf. Acts 9:13; 1
Cor 6:1; 16:1).”65
According to this use of the term, holiness is not the final end of human life,
but rather the initial divine gift that renders it both possible and obliging to

2.3.3
The Eschatological Fulfillment
of Christian Holiness
The divine gift received by the faithful (divine filiation, grace, the Christian
virtues) can be compared to a “grain of mustard seed” destined to grow and
become a large bush, or else it can be compared to yeast which leavens the
dough.66 The final goal toward which such a development tends is presented
by Revelation in eschatological terms, making use of different concepts to do
so. We shall then study the principal concepts employed.
Eternal Life — Eternal life, a reality we profess in the creed of the faith,
represents the eschatological fulfillment of Christian holiness. The faithful
that enjoy the vision of God in eternal life are called “saints,” 67 and being also
called Saints are those solemnly proclaimed to be so by the Church, those who
“practiced in a heroic way the virtues and lived in faithfulness to the grace of
God,” and these are proposed for our veneration as models and intercessors.68
In the New Testament writings, even if with different levels of emphasis, eter-
nal life is presented as the term, fulfillment, or crowning of a life that already
begins in this world—the life of the children of God—that has precise ethical
demands. In the Synoptics eternal life is promised to those who will have cer-
tain attitudes in relation with their neighbors and earthly goods: “Blessed are
the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven [ are the clean of heart,
for they will see God.”69 In the fourth Gospel, sometimes eternal life is spoken
of as something that has already begun: to have eternal life is to belong to
Christ through faith, love, and the observance of the commandments,70 and
is possessed in some way by those who eat the bread of life;71 but, above
all, it appears linked to the resurrection promised by Christ,72 and its na-
ture becomes expressed in terms of knowledge: “Now this is eternal life, that
they should know you, the only true God, and the one whom you sent, Jesus
Christ.”73 Finally, eternal life is the ultimate reason for the mission of Christ:
“For God so loved the world that he gave his only Son, so that everyone who
believes in him might not perish but might have eternal life.” 74

Chapter 2
The nature of eternal life put in terms of knowing God is also found in the First
Letter of John75 and in St. Paul.76 Both sacred authors teach that eternal life
will be the full manifestation of the life of the children of God.77 In St. Paul,
divine filiation is linked to the idea of inheritance, and the reception of the
Son's Spirit demonstrates that we are truly children of God: “So you are no
longer a slave but a child, and if a child then also an heir, through God.” 78 The
filial condition involves a walk of life according to the Spirit, without allowing
oneself to be pulled down by the desires of the flesh.
“Now the works of
the flesh are obvious: immorality, impurity, licentiousness, idolatry, sorcery,
hatreds, rivalry, jealousy, outbursts of fury, acts of selfishness, dissensions,
factions, occasions of envy, drinking bouts, orgies, and the like. I warn you,
as I warned you before, that those who do such things will not inherit the
kingdom of God.”79
The Kingdom of God — Principally in the synoptics, the Kingdom of God
(in Mk and Lk) and the Kingdom of heaven or Kingdom of the Father (in
Mt) express both the eschatological and at the same time imminent character
of Christian holiness (“eschatological in the phase of realization”, according
to the formula of J. Jeremias80). The Kingdom of God is a future reality, as
well as a present reality that approaches us; that comes and bursts into our
life. “A special feature of the announcement of Jesus is that he sees already
in its occurrence, and in His works, the bursting through of the dominion
of God (Lk 11:20; Mt 12:28) and yet still awaits its completed form (as the
Kingdom of God). This last feature is alluded to in the parables of the festive
and nuptial banquets (Lk 12:38; Mt 8:11; Lk 14:16–24; Mt 22:2–10), of the
harvests (parables of growth), the Our Father prayer, “Thy kingdom come!”
(Lk 11:2; Mt 6:10), and also in the certainty of Jesus on the vigil of his death
(Mk 14:25 and parallels). Jesus announced the coming of the dominion of
God for the immediate future, but without exactly fixing its timeframe.” 81
The principal dimension of the announcement of the kingdom of heaven is
undoubtedly eschatological: the participation in the future Kingdom of God.

Such participation is seen as a gift of God,82 that man can only receive when
he becomes like a child.83 In this sense the Kingdom of God is eternal life,
and both expressions come to be used indistinctly: “If your foot causes you
to sin, cut it off. It is better for you to enter into life crippled than with two

out. Better for you to enter into the kingdom of God with one eye than with
two eyes to be thrown into Gehenna.”84 The idea to “enter into the Kingdom
of God” is used frequently,85 and the conditions for entering the kingdom are
the same that are requested for “entering into life” or for “inheriting life”.
The Kingdom of God is also the Kingdom of Christ.86
It is linked to the
person of Jesus. The position one takes with regard to Jesus and His words
determine the position in which man will find himself at the end of his life:
“Everyone who acknowledges me before others I will acknowledge before my
heavenly Father. But whoever denies me before others, I will deny before my
heavenly Father.”87 The realization of the Kingdom of God commences with
the preaching of Jesus; and the positive response to the appeal of Christ—the
following of Christ—is the path for entering the kingdom. To make present
Christ's appeal to all people constitutes the mission of the Church.
The Church is the seed of the Kingdom of God on earth. “To carry out
the will of the Father, Christ inaugurated the Kingdom of heaven on
earth and revealed to us the mystery of that kingdom. By His obedience
He brought about redemption.
The Church, or, in other words, the
Kingdom of Christ now present in mystery, grows visibly through the
power of God in the world [ with the gifts of its Founder and faithfully
guarding His precepts of charity, humility and self-sacrifice, receives the
mission to proclaim and to spread among all peoples the Kingdom of
Christ and of God and to be, on earth, the initial budding forth of
that kingdom. While it slowly grows, the Church strains toward the
completed Kingdom and, with all its strength, hopes and desires to be
united in glory with its King.”88
The Church is, therefore, the universal sacrament of salvation and of ho-
liness:89 “God, however, does not make men holy and save them merely
as individuals, without bond or link between one another. Rather has
it pleased Him to bring men together as one people, a people which
acknowledges Him in truth and serves Him in holiness.”90 Holiness is a
personal effort, but not individualistic: since it is a participation in the

Chapter 2
trinitarian life of Jesus, it realizes itself in the Church, which is Christ's
mystical body. It is in the Church, in fact, that by means of grace, we
obtain holiness; and indeed, all of its activities direct themselves, as to
its end, to the glorification of God in Christ and the sanctification of
people.91 From here the ecclesial character of Christian life is apparent,
and consequently, the ecclesial character of its systematic study, moral
theology. We must then strongly underline the necessary role of the
Church in the correct development of moral theology.92
The Father's House — The idea of the Father's house especially highlights
that the final and definitive holiness is the fullness and goal of the life of the
children of God, which is expressed in the attitude of complete docility to the
Father's will demonstrated by Christ. “In my Father's house there are many
dwelling places. If there were not, would I have told you that I am going
to prepare a place for you? And if I go and prepare a place for you, I will
come back again and take you to myself, so that where I am you also may be.
Where [I] am going you know the way.”93 The Father's house is the definitive
dwelling place of the faithful with Jesus along with the Father.
Only those that Christ has liberated from sin, those that are children
and no longer slaves, have a permanent dwelling in the Father's house:
“Amen amen, I say to you, everyone who commits sin is a slave to sin.
A slave does not remain in a household forever, but a son always re-
mains.”94 In the beautiful parable of the prodigal son, the conversion of
the sinner is presented as a return to the Father's house,95 and this also
allows us to see how this concept gives evidence that the eschatological
fulfillment is already developing in our earthly life.
The Full Participation in the Holiness of God — The participation in
the holiness of God also connects the actual situation of the faithful with its
eschatalogical development, adding to it the prospect of the imitiation of God,
that was already present in the Old Testament.96 The First Letter of Peter
exhorts:“Therefore, gird up the loins of your mind, live soberly, and set your
hopes completely on the grace to be brought to you at the revelation of Jesus
Christ. Like obedient children, do not act in compliance with the desires of
your former ignorance but, as he who called you is holy, be holy yourselves in
every aspect of your conduct, for it is written, `Be holy because I [am] holy.” 97
These words intend to strengthen hope, purify the desire from all egoism, and

Chosen in Christ before the Creation of the World: The Universal Call to Holiness
to show that Christian conduct must be holy conduct; only this, in fact, will
allow us to enter into union with God, the Holy One, to whom we were called.
So there is a double sense in which an intimate relation is established between
holiness and glory: ascending and descending. In fact, God communicates
His glory to man, calling him to participate in the divine holiness98 and man
seeks out the glory of God responding to divine grace through holy conduct,
because God is “glorified in His saints.”99
Holiness as the Definitive Good of Human Life — The concepts of
eternal life, the Kingdom of God, the Father's house, holiness and others
like them—either considered in their first announcement or when the faithful
who are inclined to lukewarmness or exposed to temptation are reminded of
them—intend to illuminate the Christian moral life in light of what constitutes
the comprehensive and definitive good. With such a reminder, the faithful
are exhorted to moral effort and vigilance: “Watch, therefore; you do not
know when the lord of the house is coming, whether in the evening, or at
midnight, or at cockcrow, or in the morning. May he not come suddenly and
find you sleeping. What I say to you, I say to all: `Watch!'.” 100 To “watch” is
to reorder, once more, the desire toward that which is truly and definitively
good—the communion of knowledge and of love with God—and, consequently,
to re-examine under such a perspective one's own values and choices, even in
a decisive and radical way if necessary.
And so Jesus teaches: “If your hand causes you to sin, cut it off. It
is better for you to enter into life maimed than with two hands to
go into Gehenna, into the unquenchable fire.”101 It is in light of the
eschatological completion of life that the hand can be wisely valued;
it is the same for the “foot” and the “eye” of which He speaks in the
successive verses. The unfaithful steward102 is praised by his master,
“for acting prudently (fronímôs),”103 that is to say, because he had
known to think prudently at the moment in which his stewardship would
have been taken away, after which there would not be the possibility
of manipulating the received goods. The rich man is instead rebuked
for having used his wealth, thinking only of the present and not also of
the future: “But God said to him, `You fool, this night your life will be
demanded of you; and the things you have prepared, to whom will they
belong?'.”104 The reflection on one's own life and on one's own choices
in the light of the eschatological completion of life, and the lack of such
a reflection, determine whether one's use of received goods is prudent

or foolish. Significant in this regard is the connection, in the parable
of the prodigal son, between the distance from the father's house and
the son's wasting of his inheritance “on a life of dissipation.”105 The
thought and the desire of the definitive dwelling in the Father's house
works to purify the heart, which then feels liberated from the pressing
stresses of earthly goods.
2.3.4
Moral Holiness
The holy conduct illustrated in the aforementioned biblical citations is pre-
cisely moral holiness. It represents the development of the initial holiness,
through good and excellent acts, that tends toward its eschatological comple-
tion. Moral holiness is the holiness of action.106 The development through
action of one's condition as a child of God, a condition received with faith
and baptism, carries out, in an analogous way, a general metaphysical prin-
ciple that regards every living being and man in particular: action involves
a development and a completion of one's own being, a development which at
the same time flows out of that same being.
From this point of view it can be rightly seen that through good works—
already on the natural ethical plane—we reach a greater likeness with
the Lord: “God said: Let us make man in our own image and likeness;
and it is added: And God made man: he made him in the image of God,
He made them male and female and he blessed them. The fact that it
said: He made him in the image of God, and He was silent about His
likeness indicates that man since the first creation obtained the dignity
of the image, while the perfection of the likeness was reserved for him
for the end, in the sense that he must obtain it, imitating God with his
own hard work; so that having been conceded from the beginning the
possibility of perfection by means of the dignity of the image, he can in
the end realize the perfect likeness by means of works.”107 It can then
be seen—with the terminology used by Origen and some Fathers—that
the possibility to achieve a likeness with God derives from being created
in His image. Holiness, like all goods, proceeds from the Creator, as He
infuses in being the capacity to act, provides the necessary capacity for
the same action, and points out to man his final transcendent end.108
What God willed with the creation of spiritual beings is that they may reach
their own fulfillment, not in a passive way, but as participants of the divine

Chosen in Christ before the Creation of the World: The Universal Call to Holiness
work.
It is especially important to understand that such a divine plan is
intrinsic to the creative act and, consequently, forms part of the most intimate
nucleus of each person: it can be said that the human being needs moral
behavior and that man's action is none other than an exposition of his own
being; for this reason there exists an intimate relation between the human
person, the perfection to be reached, and the human or moral act. “The moral
imperative that is born from the tension between present and future, and
precisely by one's view of Jesus, receives thereby a particular dynamic power.
It necessarily leads us to behave in this world according to the prescriptions
of Jesus [ driving force which leads us forward, which, despite every resistance
and all personal failings, does not lead us to yield or abandon hope. It will
be, in fact, once again God who carries His dominion to completion, and will
draw to full realization that which is seen in a symbolic way in the person
and works of Jesus.”109
We shall not yet move to a detailed analysis of the demands of Christian
holiness. For the moment what interests us is to provide a description
that is more general, in such a way as to render intelligible what it
means that sanctification, or the reaching of moral holiness, constitutes
the proximate final end of human life, that is to say, the only type of life
which is reasonable to will in itself in light of Revelation; this life not
being subordinated to any other earthly good or condition, and being
ordained solely toward definitive communion with God in eternal life
and, in the last analysis, to the glory of God, which is the absolute final
end of man.
From a material point of view, moral holiness is not a particular activity
that can be placed alongside others. Moral holiness is sought and reached
through and in the accomplishment of normal human activities: professional
work,
family life, social and political activities, religious duties, etc. From
a formal point of view, it consists in the principles that inspire and bring
to completion such activites—charity being the chief principle—and also in
the mode in which they are accomplished, i.e. in the criteria by which they
are regulated, whether they are activities or goods that are accomplished or
acquired. Moral holiness is a type of life or, if one prefers, a way of life that
admits of multiple modes of practical realization. Diverse, at least partially,
are the way and contents of moral holiness to which are called a faithful lay
spouse with respect to a celibate person; and the life of both is, and must
be, different in many aspects to that of a priest or a member of a religious
congregation, and so forth.
That which is common to all is that Christian holiness consists in all cases
of an imitation and following of Christ, configuring oneself always more to
Him, until arriving at the fullness of charity which is the essence of Christian
109 R. Schnackenburg, Il messaggio morale del Nuovo Testamento (1989), vol. I, 43.


Chapter 2
perfection.110
It needs to be repeated that there does not exist a unique
or privileged concrete form of following Christ: to follow Christ is to act
in such a way that the theological and moral virtues, the virtues practiced
or taught by Christ, be respectively the deep inspiration and criteria of the
practical regulation of activities and life that each carries out following his own
vocation. But it should be borne in mind that holiness is always excellence,
and therefore the realization of the virtues should not be understood in a
minimalist sense as a battle against the sinful actions which they oppose, but
should be deepened and consolidated to the point of achieving the maximum
expressions which God allows and which He asks each person to achieve.
Before concentrating our attention on the following of Christ and the specifi-
cation of its content, we must first reflect on the the doctrine of the universal
call to holiness, which we have not yet mentioned until now.
2.3.5
The Ecclesial Doctrine
on the Universal Call to Holiness
Although from the biblical and dogmatic point of view the call to holiness
was always an undisputed fact, the reproposal of this doctrine in the Second
Vatican Council, in all its practical and moral value, was considered, and
really was, a true theological novelty.111 The novelty consists in having pro-
posed holiness, with all of its implications of excellence, as the practical and
achievable end for all Christians, even those who—being the overwhelming
majority—are not called by God to the priestly state or consecrated life.
Although one could say that the doctrine of the Second Vatican Council con-
stituted an important event in the history of Christianity, it is also true that
it was prepared by the inspiration of the Holy Spirit in the life of the Church
itself, through the theology of earthly realities, the liturgical renewal with
its reflection on baptism and its sanctifying character, the experiences of the
lay apostolate, and the vitality of pastoral phenomena like Opus Dei.112 The
110 Cf. Col 3:14.

charge is not a simple moral exhortation, but an undeniable requirement arising from the
mystery of the Church” (Christifideles Laici, 16).

their message, shed light on various periods of history. Among these distinguished figures,

day of his beatification, he reminded the contemporary world of the universal call to holiness
and of the Christian value which professional work can have in the ordinary life of each


Chosen in Christ before the Creation of the World: The Universal Call to Holiness
latter is characterized by the emphasis it gives to the sanctifying value of pro-
fessional work and in the accomplishment of the ordinary duties of the Chris-
tian, as one can infer from these especially significant words of its founder:
“Ever since 1928 my preaching has been that sanctity is not reserved for the
privileged few and that all the ways of the earth can be divine. The reason
is that the spirituality of Opus Dei is based on the sanctification of ordinary
work.” “Opus Dei proposes to help ordinary citizens like yourself to lead a
fully christian life, without modifying their normal way of life.” “You must
understand now more clearly that God is calling you to serve him in and from
the ordinary, material and secular activities of human life. He waits for us
everyday, in the laboratory, in the operating theatre, in the army barracks,
in the university chair, in the factory, in the workshop, in the fields, in the
home and in all the immense panorama of work. Understand this well: there
is something holy, something divine hidden in the most ordinary situations,
and it is up to each one of you to discover it.” 113
All of this is not just a mere theoretical postulate, but generates day by
day the firm and concrete desire to accomplish this ideal in ordinary life, as
teaches the fifth chapter of Lumen Gentium. This chapter begins by pointing
out the ultimate foundation of such a commitment: the holiness of God—
Father, Son, and Holy Spirit—that Christ has transmitted to the Church;
“In the Church, everyone whether belonging to the hierarchy, or being cared
for by it, is called to holiness, according to the saying of the Apostle: `For
this is the will of God, your sanctification' (1 Thess 4:3; cf. Eph 1:4)”.114
The successive point develops this idea, putting the holiness of the faithful in
connection with Jesus, the master and model; the Holy Spirit, who leads us
to love God and our neighbor from within; the sacramental life (baptism); the
virtues; and prayer. This section speaks also of the relation between initial
holiness (or sanctity) and moral holiness: “The followers of Christ are called
by God, not because of their works, but according to His own purpose and
grace. They are justified in the Lord Jesus, because in the baptism of faith
they truly become sons of God and sharers in the divine nature. In this way
they are really made holy. Then too, by God's gift, they must hold on to and
complete in their lives this holiness they have received.” 115
Next to be remembered is that holiness is one and the same for all: “The
classes and duties of life are many, but holiness is one—that sanctity which

From here derives the invitation to seek God above all things, with all one's
heart, with all one's soul and with all one's might: every person is called to
love God with a maximum intensity.120 This makes up the basis of Christian
holiness: the love of Christ that leads us to respond with a maximum love
toward God and toward our neighbor, that is made a reality in the present
situations and moments throughout the course of a lifetime.
Fixed limits
should not be placed on this growth, because no person merits to be called
good who does not desire to be better, and from the moment in which a
persons stops desiring to be better is when he ceases to be good:

2.4
The Following of Christ as the Essential
and Original Foundation
of Christian Holiness
2.4.1
Christ as the “Way, the Truth, and the Life”
We shall now concentrate our attention on the earthly realization of the vo-
cation to holiness (moral holiness), because such a realization is a moral and
spiritual work that has need of being illumined and directed by theological
reflection.
As we know, the Christian moral life is the walk toward the Father's house,126
that has in Christ its fundamental point of reference.127 Christ is He who both
renders it possible and at the same time constitutes its human and divine end,
norm, and model. He is “the way, the truth, and the life.” 128 Jesus is “the
way” to the Father's house in that He is the personal mediator of salvation
and inasmuch as He is the norm of life. He is the way because He is “the

truth”, that is, the personal revelation of the Father and of His design of love

Christian holiness therefore consists, in its earthly realization, in the following
of Christ. “It is Jesus himself who takes the initiative and calls people to follow
him. His call is addressed first to those to whom he entrusts a particular mis-
sion, beginning with the Twelve; but it is also clear that every believer is called
to be a follower of Christ (cf. Acts 6:1). Following Christ is thus the essential
and primordial foundation of Christian morality: just as the people of Israel
followed God who led them through the desert towards the Promised Land
(cf. Ex 13:21), so every disciple must follow Jesus, towards whom he is drawn
by the Father himself (cf. Jn 6:44). This is not a matter of merely dispos-
ing oneself to hearing a teaching and obediently accepting a commandment.
More radically, it involves holding fast to the very person of Jesus, partaking
in his life and destiny, sharing in his free and loving obedience to the will of
the Father.”130 He assumed the human condition in all things but sin in or-
der to render it—through His Passion, Death, Resurrection and Ascension—a
participant in His glorification.131
Christ has recapitulated in Himself all
that which man had scattered with sin.132 In Him is renewed, in a definitive
manner, the salvific yes of the Father, with a new and eternal covenant that
culminates in the eschatological participation in the glory of God.133
The risen Christ sends the Holy Spirit who sustains our condition as being
children of God, makes us joint heirs of Jesus Christ, and reconciles creation
with the Creator and with humanity itself, inasmuch as the latter participates

in the dominion that Christ has over it.134 The dominion of Christ over sin and

2.4.2
The Following of Christ as Life
According to the Christian Virtues
Leading to the Fullness of Charity
We shall now pain ourselves to explain what it means, in operative terms,
to follow Christ. As it was emphasized earlier, to follow Christ means con-
cretely to live according to the Christian virtues, that is to say, according to
the virtues taught with the words and example of Christ, “perfectus Deus,
perfectus homo.” Moral theology is none other than an explanation of this
reality, of its anthropological presuppositions, of its normative implications,
and of its modes of realization.
The theological and moral virtues are at the same time intrinsic principles—
possessed as habits—of life in Christ, its norm and in a certain sense also its
end (they are an end inasmuch as progressing in the Christian virtues and
identifying oneself with Christ are, in practice, the same thing). Naturally,
the role of the vital principle of Christian existence is preeminently found
in the theological virtues—faith, hope, and charity–, which render man able
to believe, to desire, and love God in Christ through the Holy Spirit. The
theological virtues purify and elevate the human will and conscience, directing
them toward the end of Christian life.137 They modify the criteria according
to which the moral virtues regulate activity as well as the attainment and use
of human goods in such a way as to render union with Christ possible through
them.138 The moral virtues are not norms in the sense in which human laws
are norms, but are norms inasmuch as they are cognitive, appetitive, and

Worth underlining is the central role of the virtue of charity.139 It expresses
the moral value of the person and the level of his union with Christ. Union
with Christ through love is above all human values and is not to be identified
with their harmonious sum. Through the theological virtues and the gifts of
the Holy Spirit, but especially through charity, a union with God is possible
in this life which is the greatest good of which man is capable in this world.
He who has experienced it would be disposed to any kind of sacrifice in order
to not lose it. Even if the union consists essentially in love—in charity—it
gives rise to a true contemplation of Christ and of God. By contemplation,
we do not mean an extraordinary mystical phenomenon, but the effort and
capacity to discover God in every event—great or small—of one's own life,
even in the midst of many temporal preoccupations,140 without forgetting
that He is present at the center of the soul in grace, as St. Augustine says:
interior intimo meo, more inward to me than my most inward part.141 Here

teach us to associate with and imitate Jesus: Mary, Joseph, the angels, and
the Saints.144

Chosen in Christ before the Creation of the World: The Universal Call to Holiness
It is worth the effort to include some reflections, taken from a homily of
St. Josemaria Escrivá, that illustrate effectively the nature of ordinary
contemplation that is achievable for every Christian who wishes to make
a serious effort at following Christ. “First one brief aspiration, then
another, and another till our fervor seems insufficient, because words

needing rest or feeling tired. We begin to live as captives, as prisoners.
And while we carry out as perfectly as we can (with all our mistakes
and limitations) the tasks allotted to us by our situation and duties,
our soul longs to escape. It is drawn towards God like iron drawn by
a magnet. One begins to love Jesus, in a more effective way, with the
sweet and gentle surprise of his encounter [
Our heart now needs to distinguish and adore each one of the divine

Charity is the form of all the virtues;146 it is both the mediated principle
of all the good works and also their fruit.147
Therefore, given the multi-
dimensionality of the life that must be lived in Christ, the following of Christ—
while unifying the Christian life—is not one-dimensional, nor can it be reduced
to a single type of human activity: it requires the carrying out of activities
in different human dimensions according to a virtuous ordering that, in its
more concrete expressions, depends also on circumstances and especially on
the particular vocation of each person.

transcendent good destined to endure for eternity, is accomplished or not
accomplished by the person in his moral regulation of the diverse human
activities and the diverse personal and social goods.
2.4.3
The Unitary Identity of Christian Morality
as the Following of Christ
We must finally discuss the problem, very controversial in contemporary the-
ology, as to whether the walk toward Christian holiness—which we have
described—is capable of being the basis for a morality with a sufficiently
unitary characterization. Among scholars, there is almost universal agree-
ment that within the New Testament there exists an ethics with a specific
identity and unity that is detectable in its Theological-Christological founda-
tion and in its eschatological motivation.149 But the opinions are much more
varied concerning the possibility of finding in the Sacred Scriptures a uni-
tary and perennially valid ethics, with regard to its content and instructions,
concerning personal, interpersonal, and social behavior.150
In fact, it is evident, on one hand, that the authors of the New Tes-
tament writings elaborate the preceding oral traditions in a concrete
historical-cultural situation in view of the needs of the young Chris-
tian community, keeing in mind their respective environment;151 on the
other hand, we also live in a concrete context, quite different from that
of the Christians in the first generations, in which new problems emerge
that the Sacred Authors could not have taken into consideration. The
question arises as to whether the following of Christ brings with it a
concrete, universal, and immutable morality that is valid for our time.
This problem become so complex today because of the “normativistic
148 S. Th. suppl., q. 82, a. 3, ad 4. Thomas applies this reasoning to contemplation in
paradise; anyhow, in an analogous way, one could apply it to loving contemplation in this
life.
149 Cf. G. Segalla, Introduzione all'etica biblica del Nuovo Testamento, 234–235.
150 This theme will be taken up again in a more complete fashion in Chapter VIII when
the New Law, the lex gratiae, is studied.
151 Cf. R. Fabris, “Morale del Nuovo Testamento”, in Nuovo Dizionario di Teologia
Morale, (Cinisello Balsamo: Paoline, 1990), 799.


Chosen in Christ before the Creation of the World: The Universal Call to Holiness
preunderstanding” that often accompanies the study of the New Testa-
ment. Some theologians start from ethical premises that human moral
knowledge is primarily an activity produced by norms, and then search
the Sacred Scriptures for a systematic and perfectly elaborated moral
“code” containing also a completely casuistic account ready for every
epoch, even our own. But it seems to us that such a “preunderstanding”
is not adequate for the nature of moral knowledge and for the ways in
which it comes about.
Moral knowledge regards primarily the question of which type of life is best
or, if one prefers, what is the ultimate good of human life taken as a whole.
The best life springs about from certain modes of accomplishing and order-
ing human activities, and of using and managing personal and social goods.
These regulating modes are vital principles of the human practical reason: the
virtues. On the foundation of these virtues, the reason, following its sponta-
neous and not yet reflexive operation (ratio practica in actu exercito),152 is
able to identify programs of action as well as singular actions that accomplish
here and now the desired type of life.153 Now, considering things from this
point of view, the unitary identity of Christian morality is guaranteed by the
fact that the New Testament contains an indication of the type of life proper
to the Christian—life in Christ, the following of Christ–, that encompasses all
of a person's life and not only an area of it; its eschatological purpose; and
the Christian principles of the practical reason—the Christian theological and
moral virtues–, on the basis of which one is able to identify the Christian way
of living in every circumstance and situation.154 Naturally, the moral knowl-
edge so obtained can be expressed also in universal normative terms in the
modern sense of the word, but such statements are always a derived reality,
even if they are most important for pedagogical (catechetical) effects and to
communicate moral knowledge.155 However, what is really of importance is
not so much the more or less systematic form which such practical principles
explicitly have in the New Testament, but rather the fact that these principles
(the Christian virtues) are given to the Christian with grace, in such a way
that they constitute themselves as real and vital principles of the Christian's
152 Cf. Chapter I, section 1.2.2.
153 We shall see throughout this book that the virtues, as we understand them here and
as it seems to us that St. Thomas understood them, are not simply habits, in the usual

the good that was specified independently of them, but they are in the first place principles
according to which and through which the practical reason can reach a certain knowledge,
in the practical sense, of the good to be done or the evil to be avoided.
154 “whoever claims to abide in him ought to live (just) as he lived” (1 Jn 2:6); cf. Jn

155 In Chapter VIII, under section 8.2.2 and 8.2.3 the difference between spontaneous
