Chapter 2
knowledge and moral behavior.
We retain, in synthesis, that Christian morality as identification with Christ
through the Holy Spirit possesses a well defined unitary identity, so long
as it is understood in the sense which we have now explained. The Sacred
Scriptures, and in particular the New Testament, contain under the form of
moral teaching a more than sufficient illustration of the practical principles
which the Christian receives with grace and which render him a child of God.
To bring these vital principles to reflexive and scientific awareness, explaining
their inner logic and their possible abstract and normative applications, is
the work of moral theology.156
But the theological and moral virtues, as
real principles of Christian morality, are the cornerstone for arriving at a
theological understanding of the real specific identity of Christian moral life,
as a following of Christ. In fact, moral theology requires a “careful inquiry
rooted unambiguously in the word of God. In order to fulfill its mission, moral
theology must turn to a philosophical ethics which looks to the truth of the
good, to an ethics which is neither subjectivist nor utilitarian. Such an ethics
implies and presupposes a philosophical anthropology and a metaphysics of
the good.
Drawing on this organic vision, linked necessarily to Christian
holiness and to the practice of the human and supernatural virtues, moral
theology will be able to tackle the various problems in its competence, such
as peace, social justice, the family, and the defense of life and the natural
environment, in a more appropriate and effective way.157
156 Cf. Chapter I, section 1.2.
157 Fides et Ratio 98.


## CHAPTER 3 {#colom-scelti.3}
Moral Conduct
as the Response of Man
to the Divine Call
3.1
Moral Conduct and Christian Holiness
A purely philosophical analysis sees moral life as an effort in which man
intends to carry out, through his actions, the complete and definitive good of
his existence. For such a purpose, it leaves completely exhausted the practical
reason, which is able to perform a concrete operative “translation” of the final
end, specifying the priorities, the measure and the modes in which the diverse
goods and various activities which make up human life must be desired and
accomplished.1
In the light of Revelation, we understand that, in the call to holiness that
occurs in the configuration with Christ, the complete human good is assumed,
purified, elevated, and completed, but not altered. The Christian moral life
is lived as an active pursuit of holiness, supported by the grace of the Holy
Spirit. The natural practical capacity of the human reason is enriched by
the breadth of meaning and by the concrete moral teachings of Revelation.
The natural human operative resources are analogously rectified and elevated
by the Christian virtues. All moral existence can be then more profoundly
understood as the response of man to the divine gift which has made him
become—along with the other members of the Christian community and,
potentially, all people—a child of God in Christ through the Holy Spirit.
1 Cf. Chapter II, section 2.1.2 and 2.2.


Chapter 3
It needs to be understood correctly in what sense the Christian moral life is
a response to a divine call. In a certain way, all moral life pertains to the call
that God directs to man, whether he is aware of it or not, through the natural
conscience and the natural desire for good.2 But in the Christian is found also
a clear awareness of having been the object of a divine communication that
requires correspondence. He also knows himself to be the intended recipient
of precise moral teachings, which illustrate the fundamental paths of his re-
sponse. But it should not be thought that every single action of the Christian
is a response to a divine request with precise and unequivocal content. Better
yet: in reality it is so, but it is inasmuch as the Christian sees in God the
origin and foundation of every good, and believes that the following of Christ
may be implemented as an obedient effort toward all that appears to be good,
both in the light of the natural reason (natural moral law3), and in the light
of faith (the Gospel law4), even if in reality the Christian normally acts un-
der the light which results from a collaboration between these two cognitive
principles. What we are compelled to underline is that the Christian is not
spared the active and creative effort of identifying the ways of reaching union
with Christ through his own works and activities.
All of moral theology has the task of helping the Christian to perform this
active and creative effort. At this point we can trace only a few general lines
that may offer a synthetic and dynamic vision of what will be seen further
on from an analytical perspective throughout this book and in special moral
theology.5
3.2
The Moral Cooperation of Man
with the Gift of God
It can be affirmed in general terms that every free initiative of God toward us
requires the free response of man.6 Even in what we have called initial holiness
there is already a first and fundamental response of man: the free acceptance
of the justice of God through faith in Jesus Christ wherein justification takes
place.7We shall not consider this perspective any further, because for now we

Moral Conduct as the Response of Man to the Divine Call
shall occupy ourselves more directly with the person who, with his life and
always under the influence of grace, simultaneously expresses and develops
the gift with which he was sanctified and renewed.
Faith, which follows charity and the desire to arrive at full communion with
God (hope), must be faithfully preserved each day: neither can the first accep-
tance of faith be considered as something acquired once and for all. As Saint
Augustine writes, “All proceeds from God, not however with us remaining as
sleepers, as reluctant of making any effort, almost unwillingly. Without your
will, there will not be God's justice in you. Undoubtedly the will is nothing
but your own, justice is only of God. Without your will the justice of God can
still be there, but it will not be in you if you are opposed to it [ you, will not
render you just without you.”8
On man depends, ultimately, cooperation
with the divine gift, that manifests itself in the decision to live, primarily and
above any other interests, as holy in Christ Jesus.9 The effort to live in Christ
involves two aspects: to eradicate what takes us away from the Lord and to
practice what leads us closer to Him.
The Apostolic Letters distinguish between these two aspects. The Letter
to the Ephesians, for example, describes them as “putting away the old
self” and “putting on the new self”: “that you should put away the old
self of your former way of life, corrupted through deceitful desires, and
be renewed in the spirit of your minds, and put on the new self, created
in God's way in righteousness and holiness of truth.” 10 In the Letter to
the Galatians the first aspect is seen as a battle against the desires of
the flesh; the second, as life according to the Spirit.11 The First Letter
to the Thessalonians asks the faithful to abandon the passions and sins
of the pagans who do not know God, and to behave in a manner pleasing
to God, seeking to always make progress.12 The Letter to the Romans
speaks of not conforming oneself “to this age” and of being transformed
and renewed, “that you may discern what is the will of God, what is
good and pleasing and perfect.” 13 Ultimately, both the effort to battle
against sin and vice, and the practice of the virtues and use of the means
of sanctification are necessary.

Chapter 3
3.3
The Negative Aspect of the Moral Effort:
“Put Away the Old Self
of Your Former Way of Life”
3.3.1
The Battle against Sin
In speaking of the “negative aspect” of the moral effort, we are adapting to a
common mode of speech, that must however be understood well. In Christian
life, the negation always proceeds from a previous affirmation and is ordered
toward a further and full affirmation. It is written well that in the Christian
announcement sin is not “a primary theme, but is an indirect theme that is
reflexive: a theme that occurs, obviously, but does not take the foreground [ at
least the first letter to the Corinthians where we have this archaic formula of
faith: “Christ died for our sins in accordance with the scriptures; that he was
buried; that he was raised on the third day in accordance with the scriptures;
that he appeared to Kephas, then to the Twelve” (1 Cor 15, 3–5). Here we
have right away the mention of sin, but it is put in a secondary position in
light of the fact that Christ died for this reason. The confession of faith is
Christological.”14
This consideration, far from softening the importance of sin, emphasizes it,
while placing it in the proper perspective. Whoever lives in Christ is dead to
sin: “If, then, we have died with Christ, we believe that we shall also live with
him [ As to his death, he died to sin once and for all; as to his life, he lives for
God. Consequently, you too must think of yourselves as (being) dead to sin
and living for God in Christ Jesus. Therefore, sin must not reign over your
mortal bodies.”15 Between the life of man in Christ and sin exists an absolute
opposition. Sin is opposed to the holiness of God and to life in Christ; it
represents the “no” of man to the divine call to holiness. Sin is a distancing
of oneself from God who in Christ came and approached us.16 Therefore the
battle against sin constitutes the first, radical, and immediate requirement of
the divine call to holiness.
This is one of the first things that strikes us in the moral teaching of the
letters of the New Testament. Thus, for example, St. Paul reminds the
Thessalonians of it:
“This is the will of God, your holiness: that you
refrain from immorality, that each of you know how to acquire a wife for
himself in holiness and honor, not in lustful passion as do the Gentiles
who do not know God; not to take advantage of or exploit a brother in
this matter, for the Lord is an avenger in all these things, as we told
you before and solemnly affirmed. For God did not call us to impurity

15 Rom 6:8,10–12.
16 Given the capital importance of sin, Chapter XI will be dedicated to its treatment.


Moral Conduct as the Response of Man to the Divine Call
but to holiness. Therefore, whoever disregards this, disregards not a
human being but God, who (also) gives his holy Spirit to you.” 17 No
less radical is the warning of the First Letter of John:
“You know that
he was revealed to take away sins, and in him there is no sin. No one
who remains in him sins; no one who sins has seen him or known him.
Children, let no one deceive you. The person who acts in righteousness
is righteous, just as he is righteous. Whoever sins belongs to the devil,
because the devil has sinned from the beginning. Indeed, the Son of
God was revealed to destroy the works of the devil.
No one who is
begotten by God commits sin, because God's seed remains in him; he
cannot sin because he is begotten by God.” 18
Those who follow Christ
do not sin. The absence of sin pertains to the reality of divine filiation
itself. To sin is to reject divine filiation and to offend the love of God
who bestows it as a gift.
3.3.2
Lukewarmness as Failure to Respond
to the Christian Vocation
The Christian vocation, inasmuch as it is a vocation to accomplish holiness in
the world, must overcome another obstacle beyond sin that is in appearance
less serious, but in practice more insidious: lukewarmness or acedia, “to which
pertains the negligence of a man who declines to acquire spiritual goods on
account of the attendant labor.”19The lukewarm person does not want to
offend the Lord gravely, but neither does he want to seriously put forth the
effort to have union with Christ throughout his life. Such a person may not
clearly say “no” to the divine calling, but habitually holds onto a response of
“later” or “tomorrow,” but that tomorrow never comes. His weak love of God
considers every effort to be too difficult. This explains the strong words that
Scripture uses regarding such a person: “I know your works; I know that you
are neither cold nor hot. I wish you were either cold or hot. So, because you
are lukewarm, neither hot nor cold, I will spit you out of my mouth.” 20 The
point is that the lukewarm person forgets the great love that God has shown
him, leaves aside the dynamism toward growth which is intrinsic to charity,
17 Thess 4:3–8.
18 1 Jn 3:5–9.
19 S. Th. I-II, q. 84, a. 4, ad 5. Lukewarmness should not be confused, however, with a
state of interior dryness, because it pertains to a condition of voluntary spiritual languor
that is characterized by a withdrawal from the effort to grow in one's own holiness.
20 Rev 3:15–16.
“[an author says] that lukewarmness is an ethical fever, which is not
very scary, because it is known right away; but it is so malign that one is healed of it
with difficulty.
The comparison is very appropriate, because lukewarmness renders the
soul insensible to the remorse of conscience, so it will happen, that because one is made
insensible to the remorse of venial sins, so with time this person will be rendered insensible
to mortal sin.” (Saint Alphonsus Maria de Liguori, Sermoni compendiati, XIX, 12: Opere,
vol. III, (Turin: Giacinto Marietti, 1880), 426.)

and is satisfied with how he is and what he does. “For you say, 'I am rich and
affluent and have no need of anything,' and yet do not realize that you are
wretched, pitiable, poor, blind, and naked.” 21 Lukewarmness or the “bourgeois
attitude” is ultimately the failure to respond to the vocation of holiness, and
undoubtedly represents a failure.
The lukewarm person is carried away by a temptation to think that the
path toward happiness is a happy medium between Christian holiness—
seen as too burdensome—and a distancing of oneself from God—seen
as a dark road with no exit. The lukewarm person wants to be “good”,
but ignores his filial relation with the Lord, primarily concerns himself
with earthly goods (money, power, material well-being, etc.), does not
give ear to inspirations of grace, is superficial, often irresponsible in
the carrying out of familial, professional, and social works; he does not
demonstrate any consideration of his spiritual growth and is fatigued
by any efforts to do anything that goes beyond what can be seen or
touched.

towards holiness: “Be earnest, therefore, and repent;” 4) to listen to, with
a firm intention of acting on, the call of the Lord: “Behold, I stand at the
door and knock. If anyone hears my voice and opens the door, (then) I will
enter his house and dine with him, and he with me.” This last remedy must
be accomplished in two complementary ways: a) by improving one's prayer,
“because the more we think about spiritual goods, the more pleasing they be-
come to us, and forthwith sloth dies away;”23 b) by frequenting the sacrament
of confession and through spiritual direction, in order to have a more clear
perception of what God asks of us.
3.3.3
The Battle against Concupiscence
The freedom of man is the freedom of a being composed of spirit and flesh,
immersed in temporality, and is a freedom not fully decided by a single choice,
but painstakingly throughout one's life. So, while it is a walk, the person must
concern himself with his own salvation in fear and trembling,24 and what
21Rev 3:17.
22 Cf. Rev 3:18–20.
23S. Th. II-II, q. 35, a. 1, ad 4.
24 Cf. Phil 2:12.


Moral Conduct as the Response of Man to the Divine Call
inevitably results is the battle to overcome resistance and uphold one's own
decisions, for in this life it is always possible to turn backwards.25 On account
of original sin, such moral effort causes fatigue: the natural ordination toward
God is contrasted by the disorder caused by original sin and by actual sins;
this principle of disorder in the moral life, called “concupiscence” or “fomes
peccati,”26 is attributed to the “flesh.”27
Such moral disorder makes itself known above all in the immoderate
love of oneself and in the will for self-affirmation, and maximally in the
closing of oneself off to God which is in pride:28 the worst of all con-
cupiscence is found in the inordinate love of self, which embodies itself
in diverse human appetites (both spiritual and sensitive) and leads to-
ward sin.
“It is St. Paul who describes in a particularly eloquent
way the tension and struggle that trouble the human heart. We read
in the Letter to the Galatians: `But I say, walk by the Spirit, and do
not gratify the desires of the flesh.
For the desires of the flesh are
against the Spirit, and the desires of the Spirit are against the flesh; for
these are opposed to each other, to prevent you from doing what you
would' (Gal 5:16ff). There already exists in man, as a being made up
of body and spirit, a certain tension, a certain struggle of tendencies
between the `spirit' and the `flesh.' But this struggle in fact belongs
to the heritage of sin, is a consequence of sin and at the same time a
confirmation of it. This is part of everyday experience. As the Apostle
writes: `Now the works of the flesh are plain: fornication, impurity,
licentiousness drunkenness, carousing and the like.' These are the sins
that could be called `carnal.' But he also adds others: `enmity, strife,
jealousy, anger, selfishness, dissension, party spirit, envy' (Gal 5:19–21).
All of these constitute the `works of the flesh.' But these works, which
are undoubtedly evil, Paul contrasts with `the fruit of the Spirit,' such
as `love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faithfulness, gentle-
ness, self-control' (Gal 5:22). From the context it is clear that for the
Apostle it is not a question of discriminating against and condemning
25 Cf. Lk 9:62.
26 “Etymologically, `concupiscence' can refer to any intense form of human desire. Chris-
tian theology has given it a particular meaning: the movement of the sensitive appetite
contrary to the operation of the human reason. the apostle St. Paul identifies it with the
rebellion of the `flesh' against the `spirit' (cf.
Gal 5:16,17,24; Eph 2:3).
Concupiscence
stems from the disobedience of the first sin. It unsettles man's moral faculties and, without
being in itself an offense, inclines man to commit sins (cf. Council of Trent: DS 1515)”
(CCC 2515).
27 “Flesh” in the sense of the old self, of the person marked by the disorder of sin: cf.
Chapter XI, subsection 11.6.3. On the battle against the flesh in Saint Paul, see R. Schnack-
enburg, Il messaggio morale del Nuovo Testamento, vol. II, (1989), 53–56.
28 So it is written in the Vulgate and the Neo-Vulgate: “Quoniam initium omnis
peccati est superbia” (Ecclus-Sir 10:15), of which the NAB version differs : “For
pride is the reservoir of sin” (Sir 10,13).
Citing Sirach, Augustine and Thomas
write: “Initium quippe omnis peccati superbia» (Saint Augustine, De Civitate Dei,
12, 6: NBA 5/2, 158). “Initium omnis peccati superbia vel amor proprius” (S. Th.
I-II, q. 84, a. 2, ad 3).


Chapter 3
the body, which along with the spiritual soul constitutes man's nature
and personal subjectivity.
Rather, he is concerned with the morally
good or bad works, or better the permanent dispositions—virtues and
vices—which are the fruits of submission to—in the first case– or of
resistance to—in the second case—the saving action of the Holy Spirit.
Consequently, the Apostle writes: `If we live by the Spirit, let us also
walk by the Spirit' (Gal 5:25).” 29
A direction toward holiness cannot be maintained without a battle to overcome
disordered interior movements. Already in the Old Testament life on the earth
is compared to military life, as a battle between the woman's descendant with
that of the serpent, along with many other passages of battle allegory.30 The
theme is taken up again in the New Testament, both with the metaphor of
war,31 and with that of sports competition,32 as a battle leading up to the full
victory of Christ in the eschatological battle.33 The Second Vatican Council
also reminds us: “For a monumental struggle against the powers of darkness
pervades the whole history of man. The battle was joined from the very origins
of the world and will continue until the last day, as the Lord has attested (Mt
22:39). Caught in this conflict, man is obliged to wrestle constantly if he is to
cling to what is good, nor can he achieve his own integrity without great efforts
and the help of God's grace.”34 The Christian, however, is not moved by a
earthly desire for perfection; his goal is not self-affirmation in his domination of
disordered nature, but in loving God above all things and identifying himself
with Jesus Christ by means of the grace of the Holy Spirit.
The ascetic
battle is principally an effort of transformation in Christ. Therefore, it is an
optimistic and more direct effort for doing good and avoiding evil: “Do not
be conquered by evil but conquer evil with good.” 35
3.4
The Positive Aspect of the Moral Effort:
Renewal in the Spirit and the Means
of Sanctification
The positive aspect of the moral effort is that of better responding to the pro-
found nature of the carrying out of the divine call to holiness. The moral life is
primarily spiritual progress that tends to an always more intimate union with
Christ. This union is called “mystical”, because it is a participation by means

Moral Conduct as the Response of Man to the Divine Call
of the sacraments—“the holy mysteries”—and, through Him, in the mystery
of the Most Holy Trinity.
God calls all of us to this intimate union with
Him.”36 The Second Vatican Council concludes its exposition of the doctrine
of the universal call to holiness with a concise vision of the principal means
of achieving union with Christ: “the first and most necessary gift is love, by
which we love God above all things and our neighbor because of God. Indeed,
in order that love, as good seed may grow and bring forth fruit in the soul,
each one of the faithful must willingly hear the Word of God and accept His
Will, and must complete what God has begun by their own actions with the
help of God's grace. These actions consist in the use of the sacraments and
in a special way the Eucharist, frequent participation in the sacred action of
the Liturgy, application of oneself to prayer, self-abnegation, lively fraternal
service and the constant exercise of all the virtues.” 37
3.4.1
Growth in Holiness
The Christian moral life is a process of progressive sanctification.
This is
expressed in the New Testament as growth toward union with Christ,38 or as
an always greater filial identification with the will of God the Father39 or, more
simply, as growth in charity, which is the most properly unifying virtue. Thus
Saint Paul says to the Phillippians: “And this is my prayer: that your love
may increase ever more and more in knowledge and every kind of perception,
to discern what is of value, so that you may be pure and blameless for the
day of Christ, filled with the fruit of righteousness that comes through Jesus
Christ for the glory and praise of God.”40 According to the Apostle, charity
is the moving inspiration of the knowledge and moral discernment of the
Christian, that orders all his conduct toward the glorification of God through
Jesus Christ. In the Letter to Thessalonians he expresses it in a similar way
and adds that charity, as a principle of the Christian path, proceeds from God:
“And may the Lord make you increase and abound in love for one another
and for all, just as we have for you, so as to strengthen your hearts, to be
blameless in holiness before our God and Father at the coming of our Lord
Jesus with all his holy ones.”41
The progressive identification with Christ and with the Father through charity
requires that one follow the commandments.42 The Gospels report many moral
discourses of Jesus, among these the tradition has privileged the “Sermon

Chapter 3
on the mount”, which has at its core “the beatitudes”; these, together with
the “commandment of love” and the confirmation of the decalogue, can be
considered as a summary of Christian moral praxis.43 This nucleus is clarified
and explained in other passages of the New Testament, which also underline
the radicality of the whole Christian life.44 Moral conduct is not, however, a
collection of disconnected activities. It does not consist only in doing certain
things and not doing others.
Rather, the Christian finds himself needing
to trace for himself a plan of conduct, a program of life, so that he may
accomplish and exhibit life in Christ, where he is called and also where he
discovers his human and Christian fullness, in his concrete personal, familial,
professional, and social circumstances.
Life in Christ is the criterion with
which actions, human and social relationships, and the modes of using goods
must be congruent. Everything is presided over by the need for consistency,
which gives rise to the “unity of life” of the Christian.45
It is not possible to divide the life of the Chrisitan into two great parts ruled,
respectively, by obedience and by freedom, as if to the first would pertain the
commanded and forbidden actions of moral norms, and to the second would
pertain actions that have nothing to do with morality, in which one could move
about “freely”, seeking merely human goals or interests. In reality, whoever has
been touched by the grace of God conceives of his own existence and activities
as means to union with God through Christ: “So whether you eat or drink,
or whatever you do, do everything for the glory of God.” 46 Even if there exist
activities that are considered morally indifferent considered in abstraction,
and admitting that one is not always able to actually and explicitly refer
all his actions to Christ, the intrinsic dynamic of the Christian life tends in
itself to render always more present, and always more actual and known, the
supreme goal of the love of God or, if one prefers, the filial attitude that
discovers in all things the way to “discern what is the will of God, what is
good and pleasing and perfect.”47 From filial charity, as from “a spring of

As Saint Cyprian writes, “the will of God is that which Christ performed
and taught. It is humility in conversation, firmness in faith, discretion
in words, justice in actions, mercy in works, discipline in morals; it is
to do no wrong and to tolerate wrongs immediately, to maintain peace
with the brothers, to love God with all one's heart, to love Him as
Father, to fear Him as God, to prefer nothing to Christ, for neither has
he preferred anything to us; it is to stand inseparably united in His
love, to remain close to His cross with courage and steadiness, when
his name and love our questioned, to show in love the constancy which
we confess, in controversies the trust by which we walk, in death the
patience by which we shall be rewarded: this means to want to be
coheirs of Christ, this is to do the command of God, this is to fulfill the
will of the Father.”49

these proceed the impetus to seek out Christ even in the fulfillment of secu-
lar tasks. Such a movement has some concrete manifestations: as Christ, to
strive to do all things well;61 to sanctify one's daily life;62to rule the world

3.4.2
The Sacraments
The effort to conform all the dimensions of human life to the theological and
moral virtues, making them become means of union with Christ, is not gen-
erated by man nor can it be sustained with human effort alone, as Jesus79and
the Apostle Paul both teach.80
We intend now to point out the principal
means—sacramental and non-sacramental—through which it is possible for
the Christian to follow the loving words of the Lord, “Come to me, all you
who labor and are burdened, and I will give you rest.”
According to the sacramental character of the economy of salvation,81 the
initial gift of the Christian life is received ex opere operato with baptism and
confirmation.
These two sacraments, along with holy orders, can only be
received once in a person's life. Marriage and the anointing of the sick, even
if they sometimes can be received more than once (if the first spouse dies or
when the Christian finds himself in the peril of death again), are ordained
toward completely special effects; while the sacraments of penance and the
Eucharist are the means of sanctification par excellence.82
“Christ instituted the sacrament of Penance for all sinful members of his
Church: above all for those who, since Baptism, have fallen into grave sin,
and have thus lost their baptismal grace and wounded ecclesial communion.
It is to them that the sacrament of Penance offers a new possibility to con-
vert and to recover the grace of justification.83 Even for those who receive

Chapter 3
it without having committed a grave sin, the sacrament of penance produces
an increase of grace, builds up the spiritual forces for Christian combat,84
progressively heals concupiscence and the wounds caused by sins of one's
past life, contributes to the formation of the conscience, and is an occasion
of effective spiritual direction. It is for these reasons not only a means of
healing, but also an important means of sanctification and union with Christ:
applying to the Christian the merits of the Redeemer, it is very effective
for the moral and spiritual development of the faithful, such that it consti-
tutes a true “personal encounter with the crucified forgiving Christ;” 85 for
this reason, the Church insistently recommends the practice of frequent con-
fession.86
Not less important for the Christian life is the sacrament of the Eucharist.87
The love of Jesus for men manifests itself clearly in his passion and death;
in fact, “no one has greater love than this, to lay down one's life for one's
friends;”88 and it is this same love that leads the Lord to seek to draw close
and have more intimate union with us. Such a love led Him to “invent” a
sacrament that would be a memorial of His passion, presence among men and
a special kind of nourishment:89 “at the Last Supper, on the night when He
was betrayed, our Saviour instituted the eucharistic sacrifice of His Body and
Blood. He did this in order to perpetuate the sacrifice of the Cross throughout
the centuries until He should come again, and so to entrust to His beloved
spouse, the Church, a memorial of His death and resurrection: a sacrament
of love, a sign of unity, a bond of charity, a paschal banquet in which Christ
is eaten, the mind is filled with grace, and a pledge of future glory is given to
us.”90 Thus the Christian life is strictly connected to the Eucharist because in
it are contained all of the spiritual goods of the Church and it is placed as the
center and root of evangelization and of all Christian life.91 It is the center
and summit of the Christian life because to it is directed all that the Church
and the faithful must accomplish; and it is also the root and source in that it
contains not only grace, but the very Author of grace. Consequently, the life
of holiness must be an eminently eucharistic life.

Moral Conduct as the Response of Man to the Divine Call
The Holy Sacrifice, not only a memory of an event, but rather a memorial,92
a representation –or even better, a re-presentation—of the salvific event of the
Cross that renews it and applies it throughout history. The Mass, therefore,
in its connection with the redemptive Sacrifice, is the culminating act of the
history of salvation and for each person it is the culminating act of his own
salvation and holiness. The effort for holiness is found intimately connected
with the participation in the eucharistic sacrifice; therefore the Church rec-
ommends frequent attendance at the Mass and asks the faithful that they
participate at it, at least, every Sunday.93
A second aspect of the Eucharist is Communion, whereby the Christian unites
himself intimately to Jesus and identifies with Him:94 because such identifi-
cation coincides with the goal of holiness, it is evident that Christian holiness
cannot prescind from assiduous reception of Communion. The Eucharist re-
inforces the human energies in the path toward holiness; prevents perils, dif-
ficulties, and sins; facilitates one's ascetic battles; is the pledge of eternal life;
and strengthens the union between men.95 A person must be well disposed
in order to receive communion fruitfully96 and to thank the Lord with deep
fervor.
Finally, it should be remembered that Jesus is found truly, really, and sub-
stantially present in the eucharistic species. This explains why the Church has
multiplied the acts of eucharistic worship: visits to the Blessed Sacrament,
expositions and benedictions, processions, eucharistic congresses, etc.; “the
Church and the world have a great need of eucharistic worship. Jesus waits
for us in this sacrament of love. Let us be generous with our time in going
to meet Him in adoration and in contemplation that is full of faith and ready
to make reparation for the great faults and crimes of the world[.] [May] our
adoration [certainly] never cease.”97
92The word memorial, that translates the Hebrew zikkaron and the Greek upomnéma,
does not mean a memory of the past, but a divine invocation of today in which the salvific
plan of the Lord is continued and made present.

Chapter 3
3.4.3
Prayer
“One does not live by bread alone, but by every word that comes forth from the
mouth of God:”98 the Christian life requires attentive listening to the word of
God; therefore one of the last recommendations of Jesus was: “watch and pray
that you may not undergo the test,”99 and the first Christians followed these
directions: “They devoted themselves to the teaching of the apostles [. . .] and
to the prayers.”100 The living and personal relationship with God—Father,
Son, and Holy Spirit—obtained in prayer, consists in being in the presence of
God and in filial dialogue with Him. Thus the universal call to holiness can
be made concrete in the universal call to prayer, to loving familiarity with the
Lord who incessantly invites each man to a mysterious, but real encounter in
prayer. So Jesus did and taught,101 and so must his disciples also do: the
prayer of Christians, like that of Christ, brings to full adhesion the human will
with that of the loving will of the Father. It requires conversion and purity of
heart, trust and filial audacity, humility, patience, and perseverance.102 This
is what is called contemplation, or rather to have one's “sight” of faith fixed
on Jesus, in order to better know his will and to always identify oneself more
with Him. Such contemplation does not demand a fuga mundi (flight from the
world), but rather one can and must carry it out in ordinary life and through
earthly activities: “When our mind is intent on temporal things in order that
it may rest in them, it remains immersed therein; but when it is intent on
them in relation to the acquisition of beatitude, it is not lowered by them, but
raises them to a higher level,”103 and uses them to establish in each moment
a loving dialogue with the Lord.104
Man tends, by nature, toward dialogue, toward communication; and
when he does not confer with someone else, he will speak with him-
self: memories, worries, doubts, desires, dreams, etc. The Christian life
must aspire to a continual conversation with the Lord, in a real, deep,
and generous way; thus the person detaches himself from egocentrism
and makes himself more theocentric: he strengthens divine friendship,
develops charity, rectifies his intention, acquires serenity and objectiv-
ity, and reinvigorates his moral action. No activity, even being earthly
and material, impedes the constant relationship with God:105 enough

In order to maintain such continual intimacy with God, it is helpful to dedicate

that regards every Christian; the Scriptures make clear “the necessity for them

has always witnessed to the need for determinate acts of piety, among which

seek His will in every event, see Christ in everyone whether he be a relative
or a stranger, and make correct judgments about the true meaning and value
of temporal things both in themselves and in their relation to man's final

examination of conscience. It should be underlined, nonetheless, that

3.4.4
The Cross
Jesus “said to all, `If anyone wishes to come after me, he must deny himself
and take up his cross daily and follow me.'”112 So all disciples of the Lord
carry their cross daily, and in fact, the cross is what separates those who are
authentic Christians from those who are not: “The message of the cross is
foolishness to those who are perishing, but to us who are being saved it is the
power of God.”113 Hardly could there be a coherent Christian life without a
willingness to die with Jesus, to complete in one's own flesh what is lacking in
the Lord's Passion.114 This is Christian self-denial or mortification: its pri-
mordial purpose is identification with the Lord, but for such identification it is
necessary to deny one's self, one's own ego. “The way of perfection passes by
way of the Cross. There is no holiness without renunciation and spiritual bat-
tle (cf. 2 Tim:4). Spiritual progress entails the ascesis and mortification that
gradually lead to living in the peace and joy of the Beatitudes.” 115 Therefore,
the Church has established some concrete times for penitential practice and
highly recommends voluntary privations such as fasting or almsgiving;116 fur-
thermore, each person can and must seek out in his own life practices adapted
to unite himself to Jesus's cross: mortification of the senses and of the imag-
ination, of the intelligence and the will, the effort to serve others and to
accomplish one's duties with perfection, the joyous acceptance of opposition,
etc.

Moral Conduct as the Response of Man to the Divine Call
3.5
The Virgin Mary's Role
in Christian Sanctification
Without wishing to take up the contents of the dogmatic study of the Virgin
Mary, it seems however necessary to bring to light the essential Marian di-
mension of the Christian life. The role of Mary in the life of the Church and
of individual Christians derives from her singular union with Christ and, in
the last analysis, from her divine maternity. “By her complete adherence to
the Father's will, to his Son's redemptive work, and to every prompting of the
Holy Spirit, the Virgin Mary is the Church's model of faith and charity. Thus
she is a 'preeminent and . . . wholly unique member of the Church'; indeed,
she is the 'exemplary realization' (typus) of the Church.” 117 But her role does
not finish there, because Mary “cooperated by her obedience, faith, hope and
burning charity in the work of the Saviour in giving back supernatural life to
souls. Wherefore she is our mother in the order of grace.” 118 Mary is truly
the spiritual Mother of Christians, and exercises in our regard a constant and
efficacious maternal mediation. This is one of the most proposed doctrines of
the Roman Pontiffs,119 and was recently reproposed by the Second Vatican
Council,120 by the enyclical Redemptoris Mater,121 and by the Cathechism of
the Catholic Church.122
The maternal mediation of Mary is born out of God's good pleasure and
“flows forth from the superabundance of the merits of Christ, rests on His
mediation, depends entirely on it and draws all its power from it. In no way
does it impede, but rather does it foster the immediate union of the faithful
with Christ.”123 What the Church understands by the mediation of Mary is
that, according to the design of God, nothing is communicated to us from
the immense treasure of the grace of Christ if not through Mary. “So, just
as no one can approach the highest Father except through the Son, so no
one can approach Christ except through His Mother.” 124 “ Since she excels
all in sanctity, and by her union with Christ and by her adoption by Christ
for the work of man's salvation, she merited for us de congruo, as they say,

Chapter 3

The mediation of Mary has a maternal character. The work of Mary
possesses a fortiori all of the characteristics that are proper to a good
mother: affection, understanding, tenderness, and unwavering love de-
spite all circumstances. On the Cross, Christ experienced the suffering
of abandonment foreseen by the redeeming design of the Father. Those
who had been following him remained hidden, his enemies were instead
surrounding him, watching him, and savoring their apparent victory.
Jesus then “cried out in a loud voice, `Eli, Eli, lema sabachthani?' which
means, `My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?'.” 126 The price
to pay for our sins appeared in all of its gravity. Nevertheless, even
in that moment, the Father did not deprive the Son of the support of
His mother, who stood “by the cross of Jesus.” 127 Giving Mary to us
as Mother,128 Christ seems to want to explicitly confirm that no one of
those who want to follow in His footsteps throughout the centuries will
ever be deprived of the consoling and maternal presence of the Virgin
Mary. From that moment Mary became the refuge of all Christians,
always available, a motive of sure hope, and a presence that never fails.
The Second Vatican Council underlines that Mary is also the model of
the Church whom Christians must imitate. “But while in the most holy
Virgin the Church has already reached that perfection whereby she is
without spot or wrinkle, the followers of Christ still strive to increase
in holiness by conquering sin.
And so they turn their eyes to Mary
who shines forth to the whole community of the elect as the model of
virtues.”129 Our Lady is the most clear reflection of the moral life. “By
accepting and pondering in her heart events which she did not always
understand (cf. Lk 2:19), she became the model of all those who hear
the word of God and keep it (cf. Lk 11:28).” 130
In response to the maternal protection and example offered by Mary,
the Christian responds by entrusting himself completely to her. “The
Marian dimension of the life of a disciple of Christ is expressed in a
special way precisely through this filial entrusting to the Mother of
Christ, which began with the testament of the Redeemer on Golgotha.
Entrusting himself to Mary in a filial manner, the Christian, like the
Apostle John, `welcomes' the Mother of Christ 'into his own home' and
brings her into everything that makes up his inner life.” 131
It needs to be emphasized that from the practical point of view, that is,
from the perspective of the Christian who, despite his own limitations, desires

reach the fullness of maturity in Jesus Christ is that Mary, forever Mother of
Jesus Christ and fruitful Spouse of the Holy Spirit, is not formed well enough
in their hearts. Whoever wants to have well matured and formed fruit must
have the tree of life, that is Mary; whoever wants to have in himself the
working of the Holy Spirit must have the fruitful and indissoluble Spouse, the
heavenly Mary, who renders it fertile and fruitful.” 132 The patron of moralists
affirms it even more concisely: “One does not reach God but through Jesus
Christ, and one does not reach Jesus Christ but through Mary.” 133
3.6
The Apostolic Dimension
of the Christian Vocation
The active response of the Christian to the call to holiness includes also the
active participation in the mission of Christ and of the Church. The Chris-
tian vocation “by its very nature is also a vocation to the apostolate.” 134 We
do not speak now specifically of the tasks derived from various ecclesiasti-
cal ministries, but rather of the apostolic effort instrinsically connected with
the following of Christ that is proper, therefore, for all the faithful, even the
lay faithful, as was emphasized by the decree Apostolicam Actuositatem of
the Second Vatican Council and, more recently, by the Apostolic Exhortation
Christifideles Laici.
The Church has the purpose of “spreading the kingdom of Christ throughout
the earth for the glory of God the Father, to enable all men to share in
His saving redemption, and that through them the whole world might enter
into a relationship with Christ.”135 All of the activity of the Church ordered
toward this end is called the “apostolate”. The radical call to the apostolate
derives not from a ministry or from particular circumstances, but from union
with Christ the Head,136 and therefore all of the faithful contribute to the
apostolate, though in different ways and according to their own situations
and circumstances. It is not possible to separate the following of Christ from
the apostolate:
“Just as there is no way to separate Christ, the God man,

came down from heaven 'for us men and for our salvation', as we say in the
creed. For a Christian apostolate is something instinctive.” 137
The Christian
apostolate, in the final analysis, is always evangelization and sanctification.
It is directed, in fact, “to manifest Christ's message by words and deeds and
to communicate His grace to the world.”138
The apostolate is carried out spontaneously when the faithful set out to
order their own activities seeking primarily union with Christ. Clerics
accomplish it through the ministry of the word and the sacraments;
those in religious life do so through prayer, works of charity, and es-
chatological witness; the lay faithful through their own Christian life,
words, fraternal help, etc. The specific task of the laity is the Christian
animation of the temporal order,139 an important theme that will be
treated further on.140 Now we only wish to underline that the Christian
apostolate involves for everyone also “the proclamation and presenta-
tion of morality,”141 that is, proclamation through word and deed of
the path to follow in order to be disciples of Christ.
“Just as it does in proclaiming the truths of faith, and even more so in
presenting the foundations and content of Christian morality, the new
evangelization will show its authenticity and unleash all its missionary
force when it is carried out through the gift not only of the word pro-
claimed but also of the word lived. In particular, the life of holiness
which is resplendent in so many members of the People of God, hum-
ble and often unseen, constitutes the simplest and most attractive way
to perceive at once the beauty of truth, the liberating force of God's
love, and the value of unconditional fidelity to all the demands of the
Lord's law, even in the most difficult situations.” 142 This reality offers
a perspective for the teaching and study of moral theology that should
never be forgotten.

Part II
The Human Person
Called by God:
Moral Anthropology


## CHAPTER 4 {#colom-scelti.4}
The Freedom of the Sons
of God
4.1
A Comprehensive Vision of the Themes
of Christian Moral Anthropology
We studied in Part I the vocation of the Christian to holiness, or rather,
the call to participate in the Trinitarian life in Christ. Between the initial
justification and the eschatological fulfillment of salvation sits the process of
sanctification; the earthly and historical carrying out of the Christian voca-
tion, whose more general aspects were discussed in the last chapter. Before
dealing with the study of the normative aspect of moral activity (Part III),
the nature and structure of the realities that must be regulated will first be
studied analytically (actions, affections, etc.), as well as the mode in which
they are regulated. That is to say, we first must study the conditions and
structures that make a Christian a being capable of collaborating freely with
God, elaborating–with the help of grace—a type of life (moral conduct) that
not only is consistent with his identity as a son of God but also permits him
to express himself and grow “to the extent of the full stature of Christ.” 1
Christian moral anthropology is not concerned with all the themes of theologi-
cal anthropology, while the latter is nonetheless presupposed. Rather, the sole
object of our attention is the Christian as a moral agent and thus inasmuch
as he is free; for this reason, this chapter shall be dedicated to a discussion
of freedom. The Christian sees freedom as part of his self-understanding as
a child of God in Christ, and therefore as the freedom of a child that desires
1 Eph 4:13.


Chapter 4
above all to fulfill the will of the Father.2 A prior study of the dimensions
of the philosophical concept of freedom will provide us with the analytical
framework necessary for adequately framing this entire theme.
Free behavior has a rather complex articulation.
Such complexity unfolds
itself along two axes. According to its horizontal axis, free behavior can be
conceived as a process of communication between man, the world, and God,
which, in its entirety, tends to carry out life in Christ in a concrete way. Ac-
cording to its vertical axis, free behavior represents the culminating moment
and the supreme integrating principle of a set of processes, contents, and states
of the psyche that, due to the phenomena of interconnection and retroaction3
that verify themselves in it, possesses a certain circular character.4
In this process it is possible to analytically distinguish five fundamental ele-
ments.
1. The inclinations and tendencies, which we shall generically call desire, in
the sense of being non-deliberated desire, that is, prior to a free choice.
2. The perception regarding the presence or absence of goods to which
human desire is referred.
3. The affective reactions (sentiments, emotions, passions) which follow
perception. The person reacts positively or negatively depending on the
meaning that the perception has in relation to his tendencies.
4. Human acts or free acts, governed by the intelligence and the will,
through which the person leads himself (conduct) toward the type of
life he has decided to live; governing his own tendencies and respond-
ing, positively or negatively, to the call of God.
5. The habits: the principal expressions of the person's freedom, through
which he manages to modify, for good or bad, his operative makeup,
i.e. the inclinations; tendencies; and the capacity to judge, decide, or
execute. Alongside the habits acquired through moral effort, Christian
moral anthropology must study the infused habits (the infused moral
virtues, the gifts of the Spirit) through which the Christian is guided by
the Holy Spirit toward the life of the children of God in Christ. This
fifth element—acquired and infused moral habits—closes the circle and
becomes in reality the first element of the series, in the sense that in real
2 Cf. Jn 4:34; 5:30; and 6:38 in reference to Jesus. See: Jn 7:17 in reference to the
Christian.
3 For example: reflecting on prior choices, changing one's mind, etc.
4 In virtue of such circularity the study of moral theology presupposes the knowledge of
the essential structures of being and of human action: spiritual faculties, sensitive appetites,
conscience, etc., themes that are not possible to develop here in all their extension. Only
the aspects which directly regard moral behavior will be treated.


The Freedom of the Sons of God
life the human inclinations and tendencies are not found in persons who
are in a pure state. We find instead inclinations, tendencies, sentiments,
etc., which are modified—for good or bad—by the moral habits, and
therefore by the ethical effort of the person and by his cooperation with
the saving action of the Holy Spirit.
Of the five elements just cited, the first three will be studied in Chapter V.
They are of extreme importance for forming an exact idea of human freedom,
its motivations, and of the goods that attract it. Human freedom is certainly
a spiritual reality, but not a pure option of a spirit that stands outside of space
and time. Our will is not a pure initiative, nor is it without roots. Man pos-
sesses inclinations and necessities connected with his corporeity, sensibility,
and rationality, as well as “inclinations” and demands received with the grace
of the Holy Spirit that can be satisfied only with free behavior. So, in the
moral life, issues and needs proceeding from what are not free are continually
elevated to the level of freedom, where they are always in some way elabo-
rated and transformed, and sometimes corrected or even rejected. Freedom is
nourished by motivations that often do not proceed from itself. Among these
motivations, some proceed from inferior levels of the human psychophysical
complex; others proceed from a superior ambit which is determined by the
presence of the Holy Spirit in the Christian. In any case, without consider-
ing these elements attentively, it is not possible to have an adequate idea of
man—including the Christian—as a moral agent. Man as a moral agent is
not an indifferent agent who then comes in contact with a law, nor is he an
autonomous subject that carries out transcendental choices outside of space
and time.5
Two last elements remain to be discussed which are more familiar to moral
theology: moral action and the moral habits.
To these elements we shall
dedicate Chapters VI and VII respectively.
4.2
The Dimensions
of the Philosophical Concept of Freedom
Philosophical ethics, and the same goes for moral theology, presupposes the
reality of human freedom. If we did not have the real psychological possibility
of deciding freely between good and evil, there would not be moral conduct
(man would not be able to “conduct” himself) nor could there be imputed
any responsibility, and such things as praise or blame regarding our behavior
would not make any sense. The juridical and political experience of humanity
5 On the diverse conceptions of the moral agent in contemporary ethical approaches, cf.
G. Abbà, Quale impostazione per la filosofia morale? (1996), 239–274.


Chapter 4
relies on this same presupposition as well.
Now, the existence of various
factors which condition human action do not carry any essential argument
against this reality of human freedom, for these conditioning factors always
leave a certain margin for a final autonomous decision6 and, as Hans Reiner
observes, no one up to this point has succeeded in rigorously demonstrating
that such a margin does not remain.7 The negation of freedom depends on
premises of a general nature whose legitimate applicability to the entire scope
of reality has never been demonstrated.
It needs to be recognized, nevertheless, that human freedom is a reality so
profound, multifaceted and, in some ways, mysterious, that it is easy to under-
stand why it has been, still is, and probably always will be a principal object
of man's reflection. It is primarily the task of philosophical anthropology and
metaphysics to clarify the myriad theoretical aspects of the concept of free-
dom.8 Here we must limit ourselves to mentioning the principal dimensions of
the philosophical concept of freedom, in order to be able to adequately frame
what Christian anthropology teaches regarding it.
If we consider the expression “we must have freedom in order to be free to be
free”, we see that the concept of freedom is used with three different meanings.
The first part (“we must have freedom”) means the absence of restrictions or
coercion; the second part (“to be free”) means freedom of choice, the capacity
to choose autonomously; the third part (“to be free” again) means instead
a condition that is the object of choice or of achievement, and represents a
quality of the purely ethical order, whose nature we must explain further along.
Around these three meanings the principal problematic nuclei of the concept
of freedom can be divided, though certainly not all of them.
4.2.1
Freedom from Coercion
“Freedom from coercion” or “freedom from restrictions” is the condition of
the person who is not compelled or impeded in his action by external agents.
A slave, a prisoner, or any who are prohibited by law or by other people
from expressing themselves or doing what they want, do not have this type of
freedom. It is a freedom that refers principally to the power to do externally

Verantwortung, (Cologne: Adamas, 1982), 65–83; A. Rodríguez Luño, Etica (1992), nos.
111–115. A reader interested in an interdisciplinary approach can consult: F. Russo and
J. Villanueva (eds.), Le dimensioni della libertà nel dibattito scientifico e filosofico, (Rome:
Armando, 1995).


The Freedom of the Sons of God
what one has decided to do, although it can also refer to the will inasmuch as
it can undergo exterior coercion, for example, through some types of drugs
or systems of torture. Diverse moral, political, and legal standpoints of view
deal with this type of freedom and its many manifestations.
The first reflections concerning freedom in ancient Greece before the
time of Aristotle moved in this area. Freedom came to be defined in
contraposition to that from which it was free, and so a fundamentally
political notion of freedom came to be formulated: the citizen is free, he
that is neither a slave nor a prisoner of war. In the Modern Age of Eu-
rope, this concept of freedom was the principal object of the attention
of some philosophers, even if it came about in a very different context
than that of ancient Greece. With the advent of modern science, the
reduction of causality to material and efficient causality rendered reflec-
tion on freedom very difficult, since between the preceding state of the
soul and the will that derives from it, a causal relation is established
of a material/efficient type, understood as a necessary connection be-
tween two events or instances (given the motivation or state of soul
A, action B necessarily follows). To affirm the freedom of the will was
supposed at the time to deny the existence of this necessary connection
between motivation and action and, consequently, causality. Now, since
the theoretical exercise of the reason appears ruled by the categories of
causality, to affirm freedom in limiting causality would be to support
the impossibility of theoretically understanding human action, which
would in the end be conceived as the irrational or unpredictable par
excellence.
For this reason, philosophers like Hobbes, Locke, Hume,
and Voltaire prefer to think of freedom not as an internal property of
the will, but rather as the capacity to externally put into effect what
is willed. Freedom would be the power to act as one wills, but not the
faculty of willing freely. Leibniz rightly pointed out to them that the
true problem was the freedom of the spirit, and not that of the free-
dom of the arm or the leg, even if Leibniz did not succeed in resolving
satisfactorily all of the problems associated with the freedom of the will.
4.2.2
Freedom of Choice
The second meaning of freedom looks no longer for the opportunity to do what
which one decides to do, but seeks, rather, the absence of an interior neces-
sity to make one decision or another. It is properly the freedom of the will,
which is commonly called psychological freedom. The philosophical doctrine
that denies the existence of this freedom is generically called psychological
determinism, and it sustains, in synthesis, that the apparent choices of man
are subjected in reality to an internal necessity, for example, the strongest
rational motivation, in the face of which the will would be determined in its
act. Indeed, the existence of diverse internal conditions which limit (or even


Chapter 4
nullify) psychological freedom cannot be denied; this indicates that human
freedom is limited, yet the presence of such conditions does not deny the re-
ality of freedom; personal experience of the human act shows that, in normal
conditions, the person freely chooses what she wills.
Freedom of choice, called “free will” by classical philosophy, implies the au-
tonomous position of an act of the will, which situates itself between “I can”
and “I am not compelled”. On the level of lived reality it is linked to the
awareness that, regarding my will, there must exist something that may as
well not have existed, or that there does not exist something which could
have. On account of freedom of choice, man is the cause and principle of his
own acts (Aristotle), or in other words, the master of his own action (Saint
Thomas). Man does not necessarily will what he wills, he can choose or take
preferences, and when there is no real possibility of choosing he can nonethe-
less take an interior position: to affirm or deny, or to accept or refuse what is
given to him. It is an interior freedom that is even compatible with coercion
in extreme cases: the prisoner, for example, still has the freedom to take a
position regarding his own situation, accepting it because he considers it a
just penalty for his crimes, or by not accepting it because he knows himself
to be innocent and unjustly condemned.
Regarding the freedom of choice, it is possible to conceptually distin-
guish two dimensions: self-determination and intentionality. The idea
of self-determination expresses faithfully, in our judgment, the essence
of the free act.9 It says in effect that in every free action, it is I (and
not another person or an internal necessity) who decides or determines,
and who, moreover, decides or determines myself, or who I am to be-
come. The first aspect (“It is for me to decide, and not another in my
place”) is that recalled by the same concept of freedom. But the second
is no less important: in every free action, even if one treats of an action
that is directed toward another person or external matter, I decide also
who I am; I modify and form my moral being. The second dimension
of the freedom of choice, intentionality, is found in the opening of the
will toward its object. The will is the faculty which the person uses to
achieve his objectives and, in this perspective, freedom implies that the
objects presented by the intelligence do not necessarily determine the
act of the will. This is the perspective that is unduly made absolute by
those who conceive of the discussions concerning freedom as being in the
form of an opposition between determinism and indeterminism. With
the idea of indeterminism regarding the objects of the will, it is possible
to form only a negative (what it is not) and inadequate idea of freedom;
for it implies a form of dependence and of determination qualitatively
superior to the dependence and independence with respect to the ob-
jects of the will: this superior form of determination and dependence
9 We follow here the analysis of self-determination of K. Wojtyla, Persona e atto,
(Vatican City: Lib. Ed. Vaticana, 1982), Ch. III.


The Freedom of the Sons of God
is self-determination or self-dependence. The person is not determined
by the objects of the will, in that he is determined and ruled only by
himself (self-determination). Self-determination would therefore be the
fundamental dimension of freedom, while intentionality on the level of
the objects is a derived dimension.10
Saint Thomas makes a distinction regarding the freedom of choice be-
tween the level of exercise and that of specification,11 comparable to
that already indicated between self-determination and intentionality,
which we shall not treat of now. Rather, needing to be considered is
the fact that for Aquinas the root of the freedom of choice is found
in the universality of intellectual knowledge. The known objects are
certainly individual, but of them we say that they are respectively a
house, a table, etc. We know them, that is, also in their universality—
house, table—and, in the final analysis, inasmuch as they are entities
and goods. So, just as we hear something insofar as it produces sound,
and see it insofar as it gives off light, so we comprehend something inas-
much as it is, and we understand it “practically” when we consider it
as a good. The intellectual capacity is in itself related to being and the
universal good, and for this it cannot be saturated by individual ob-
jects. The universal horizon of the reason—virtually infinite—renders
possible the practical reason's freedom of judgment about the goodness
of individual things, and makes it so that there always remains a real
margin for the self-determination of the will, whose horizon—the moti-
vation of good in general—participates in the virtual infinitude of the
intellect. Therefore, no finite good (or infinite, but known in a finite
way) is perfectly commensurate to the intellect and to the will so as to
produce a necessary judgment or consent.
Usually the cognitive evaluation of concrete goods does not produce any
necessity in the will. The person is not necessarily driven by the known
goods; rather it is up to her to determine her own self in relation to
the goods. It could be said that the personal will forms itself; it gives
itself a formal determination while certainly making use of knowledge.
It can also be said that the intellect merely introduces the formal de-
termination that the will accepts. In any case, when faced with a good
whose attraction seems almost irresistible, the person can will to not
consider this good, and think of another thing, etc.: this is the case of
those who do not understand “because they do not want to understand”
and of those who do not listen “because they do not want to listen.” We
must conclude that the exercise of the intellect depends on the will, and
conversely, that the intellect certainly guides in some way the apparent

See the interesting observations concerning this in:
M. Scheler, Zur
Phänomenologie und Metaphysik der Freiheit, in Id., Gesammelte Werke, vol. X,
(Bern: Francke, 1957) 176–177.

Chapter 4
transcendence of the will; for the person would reject the intellectual
consideration only if such a consideration were held to be opposed in
some way to the person's own good. To summarize all of this: the will
is preceded by an intellectual act that is not objectively established by
the will; nevertheless it depends on the will that such a consideration,
and not another, be decisive on the level of practice. It is in this sense
that we say that self-determination is the fundamental dimension of the
freedom of choice.
4.2.3
Freedom as a Value and Ethical Task
We refer now to the value and moral task represented by the good use of the
freedom of choice or, in other words, to the value represented by the free affir-
mation of the good and, in contrast, to the negativity that is introduced into
the spiritual world every time that an intelligent being chooses what he knows
to be evil or rejects what he knows to be good. We speak, therefore, not of
something that man has by nature, in virtue of his ontological or psychological
constitution, but of an object of choice and of achievement on the part of man
that can be expressed negatively as a third type of freedom: “freedom-from”.
If previously we spoke of freedom-from-external-coercion and freedom-from-
interior-necessity, now we shall speak of freedom-from-disordered-impulses; the
freedom from sin and from moral misery. It represents the ethical perfecting of
psychological freedom: its being consolidated in the good through moral virtue,
which is the goal sought by moral education. Christianity had a very impor-
tant influence in the formation of this third meaning of freedom, which it sees
as the collaboration between human (psychological) freedom and the grace of
God, with it not being, however, an exclusively theological concept.12
4.2.4
Freedom and Love
Philosophical reflection cautions that the consideration of freedom as “freedom-
from”, in the three indicated senses, is insufficient. All three cases treat of
negative notions that paradoxically need what they deny in order to affirm
themselves.
We saw freedom, in fact, as a negation of coercion, of neces-
sarily determined interior motivations of the choice, and as liberation from
12 Concerning this, V. Mathieu writes: “To be free, it is necessary and sufficient to will
it: but to say “no” to the will, one must not forget the intrinsic difficulty of such a volition,
which does not depend on a simple act of the will, but is, rather, the most difficult of
accomplishments.
The problem is in succeeding to be free; and to have put grace and
freedom in relation to one another was, for the knowledge of such a problem, a precious
acquisition; precisely because it has drawn attention to the problems regarding the will
[. . .] Even apart from any theological interest, a concept of “grace” is necessary to help one
understand in all its depth, even in plainly philosophical grounds, the problem of freedom.”
(V. Mathieu, voce Libertà (1957), col. 23), our translation.


The Freedom of the Sons of God
disordered passions and sin. But even if these three types of “freedom-from”
were guaranteed, human life would not yet reach its fullness. Freedom, de-
spite being a great good, does not satisfy the person's will, but is rather a
necessary condition for reaching such a good. Without freedom, no good is
a human good; but without good, freedom is empty. Freedom is the freedom
of a person that “conducts himself”: freedom of conduct. And the idea of
“conducting oneself” grants importance to the question regarding the jour-
ney's destination; to the “why” of freedom. “Freedom-from” opens the door
to “freedom-for” and, therefore, for the human good to be affirmed and the
evil to be denied.
The study of freedom leads into a consideration of love
which, in all of its forms, is always an affirmation of the good.
In Part I of the book we reflected sufficiently on the response that Christian
faith gives to the question concerning the ultimate good of man. Now we
can note that a philosophical consideration of freedom can show that it pre-
supposes the transcendence of the human will with regard to the goods that
surround it, a reason why the choice, though motivated, is not determined by
such conditions. Freedom seems animated by an aspiration toward absolute
good. Saint Thomas Aquinas refers to this with the technical concept of vol-
untas ut natura (natural inclination of the will). He designates the intentional
horizon of the voluntas ut natura with technical expressions that emphasize
its potentially infinite breadth.13
In its initial natural givenness this aspiration is formal, and implies a ratio
volendi and not properly a concrete act of the will. In every concrete person
such an aspiration is personally developed in different ways, often with a
development of a religious character; but in any case such a development is not
a stranger to something very similar to faith, which thus shows itself to be an
anthropological category of the first order. Moreover, in order to live we also
need hope, an expectation of the good which does not always find empirical
evidence, because people who lack these expectations become discouraged or
disheartened and lack courage and trust, which are both necessary for the
moral life. It is thus meaningfully said of such people that they have become
demoralized.

Chapter 4
4.3
Freedom in Christian Anthropology
4.3.1
Freedom as a Gift of God
in Light of Salvation History
Sacred Scriptures do not contain abstract philosophical reflections on the con-
cept of freedom, even if some considerations of the wisdom literature reach a
certain level of abstraction. Particularly in the New Testament, an existential,
or salvation-historical, perspective is prevalent, which sees freedom—shown to
be sinful—as redeemed by Christ and called to cooperate with grace in order
to freely become a good will and, eventually, a holy will. In the general bibli-
cal perspective, freedom of choice is simply presupposed by what is affirmed
about the behavior of individuals or the elect people, even if some explicit
statements are not lacking. To be noted, for example, is that of Deuteron-
omy: “Here, then, I have today set before you life and prosperity, death and
doom [ Choose life, then, that you and your descendants may live” 14; and
another passage that is a little more abstract from Sirach: “When God, in
the beginning, created man, he made him subject to his own free choice. If
you choose you can keep the commandments; it is loyalty to do his will. There
are set before you fire and water; to whichever you choose, stretch forth your
hand. Before man are life and death, whichever he chooses shall be given
him.”15
In the Old Testament, the episode of the Exodus occupies an important
place in the study of liberation: God saw the oppression of his people
and decided to free them from this situation of suffering and exploitation
in order to lead them to the Promised Land.16 One treats of a liberation
that has a socio-political aspect, although it cannot be interpreted in
either an individualistic sense nor in the sense of being the liberation of
a class, for it pertains to the whole people of God. On the other hand,
it is not for man to emancipate himself but to receive liberation from
God,17 although this does not exclude—but rather implies—human me-
diation.18 The socio-political liberation, however, does not exhaust the
meaning of the Exodus, and neither is it the principal meaning: the lib-
eration is directed toward the Covenant, it has a transcendental value
of relationship with the Lord, with its ritual, moral, and juridical pre-
scriptions. The deep meaning of the Exodus is moral-religious; it is not
so much a liberation aimed at avoiding human exploitation as it is to
show the glory of God, who of course demands the disappearance of all
kinds of oppression. This is seen more clearly when one considers that

The Freedom of the Sons of God
the Promised Land, more than a geographic area, designates the “peo-
ple of God” in which reigns justice, as is especially emphasized by the
prophets.19 It is to be further noted, that in the Septuagint, the term
eleuthería (freedom), used often in opposition to the idea of slavery, is
not used in the context of the Israel's liberation from Egypt, nor is it
used in the traditions relating to the return from exile.
It should be emphasized that freedom—both freedom of choice, and liberation
from oppression—is seen, nonetheless, as a gift of God, always connected to
the salvific action of Him who bestows it. The great value of human freedom
as a gift of God became a characteristic thesis of Christian anthropology.
“Authentic freedom” in man “is an exceptional sign of the divine image.” 20 It
marks the transcendence of man over the material world: “For by his interior
qualities he outstrips the whole sum of mere things.
He plunges into the
depths of reality whenever he enters into his own heart; God, Who probes
the heart, awaits him there; there he discerns his proper destiny beneath the
eyes of God”.21 It can be considered that on the human level, i.e. the natural
level, freedom is the greatest gift that God has granted to men.22The value of
freedom consists in the fact that only it renders possible the free affirmation
of good for its own sake, and therefore, the love of God inasmuch as it is the
supreme good; the act of free adhesion to the good that constitutes, on the part
of the creature, the imitation or participation in the beatifying goodness of
God. Without freedom, union with God through love would not be possible,
nor would man's eternal beatitude. “For God has willed that man remain
`under the control of his own decisions' (cf. Sir 15:14), so that he can seek
his Creator spontaneously, and come freely to utter and blissful perfection
through loyalty to Him. Hence man's dignity demands that he act according
to a knowing and free choice that is personally motivated and prompted from
within, neither under blind internal impulse nor by mere external pressure.” 23
This perspective demands a movement toward freedom as an ethical task and
that which we have called “freedom-for”, and in such a direction goes, in fact,
the Second Vatican Council: “Man achieves such dignity when, emancipating
himself from all captivity to passion, he pursues his goal in a spontaneous
choice of what is good, and procures for himself through effective and skillful
action, apt helps to that end. Since man's freedom has been damaged by sin,
only by the aid of God's grace can he bring such a relationship with God into

Chapter 4
full flower.”24 In a little while, we shall return to this point, but first we shall
propose another consideration.
The possibility of adhering freely to the good implies, and cannot but imply,
the possibility of not adhering to it. The possibility of love implies the possi-
bility of hate. In the face of the historical experience of evil, which sometimes
took on brutal and degrading forms, doubts may arise that human freedom is
worth the pain. It is a problem that has tormented the most acute philosoph-
ical and theological minds for ages. From the theological point of view we
can respond that, if faced with the two possibilities and there were something
to ponder, something to consider, then this was done by God once and for
all and His wise choice was a yes to man; even knowing that to sustain man
the blood of His Son would be shed. All of this means to say that Christian
anthropology, while holding firm the distinction between liberty and libertin-
ism, between freedom as a value and the corruption of freedom, must affirm
without any pusillanimity, with “divine” greatness of soul, the value of human
freedom: an affirmation on which it is not possible to waver.
4.3.2
“For Freedom Christ Set Us Free”
As was mentioned, the attention of the Sacred Scriptures, and particularly the
New Testament, was focused on the last two dimensions of freedom, namely,
freedom from sin and the freedom that expresses itself in love (“freedom-
for”)—as seen always from the standpoint of salvation history. A point of the
highest importance is treated here on account of its soteriological, anthropo-
logical, and moral implications.
The central idea is that all humanity can be free from sin only if, and in
the measure in which, it accepts the salvific action of God in Christ. This
is brought to light with particular force in the Letter to the Romans, Saint
Paul's most complete and articulate exposition of the Gospel. In this letter
the present reality, the events of the past, and those that we await in the
future are read in light of faith in Christ the Redeemer, whose work can
be understood in its depth only in reference to the power of sin, which had
reduced humanity to slavery—a sin that is the personified power (hamartía
is in the singular) so characteristic of this Pauline letter.25
