The Freedom of the Sons of God
is not an idea or a hypothesis, but rather, it exists in concrete sinful actions.
Likewise, the act of sinning is not an exclusively autonomous resolution of
a single individual, who now and then falls in a healthy world, but rather,
it always carries with it an assent that concretely makes that regime exist.
To sin means, in short, to manifest the reality of sin in committing a sinful
action.”41
Only the grace given to those that believe in Christ renders the complete victory
over sin possible.
The power of sin, which accompanies the choice of the
individual in order to manifest itself, draws its origins from the fundamental
rupture of the relationship of man with God. Such power is overcome only
when that relationship is renewed by the grace of Christ. Nevertheless, even
the believer finds in himself an opposition between his interior self and his
members; between an interior critical aspiration that distinguishes between
the good and evil and another law that resists it and would like to prevent
that aspiration from transforming his life for its good: “For I take delight in
the law of God, in my inner self, but I see in my members another principle at
war with the law of my mind, taking me captive to the law of sin that dwells
in my members. Miserable one that I am! Who will deliver me from this
mortal body? Thanks be to God through Jesus Christ our Lord. Therefore,
I myself, with my mind, serve the law of God but, with my flesh, the law of
sin.”42Freedom from sin is an ethical task for the believer, a battle against the
interior division which he experiences each day. But now, in Christ, victory
is possible: “For freedom, Christ set us free.”43
4.3.3
Freedom, Charity, and the Law of Christ
Faith in Christ opens the road to the fulfillment of Christian freedom in love,
to a freedom that does not raise up barriers before the needs of one's neigh-
bor, but understands itself, rather, as a gift of putting oneself in the service of
others. He that was freed by Christ is at the same time a servant of Christ,44
subservient to the law of Christ,45 that is, the law of freedom,46 and of love:
“For the whole law is fulfilled in one statement, namely, `You shall love your

and toward the love that comes from the Holy Spirit. Christian freedom man-
ifests itself as freedom from one's own egoism, as availability for the service
of God, justice, and neighbor.48 “For the love of Christ impels us [. . . ] so
that those who live might no longer live for themselves but for him who for
their sake died and was raised.”49 Love for the brothers and sisters, for whom
Christ died, can require even that in certain circumstances, in order to live in
the fullness of ethical freedom, one not exercise his own freedom of choice.50
Of notable interest for morality are the references in New Testament letters to
freedom as a “pretext” or as a “cloak for maliciousness”.51 Christian freedom
can never become “a pretext for living according to the flesh”; rather it en-
courages, through charity, one to serve God and others.52 Christian freedom
means walking according to the Spirit and it is therefore incompatible with
the “works of the flesh.”53 In fact, in walking according to the Spirit and,
therefore, distancing oneself from the “works of the flesh”, the person reaches
the fullness of his human and Christian freedom. Thus, the free development
of charity that was poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit,54 implies
a precise regulation of our relations with others (peace, benevolence, etc.), and
of our actions and of our sentiments (joy, patience, fidelity, meekness, self-
control); which is to say that grace gives rise to the consolidation of all the
moral virtues, informed by faith and charity.
Inasmuch as precise normative
demands also derive from this reality, one rightly speaks of a law: the “law
of faith”,55 the “law of Christ”,56 or the “law of the Spirit.”57 But inasmuch
as this law is not a norm that compels from the outside, but a supernatural
vital principle destined to develop itself with spontaneity and naturalness, one
can and must speak of a “law of freedom”58 or, simply speaking, of Christian
freedom.59
In any case, there does not remain any space for the dialectic

Ultimately, in addition to the moral dimension of Christian freedom (free-

dimension of the divine filiation of the Christian in Christ.
Furthermore, the Johannine perspective provides for the collaboration of man

obedience to the will of God. His crucified flesh fully reveals the unbreakable
bond between freedom and truth, just as his Resurrection from the dead is
the supreme exaltation of the fruitfulness and saving power of a freedom lived

Chapter 4
We can say in synthesis that Christian freedom presupposes freedom of choice
or psychological freedom, but adds a new element to it: a stable moral “per-
fecting”, or empowerment, of the capacity to choose with which the Christian
can regulate his actions and sentiments in such a way as to be able to accom-
plish day by day the following of—and union with—Christ. This stable moral
empowerment of the freedom of choice is ultimately established by grace and
by the theological virtues, and in itself consists of the Christian moral virtues.
Of the latter we have more yet to say, however, for the moment it is enough to
note that such virtues are not the simple result of human effort, and still less
are they expressions of an effort toward human self-affirmation, but rather
they are the fruit of the collaboration between human freedom and divine
grace given to those who believe in Christ.67 A true collaboration is dealt
with here, in which the two parts are equally necessary and equally insuffi-
cient. Grace cannot be directed but to a free creature, and human freedom,
after the fall of the first parents, is not alone able to be exercised to freely will
the good in all of its fullness, being itself stifled by evil inclinations and sin.
4.4
Transcendental Freedom
and the Fundamental Option
In the second half of the twentieth century, some theologians considered it
appropriate to distinguish a new and deeper level of freedom called transcen-
dental freedom, whose exercise has come to be called a fundamental option.
Not all conceived of the fundamental option in the same way, but in general
such a concept was intended to overcome the atomistic conception of human
acts, to deepen the relationship between the person and his singular acts, and
to reach a more adequate understanding of the nature of sin.
It is a matter of fact that some authors (therefore not all), developing such a
notion, formulated theses concerning freedom and sin which merited clear doc-
trinal reservations. For this reason, the encyclical Veritatis Splendor treated
of this theme,68 marking clearly the limits within which the concept of funda-
mental option is doctrinally acceptable.69 However, according to this encycli-
vigorously emphasized by the different points of view in this encyclical.
67 For a deepened understanding of the relation between freedom and grace, with spe-
cial reference to Pelagianism, see: E. Gilson, Introduzione allo studio di Sant'Agostino,
(Genova: Marietti, 1989), 182–191.
68 Cf. Veritatis Splendor 65–70.
69 In this doctrinally acceptable line, see, for example: A. Sarmiento, “Elección funda-
mental y comportamientos concretos”, Scripta Theologica 26, (1994), 179–197; G. Gatti,
Opzione fondamentale sì, ma, (Rome: LAS, 1994). A very interesting study of this notion,
centered around the thought of Dietrich von Hildebrand, is: J.M. Yanguas, La intención
fundamental, (Barcelona: Ediciones Internacionales Universitarias, 1994).


The Freedom of the Sons of God
cal, it must be accepted “that the so-called fundamental option, to the extent
that it is distinct from a generic intention and hence one not yet determined
in such a way that freedom is obligated, is always brought into play through
conscious and free decisions.
Precisely for this reason, it is revoked when
man engages his freedom in conscious decisions to the contrary, with regard
to morally grave matter. To separate the fundamental option from concrete
kinds of behaviour means to contradict the substantial integrity or personal
unity of the moral agent in his body and in his soul.” 70
While recognizing that the concept of fundamental option is doctrinally ac-
ceptable within the limits marked by the encyclical Veritatis Splendor, we,
nonetheless, do not adopt it because it is not consistent with our theological
approach. For an ethics of virtue, the concept of fundamental option is not
suitable for expressing the true modus operandi of the practical reason or of
human freedom, and is therefore unfounded and superfluous. Furthermore,
we believe that such a notion presupposes a certain philosophical background,
determined by the “transcendental” conception of freedom, present undoubt-
edly in authors who have given it a more profound and consistent formulation,
which renders it difficult and artificial to use within the limits marked by the
Church's Magisterium.71 In order to respect these limits, such a concept must
be revised, giving rise to a hybrid approach which in the end loses its internal
coherence.
We would like to clarify that our position regarding the theorem of the
fundamental option is not in response to the fact that it may have re-
ceived or could yet receive doctrinally questionable or even erroneous
formulations. We retain, rather, that the theorem of the fundamen-
tal option, considered in itself and its philosophical presuppositions, is
substantially unfounded; it does not correspond to the realities of the
conscience nor human moral action.
In our judgment, we have ade-
quately expressed previously the reasons for which they sustain this
theorem.72 Concerning the fundamental option, Angelini has written
recently: “Similarly and equally problematic seem to be the results from
those movements of recent moral theology which are inspired by the an-
thropology of Rahner. Despite repeated claims to the contrary, such a
theology does not appear capable of giving an account of the historical
mediation of the fundamental option. The so-called fundamental free-
dom of the person cannot be carried out other than through reference
to determinate historical experience; in its historical determination, a
particular action may disclose the unconditioned good (God) in varying
degrees. The person understands that he has a determinate duty, but

nonetheless, it does not immediately manifest itself adequately to him

moralists of the 'transcendental' approach tend to establish a disassocia-
tion between the transcendental instance of conduct and its “categorial”
instance; such a disassociation then impedes the person from giving a
rational account of the process spread out in time as freedom knows it.
Only through the distinction of time, in fact, is it possible that the per-
son may reach the meaningfulness of time, in which alone his absolute
self-determination may become possible—in fact, necessary.” 74
Nevertheless, Angelini adds that the pertinence and necessity of intro-
ducing into moral theory the concept of fundamental option cannot be
put into doubt, provided that by such a category is not intended “a
sort of arcane, transcendental super-choice, as being right alongside the
many so-called `categorial' choices.” 75 The category should instead be
understood as referring to a formal way of looking at human action:
“As a matter of fact, in every free act his ultimate destiny is in ques-
tion that can never be recognized as a destiny concluded in time.” 76
We are in full agreement that in every act the ultimate fate of man
is in question. But this was, and must still be, brought to light with-
out need of recourse to a distinction like that between a transcendental
level and another “categorial” level—a distinction which does not seem
founded, and carries with it the already alluded to problems.
It is
enough to think of the writings of Saint Thomas, who at the beginning
of his treatment of morality asks: “utrum homo omnia quae vult, velit
propter finem ultimum.”77 Ultimately, we have sought to present the
meaning of such a Thomistic thesis, recognizing also the more common
objections raised against it. As Angelini emphasized, the fundamental
option, rather than effectively showing the connection between the free
act and the good accomplished by man, actually finishes by disassoci-
ating them: rendering it very difficult to maintain a unitary conception
of man as a moral agent. What will be said in the next three chapters
should further clarify the position we have taken.

## CHAPTER 5 {#colom-scelti.5}
Tendencies, Sentiments,
and Passions
5.1
The Human Person as an Agent
with Desires and Passions
We shall begin the study of the makeup of free behavior. In this chapter and
in the successive chapter we shall move along from the base on upward along
the vertical axis which we described synthetically in the first section of the
last chapter.
First of all, the criterion according to which we situate the different experi-
ences of the soul along the vertical axis needs to be clarified. Moral experience
renders us aware of actions or movements that are initiated, planned, and ac-
tively monitored by our own I 1, or active personal center of consciousness; so,
for example, we concentrate our attention in order to resolve a mathematical
problem or a moral dilemma, we make the effort to remember where we placed
a book which we need, or we plan an outline of an article which we are going
to write. But experience also renders us aware of other experiences which are
neither initiated nor actively planned by our I. We refer, for example, to the
passions, sentiments, and states of the soul which proceed from a stratum of
our psyche that stands underneath the level determined by the free initiative
of the I, which Phillip Lersch calls the base affective stratum.2
1 Translator's note: The Italian word Io can be translated either I or ego. We decided
to use the word I to avoid some of the connotations attached to the word ego; though ego
will be used at times when it seems most appropriate.
2 Cf. Ph. Lersch, La estructura de la personalidad, 4th ed., (Barcelona: Scientia, 1966),
80–81. This is the Spanish translation of the eighth edition of the German text (Aufbau
der Person, Munich: J.A. Barth, 1962).
We do not know of any English translation of


Chapter 5
In pondering the meaning of this lower stratum of our psyche, it is helpful to
not forget that even it has a horizontal dimension, that is, through it man
communicates in some way with those who surround him (things, persons, and
even God). These phenomena express an exclusively human way of manifest-
ing the relational character proper to personal being. For each person “to be”
is “to be with,” his being is in reality “co-being,” or “co-existing,” in the most
profound metaphysical sense in which it can have being.3 We cannot imag-
ine the existence of a person alone in the Universe by himself (either human
or divine), without having the clear impression that such solitary existence
would be an absurdity and a metaphysical tragedy. “To be-with,” in the case
of the human person, is carried out in accordance with his essential makeup.
The phenomena of which we speak (tendencies, sentiments, passions) mean
in this perspective that “being-with,” in man, is also carried out as a coming
together with others and with one's environment, so as to suffer a reaction or
subjective modification caused by the presence or absence of persons or goods.
In the last analysis, the human experience of “being-with” is also exercised as
affectivity and as passion.4 Man, therefore, is not only an active, but also a
reactive subject and author of his actions.
In order to better understand this properly human mode of personal relation,
it is necessary to consider man's corporeity as well as the particularly human
synthesis of nature and freedom.
5.1.1
Body and Soul
The human person is a unified whole of body and spirit (body and soul), con-
ditions to which Christian anthropology attributes notable importance.5 The
human body is not independent from the spirit, and neither is the human

Spanish translation as the fondo endotímico.
This technical term shall be used several
times throughout this book, sometimes in shortened form as affective stratum.

L. Polo, Antropología trascendental.
Tomo I: La persona humana, (Pamplona:
Eunsa, 1999); F. Haya Segovia, El ser personal. De Tomás de Aquino a la metafísica del
don, (Pamplona: Eunsa, 1997).
4 In this line of thought, it can be of use to consult the interpretations of the passions

have been useful.
Cf. O. Flanagan and A. Rorty Oksenberg, eds., Identity, Character,
and Morality.
Essays in Moral Psychology, (Cambridge, MA-London: The MIT Press,
1990); J.J. Kupperman, Character, (New York-Oxford: Oxford University Press, 1991);
A. Manenti and C. Bresciani, eds., Psicologia e sviluppo morale della persona, (Bologna:
Dehoniane, 1992); L.A. Blum, Moral Perception and Particularity, (Cambridge: Cambridge
