Tendencies, Sentiments, and Passions
spirit independent from the body, while still giving it life. The dependence is
so strict that even the most spiritual human activity is in a certain way per-
meated by bodily conditions in an analogous way to how the body is governed
and given form by the spirit.
From the fact that the soul informs a body, it follows that man possesses the
functions proper to vegetative and sensible life, beyond that of rational life.
The principal functions of vegetative life are nutrition, growth, and repro-
duction. The sensitive life is characterized by its possessing, furthermore, a
perceptive system (external and internal senses) and an appetitive system,
through which the living being establishes a relationship with its own envi-
ronment that tends toward the satisfaction of its vital needs. Through sense
perception, the animal receives stimuli which proceed from the environment
to which are given an instantaneous appetitive response: that is to say, a re-
sponse that is automatic and not modifiable. Moreover, rational life, proper
to humans, is characterized by intellectual knowledge and by free will. This
enables humans to escape the necessity of the stimuli-response cycle, because
between the stimuli and the response there lies an intellectual judgment and
free decision of the will. These are the principles of human action: both in
instances of satisfying vegetative needs, which are no longer regulated solely
by instinct but generally remain subordinate to moral control, and in in-
stances proper to the rational life: understanding of the meaning of things,
interpersonal love, adhesion to ideals, the promotion of justice, technological
development, etc.
According to the three degrees of life—vegetative, sensitive, and rational—
a hierarchy and interconnection is established between the vital human
activities, and not simply a juxtaposition. We intend by interconnec-
tion the reciprocal dependence that exists between their functions, in
such a way that the alteration of one of them provokes alterations in
the others. Each degree of life presupposes the inferior degree, and is
benefited by the positive development of the degree superior to it. So,
on the one hand, the activities of the reason and the will presuppose
the execution of knowledge and the sensible appetite, and these oper-
ations imply, on their part, the integrity of their organic bases: of the
brain, etc. On the other hand, the ordered or disordered exercise of
freedom modifies, positively or negatively, the dispositions of the sensi-
ble appetites by means of the moral habits (virtues and vices), and can
even modify the vegetative functions (e.g. sicknesses that have a strong
psychosomatic component).
The interconnection of which we speak should not be interpreted simply
as causality. Causality takes place between different organisms, each of
which constitutes its own integrated whole. But the soul and the body
are not two diverse realities that interact with one another, so it is not
exactly correct to claim that the soul exercises causality over the body


Chapter 5
or vice versa. Rather, body and soul constitute a single reality—a uni-
fied whole—in humans, in which phenomena occur that are initiated
sometimes by dimensions more connected with corporeity and some-
times by dimensions which are proper to the spirit, but in the end both
pertain to and reflect characteristics of the whole person.
In humans it is difficult to isolate purely sensitive or purely rational func-
tions. From an analytical point of view, the difference between sensibility
and rationality is clear, but on the functional and practical level sensibility
and reason are exercised together. The phenomena of the human sensitive ap-
petites are in practice different to those found in animals, because in humans
they presuppose self-knowledge and the will. It is enough to think of the fact
that in the human sensitive appetites there are moral habits that modify their
intentionality.
Human corporeity and, in a functional sense, vegetative and sensitive life,
imply a structure and set of already given vital activities and needs, which
the active center of the person did not choose to possess. They are the realities
through which the human person lives and acts and from which frequently
proceed motivations, sentiments, and goals that each person elaborates and
carries out in his own way. We have here a primary and important source
of passivity, of emotions and passions, with it being well understood that
passivity cannot be identified with negativity, slowness, or absence of meaning.
Far from it, rather it means that the phenomena of which we speak do not
come about from the initiative of the person's active source: his I.
5.1.2
Nature and Freedom
Even on the level of the higher human operations, those of knowledge and
the will, not everything responds to the initiative or free choice of the person.
There is on this level a synthesis of nature and freedom, that is to say, of two
clearly diverse modes of action characterized, respectively, by a determination
ad unum and by self-determination.6 It is not that the concrete acts of the
person's will are sometimes chosen freely and other times determined choices
ad unum. Rather, this means that the human free will also has a determi-
nate nature, and in virtue of this nature—and therefore, necessarily before
and independently of any choices made by each particular person—the will
possesses a (natural) inclination toward its own formal object, the ratio boni
cultivated by the reason. This object possesses the same potentially infinite
breadth as the reason and manifests itself as an aspiration toward happiness.
We already know that Saint Thomas refers to such an inclination with the ex-
pression “voluntas ut natura.”7 This natural inclination toward the intelligible
6 Cf. S. Th. I-II, q. 10, a. 1, ad 1.
7 Cf. Chapter IV, subsection 4.2.4.


Tendencies, Sentiments, and Passions
good constitutes the basic intentional horizon of the human will and is the
foundation of its capacity to move itself. It stands at the base of all concrete
acts of the human will, which always remain free (“voluntas ut ratio”). Noth-
ing can be the object of a free choice if it is not because the reason discovers
in it the motivation of a good, whether it be real or only apparent.
The reason also possesses its own natural dimension, which Saint Thomas calls
“ratio naturalis,”8 that has as self-evident principles, of both a speculative and
practical character, the so-called first principles. We shall occupy ourselves
with these when we study the natural moral law. At the moment, it interests
us to note that both the composition of body and soul, and the synthesis of
nature and freedom, make it so that human freedom is not a pure initiative
without roots.
Man possesses inclinations and needs linked to corporeity,
sensibility, and even rationality, which can be satisfied only by free behavior.
In the moral life, the person must confront and take a position with regard to
issues and needs that he did not choose to have—one may think, for example,
of the desire for fulfillment or happiness, the need for nourishment, or of the
sex drive—and the same goes for the moral life of the Christian, who must
identify a mode of drawing up and accomplishing such goals that is proper to
a child of God in Christ.
The distinction between nature and freedom, valid as a distinction be-
tween two modes of action in the sense just explained, cannot be under-
stood, conversely, as a distinction between persons on the ontological
plane. In a human there are not, in fact, two beings: one natural and
one personal. The human person is not a sum of nature and reason,
but an individual of a rational nature. On the entitative level, the term
nature does not come understood in a physical or cosmological sense,
as a mode of being opposed to spiritual and free being; it is taken, in-
stead, in its rigorously metaphysical usage, as the proper character or
peculiar mode of being of an entity, seen as a principle of its specific
dynamic. Nature in the metaphysical sense is not per se a principle of
uniform operations (as is the nature with which physics is occupied),
but a uniform principle of operations, which may very well be free, as is
the case with humans. For this reason, the spirit is a nature in no less a
degree than an irrational living being. The fact that it is proper to the
spirit to be open to the universal does not invalidate the metaphysical
concept of a spiritual nature.
From what we have said, it follows that the distinction between nature
and person proposed by some authors9 does not seem realistic, and
among these authors this notion is strictly linked to the concept of a
fundamental option. In this perspective, nature would be all that which
8 Cf. for example De Veritate, q. 11, a. 1.
9 Cf. K. Rahner, Zum theologischen Begriff der Konkupiszenz, in Idem., Schriften
zur Theologie, vol. I, (Einsiedeln: Benziger, 1962), 377–414; F. Böckle, I concetti
fondamentali della morale, 8th ed., (Brescia: Queriniana, 1981), 45–47.


Chapter 5
is given to the human being at a level which is physical, psychological,
spiritual, etc., while freedom—or the person—would be considered as
the pure capacity for self-determination along with the consequences of
its exercise. To nature would pertain all of the inclinations and spon-
taneous dispositions, while to the person would pertain the actions and
dispositions caused entirely by the I . Such a contraposition between
nature and person which would forcefully divide man, introduces an
ambiguity in the determination of moral responsibility (one would not
know in what degree that observed conduct could be imputed to the
person, for it is mediated by “nature”), and renders particularly diffi-
cult a unitary articulation—within ethics, pedagogy, etc.—between the
elements offered by philosophy with those given by medicine, experi-
mental psychology, etc. (“Natural Science”); for between the two types
of knowledge there tends to be produced the same lack of integration
that there would be between the two parts of the human being: the
object of these sciences.
It is true that the integration between different human dynamics can
sometimes constitute a very difficult ethical-practical problem which
must be solved by the moral virtues. But as we shall see immediately,
to conceive of the tendencies and sentiments substantially as resistances,
and not as basic motivations of freedom, seems rather reductive. In any
case, on the ontological level the necessity to integrate diverse psycho-
logical and characterological elements in free action, with what this
implies in terms of tensions and the search for balance, pertains to the
essence of human freedom, and responds in the end to the metaphysi-
cal conditions of each finite spirit: the act is different from the agent,
and derives from it; the agent is not pure act. Therefore, it is neces-
sary to presuppose in the agent something not set there by himself, for
its placement would be an act and an act cannot set its own intrinsic
conditions, i.e.
those which are determining from within the typical
structure of the act. The act of a finite spirit presupposes a spiritual
nature. And in this sense, the spirit also has a natural dimension, so
that one treats of a nature which is open to being in all its universality
(anima quodammodo omnia). In the case of the human person, the nat-
ural condition is a corporal and spiritual whole; for the human spirit,
beyond being finite, is essentially the form of the body.10 The contra-
position between nature and person, of which we are referring, depends
on an initial presupposition: that of interpreting the intentional open-
ness of the human spirit as a sort of entitative quasi-infinitude (spirit
as complete self-transparency and self-possession) which, in fact, would
be limited by a foreign element, denominated as nature. This would
all be as if the finitude were an extrinsic condition of the human spirit
derived from its union with the body (the body would be, then, the
prison of the soul).
10 Cf. regarding this argument J. De Finance, Etica generale, (Cassano Murge
(Bari): Tipografica Meridionale, 1984), 459–478.


Tendencies, Sentiments, and Passions
5.2
Human Desire
Desire is the form in which the vital needs of humans are manifested in their
interaction with the world. To each need corresponds an impulse, and vice
versa. The animal impulses correspond substantially to vital needs (nutrition,
reproduction, and defense). The human tendencies, on the other hand, have
a broader subject matter (sociality, the need to love and be loved, the desire
to know, religiosity, etc.), which is further expanded in the Christian.
In
both cases it is true that the inclinations or tendencies constitute a principle
of selection of meaningful objects and, for the human person, a principle of
configuration for his own world. The world of each of us is also the result of our
own interests, even if one must add that man, in virtue of having more elevated
processes of thought and of the will, can reach a high level of objectivity in
the comprehension of himself and his world (even if, in practice, he does
not always reach it).
This cognitive dimension of desire is also extremely
important for the perception of the good which, in lived moral experience, is
not only the object of abstract reasoning but presupposes personal conditions
and, in particular, an adequate affective balance. The “cognitive” dimension
of desire is the anthropological foundation of the cognitive function of moral
virtues.
We take on the study of human desire from two diverse, but complementary,
perspectives. We shall occupy ourselves in the first place with the Thomistic
conception of natural inclinations, which bring to light the ontological foun-
dation of human desire. In the two successive subsections we shall assume the
standpoint of psychology, in order to then proceed to tracing a “map” of the
human tendential 11 system.12
5.2.1
The Ontological Dimension of Human Desire:
The Natural Inclinations
The Thomistic conception of the natural inclinations13 is a metaphysical con-
cept, and not a psychological one, and it emphasizes the ontological founda-
tion of the human tendencies. Starting from his metaphysical, creationistic
conception, Saint Thomas considers that every created nature is ordained
or directed toward its own perfection, and such a metaphysical teleology is
generically called natural appetite. We are not treating yet of a conscious in-
clination or desire, but of an ordering of every being toward its comprehensive
11 Translator's Note: We use “tendential” as a proper technical term for translating “ten-
denziale” as an adjective which denotes something pertaining to the tendencies.
12 We are borrowing, with broad modifications, what was written by A. Rodríguez Luño,
Ética General (2001), Chapter V.
13 Cf. S. Th. I-II, q. 94, a. 2. A previous study of the natural inclinations had already
been accomplished in the Scriptum Super Sententiis, lib. IV, d. 33, q. 1, a. 1.


Chapter 5
end (a metaphysical teleology), prior to any act or option of the individual.
The natural inclination or appetite manifests itself on the level of the psyche
in a way adequate to the nature of each being. In animals it is manifested as
instinct, in man as a conscious tendency that comes about as a sensible desire
and an aspiration of the will.
Saint Thomas occupies himself with the natural inclinations primarily when he
treats of the natural law.14 In such a context, he underlines that the practical
reason “naturally” accepts as human goods all of those goals toward which man
is naturally inclined (the term of the natural inclinations). Therefore, it can
be affirmed that the precepts of the natural law are related to the objects
of the natural inclinations and constitute their basic moral regulation. The
natural inclinations play a primary role in the constitution of the fundamental
practical principles.
He distinguishes three main groups of natural inclinations:
1. The inclinations that humans have in common with all living beings:
inclinations toward the conservation of being, self-defense, nutrition,
etc.
2. Those which they have in common with animals: reproduction and the
care of offspring, which in humans are extended to marriage, etc.
3. Those that are proper to man inasmuch as he is a rational being: so-
ciality, friendship, knowledge, love, metaphysical transcendence, etc.15
This step in our study, as has been said, is only intended in order to put in
evidence the relationship between the natural inclinations and the precepts of
the natural moral law. It proceeds rather schematically, and certainly does
not have the pretense of providing a complete picture of human goods. For
the moral virtues contain the criteria according to which each of the human
goods are sought and achieved, and only a detailed study of the particular
moral virtues permits one to have a more complete idea of Saint Thomas's
vision of fundamental human goods.16
5.2.2
The Phenomenology of Human Desire:
The Tendencies
The concept of a tendency is used by empirical psychology to describe the
dynamic which provides the basic motivations for human conduct. As per-
taining to empirical psychology, the concept of tendency places itself at a level
14 Cf. S. Th. I-II, q. 94, a. 2.
15 Cf.
ibid.
Still useful is the study of D. Composta, Natura e ragione.
Saggio sulle
inclinazioni naturali in rapporto al diritto naturale, (Zürich: Pas-Verlag, 1971).
16 Cf. S. Th. II-II, qq. 47–170.


Tendencies, Sentiments, and Passions
of conceptualization diverse from that which is proper to metaphysics; and
therefore, a tendency is not exactly the same thing as a Thomistic natural
inclination. Nonetheless, they are complementary concepts, and it could be
affirmed that the tendencies are the dynamic manifestations of the natural
inclinations of humans on the level of experienced psychology.
The characteristics of the tendencies are as follows:
1. The tendencies are a psychological reflection of the vital law of communi-
cation between humans and the world. In the tendencies, our needs (the
natural inclinations) are manifested as psychological necessities (hunger,
desire to be esteemed, need to perform work, etc.) which must be sat-
isfied through adequate behavior.
2. The tendencies are experienced as a movement which goes from a per-
sonal state of need toward a future state of satisfaction, which comes
perceived in a still obscure and confused way and, in this sense, the
tendency is something which anticipates and suggests.
3. Every tendency is aimed toward a goal. If the tendency opens itself up
to the world as a “search for something,” the goal is that “something”
that comes to be sought. The sought goal is seen as a value, as a good
in the broadest sense of the term, because it responds to our need.
4. The tendency presents itself as something that is given to us. It does
not respond to an initiative of the individual; just as our need for food
or to live in society do not respond to one of our personal choices. In
this sense, it has a passive character.17
It is not difficult to understand that the tendencies, taken as a whole, tend
toward the development and complete fulfillment of humans, and to have a
“map” of the human tendencies would be the same thing as having a com-
plete picture of human goods. Nevertheless, among psychologists there exist
various conceptions concerning the concrete goods which integrate human de-
velopment and perfection. Therefore, psychologists propose different numbers
and classifications of human tendencies.
Some authors sustain a monothematic conception of the tendencies,
because they trace the entire teleological dynamic of the human psyche
to a single fundamental motive, which would be, in the last analysis,
the explanation and common denominator of all the phenomena of the
tendential sphere. An example would be Freud, for whom the libido
(sex drive) is the basic theme of the psyche's dynamic. One could also
17 Regarding this characteristic of the tendencies, cf.
P. Lersch, La estructura de la
personalidad (1966), 99–100.


Chapter 5
mention Epicurus, Hobbes, Bentham, La Rochefoucauld, and Adler as
having monothematic visions of human desire.
Others—e.g.
MacDougall, Pfänder and Klages— support a polythe-
matic classification, in which diverse tendencies or groups of tendencies,
not reducible to each other, come to be specified.
A third group of authors, among whom stands Gehlen, propose an
athematic conception, which, while recognizing the possibility of spec-
ifying a diversity of tendencies on the experiential level, consider them
as transitory adaptations for the diversity of situations we experience.
It would not be possible to trace a classification, according to these
authors, because there does not exist any fixed tendential system in
humans.
The classification of the human tendencies certainly constitutes a difficult
problem for which perhaps there will never be found a solution which satisfies
everyone. It is rather difficult to successfully express the richness of human
life in a closed and definitive classification, and perhaps neither would it be
helpful to try. Regardless, for morality it is important to be able to have at our
disposal a descriptive foundation which, while being open and not definitive,
is not reductive, that is, which does not exclude a priori essential dimensions
of life and of human development: for the image itself of man as a moral
agent is at stake. We shall adopt the polythematic classification proposed by
Lersch,18 which we consider open to further improvements, but which, in any
case, seems to us to be sufficiently complete and balanced.
5.2.3
Classification of the Tendencies
Lersch distinguishes between three groups of tendencies: a) vital tendencies,
which are the tendency toward activity, the tendency toward enjoyment, the
sexual tendency and the experiential tendency to relive one's own emotive
experiences; b) the tendencies of the individual ego, which comprise the ten-
dency toward individual conservation, the tendency toward possession, the
desire for power, the need to be esteemed by others, the desire for revenge,
and the desire for self-esteem; c) the transitive tendencies, which are the ten-
dency to be with others (sociality), the tendency to be for others, the creative
tendency (creativity), the desire to know, the amatory tendency (tendency for
romantic love), the normative tendency, and the transcendent tendencies.
Before briefly discussing the content of each of the tendencies, it needs to be
recognized that the classification we present was elaborated by a phenomeno-
logical, descriptive perspective. It intends to describe human experiences as
they present themselves in attentive observation, and not to establish whether
they ought to be that way, or how they ought to be, morally speaking. It is
18 Cf. ibid., 99–183.


Tendencies, Sentiments, and Passions
the task of morality to specify the criteria for distinguishing between impulses
and sentiments which are ordered from those which are disordered.
Vital Tendencies — The tendency toward activity seeks activity and move-
ment for its functional value. The organism has need of movement and it is
through activity that life develops. No one manages to remain completely im-
mobile for very long. The need for activity is very particular in children, and
tends to diminish with the passing of years. There are, nonetheless, notable
individual differences: from those who are hyperactive or restless to those who
are sedentary or passive, the latter being those for whom any movement is a
cause of anxiety and interior suffering.
The more elementary form of the tendency toward enjoyment is the impulse
toward pleasure, already present from early childhood. Throughout the devel-
opment of individual life, the content of this tendency suffers many changes,
entering into relation with the content of other tendencies (alongside the plea-
sure of eating and drinking, the enjoyment linked to higher functions appears:
from intellectual knowledge to humor, from affirmation to the pleasure of see-
ing one's orders followed).
This tendency acquires a particular accent in
hedonistic behavior, for which enjoyment is constituted as the final end of
existence. The hedonist refuses all restraint or responsibility, avoids effort, is
not demanding on himself, and in the end has a sense of interior emptiness
(it might make one think of the character of Dorian Gray created by Oscar
Wilde).
The sexual tendency is a basic form of the vital tendencies. It tends toward
union with the other sex, and is distinguished from the simple tendency to-
ward enjoyment for its objective reference to the transmission of life and,
therefore, to human conservation. Its genetic relationship with the preced-
ing tendencies renders possible that an individual may transfer its dynamic
from an ambit of procreation to that of sexual pleasure alone, and then the
search for voluptuousness is rendered autonomous, something that has nega-
tive consequences for the personal possibility of developing certain transitive
tendencies in a mature way.
The aim of the experiential tendency is to make oneself aware of his own
vitality, interiorly living and reliving the phenomena which arise from his
own base affective stratum (fondo endotímico), whatever they might be. This
tendency manifests itself especially in puberty, in concordance with sexual
maturation. It admits of great variability between individuals, and in certain
cases can manifest itself as a search for always more exciting experiences.
The Tendencies of the Individual Ego — The tendency toward individ-
ual conservation is, in its most basic evolutionary form, the instinct for the
conservation of the biological-corporal existence of the individual that tends
toward nourishment, defense, and flight from danger. But normally it goes


Chapter 5
beyond this, leading man to elaborate and produce tools, resources, and all
the useful things for life which we consider part of human culture in general.
The possessive tendency is in relation with this last tendency, but is only
carried out properly in response to competition with other persons, and not
dangers which come about from nature or natural disasters. Furthermore,
while the instinct of conservation contents itself with maintaining life, the
possessive tendency tends toward living better (even better than others), and
gives rise to phenomena of hoarding goods which are not strictly necessary.
It can be called, in a broad sense, egoism, and acquires various forms from
what may be considered a “healthy egoism” to egomania. An egomaniac is
cold and indifferent in confrontation with others, easily envious, aggressive,
and inconsiderate, or—if the person feels weak—excessively worried for his
security. This tends to inhibit the transitive tendency.
The desire for power tends towards the taking control of one's own environ-
ment, including other persons. It has a genetic relation with the two preceding
tendencies, inasmuch as taking control of an environment is a sure means for
securing one's own conservation and security, but it acquires its own auton-
omy in the form of a confirmation of one's own superiority, which goes well
beyond the needs of conservation.
The need to be esteemed by others is manifested when the person seeks recog-
nition and to be appreciated by others. It does not pertain to any conservation
or affirmation of biological-corporal life, but to one's sense of his own value
inasmuch as that value is recognized in the judgments of others. Primarily
in the period of infancy, but in some measure always, the esteem of others is
necessary for the normal constitution of one's personality. The normal and
moderate need to be esteemed gives rise to the prudent, simple, and modest
person. An exaggerated and disordered manifestation of this is the anxiety of
notoriety: this is found in persons who seek, above all, to strengthen their ego
through appearances. They will do anything (even faking sickness) to draw
the attention and appreciation of others. They are often inflexible, obstinate,
and emotionally sensitive persons with whom it is difficult to collaborate.
Moreover, they can easily become isolated.
The vindictive desire draws a person to want to compensate for the damage
done to his own aspirations (legitimate or illegitimate) causing harm to the
person who is responsible. It follows the common conviction that “whoever
erred must pay” or the law of “an eye for an eye, a tooth for a tooth.” It
admits of a diversity of forms and can manifest itself also as resentment. If it
is well integrated and ordered, it is perfectly compatible with forgiveness and
generosity.
The desire for self-esteem pertains to the sense of one's own value as a person,
necessary for the normal constitution of the personality and for relations with


Tendencies, Sentiments, and Passions
others. With the arrival of puberty, it manifests itself as a desire for autonomy,
independence, and freedom. The exaggerated and disordered sense of one's
own value expresses itself in negative (pride) and sometimes comical or even
ridiculous forms. The complete absence of self-esteem is characteristic of some
criminological typologies.
The Transitive Tendencies — The tendency to be with others, or toward
sociality, responds to the need to live in society, to communicate, and to share.
It is not simply a gregarious instinct: the existence of language makes it so
that human life in common is something completely different. It presupposes
individuality, and transcends it without negating it.
Furthermore, at the
level of personal character there exist differences between individuals, along
a continuum going from introversion to extroversion.
The tendency to be for others means the awareness of a true responsibility
toward others: true devotion.
In the context of closer and more intimate
communities, like the family, the different aspects of this tendency develop,
which involve a profound sense of belonging and participation.
The tendency toward creativity, in its diverse expressions, is the impulse to
leave a mark on the world and in society with the fruit of one's own work,
whether that follows the paths of good performance or creative configuration.
In any case, what is intended is to make a worthwhile contribution for others
and society: to produce an increase in value.
The desire to know is the tendency to expand one's own vital horizon through
knowledge. It is not simply the desire to know understood as a power or source
of power, which would be put in relation with the tendency of the individual
ego, but rather a search for meaning. From the evolutionary point of view,
the aspiration for knowledge is first ordained to individual and social survival,
to the conservation and affirmation of the ego on the vital, professional, eco-
nomic, and social plane: as instrumental reason. Extended further, the desire
to know is manifest in all its purity and depth as the autonomous search for
meaning.
The tendency to love and be loved expresses the most radical interest of man.
In part, its subject-matter crosses paths with that of the tendency to be for
others. It comprises the diverse forms of friendship, benevolence, and love; as
well as their opposites: enmity, malice, and hatred. For the morality of the
person, this tendency is of capital importance.
The normative tendencies draw one towards abstract values: truth, justice,
solidarity, etc., and express the human capacity and need to work for the
affirmation of such values, seen as having foundations beyond that of the
individual. If it is rightly interpreted, there is no doubt that this tendency
represents a true self-transcendence of the person.
The transcendent tendencies seek “in the world a sphere of being that over-


Chapter 5
comes the relativity and transience of the individual ego [. . . ] What is sought
and investigated is always an absolute.”19 They include the artistic impulse,
metaphysical aspiration, and religious seeking. If the phenomenological anal-
ysis is limited to noting the existence of these tendencies and the forms which
they assume in a determinate cultural or historical context, theological re-
flection inquires about their foundation. Such reflection discovers in the ten-
dencies the fingerprints left in the human being of the One who created him
through, and in view of, Jesus Christ.20
The process of specification brings to light these tendencies which draw hu-
mans to transcend themselves, and these tendencies possess a particular im-
portance in the moral life. They tend toward participation in the world, but
not in the sense of a desire for possession, but rather emphasizing the individ-
ual's dependence on and dedication to persons and values. The person feels
himself attracted to something which lies beyond his own ego. In particular,
the existence of a tendency to be with others and for others illuminates the an-
thropological foundation of justice and solidarity and, in more general terms,
social and political ethics: they presuppose, in fact, the radical recognition of
the other as one's equal. That is, man is able to recognize others as equals,
and therefore, to promote their good as such, and not only because this has
positive repercussions for his own good. This capacity for self-transcendence
permits us to escape the annoying tendency to want to found social ethics
exclusively on self-interest.
The autonomy of the transitive tendencies in relation to the tendencies of the
individual ego manifests the importance in itself of the exercise of the reason
which tends toward grasping the meaning of life and the world, and toward
seeking after the absolute. This exercise of the reason, which we could con-
sider as pertaining to wisdom, cannot be reduced to, or be substituted with,
instrumental reason, that is to say, to the exercise of the reason, necessary
as it is, oriented toward the control and utilization of nature with the goal
of guaranteeing security and the expansion of the ego (desire to possess, for
security, for self-affirmation, etc.). For the desire to know the truth does not
represent, from the anthropological point of view, something less important
and necessary than the goods connected with biological sustenance.
The coordination and integration of the diverse tendencies is not something
that is already given, nor is it something that cannot be modified. It is condi-
tioned by individual characterological differences, and also by the conceptions
of life which are affirmed in each culture.
Every individual temperament
and every culture represents a different point of departure, at least partially
unique, for reaching the balance and integration required for successful living.
19 Ibid., 170.
20 Cf. Col 1:16; Eph 1:3–7.


Tendencies, Sentiments, and Passions
The regulation and education of the tendencies is the work of virtue ethics.
Furthermore, the Christian moral virtues, in light of the theological virtues,
introduce new subject-matter and specific criteria for the regulation of these
tendencies.
5.2.4
The Tendencies and the Will
Now we shall put forward the question of how the will ought to be conceived in
relation to the tendencies, moving always on the level of a phenomenological
description of the phenomena of the soul. Is the will an impulse of the base
affective stratum, even if specific to man, or is it autonomous with regard to
the tendencies we have just studied? As it was said at the beginning of this
chapter, phenomenologically the will does not appear at first glance to be
another tendency, but rather as a superior command center that has the task
of regulating “the traffic” of the tendencies, determining which impulse must be
carried out and how it must be carried out, and overcoming the resistances that
it encounters. Nonetheless, some authors—for instance, Wundt—retain that
the will is none other than a particular emotion, pertaining rather to the base
affective stratum. Such an identification, however, does not seem acceptable.21
The tendencies and the other phenomena of the base affective stratum have a
point in common: they both come about out of a psychological stratum which
is not directly controllable by the consciousness of the I, and tend per se to
push the I toward a determined goal, anticipating and suggesting a form of
behavior. They have a pathic22 (from the Greek pâschein, to suffer) character.
On the other hand, in willing, man senses in himself an active center which is
conscious and unitary and not determined necessarily by any impulse, because
it is he himself who actively decides to plan and direct. In volition, the I
experiences itself as an active command center that decides what to do and
how to do it. Raising itself over the pathic phenomena as an island on the
sea, the experience of self-control and determination23 is distinguished from
the flux of base affective phenomena as stable land to the water in motion.
It is true that many of the types of objects of the will, considered “materially,”
proceed from the tendencies. Nonetheless, the distinction subsists, because
the will appears as the personal decision-maker concerning that which the
tendencies suggest. The person accepts or rejects, favors, elaborates, modifies,
or suppresses. And then, the will is concerned with the accomplishment of
the chosen goal, revealing itself as a force capable of again taking positions in
response to internal or external resistances, and also of overcoming them.
21 Cf. Ph. Lersch, La estructura de la personalidad (1966), 435–437.
22 Translator's Note: We have opted to follow closely the use of this technical term which
is, in fact, not a common Italian word and reads as “pathico.”
23 Cf. Chapter IV, subsection 4.2.2.


Chapter 5
The autonomy of the will is certainly based on a specific dynamic, an aspi-
ration which follows the reason, and therefore is not of the character of the
phenomena of the base affective stratum; this dynamic is the “desire”24 for
the good which we previously called the voluntas ut natura: the constitutive
inclination of the will as a desire for the good grasped as such by the reason.
Therefore, the will is also desire, and desire which has a specific type of object,
at least from the formal point of view, inasmuch as even the types of objects
which proceed from the particular tendencies are now seen and evaluated in
their relation to the comprehensive good of the person.
Nonetheless, the human will is not only desire. The human will is exercised
also in a sense that is different from “receiving” or “tending,” and for this we
must come to a concept of the will which is not reduced to desire, to a “hy-
perteleological concept of the will,” which is very characteristic of Christian
anthropology.25 For Greek thought, the will is a faculty which is fundamen-
tally one that tends and desires; only knowledge came to be considered as an
immanent operation which possesses its own end (the Aristotelian theory of
friendship would perhaps oblige us to clarify further, but not to substantially
change this last affirmation).
Regarding this, “Thomas Aquinas says that
more or less all of the philosophers intuited that God is Logos, but that God
is love no one conjectured. It is clear that if the will is only a tendency and
desire, it is not possible to put it in God (a god that desires is a mythical
notion or aberrant gnostic illusion), for from this it would follow that God is
imperfect, and an imperfect god is a contradiction. Only Christianity knows
that God is Love.”26 Love which consists in the giving of oneself represents a
specific exercise of the human will. In the giving of self the elements proceeding
from the tendencies can be reunited and purified to an axiologically superior
level, particularly those which come about from the ambit of the transitive
tendencies.
5.3
Human Affectivity:
Sentiments and Passions
If the tendencies are like an impulse that leaves the person and are projected
on the world, orienting a person's pursuits and perception, the emotions and
sentiments are the interior resonance of the tendencies which come after per-
24 With regard to the will, we speak of desire in the sense of being deliberated desire, and
not as a desire previous to choice, as we understand it with regard to the tendencies.
25 Cf. L. Polo, “Tener y dar. Reflexiones en torno a la Segunda Parte de la Encícilica
`Laborem Exercens',” in Various Authors., Estudios sobre la Encíclica “Laborem Exercens,”
(Madrid: BAC, 1987), 223–227.
26 Ibid., 224.


Tendencies, Sentiments, and Passions
ception. In the sentiments there is captured and evaluated the response com-
ing from the world to the question contained in the tendencies.
The sentiments have a passive character (they do not respond to the initia-
tive of the I ), and for this reason they are called passions in philosophy. The
sentiments are not a taken deliberated stance, even if they tend and suggest a
position and free behavior to take. In themselves they are organic, psycholog-
ical, and spiritual reactions caused by the perception of the good (happiness,
enthusiasm) or of evil (fear, sadness, worry) in relation to the tendencies. So,
for example, given the fact that we have a need to be esteemed by others (and
we did not choose to have this need), in response to the praise of an employer
there spontaneously follows a feeling of satisfaction; to a reproach, a feeling
of sadness or depression.
5.3.1
Phenomenology of the Sentiments
The sentiments or emotions are strictly connected with and dependent on the
tendencies, and therefore it is fitting for them to have the same classification
as the tendencies. There are sentiments linked to the vital tendencies, such
as: pleasure or pain, boredom, repugnance, frivolity, annoyance, panic;—as
well as there being sentiments linked to the tendencies of the individual ego:
fear, agitation, trust or distrust, jealousy, contentedness or discontentedness,
a feeling of inferiority, vengefulness, shame, sense of defeat, remorse, self-
disdain. And, finally, there are sentiments linked to the transitive tendencies:
sympathy and antipathy, love and hate, respect and disrespect, esteem and
contempt, compassion, open-handedness, artistic sentiment, religious senti-
ment, etc. In order to elaborate a complete phenomenology of the sentiments,
we would have to return to look at the different types of objects of each of
the tendencies, identifying the particular sentiments associated with each of
them. However, in order to avoid repetition we shall skip this step.
Psychology distinguishes sentiments from states of the soul. The first are emo-
tions of brief duration and are punctual, while the second are more persistent.
Nonetheless, an exact distinction cannot always be made, because there exist
border phenomena. To understand the origin and dynamic of the persistent
states of the soul is a rather complex question. Here we shall limit ourselves
to note that persistent states of the soul can play an important role in the
way a person lives. Consider, for example, persons who have a state of soul
which is prevalently joyful or, in contrast, melancholic or almost depressed;
or those who have a marked hyperesthesia of sentiment concerning their own
power or value; or those who are conditioned by a persistent sense of inferior-


Chapter 5
ity. Also well-known are the states of the soul marked by anxiety, pessimism,
or a nihilistic sense of the world.27
5.3.2
The Passions
Now we shall discuss the appetites and the passions, and thus move back to
terminology which is more familiar to moral theology. In living beings that
possess knowledge, the natural inclinations manifest themselves as elicited
appetites (for psychology, as tendencies), which act in dependence on an ob-
ject which is intentionally grasped by the senses (sensible appetites) or by the
reason (the will).
Saint Thomas gives the name passion to the acts of the sensible appetites.
The Thomistic concept of passion does not have the negative connotation
which it was later given. All of the acts of the sensible appetites are passions
(joy, desire, the flight response, etc.), whether they are positive or negative
acts, violent or non-violent, caused by the will, accepted by the will, or com-
pletely involuntary. Passion is not, then, in itself a violent impulse toward a
morally evil action which renders the rational governance of behavior difficult,
but is rather a normal component of human life, which often constitutes the
motivational basis of a person's conduct.
Moreover, the term “passion” implies the idea of passivity, of something the
person suffers or that happens in him and for which he has not taken an
initiative (even if this is not always the case). Saint Thomas dedicates much
space to the study of the passions.28
This is due to the fact that he sees
in them movements toward concrete objects here and now suitable to the
sensibilities of the acting person, and which for this reason are seen as goods.
Their integration into, or “dis-integration” from, the comprehensive good of
the person is of capital importance for morality.
The different passions are distinguished according to three criteria:
1. Their generic distinction is based on the distinction between the two
appetive faculties in human sensibility: the concupiscible appetite or
the pleasure impulse, which has as its object the good which is pleasing
to the senses, and the irascible appetite or the aggressive impulse, which
has as its object the pleasing good which is difficult to reach or the evil
which is difficult to evade, and which therefore requires effort and battle.
According to this criterion, the passions of the concupiscible appetite
are always different from those of the irascible appetite.
2. The differences between the objects of the passions inasmuch as they
27 On the persistent states of the soul, see Ph. Lersch, La estructura de la personalidad
(1966), 267–309.
28 Cf. S.Th. I-II, qq. 22–48.


Tendencies, Sentiments, and Passions
are good or evil, and according to the presence or absence of good or
evil. The passions which tend toward a pleasing good which is absent
(desire) are different from those which tend toward a pleasing good
which is present (joy) and of those which tend toward an evil which is
present or absent (sadness, flight-response).
3. Only for the passions of the irascible appetite is there a third criterion of
distinction, which consists in the different type of movement one makes
with respect to the same object: to draw closer to a difficult, yet pos-
sible to achieve, good (hope) or to distance oneself from the same good
inasmuch as it is thought that it cannot be achieved (discouragement).
Having stated these three criteria, Saint Thomas distinguishes between the
following passions:
1. In the concupiscible appetite: a) prescinding from the presence or ab-
sence of the object, love toward the good or hatred toward the evil;
b) toward an absent object: desire for a good or avoidance of evil; c)
regarding a present object: joy for the good or sadness on account of
an evil.
2. In the irascible appetite: a) regarding an absent good which is difficult
yet considered possible to achieve: hope; if it is seen as unachievable:
desperation or discouragement; b) regarding an absent evil which is seen
as possible to avoid: audacity; if seen as inevitable: fear; c) with respect
to a present evil: anger.
The Thomistic classification of the passions intends to clarify the formal dif-
ferences between the diverse acts of the sensible appetites, setting off to the
side the diversity of goods and evils, that is, the specific subject-matter of the
tendencies. Therefore, this leads to a classification which is extremely formal,
and of little descriptive use. Desire is, for Saint Thomas, a passion, while from
the phenomenological perspective the desire to eat, to know, for revenge, or
to make another suffer are very different from one another. Nevertheless, this
formalism is intentional. The Thomistic perspective is not concerned with tak-
ing up the task of describing the diverse themes or contents of the phenomena
of the soul, but to the task of classifying the role which such phenomena play
in relation to the reason. Aquinas is interested in distinguishing between the
passions which impel from the passions which inhibit, because their respective
modes of influencing the will are very different. Consider, for example, the
different effects on marital consent there are between intense desire and fear.
Marital consent given under the influence of fear is not perfectly voluntary
and can easily be canonically invalid. In contrast, the strong desire to enter


Chapter 5
into a marital bond renders the consent to be even more voluntary, except in
the case in which it reaches a point that inhibits the use of the reason.
Nonetheless, it should be noted regarding the passions that when he discusses
the moral virtues that must moderate them, Saint Thomas introduces the-
matic distinctions, according to diverse goods and evils, and so distinguishes,
for example, the virtue which regulates the desire to eat (temperance) from the
virtue which regulates the desire to know (studiositas) and from the virtue
which regulates the desire to obtain the esteem of others (humility). This
demonstrates that the study of the ethical virtues bears in mind the subject-
matter of the different tendencies, just as psychology does.
5.4
The Passions in the Moral Life
5.4.1
The Role of the Passions in the Moral Life
The presence of the passions in human life is an absolutely normal reality,
which pertains to the human psychological condition, as was said in the pre-
ceding pages. Sentiments and passions were present in the lives of the Saints
and also in the life of Christ.29 It would be rather abnormal if the passions
and sentiments were absent; in fact, for this to happen is one of the charac-
teristics of a psychopathic personality. If it is natural that every living being
react in some way in the face of that which favors or compromises its own
development, it is also natural that man, as a being gifted with sensibility,
interiorly relive these reactions. The undisturbed development of one's being,
or the acquisition of vital objects, marks interior experience with a positive
affective tonality, whereas the frustration of a tendency provokes an affective
state which is negative.
Neither does it respond to reality the idea that the passions are in themselves
obstacles to the voluntariness of human action. Rather, the passions of normal
intensity are one of the most frequent motivations of voluntary action.30 The
passions and the sentiments constitute the foundation which, further elab-
orated and when necessary moderated by the I, explains many projects of
human action, as well as the psychological and moral character of the person.
The passions are not, then, considered fundamentally as an enemy to combat
or suppress, but as a part of one's being that is to be integrated and regulated
according to the person's well-being, or comprehensive good.
The tendential and sentimental sphere, then, is not in itself something which
resists or impedes the free expression of the person. Rather, it seems to us that
the affective structure is one of the most clear and—at times—immediate ex-
29 Cf. Mt 26:37–38; Lk 10: 21.
30 Cf. S.Th. I-II, q. 6, a. 7.


Tendencies, Sentiments, and Passions
pressions of the human moral personality. Except in the case of mental illness
or of a personality disorder, each person definitively has the affective struc-
ture which, little by little, is given to him. It is true that innate temperament
and certain educational, cultural, and social conditionings have sometimes a
notable influence. However, in the last analysis, the person always maintains
the capacity to take a stand in relation to them, and to control—consenting
to them or opposing them—their effect on one's character. The fact that the
character is formed and modified gradually, and that a point can be reached
in which it is not easy to turn back, does not negate in the least that the cause
of certain positive or negative personal characterological traits is the person's
freedom, under the form of an effort, or negligence, to form one's affectivity.
What must, instead, be underlined above all is the role of the sentiments in the
formation of our relationship with others and with the world. The sentiments
manifest that we are not indifferent to others or the world.
Rather, they
cause in us interior reactions which permit us to evaluate their effect on our
life and our projects. The joy of finding one's beloved, the fear in response
to a new situation, or the shame experienced on account of one of our errors
all respond to our way of experiencing and being affected by our encounter
with the world and with others. In the sentiments the world is seen from
the perspective of value and, therefore, the sentiments oscillate between being
positive and negative: pleasure-pain, sympathy-antipathy, respect-disrespect,
etc. Because of their positive or negative tonality, never being neutral, the
sentiments are called upon to play an important role in the perception of what
is morally good or evil.
This important role of the sentiments is, nonetheless, a rather delicate ques-
tion, because they are, or can be, morally ambiguous. The moral ambiguity
of the sentiments responds:
 To the fact that they depend also on the way and level in which a
person's affectivity has been educated;
 To the fact that we are referring to a tendency or various tendencies,
without being able to express in their content (positive or negative) the
role which the relevant tendency or tendencies have toward the integral
good of the person. Sentiments do not integrate themselves alone, but
the integrating activity of the reason and will is always necessary.
If the tendencies and sentiments are adequately educated, the knowledge fur-
nished by them will be true. With the words of Aristotle: the virtuous one
“judges rightly of all things, and in each the truth is apparent to him. For,
truly, there are good and pleasing things to each kind of disposition, and per-
haps the man of value is distinguished primarily for the fact that he sees the


Chapter 5
true in everything, inasmuch as he is the rule and measure of it.” 31 Indeed,
the cognitive dimension of virtue ethics –namely, the fact that virtues are not
only necessary for doing what we know is good but, first and foremost, that
they are necessary for knowing what is good to do in a concrete situation—
has for its anthropological foundation the anticipative character proper to the
question contained in the tendency and in the valuation contained in the sen-
timent. Moral virtue cultivates the capacity of anticipation and penetration
proper to a morally ordered affectivity.
5.4.2
The Passions in Christian Anthropology
The Christian moral teaching sees the passions as natural components of the
human psyche.32 The Sacred Scriptures, in offering a portrait of man as he
is, also emphasizes his emotional and passionate elements. At first glance,
it could seem that Saint Paul considers the passions in an ethically negative
perspective: “Now those who belong to Christ (Jesus) have crucified their flesh
with its passions and desires”33; however, such an impression is not entirely
accurate. He values negatively the “degrading” passions34 which dominate
those who do not know God.35 In fact, in the context of Sacred Scriptures the
passions do not receive a purely negative assessment, for they are attributed
to God Himself,36 and to Jesus.37
For the doctrine of the Church, the passions become positive or negative from
the moral point of view “only to the extent that they effectively engage reason
and will. [. . . ]. It belongs to the perfection of the moral or human good that
the passions be governed by reason. (cf. S.Th. I-II, q. 24, a. 3).”38 In the
state of original justice there existed a perfect harmony between the sensitive
tendencies and the will; after the original sin, such harmony was altered,
so that human nature was deteriorated by concupiscence or the desire for
pleasure which comes about by sin and inclines toward sin.39 Grace did not
fully restore the lost harmony, so that fallen man, even if redeemed, does
not possess complete self-control over his passions, though—with grace—he
is able to overcome grave disorders.40
31 Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics, III, 4: 1113 a 28–32.
32 Cf. CCC 1764.
33 Gal 5:24.
34 Rom 1:26.
35 Cf. 1 Thess 4:5.
36 Cf. Deut 28:63; Isa 30:27, 30; Am 5:21.
37 Cf. Mt 21:12–13; Lk 22, 44; Jn 11, 33–35.
38 CCC 1767.
39 Cf. Council of Trent, De Peccato Originali, can. 5: DS 1515.
40 Cf. Gaudium et Spes, 17.


Tendencies, Sentiments, and Passions
The Christian doctrine does not share the idea of some currents of thought—for
example, those of the Stoics or Kant—for whom the passions are seen with
an aura of suspicion, inasmuch as they would preclude the judgment of the
reason and would be incompatible with authentic moral purity: for, this is
true only for the disordered passions; ordered passions, instead, contribute to
good moral behavior. What is more in accord with human nature is to order
all the passionate movements in a way that the entire man is engaged in the
achievement of the good: “so also does it belong to the perfection of moral
good, that man should be moved unto good, not only in respect of his will, but
also in respect of his sensitive appetite; according to Psalm 83:3: 'My heart
and my flesh have rejoiced in the living God': where by 'heart' we are to
understand the intellectual appetite, and by 'flesh' the sensitive appetite.” 41
The impulse toward the good can come out of the tendential sphere: it is not
only the case that the passions can obscure the understanding, they can almost
make it more acute in order to show the best way to please the beloved. In
such a perspective, Christian life cannot just be conceptual and voluntaristic,
it must also take into account human sentiments, otherwise it would not be
sufficiently rooted in the person and could easily fall apart (certainly, this
does not mean it should be a “merely sentimental” religion). This does not
deny that, in the actual economy of salvation, the passions frequently have
a negative moral influence, but not because of the passions themselves, but
rather a previous voluntary disorder: “Sin [. . . ] produced in me every kind of
covetousness.”42 The disorder introduced by sin makes it so that every appetite
seeks its own object independently from the rational order, so that instead of
facilitating the right intention of the will, the passions render it difficult, on
account of their 'dis-integrated act'; such insubordination is clear enough from
experience, but its origin due to original sin is clearly known only with the
help of faith.
Furthermore, personal sins aggravate this disorder, especially in the areas
in which sins are more frequent or intense in each person, for example, the
tendency to be angry in a person who does not battle to remain calm, or does
so weakly, etc. Sin obscures the understanding and causes the disorders of the
passion to grow, which then more strongly incline one toward sin: “Rather,
each person is tempted when he is lured and enticed by his own desire. Then
desire conceives and brings forth sin, and when sin reaches maturity it gives
birth to death.”43 In sinful man, the affective disorder is more prevalent and
more difficult to resist: “For the flesh has desires against the Spirit, and the
Spirit against the flesh; these are opposed to each other, so that you may not
41 S.Th. I-II, q. 24, a. 3.
42 Rom 7:8.
43 Jas 1:14–15.


Chapter 5
do what you want.”44 The Church Fathers compare the passions—good and
evil—to trees which grow in the field of the soul; they can be easily pulled
out of the ground when they are still young, something which is much more
difficult when they have been allowed to grow for long; “so are the passions:
when they are little, if we want, we tranquilly succeed in pulling them out.
But if we leave them be because they are small, they will toughen, and the
more they toughen, the more fatigue will they require. If they place their roots
deeply in us, not even with great effort can we remove them by ourselves.” 45
We can say in summary that also for Christian doctrine the sentiments and
passions are most important parts of the human person; they are expressions
of his being and moral specificity, and are at the same time one of the scenes
where the great battle occurs between the good will and grace on one side,
and sin on the other. The decisive point is that of the moral education and
formation of the person's affectivity.
5.4.3
The Moral Education of Affectivity
Even if it is true that the sentiments and the passions are moral acts (good
or sinful) only inasmuch as they are deliberately provoked or consented to by
the person, it is still the case that the sentiments and passions, considered
in themselves, are not neutral realities from the point of view of their value.
We know that the sentiments and the passions move between a positive and
negative pole (pleasure-pain, sympathy-antipathy, respect-disrespect, etc.),
and therefore they play an important role in the practical perception of good
and evil. The sentiments and the passions, considered in themselves, contain
a first evaluative judgment, trace a position to take, and suggest a possible
choice of action. In this perspective, their value depends on the truth or falsity
of the evaluation which they contain, that is, they depend on the correctness
or incorrectness of the stance to be taken which they trace and on the morality
of the line of conduct which they suggest or toward which they push.46 Their
quality depends, therefore, on their content and on their intensity. It is good
to rejoice over, or feel spontaneously attracted by, that which is truly good,
and it is not good to react in the same way to that which is evil. Indeed, the
positive sentiments are a great help in the moral life, while negative sentiments
44 Gal 5:17. Cf. Dominum et Vivificantem, 55.
45 Saint Dorotheus, Insegnamenti, 11, 115: SC 92, 361, our translation.
46“Strong feelings are not decisive for the morality or the holiness of persons; they are
simply the inexhaustible reservoir of images and affections in which the moral life is ex-
pressed.
Passions are morally good when they contribute to a good action, evil in the
opposite case. the upright will orders the movements of the senses it appropriates to the
good and to beatitude; an evil will succumbs to disordered passions and exacerbates them.
Emotions and feelings can be taken up into the virtues or perverted by the vices.” (CCC
1768).


Tendencies, Sentiments, and Passions
are a notable obstacle, certainly not insurmountable, but significant in the
long run. However, even good sentiments can be of an exaggerated intensity.
The task of the moral education of the affectivity is to overcome the moral
ambiguity of the affective phenomena, of which we already spoke, introducing
in them a habitual order (the moral virtues), in such a way that not only will
they no longer be an obstacle, but their promptness and immediateness can
be cultivated for the good. The ordered sentiment permits one to judge and
act with promptness, facility, and penetration, with a deep intuition of the
good.
The moral education of the sentiments gives to the person a triple task: to
interpret, evaluate, and direct or correct the affective phenomena.47 To inter-
pret means to try to understand the meaning of what one experiences. At
times, it is a rather simple task: if, for example, one gets little or poor sleep
for days on account of a sore tooth, it is not difficult to understand the cause
of a sense of tiredness or of the lack of energy which makes every task seem
difficult. In contrast, sometimes it can be extremely difficult: a person, for
whom everything seems to be going well, can experience a sense of deep dis-
satisfaction, of bitterness, or of interior emptiness for which he cannot find
any explanation. And since he cannot understand what is happening, it is
impossible to effectively remedy it.
The phenomena, after having been interpreted, are then evaluated. We must
put the good or evil which affectively interests us in relation with the compre-
hensive good of the Christian life, according to the vocation and circumstances
of each individual. We think, for example, of a person who has decided to be a
doctor. At the beginning of his professional activity he can spontaneously ex-
perience fear in response to patients with contagious diseases, or feel terribly
burdened to have to frequently witness sick patients die, those with whom he
had had a professional relationship whith a strong emotional side: this hap-
pens often in oncology. These sentiments manifest an evident difficulty, which
the person must know how to evaluate. If he decides to continue the medical
activity to which he is called, he will understand that he must learn to live
with those sentiments, without being discouraged. He must seek at the same
time to give meaning to his own suffering and that of others, to death and to
his own activity relating to the dying, in such a way that his work becomes an
element which positively contributes to his human and Christian growth. If,
instead, the difficulty seems insurmountable, perhaps he will have to consider
changing his activity. This evaluation of affectivity is an important normative
function of the practical reason.
47 Cf.
regarding this point A. Malo, Antropologia dell'affettività, (Rome:
Armando,
1999), 216–230.


Chapter 5
After the evaluation of the affectivity follows its direction. To direct is, de-
pending on the case, to accept the sentiments, with the spontaneous evalua-
tion which they contain and the line of behavior which they suggest, or else
to modify or reject them. So, for example, one rejects or modifies a negative
sentiment which does not possess any objective foundation, but which, rather,
leads to an injustice with respect to a colleague. This, for example, the person
may understand as having come about specifically on account of his envy of
a person in the same profession who is better at what he does. Sometimes it
will even be the task of the practical reason to arouse or attempt to arouse
feelings (consequent passions, of which we shall speak later).
5.5
The Influence of the Passions
and the Sentiments on the Will
As we saw in the general outline of behavior, the sentiments and the passions
come about first from voluntary action. It is normal, however, that the pas-
sions reawaken independently of the will. In some cases they can provoke an
absolutely involuntary external act which, therefore, would remain without
moral value; in such a sense it is affirmed that the morality of the matter does
not consist in experiencing a determinate passionate impulse, but rather in
allowing one.48 Nonetheless, normally the will is in grade to exercise a “diplo-
matic” control or mastery over the passions49; we say diplomatic because we
do not treat of a complete mastery: there is always the tendency of the sen-
sibility toward its proper object, which the will can redirect toward the good
of man. Therefore, usually, the influence of the passions on action depends
on the consent of the will. On the other hand, the grace of God, profoundly
strengthening the will itself, renders it more apt to be the unifying center of
the person, and augments its mastery over sensibility; this makes it so that
the saints may reach a notable equilibrium regarding the movements of the
passions.50

Tendencies, Sentiments, and Passions
The affections which are felt before the will makes a decision in their regard
are called antecedent passions. Sometimes they appear spontaneously without
any preceding warning, so that they are even less approved by the will (motus
primo primi); furthermore, when they are felt, they can even precede free de-
cision (motus secundo primi). Finally, a movement of the passions can persist
for a while even if it has been rejected by the will; in such case it continues
to be an antecedent passion. These antecedent passions can influence the will
in a two-fold way:
1. conditioning the practical judgment of the reason in a way so as to
present as suitable, here and now, that which the passions desire; when
the passion is disordered it can present as a suitable good an “apparent
good,” even contrary to a virtue which is possessed; that is, the passion
can influence the judgment, leading it to judge a concrete human action
in a way contrary to what the person would think habitually or in gen-
eral;51 when the passion is ordered, on the other hand, it strengthens
the practical judgment to seek the real good.
2. A second way in which the antecedent passions influence the will is in
weakening it: the interior energy of the person is not unlimited, and
when a passion is very strong it appropriates to itself the capacity of
one's attention and operative energy, leaving little space for a controlling
action on the part of the will.52 This does not present much of a problem
when the passions and the will are directed in the same direction, but
when they are directed in contrary directions, or at least divergent, a
robust passion can take control of the person.
Beyond the antecedent passions, which have a great importance in morality,
there exist also consequent passions, whose movement derives from the will,
either because they are instigated by a voluntary resolution, or because once
they come about in a spontaneous way they are then freely approved. Finally,
a passion can be the reflex of a strong voluntary effort: something called a con-
comitant passion. It is not sought for itself, but appears contemporaneously
to the voluntary act; if accepted freely, it becomes a consequent passion.
In the next chapter we shall study in what measure the passions can affect
the moral imputability of a voluntary action.

## CHAPTER 6 {#colom-scelti.6}
The Nature, Structure,
and Evaluation
of the Moral Act
6.1
Concept of the Moral Act
Following the plan which we laid out in the first paragraph of Chapter IV, we
now pass to a study of free acts. In these are expressed the freedom of the
human person and his response, positive or negative, to the divine call to be
saints in Christ.1 In the proper sense morality and immorality pertain only to
free acts or, more exactly, to the person inasmuch as he acts freely. Morality
(in generic contrast to amorality) and freedom have the same extension: all
free acts, and only these, are moral. The fact that what is freely planned or
carried out is private, interpersonal, or political does not make any substantial
difference: the use or abuse of alcoholic drinks at home, fulfillment or non-
fulfillment of professional duties, and the legislative acts by which a political
community gives itself juridical structure, are realities which equally pertain to
the moral order (understood in a generic sense). The reason for this identical
extension is simple: all that is not governed in man in necessary form by
instinct or by some type of causal necessity must be designed by the practical
reason and chosen by the free will, and precisely this is what it means to be
moral.
To be moral or immoral is a specific quality and is, in a rigorous sense, exclu-
sive to the personal will and its acts. The acts of the other human faculties
1 Cf. Eph 1:4–5.


Chapter 6
—thoughts, memories, acts of the nutritive or generative faculties, economic
activities, etc. and not to mention the instinctive impulses, the passions, and
the sentiments—are only moral or immoral inasmuch as they are willed or
consented to freely. Both the free acts of the will and the acts of the other
faculties that are freely commanded, or to which are freely consented, come
to be called human acts because it is proper to the human person to have
freedom in performing or not performing his acts, to perform them in one
mode or another, deliberately determining their intentionality. Human acts
are acts of which man is the master.
For these characteristics, human acts are distinguished not only from the
tendencies and the sentiments, whose intentionality is determined by the base
affective stratum, but also from the acts of man. Acts of man are, for example,
physiological processes which are performed without the intervention of the
will (e.g.
digestion), or actions which are simply reflexes, that is to say,
involuntary motor responses to a stimulus which come about from a peripheral
sense organ, and not from a personal decision (to pull one's arm away from a
hot object which suddenly burns the skin). We deal here, in each case, with
processes or actions which occur in man, more than being performed by man.
All of this can be summarized by saying that what is distinguishing about a
human act—and therefore a moral act—is the fact that it is a voluntary act.
It still needs to be defined, then, what is a voluntary act and what are its
characteristics.2
2 Regarding the theory of action, beyond the studies that will be cited through this

Ltd., 1998); J. De Finance, Saggio sull'agire umano, (Vatican City: Lib. Ed. Vaticana,
1992); A. Fumagalli, Azione e tempo. Il dinamismo dell'agire morale, (Assisi: Cittadella
Editrice, 2002); A. Léonard, Il fondamento della morale, (Cinsello Balsamo: San Paolo,
1990), Ch.I; T.H. Nisters, Akzidentien der Praxis.
Thomas von Aquins Lehre von den
Umständen menslichen Handelns, (Freiburg–Munich: Alber, 1992); M. Rhonheimer, The
Perspective of Morality. Philosophical Foundations of Thomistic Virtue Ethics (Washing-
ton, DC: The Catholic University of America Press, 2011), ch. III; P. Ricoeur, La seman-
