University Press of America, 1984).


The Nature, Structure, and Evaluation of the Moral Act
6.1.1
Definition of a Voluntary Act
The voluntary act can be defined as an act which proceeds from an intrinsic
principle and is accompanied by formal knowledge of an end.3 We shall now
explain the diverse elements of this definition:
1. The voluntary act “proceeds from an intrinsic principle”; that is, from
an operative faculty of the acting person, which is the will. Voluntary
acts come about from the interior of man, and it is this which distin-
guishes them from forced or violent actions, imposed by an external
cause against the will or desire of the agent.
2. “Formal knowledge of the end” means that the person knows the reason
for which he performs the act, and knows it expressly as an object of
his action, evaluating its suitability, in such a way that the pondered
knowledge of the object is the origin and cause of the action. Therefore,
voluntary action is also distinguished from movements or simple spon-
taneous processes which arise or occur in the person but do not proceed
from a free judgment: e.g. reflexes.
Without formal knowledge of the end, or in the measure in which there is
not such knowledge, there does not exist a voluntary act. For example,
if someone has put among some old papers a check for $500, and I
am unaware that this person has done so, when I tear up the papers
and throw them away I voluntarily perform the action of “tearing up
and throwing away old papers” (because this is what I know myself to
be doing), but I do not voluntarily perform the action of “tearing up
and throwing away a check for $500.” This is so even if it is true that
the check was torn up by my own hands, and that I did so without
being forced by another. Without formal knowledge of what one does,
it cannot be a voluntary act.
3. Lastly, the term “end” generically expresses the proper object of acts of
the will. There exists a more restricted use of the term end, which we
shall study in the second section of this chapter, but now we speak of the
end in its widest and most generic use, according to which end means
the object or term of the act of the will. When this end is reached,
the will has completely performed its act and, consequently, the act is
finished. Given that the nature of the will (voluntas ut natura) is that of
being an inclination toward the good recognized by the reason, the end
of the voluntary act is always a true good, or at least an apparent good
3 Cf. S.Th. I-II, q. 6, a. 1. “Duo igitur sunt necessaria ad constituendam rationem
voluntarii, nempe quot sit a principio intrinseco, et cum aliqua cognitione finis” (Saint
Alphonsus of Liguori, Theologiae Moralis, lib. V, praeamb., 1, 7: Opere, Turin: Giacinto
Marietti, 1880, vol. VI, p. 6).


Chapter 6
(something seen as good) which can be reached, used, or performed by
a voluntary action (practical good).
When speaking of the end (or of the object) of an act of the will, it is mislead-
ing to immediately think of a thing (a watch, pen, outfit, etc.). For since the
goods sought by the person's will normally can be performed, used, achieved,
etc. through acts commanded by it, the end of the will's act is oftentimes a
commanded act, for example, the will chooses the action “buy a pen” or the
action “give a pen as a gift,” and so the actions “to buy a pen” or “to give a
pen as a gift” are the ends of the will's act.
6.1.2
The Tendency of the Will toward the End:
Voluntariness
From the definition of a voluntary act explained in the preceding subsection
it follows that an essential constitutive element of the moral act is the con-
scious and deliberate tendency of the personal will toward its end, a tendency
which from this point on we shall call voluntariness. Voluntariness is there-
fore a “tending towards,” the embodied “aiming at” in every act of the will.
Voluntariness is the intentionality constitutive of the voluntary act.
All of moral action theory presupposes an adequate understanding of volun-
tariness. Not only because without voluntariness there is no voluntary action,
but also because the concrete mode which the tendency of the will assumes in
each particular action determines such an action as a specific type of action
(gift, theft, loan, etc.). In general terms, it is true that all action becomes
specified by its object, that is to say, by the specific principle which actuates
each particular human operative faculty.4 Hearing is actuated in response to
sound, scent in response to odor, and in response to odor and sound, scent
and hearing have no other possible act but to smell and to hear. The person,
instead, can respond in a very diverse manner to the same reality (approve of
it or disapprove of it, love it or hate it, buy it or steal it), which is the reason
for which such a reality, inasmuch as being an object or good to which the
will aims, cannot be defined independently from the way in which the person
intentionally approaches it, that is to say, it cannot be defined independently
from the voluntariness of the person who directs himself toward that reality.
So as we said before and say again because it is important, the end or good,
as the object of the will, is not properly a thing, e.g. a watch, but rather an
action which uses, or pertains in some way to such a thing: the watch is a
practical good (an end of the will) insofar as it is an object that brings with
it pleasure, or insofar as it is an object of sale or theft, or as it is given as a
gift to someone as a manifestation of friendship, etc. The good or end of the
4 Cf. S. Pinckaers, Il rinnovamento della morale, (Turin: Borla, 1968), 176–181.


The Nature, Structure, and Evaluation of the Moral Act
will is, therefore, to use the watch, to buy it, to steal it, to give it as a gift,
etc.
It would be a grave error to conceive of or describe moral action from the
outside as a simple physical occurrence, without taking account of the interior
purpose (voluntariness) out of which it proceeds and from which it is informed.
Moral action is not a simple occurrence of the physical world from which cer-
tain effects follow. The event and the effects are only the physical component
of the action, the body of the action, but voluntary action is constituted
also, in the formal sense, by voluntariness, which is likened to its soul. So,
for example, if unexpectedly a patient, Peter, dies while undergoing surgery
which was correctly performed, we have the action “surgical operation” and
the effect “the death of Peter” but this does not equal the voluntary action
“killing Peter” because in no moment and under no aspect did the surgeon
see the death of Peter as a good (end) to follow nor did he intentionally will
it through his own action.
6.1.3
Characteristics of Voluntariness
We can now explicitly highlight the characteristics of voluntariness.
Voluntariness is a deliberate and conscious “movement” toward an object not
only because the person “has awareness” of what she does: one can have
knowledge of something which is not, however, organized or regulated by her-
self (as in the case of a heart-beat); the voluntary act is a deliberate and
conscious act because it includes in its intimate structure an intellectual judg-
ment which plans or evaluates as good an action or what is achieved through
the action. Rational knowledge is presupposed in voluntariness, and it is in
a certain sense immersed in it (nihil volitum nisi praecognitum): the will is a
“judging tendency.”5 The reason why this is so is because the will is a rational
appetite which can choose an action only inasmuch as it is presented by the
reason with an intelligible meaning. Chosen actions are always willed under
a rational description, that is to say, under such a description that allows a
person's chosen action to make sense.6
Saint Thomas explains that the objects of moral actions are forms con-
ceived and constituted by the reason.7 He means by this that the object
toward which the will aims is not identified with the chosen action or the
realized object considered simply as a physical fact, or considered only
as acts of a physical faculty (nutrition, generative faculty, etc.), because
the moral action is an act of a rational agent, who with the intellect also
5 Cf. K. Wojtyla, Persona e atto (1982), 49 and 173. Italian reads: “tendere giudicando.”
6 This aspect is brought to light and studied in depth by G.E.M. Anscombe, Intention
(1957).
7 “Species moralium actuum constituuntur ex formis prout sunt a ratione concep-
tae” (S.Th. I-II, q. 18, a. 10).


Chapter 6
selects intelligible aspects; this explains why the person approaches the
object in one way and not another. So, for example, the same action
of “turning a blind eye” to the errors of a student in his exposition of
a topic can be seen by the professor, depending on the circumstances,
as an act of mercy or of undue condescension. A physiologically identi-
cal action of the generative faculty can be in one case adultery and in
another a legitimate conjugal act. The difference between the first and
the second is relevant for the person who chooses the action, but not
for a purely naturalistic (medical-physiological) consideration of such
an act.
Voluntariness is active in the sense that the way in which a person approaches
an end is chosen and decided by the person. It is not a purely passive move-
ment as the sensitive passions are. The acts of the will are not passions,
but acts or actions, because the relation between the voluntary agent and his
object comes to be chosen and set by the agent himself.
In the end, voluntariness is also always self-referential. The voluntary action,
beyond taking aim of an object in the sense indicated up to now, involves the
personal agent, modifying and qualifying him. It is not possible, for example,
to steal without being rendered a thief, while instead one can know of a theft
or a homicide without being marked by these moral faults.
Voluntariness
implies a personal identification (an evaluation and a positive position taken
with love, or a negative position taken with hate or refusal) with the willed
action,8 which is not the case with knowledge (no one becomes a thief simply
because he knows that there was a theft). Voluntariness is the immediate
expression of the person. The person remains involved as a person in each
act of his will9, and for this reason each determination of the will toward
an object is always also a self-determination, i.e. an act through which the
person determines himself. It pertains to the essence itself of the will that the
personal I reclaim for itself what is willed, approving or rejecting it, while
it does not at the same time associate itself with what is merely the object
of simple knowledge. Voluntariness is never neutral, and if it comes to be
described as neutral one can be sure that its most intimate nature is escaping
us.10 This self-referentiality of the human act explains why God “will repay
everyone according to his works.”11
8 This does not take away from the fact that there exist voluntary acts done with a
certain repugnance, as to take a medicine which has a poor taste: the goal sought, is
health, and not the taste.
9 Cf.
K. Wojtyla, Persona e atto (1982)., ch.
III; L. Polo, Curso de teoría del
conocimiento, vol. II, (Pamplona: Eunsa, 1984), 229.
10 Cf. Veritatis Splendor, 78.
11 Rom 2:6; Cf. Ps 61:13; Prov 24:12; 2 Cor 5:10.


The Nature, Structure, and Evaluation of the Moral Act
6.1.4
Elicited Voluntary Acts
and Commanded Voluntary Acts
One calls elicited those voluntary acts exercised directly by the will (to love,
to hate, to decide to buy something or to study, etc.).
The person, as a
spiritual center, takes a stance with regard to an object (loves, hates, approves,
disapproves, chooses, decides, etc.). The elicited acts can be referred also to
the objects which are in their own power; so, for example, one can love or
hate the qualities of another person, one can decide that he has had success
in his activities or has failed in them, even if the person who loves or hates
cannot do anything to promote or prevent these qualities, successes or failures.
But very frequently elicited acts plan or choose realizable and realized actions
(one decides to go on vacation in three weeks, or to purchase an outfit, etc.),
and they apply the operative faculties (hands for grabbing something, legs for
running, etc.) to the accomplishment of what has been decided. A possible
misunderstanding of the nature of elicited acts is to think “that they always
consist in acts which not only originate immediately from the will but also
terminate `in' the will, never in any power subject to the will; or in other
words, to think that per se they only constitute volitional relations and never
per se constitute any other kind of relation, that is, any relation implying any
other beyond that of the will.”12 The elicited act of willing to move the legs
in order to walk (active use) finishes in the effect of walking, which is already
a commanded act.
The accomplishment of the chosen actions are, in effect, the voluntary com-
manded acts, that is to say, the acts immediately performed by a faculty which
is not the will (the understanding, the arms, the eyes) under the influence and
the prompting of the will: so to read a book, to knock on the table, and to
lend someone attention are voluntary commanded actions. These and other
commanded acts are planned, chosen, and performed freely by the person,
and are, therefore, voluntary actions in a most rigorous sense. The planning
and interior choice of these acts constitute their “soul,” that which informs,
gives life and meaning; the commanded act in its psychological or physical
facticity is like the “body” of the action.
Two consequences of this are important for moral theology. The first is that
the elicited acts have a great moral relevance, for they are the principle and
foundation of the commanded acts. Christianity underlines the importance of
the “heart,” where man expresses himself, at least before God and himself,
in a more personal manner than he may do in the physical performance of
the act itself.
In this sense it is the elicited act which one must consider
morally good or evil in its essence, while the commanded act is good or evil
12 S.L. Brock, Action and Conduct (1998), 175.


Chapter 6
inasmuch as it participates in the elicited act.13 The second consequence is
that the moral description of the action must seek to grasp, inasmuch as it
is possible, what animates the commanded act: the elicited act characterized
essentially by voluntariness. An action described in this manner: “the muscles
of the right arm of the motorcyclist, Peter, contract” is not yet a voluntary
action, and cannot be evaluated morally: it is a “body” without a “soul,”
morally unintelligible; so described, no one could choose it. If that action
comes to be described in another mode, for example: “The motorcyclist Peter
indicates he is turning to the right by raising his arm,” or “Peter insults John
with a gesture of his right arm,” then the choice of action made by Peter
has a human meaning and is susceptible to moral evaluation. Voluntariness
cannot be left out of the description of the action, because voluntariness is the
basic level of intentionality constitutive of a voluntary commanded act. On
account of voluntariness, a type of action distinguishes itself from another,
which could sometimes be almost identical to an outside observer. Beyond
this first constitutive intentionality there can be further intentions, which
are not constitutive of the action but morally relevant nonetheless, as we
shall explain later in this chapter. Naturally, if a description of an action
which has a “body” without a “soul” is to be avoided, equally a description
which presents us with a “soul” without a “body” is also to be avoided. The
commanded action is, rather, a unitary whole.
Saint Thomas, and with him many other theologians, calls the elicited
acts of the will internal acts, and the commanded acts external acts.
The terms “internal” and “external” are utilized, then, with reference
to the will, and so a thought or a voluntary memory (which are com-
manded acts of the will but performed by a faculty external to it) come
to be considered external acts. This is the most correct use of the ter-
minology. Nonetheless, sometimes the qualifications of “internal” and
“external” come to be used in reference to that which an outside observer
can see. And then a thought or a voluntary memory would be internal
acts, while studying, hitting, or stealing would be external acts. In this
sense internal sins (evil thoughts, evil desires, etc.) are traditionally
distinguished from external sins (theft, violence, etc.).
6.2
The Different Types of Objects of the Will
6.2.1
The Direct Object of the Will
It needs to be clarified that the object of the voluntary act of which we spoke
up until now must be called with greater rigor the direct object of the will, to
distinguish it from the indirect object, of which we shall speak shortly. First
13 Cf. Scriptum Super Sententiis, lib. III, d. 23, q. 1, a. 4, ql. 1.


The Nature, Structure, and Evaluation of the Moral Act
we must propose some qualitative distinctions regarding the direct object of
the will, which shall permit us to understand the strictest use of the concept
of the end (or intention).14
We know that the direct object of the will is the good (real or apparent)
grasped by the reason. To the eyes of the acting person, an action, or what
is acquired by means of it, can possess the intelligibility of a good in diverse
ways: there are, so to speak, various classes of goods. Among these, the end in
the most rigorous use of the term is that which is presented as a good desirable
in itself, that is to say, it is that which interests in itself, and for this it can
be in itself a principle of the will's movement. Once the end which gave origin
to an act of the will is achieved, such a voluntary act is complete. The end is,
therefore, that which is seen as good or desirable in itself and for this reason it
is willed or achieved for itself. At the heart of this restricted use there needs
to be introduced yet a further distinction of a qualitative type: something can
be seen as good in itself because it is honest or because it is pleasing. What is
willed in itself because it is objectively good or worthy of being loved (that is
to say, because it possesses an objectively relevant value), is an honest good;
this has an objective character, for the human person recognizes good in it
and approves it as such. However, an action or thing can be willed in itself
also because it causes in a person a positive affective resonance (pleasure,
satisfaction, joy, etc.), and so it is called a pleasing good.
Finally, there is a third type of good which is not an end, but is put in relation
to the end, and for this reason pertains to the direct object of the will, even if
in a secondary way. This third type of good comes to be called sometimes a
useful good, a directed good (Saint Thomas denominates it with the expression
“ea quae sunt ad finem,” “those things which are directed toward the end”),
or simply the means. The directed good, considered formally as such, is not
willed in itself (neither as an honest good or as a pleasing good), but because
it is presented as ordained (directed) to the achievement or attainment of the
end: it is, therefore, willed in virtue of another good, in virtue of the end
for whose attainment it is useful. So, we submit to painful medical care, not
because it may interest us in itself, but because it allows us to recover health.
The distinction between ends and means permits us to glimpse one of the
most common forms of organizing complex moral behavior: certain actions
come to be chosen as means, for the sake of something else. The distinction
between the willing of something as an end or as means has many applications
in moral theology.15
14 We borrow from what was written in A. Rodríguez Luño, Etica (1992), nos. 87–94,
limiting ourselves to the essential aspects.
15 Cf. for example, Evangelium Vitae, 62.


Chapter 6
6.2.2
The Indirect Object of the Will
Beyond that of the end or of the directed goods (means), which are directly
willed by the person, the will can also have an indirect object which, in the
measure in which it is foreseen, remains in the realm of its intentionality.16
The indirect object is a consequence of action (a collateral effect of the action)
which does not interest the person and is in no way willed, either as an end
or as means, but is foreseen and permitted inasmuch as it is inevitably linked
to what is willed. Some examples: a person submits himself to a cure for
leukemia, which provokes, as a secondary effect, baldness; a woman who would
like to have a family allows that her uterus may be extracted on account of a
tumor having formed there, and as a consequence becomes infertile. Baldness
and infertility are indirect objects of the will, not willed, but rather known
and foreseen effects which necessity obliges them to tolerate. Whenever an
action carries with itself an indirect negative effect for the person acting or for
others, one is placed before the problem of the moral licitness of performing
such an action. So Saint Paul encourages the avoidance of any action which,
though being licit in itself, has as an indirect effect the scandalizing of those
who are weak in the faith.17 It is the moral issue of actions which have a
double effect, which will be studied in section 5 of this chapter.
In order to avoid confusion, it is good to know how to distinguish between an
indirect object (or the indirect voluntary action) and an object willed directly
as a means. If a woman does not want to have children, for it is probable
that another delivery may result in her death, and directs a doctor to extract
her uterus, the surgical operation is willed directly for the sake of rendering
her infertile and the consequent infertility is also willed directly, even if as
a means to preserve her health. The fundamental distinctive criterion is as
follows: because the foreseen effect of an action may be considered an indirect
object of the will, such an effect cannot be willed as the means (on the level of
reality, the cause) which allows the person to obtain or achieve what is really
desired. Any effect which is seen or willed as part of the causal ring between
the person and his end is willed directly as a means, i.e. as a directed good.
In the last example, the future infertility is willed directly as a means; in the
other two examples, rather, baldness and infertility are willed indirectly, so
that baldness is not the cause of the cure for leukemia, just as the fact of not
being able to have kids is not the cause for which the woman has the tumor
extracted out of her body. Speaking properly, the indirect effect is not willed,
but permitted, tolerated, or endured.
16 As an example of the distinction between direct and indirect willing, see n.
57 of
Evangelium Vitae.
17 Cf. Rom 14:14–21.


The Nature, Structure, and Evaluation of the Moral Act
In practice, the distinction between the direct object and the indirect
object of the will can be at times difficult to establish, and for this reason
it can lend itself to abuses. Recognizing this, we still retain that if one
proceeds correctly with an attentive and serene analysis, the difference
between the two types of object of the will can be established in an
objective and controllable way. Even ordinary language is sufficiently
sensible to the existing differences in the types of willing. It is enough
to examine the semantic forms of some of the words with which we refer
to human actions (to will, to approve, to permit, to tolerate, to endure,
etc.) in order to have confirmation for what we have explained.
6.3
The Discursive Structure
of Voluntary Action
Rational activity is discursive: it involves the passage from one term to
another. In the theoretical order, the progress consists in the acquisition
of new truths from those already known.
In the practical order, an
analogous relation is established between the diverse instances of the
exercise of the practical reason and the will: from the act of willing to
not gain weight, for example, we pass to a deliberation regarding the
way in which we can reach such a goal, deciding to do physical exercise
or to begin a diet. Saint Thomas, assuming and completing the analysis
of Aristotle, Saint Augustine, and Saint John Damascene, elaborated
a general scheme of diverse levels of exercising the will.18 According
to Aquinas, to the first apprehension of an end follows a delight of
the will called love. Afterwards one has a judgment which evaluates
the possibilities and the mode of reaching the end, to which follows a
firm decision to obtain it through certain actions: this decision is called
intention. Moved by the intention, the intellect deliberates regarding the
means (directed actions) ideal for attaining or accomplishing this end, to
which the will can give or not give its consent. One must then establish
which of these actions are the most appropriate and which can be put
into practice immediately (judgment of choice), and then one makes
the interior decision to act in such a way (choice). When it is decided
what is to be done here and now, the activities of the diverse operative
faculties need to be organized and coordinated (rational imperio), and
in accord with this plan the will moves the other faculties (active use
of the will and passive use of the other faculties).
Then follow the
achievement of the end and the delight from its possession. The first
apprehension, love, the intention, and the judgment which precedes it,
along with delight and the final fruition, are acts which have as their
object the end, what is desirable in itself and for itself; and among
these acts, love, intention, and fruition are elicited acts of the will.
Consent, choice, and the active use of the faculties are also elicited
18 Cf. S.Th. I-II, qq. 11–16.


Chapter 6
acts of the will, but they have as an object the actions ordained to
the end. The more modern interpretations sustain that this analysis
is of a structural character, and not psychological. It should not be
interpreted, that is, as a set of completed and independent acts, which
follow in a fixed and irreversible temporal sequence, but rather as an
analytical specification of the modality which the acts of the practical
reason and the will acquire. This all gives rise to unitary discursive
structure that, according to the particular case, can be exercised in a
partial or a complete way.19
In the study of voluntary action, moral theology has a particular interest in
choice and intention.20
We understand by intention an elicited act of the will consisting in the effi-
cacious willing of an end (something desirable in itself and for itself) which,
in its factual reality, is distant from us, so as to not be immediately achiev-
able or reachable, but which must be reached or achieved through a series of
actions directed toward it. The end which is the object of the act of intention
traditionally comes to be called the finis operantis. It is seen and formally
planned as the term of directed actions; the intention is the act completer par
excellence.
For this reason, Aquinas observes that “when the appetite is immedi-
ately directed toward something, there is not an intention for this good,
either with regard to the final end or an end ordained to it; only when
one intends to arrive at an end through what he wills now does he have
an intention for this end.”21 This characteristic of the intention can give
rise to confusion. If we separate a series of means that are related to one
another by their end, a directed action can appear as an end without
really being one. For example: health in itself is a good, and to conserve
it I am ready to take a repugnant medicine which, furthermore, I am
only able to find in a pharmacy situated at the opposite end of the city.
Abstracting from my desire to stay healthy, I could think of my act of
taking money, getting a bus, etc. to purchase and take the repugnant
medicine as becoming my intended end. But this description of the ac-
tion is erroneous, because the medicine is not properly an end (it is not
willed in itself): it is functionally an end in a certain way—mistaken
in this case—of describing the action; here the end and intention is,
rather, health.
We call choice the elicited act of the will which has for its object the action
immediately achievable in view of the desired end.22 The object of choice is,
19 Cf.
S. Pinckaers, “La structure de l'acte humain suivant Saint Thomas”, Revue
Thomiste 63/2 (1955) 393–412.
20 Already Aristotle applied himself to this investigation: cf. for example Nicomachean
Ethics, VI, 2: 1139 a 32–34.
21 Scriptum Super Sententiis, lib. II, d. 38, q. 1, a. 3. On intention, see S.Th.
I-II, q. 12.
22 On choice, see S.Th., I-II, q. 13.


The Nature, Structure, and Evaluation of the Moral Act
therefore, the directed action which is immediately in my power to do or not
do, to achieve in one mode or in another. The choice presupposes various
acts of the reason: at least deliberation and practical judgment, and also
presupposed in its act is the act of intention. The object of deliberation and
of choice cannot be an end, since to deliberate on a good and to choose it
entails orienting it toward another end, and therefore it entails choosing it as
a directed good (means).
If we compare what we are saying now with what we already know about
voluntariness23, it is immediately seen that there exist diverse levels of inten-
tionality of action. So, for example, the action “threaten to kill an officer”–
which in virtue of its constitutive intentionality (the intentionality proper to
choice) is diverse from the action “to ask” or from the action “to thank”—can
respond in a concrete case to the intention of obtaining a building permit
that one has a right to according to the law, and in another case to the in-
tention of obtaining something which this person does not have the right to,
and which is actually illegal. The presence of diverse levels of intentionality
creates particular problems when the moment for moral evaluation arrives, as
will be seen in subsection 6.4.3 of this same chapter.
6.4
The Moral Evaluation of Voluntary Action:
The Sources of Morality
After having studied the nature and structure of voluntary action, it is possible
to take on an analysis of the elements on which depends the moral evaluation
of actions with regard to their matter, or content, elements which traditionally
came to be called the sources of morality. In section 6 of this chapter we
shall study, instead, the elements relating to the psychological perfection of
an action which determines not the objective morality of its content, but its
subjective imputability.
We shall now consider the problem to be resolved, making use of some
examples. A doctor needs to define and classify the different patholo-
gies (gastric ulcer, diabetes, tuberculosis, malaria, etc.) to be able to
identify what is causing each patient harm based on symptoms, clinical
history, etc., and to be able to provide the appropriate care. A judge
makes use of the definitions and classifications of various crimes (mur-
der, arson, manslaughter, theft, robbery, extortion, etc.) in order to be
able to judge the kinds of behavior on which he must pass judgment.
Moralists also must make use of definitions and classifications of the
proper acts of the virtues and of the acts contrary to them (lying, theft,
abortion, contraception, murder, slander, etc.) in order to be able to
23 Cf. section 6.1 of this chapter.


Chapter 6
morally evaluate different kinds of behavior. Each of these analytical
categories (lying, theft, etc.) constitutes a moral species, and it is the
role of the theory of virtues and vices to define them with exactness
and to justify their morality. The problem with which we now occupy
ourselves is more restricted; we are concerned with knowing on what
depends the moral species of free behavior, that is to say, on what
elements of action depends, for example, the distinction between an
abortion and a licit therapeutic operation, or between contraception
and abortion, etc.
6.4.1
The Ecclesial Doctrine Concerning
the Sources of Morality
Concerning the sources of morality, there exists not just a centuries old the-
ological tradition of reflection,24 but also a precise ecclesial doctrine, which
was recently brought forth in the Catechism of the Catholic Church25 and in
the encyclical Veritatis Splendor.26
The exposition of the Catechism of the Catholic Church, being very concise, is
limited by concerns of practicality to enumerate all of the essential elements.
The morality of human acts depends on three elements: 1) “The object cho-
sen,” that is to say, the object of the act which in the preceding paragraph
is called choice; 2) “the end in view, or the intention,” which is the object
of the act which we called intention; 3) “the circumstances of the action,”
whose nature must still be explained. “The object, the intention, and the
circumstances make up the 'sources,' or constitutive elements, of the morality
of human acts.”27
The chosen object gives the moral species to the act of the will,28 and “can
by itself vitiate an act in its entirety. There are some concrete acts—such as
fornication—that it is always wrong to choose, because choosing them entails
a disorder of the will, that is, a moral evil.” 29 A good intention can neither
render good nor just a type of behavior which is evil in its object; contrarily,
an evil intention could render evil an act which, in itself, can be good.30 The
circumstances, which are secondary elements of the moral act, contribute to
increase or diminish the moral goodness or evil of an act but they can neither
render good nor just an action which is evil in its object (an intrinsically
24 A good synthesis of theological reflection on the material is offered by Th. G. Belmans,
Le sens objetif de l'agir humain. Pour relire la morale coniugale de Saint Thomas, (Vatican
City: Libreria Editrice Vaticana, 1980).
25 Cf. nos. 1749–1761.
26 Cf. nos. 71–83.
27 CCC 1750.
28 Cf. ibid., 1751.
29 Ibid., 1755.
30 Cf. ibid., 1753.


The Nature, Structure, and Evaluation of the Moral Act
evil action).31 In synthesis, “a morally good act requires the goodness of its
object, of its end, and of its circumstances together.” 32
The exposition of the encyclical Veritatis Splendor has a different character,
because it does not intend so much to offer a general and simple vision of the
doctrine, as to uphold and expand on some points which were recently de-
nied or put into question. The doctrinal nucleus of the section concerning the
moral act stands in the affirmation of the existence of intrinsically evil acts
(intrinsece malum), that is to say, in sustaining that there are concrete behav-
iors (adultery, abortion, etc.) which are morally evil “always and per se, in
other words, on account of their very object, and quite apart from the ulterior
intentions of the one acting and the circumstances.” 33 The term “behavior”
is not referring to actions done by someone who is incapable of performing a
free choice; when the encyclical speaks of “behavior” it refers precisely to a
possible object of free and deliberate choice.34This explicit reference to delib-
erate choice is always present when the encyclical treats of types and classes
of actions which are intrinsically evil.35 It seems evident that the insistence
on this way of expressing it was on purpose and has a precise meaning. It
affirms also that in the sustaining of the existence of intrinsically evil acts
“the Church accepts the teaching of Sacred Scripture.” 36 From the existence
of actions which are morally evil according to their species, or according to
their object37, comes a second doctrinally relevant thesis: the norms which
prohibit such acts are valid semper et pro semper, always and for all, without
any exception.38 It is a thesis which is repeated several times.39

ad 3 and q. 19, a. 7, ad 3.

evil by virtue of its object into an act 'subjectively' good or defensible as a choice” (no. 81);
“the opinion must be rejected as erroneous which maintains that it is impossible to qualify
as morally evil according to its species the deliberate choice of certain kinds of behaviour
or specific acts” (no. 82); “Judgments about morality cannot be made without taking into
consideration whether or not the deliberate choice of a specific kind of behaviour is in con-
formity with the dignity and integral vocation of the human person” (no. 67); “Such theories
however are not faithful to the Church's teaching, when they believe they can justify, as
morally good, deliberate choices of kinds of behaviour contrary to the commandments of

Chapter 6
The encyclical moves forward to furnish some necessary guidelines, both posi-
tive and negative, for adequately understanding the doctrinal assertions which
have been reiterated up to this point. In a positive sense, such assertions pre-
suppose the thesis that “The morality of the human act depends primarily
and fundamentally on the 'object' rationally chosen by the deliberate will” 40:
a thesis best expressed and given foundation by Saint Thomas, but not only
by him. Still in a positive sense, but already entering into the field of method-
ology, there is expressed a particularly important point: “In order to be able
to grasp the object of an act which specifies that act morally, it is therefore
necessary to place oneself in the perspective of the acting person. The object
of the act of willing is in fact a freely chosen kind of behaviour. To the extent
that it is in conformity with the order of reason, it is the cause of the goodness
of the will.”41 On this foundation, the existent unity between the morality of
the choice and the morality of the person is put into relief: the moral ob-
ject “is the proximate end of a deliberate decision which determines the act
of willing on the part of the acting person. Consequently, as the Catechism
of the Catholic Church teaches, `there are certain specific kinds of behaviour
that are always wrong to choose, because choosing them involves a disorder
of the will, that is, a moral evil.' ”42
Among the negative methodological guidelines, the following two are impor-
tant. The first regards, at its core, the concept of action: “By the object
of a given moral act, then, one cannot mean a process or an event of the
merely physical order, to be assessed on the basis of its ability to bring about
a given state of affairs in the outside world.” 43 The second regards, instead,
the constitution of the moral object: “The weighing of the goods and evils
foreseeable as the consequence of an action is not an adequate method for de-
termining whether the choice of that concrete kind of behaviour is `according
to its species', or `in itself', morally good or bad, licit or illicit.” 44
In substance, these brief notes have brought to light the ecclesial doctrine
concerning the sources of morality.
There are, however, points to explore
further, as we shall see in what follows.

The Nature, Structure, and Evaluation of the Moral Act
6.4.2
The Moral Object
The general principle which lies at the base of the ecclesial doctrine concerning
the sources of morality is clear and is peacefully accepted: each act of the will
is fundamentally specified by the object (by the end or good) at which such
an act is directly aimed. The chosen object gives species to the choice (it
makes it to be one type of choice and not another); the object (end or good)
to which the intention is directed gives species to the act of the intention;
and the object (end or good) to which is consented gives species to the act
of consent. The moral tradition calls the object of choice the moral object or
finis operis (end of the act); the object of the intention comes to be called
instead the end or finis operantis (end of the person who acts).
The species of voluntary acts is a moral species. The will follows the reason:
human choice is deliberated choice, and human intention is equally enlight-
ened by rational judgment. The objects of choice and of intention come to
be compared with the natural practical principles of the reason, which are
the moral virtues,45 and from such a comparison there results a moral evalu-
ation.46
When these principles come to be applied to simple behaviors, they do
not present any particular problem: the choice normally tends toward a
commanded action (for example: to steal an automobile) and therefore
the act is specified by it: the choice to steal is specified as theft. But
in more complex actions, in which different goods are involved, a doubt
can emerge over which are the elements that enter into the essence of the
commanded action, and therefore concerning the elements which should
be considered the object that gives to the choice its moral species. For
example: the doctor can prescribe to a married woman, affected by a
disease, a medicine that, for all the time that it is taken, will render her
conjugal relations to be infertile. The woman may wonder if taking the
drug is a therapeutic action or contraception. If it is explained to the
woman that it is not contraception, even if that same medicine is taken
by other women as a purely contraceptive means, then doubt may arise
as to whether in this case there is not the intention, circumstances, or
moral object to fundamentally determine the morality of the behavior
as being contrary to what is affirmed by ecclesial doctrine. To resolve
this and other similar problems we must further explore the nature and
role of the moral object, the end, and the circumstances.
The Concept of the Moral Object — A good part of the difficulty for
understanding exactly what the moral object is comes about from the error,
45 “In ratione pratica praexistunt quaedam ut principia naturaliter nota, et huiusmodi
sunt fines virtutum moralium, quia finis se habet in operabilibus sicut principium in spec-
ulativis” (S.Th. II-II, q. 47, a. 6, corp.).
46 “Omnis finis a ratione deliberativa intentum, pertinet ad bonum alicuius virtutis, vel
ad malum alicuius vitii” (S.Th. I-II, q. 18, a. 9, ad 3).


Chapter 6
rather frequent, of describing commanded voluntary acts as simple physical
occurrences that are followed by certain effects, without taking account of the
interior purpose of the choice (voluntariness) from which the commanded act
proceeds and which it embodies.47 This error is sometimes facilitated by the
terminology itself, which is not always used correctly. To speak of the object
of the act makes sense in relation to the elicited act of the will (the choice),
but not in relation to the external action chosen by the person. The object of
choice is the same chosen external action (to steal an automobile) and not a
material “something” of the external action (the automobile).48 If the moral
object were the automobile, the actions “to steal an automobile” and “to give
away an automobile” of the same brand would have the same object, which
is manifestly false. Moreover, if the moral object of either contraception or
the previously cited therapeutic action were simply sterilizing effect of the
medicin taken, the conclusion would follow that both are morally identical,
and for this reason either both would be morally licit or both would be equally
illicit. Instead, it needs to be recognized that the interior purpose of the agent
represents the basic level of intentionality, constituting the formal and decisive
element of the external choice's moral object.
To understand this we return to the example of the motorcyclist Peter.
If we say: “the muscles of Peter's right arm contract,” we speak of a
physical fact and we give a description of it proper to physiology. Saint
Thomas calls that physical event the materia ex qua of the voluntary
commanded action. But such material, alone, does not yet constitute a
voluntary action or a moral object. If instead we say: “Peter signals that
he is turning left by raising his arm,” we are already speaking of a vol-
untary action that a sensible person can choose, in which the corporal
movement (raising the right arm) responds to and embodies a delib-
erate plan or purpose which makes sense for him and for others who
see it. Saint Thomas employs the technical concept of materia circa
quam,49 which is really equivalent to the moral object of the choice,
making clear, however, that such an object or materia circa quam is in
some way a forma a ratione concepta;50 or in other words, the moral
object is formally a purpose or operative project conceived and eval-
uated by the practical reason, and this insofar as it is chosen.51The

material element of the commanded action, and therefore of the object
of the choice (to raise the arm), could be a response or embodiment
of different purposes, for example, to threaten someone, and then it
would result that the same material behavior would be the materia ex
qua of a completely different moral action. “For one to indicate that
he is turning right” is a very different voluntary action than the action
of “threatening someone by raising one's arm.” The moral object of the
first action's choice is different from the moral object of the second ac-
tion's choice, and such difference depends solely on the moral object,
and not on the intention or finis operantis. We have not spoken yet
of the intention for which Peter decides to indicate that he turns right
or for which he threatens someone with his arm, and we do not have
any need of speaking of it when we are dealing only with distinguishing
between the action of “one signaling that he is turning right” from the
action of “threatening someone.” The intentionality (voluntariness) of
indicating a right turn and that of threatening are in both cases the
intrinsic and constitutive intentionality of the action, which give their
actions their moral species, and which the theological tradition calls
the finis operis. Regarding this intentionality which is constitutive of
the action (finis operis), the intention or finis operantis represents a
further intentionality or, in other words, a second level intentionality.
The encyclical Veritatis Splendor speaks in this regard of the “ulterior
intention,”52 and the Latin edition of the Catechism speaks of ”intentio
superaddita,”53 in order to indicate that already at the level of choice
or the finis operis there exists a first constitutive intentionality of the
action (we have called it voluntariness).
In light of this clarification, the moral act of the action contraception, for
example, cannot be described as “to take an anti-ovulatry pill with a little
water.” This physical act alone would be the materia ex qua (certainly not
the materia circa quam) of the action contraception, but it could be equally
the materia ex qua of an action which has nothing to do with contraception,
e.g.
the therapeutic action spoken of in Humanae Vitae 15,54 or else the

Chapter 6
action of protecting oneself from the effects of acts of sexual violence which
can happen as soon as an enemy army enters into a city. If we want to know
what the action contraception is, or what the moral object of the contraceptive
choice is, we must define the purpose (the forma a ratione concepta) to which
the action responds and which it embodies, and then we must affirm that
contraception is any act that “either before, at the moment of, or after sexual
intercourse, is specifically intended to prevent procreation—whether as an end
or as a means.”55
In synthesis, this entire problem is resolved by understanding that the choice
(which is a voluntary action), like every other human act, is an intentional
reality; this expresses in other terms the metaphysical principal omne agens
agit propter finem. Voluntary action, also described in the abstract as a type
of action (theft, murder, slander, etc.), possesses an intentionality (voluntari-
ness) which constitutes it as a particular kind of act. When the constitu-
tive intentionality, or first-level intentionality, comes into contradiction with
a moral virtue (justice, temperance, etc.), the action possesses a moral nega-
tivity which no further intentions, or second level intentions (finis operantis),
can rectify. Naturally, there exist many types of action, according to their
constitutive intentionality, which are not opposed to any virtue, as is said in
what follows.
Moral Typology of the Object — According to their objects, voluntary
acts can be: 1) Good: if they are in themselves acts conforming to a virtue:
as are prayer or helping one's neighbor; 2) Evil: if they are in themselves
contrary to a virtue: theft, adultery, etc.; 3) Indifferent: if they are acts
which in themselves do not possess a special reason for being in conformity or
contrary to a virtue. Nevertheless, it should not be forgotten that indifferent
acts have in themselves a certain moral qualification, otherwise they would
be merely physical acts and not voluntary: we deal here with acts that are
compatible with the full truth of man, but which in themselves do not promote
it. In this perspective they are called licit acts, which to be truly good must
arise from a good will and be ordained to God by the agent who performs
them.
In reality, there do not exist concrete indifferent acts, for, when hu-
man acts are considered in concrete reality, their moral value is al-
ready determined by some circumstance or end. Some theologians (for
example, Saint Bonaventure) defend the existence of concrete human
actions which are morally indifferent; nonetheless, the overwhelming
majority—among whom are Saint Thomas and Saint Alphonsus de
Liguori—deny this possibility.
Saint Thomas concludes his study of
this question as follows: “Every human action that proceeds from de-
liberate reason, if it be considered in the individual, must be good or
55 Ibid., 14.


The Nature, Structure, and Evaluation of the Moral Act
bad.”56 This moral doctrine is a grand stimulus for ordering every per-
sonal activity, even those which seem indifferent, toward God.
How is the goodness or evil of the moral act's object know? Certainly, the
source of moral discernment is found in the human reason: on the foundation
of the natural practical principles and of their discursive development, it is
able to recognize and distinguish good from evil, virtue from vice.57 The natu-
ral capacity of the reason is aided by Revelation, which confirms the teachings
of right reason and instructs it with regard to supernatural goods. The Scrip-
tures concretely contrast good works, or fruits of the Spirit or fruits of faith,58
to works of the flesh: i.e. evil works, perverse works, works of darkness, dead
works.59 And more concisely: “Grave matter is specified by the Ten Com-
mandments, corresponding to the answer of Jesus to the rich young man: `Do
not kill, Do not commit adultery, Do not steal, Do not bear false witness, Do
not defraud, Honor your father and your mother.'” 60
Furthermore, the Magisterium of the Church constitutes another aid for dis-
tinguishing good actions from evil ones.61 “The Magisterium of the Pastors of
the Church in moral matters is ordinarily exercised in catechesis and preach-
ing, with the help of the works of theologians and spiritual authors [. . . ].
Alongside the Creed and the Our Father, the basis for this catechesis has
traditionally been the Decalogue which sets out the principles of moral life
valid for all men.”62 Other examples of this moral teaching are: the precepts
of the Church63; whatever violates the integrity of the human person64; the
teachings concerning marriage65; the doctrine concerning sexual ethics66; and
the different encyclicals and documents concerning socio-economic ethics.
6.4.3
The End of the Agent (finis operantis)
The Concept of the End (finis operantis) — Even if the object of every
voluntary act (intention, choice, consent, etc.) comes to be called an end, the
doctrine of the sources of morality reserves the term end for the object of only
one of these acts, the intention.67 The end (finis operantis) is the objective
for which the agent orders his action, that is, that which he wants to obtain

Chapter 6
through the chosen action or actions; it is, therefore, the motive principle of
the action. Moral theology dedicates particular attention to it, for it is the
source from which flow all human works, which are the realization (or less) of
the true love of God and of neighbor.68
In the Gospel, the moral relevance of the intention that inspires action is em-
phasized. In fact, it was a doctrine which Jesus explicitly wanted to inculcate
in His disciples, because it was in opposition to the moral teaching of His
time, both Jewish and pagan. The Gospel passage which perhaps develops
this concept the most is the argument Jesus has with the Pharisees regarding
the ritual washing of hands before eating; the conclusion is clear: “The things
that come out of the mouth come from the heart, and they defile. For from
the heart come evil thoughts. . . ”69 The reason for this primacy of interiority is
evident: man must seek the true good (ultimately God) with all his heart, all
his soul, and all his mind; therefore the most relevant aspect of moral conduct
is found in his interior dispositions.70
The end or intention of the agent—the real reason or motive of the
action—is not to be confused with other motives which can be acciden-
tally concurrent with it: one may think of, for example, the difference
between giving alms only to be seen, and this would be the end (if
others were not to see it, the person would not give alms), and giving
alms to help one's neighbor, but also with the pleasure of being seen.
In fact, along with the principal intention, there can exist concomitant
intentions or motives which do not nullify the principal end, but render
it more or less pure. In this regard, the importance of battling against
disordered concomitant intentions should be underlined. We refer to
those intentions which, if they are not fought, often lead to a change
in the primary purpose of the will; for example, to work with vanity or
a concomitant intention of “careerism” can easily turn into working for
vanity or “careerism.”
The presence of different levels of intentionality (intention and choice, vol-
untas intendens and voluntas eligens71) does not break the unity of human
conduct. It is true that the act of intention can be exercised separately from
the act of choice, as happens when one makes a firm decision to pursue a
goal which will be achievable in the future without having thought yet of the
means to be chosen to achieve that end. For example, a person in his junior

The Nature, Structure, and Evaluation of the Moral Act
year of high school decides to become a journalist, but has not thought yet
of the manner in which he will do it: to enroll at the University to study
Communication Studies, or by spending time doing apprenticeship work for a
newspaper and then, if it is requested, pursuing a degree, etc. However, many
other times the intention and the choice of means are two instances of the
same movement of the will, which could be described by one of two extremes:
by intending to achieve a goal through determinate means, in which case we
speak of the intention; or when determinate actions are chosen to achieve that
goal, in which case we speak of choice.72
In absolute terms, the intention of the end (of what is desired in itself) is more
meaningful and better reflects the disposition of the acting person's soul than
the choice of means. The perspective of morality, nonetheless, is determined
by the principle “bonum et malum sunt in rebus, verum et falsum in mente,”73
that is to say, morality sees the different instances of conduct as a process of
realization of particular goals having positive or negative value and, from this
perspective, the intention is seen as the interior planning of a good that is
achieved or negated through the chosen actions.
The managing director of a manufacturing company, for example, might
face a complicated economic problem with the intention of resolving it
in a just manner, that is to say, respecting the rights of his workers,
shareholders, creditors, etc. Then he establishes a program of action
which, in fact, does not respect the rights of all, rather one of the afore-
mentioned sets of people involved comes to be treated unjustly, and so
the initial just intention is nullified by the chosen actions. The inten-
tion of being just comes to be nullified the very moment in which, in
order to accomplish it, unjust actions are chosen. Justice cannot be ob-
tained through an injustice. The distinction between the just goal and
the unjust means, which is always analytically possible, should not be
overly emphasized, because in reality whoever wants to achieve justice
through means which he knows to be unjust, possesses an unjust will.
Whoever has planned the execution of a just goal by means of unjust
means never had a true intention for justice.74The proposed example
demonstrates that, in the order of the good, the practical execution of
the intention through the choice adds a new value, positive or negative,
to the merely planned intention: “good intentions are not enough.” The

Chapter 6
intention is a principle, to which must be added a proper discernment
concerning the concrete manner of accomplishing it.
The selection of what must be done here and now in order to accomplish an
intention often presents new difficulties and hindrances which must be over-
come. As a result, the choice, presupposing and preserving the ethical mean-
ing of the intention, adds new elements; the intention becomes reality—or else
comes to be negated—through the choice. A failure on the level of the concrete
choice could nullify a good intention, or else it could manifest the weakness
or scarce conviction of an intention that has succumbed in the face of its first
encountered obstacle. Furthermore, it is to be kept in mind that the execution
of the end through directed chosen actions can put in motion a network of
connections which cause indirect effects that are not desired, but are, rather,
foreseen and tolerated. These undesired, yet foreseen, effects can sometimes
be morally significant: we think, for example, of the cases in which the chosen
actions ordained toward a just end indirectly cause unjust situations that are
more serious than the just end which was directly willed.
From this it is understood that the intention is only a particular part (though
very important) of the internal organization and planning of the action. The
intentional planning is not only the establishment of the end, but also the
choice concerning the directed actions and the mode of performing them.
In
this sense the proper and principal act of virtue is the right choice, because
virtue requires not only a good intention, but also, and primarily, to carry
the intention to completion through right choices, that is to say, through
choices which truly execute the virtuous intention.75 The person would enter
into contradiction with himself if he intended to accomplish justice through
injustice or purity through impure acts.
The unity of the person implies
ethical consistency between intention and choice.
These considerations allow one to understand exactly the Gospel teaching that
interior intentions manifest themselves through their fruits, which are exterior
works: “So by their fruits you will know them.”76 At the end of the Sermon
on the Mount, the moral “magna carte” of Christianity, the Lord explicitly
said “not everyone who says to me, 'Lord, Lord,' will enter the kingdom of
heaven, but only the one who does the will of my Father in heaven [. . . ].
Everyone who listens to these words of mine and acts on them will be like a
wise man [. . . ]. And everyone who listens to these words of mine but does

The Nature, Structure, and Evaluation of the Moral Act
not act on them will be like a fool.”77 That is, from love, or good intentions,
there consistently follow good works.78
It needs to be underlined that the works of which the Bible speaks are
not something abstract, but very concrete: to be noted the different
lists of what must be done or not done, beyond what is said in the
Sermon on the Mount, found in: Rom 1:22–32; 12:6–21; 1 Cor 10:7–11;
Gal 5:19–22; 1 Pt Ch. 2, 3 and 4; etc. Throughout history there were
sects which sought to affirm a morality without the effort of concrete
works: nevertheless the attempt to establish a morality on two isolated
planes, i.e. a morality of intentions and a morality of works, was always
destined to be unsuccessful; it entailed not having understood deeply
the dynamic of the will and, still worse, to have disregarded the words
of Jesus, for it is clear that such attempts do not have the least bit
of scriptural foundation, as was recently affirmed by Veritatis Splen-
dor, 82.
The Role of the End in Moral Evaluation — The moral quality of the
end for which an action is chosen affects the morality of the action in different
ways depending on the moral qualification of the choice. Actions which are
indifferent in their object become good or evil on account of their end.79
Actions that are good in their object (e.g. friendly behavior), on account of
their end can become: 1) morally better: e.g. to make friends out of love of
God, for helping a neighbor, for finding companions in a sport; 2) morally
worse: on account of disordered concomitant motives; e.g. to make friends
with (and not for) the vainglory of being more popular; 3) evil: e.g. to make
friends in order to find accomplices for a robbery. Regarding this, the Gospel
speaks of the hypocritical “virtues” of the Pharisees;80 “an added bad intention
(such as vainglory) makes an act evil that, in and of itself, can be good (cf.
Mt 6:2–4).”81
An action which is evil in its object can become more or less evil through the
intention: and so Jesus says “Father, forgive them, they know not what they

rhetorical discourses. To speak and to promise is easy for anyone, but it is not likewise
easy to perform, moving toward action, one's ideas. Why have I said this? Because, up
until this day, there are many who say they fear and love God, while with their works they
demonstrate the opposite: God, instead, asks to be loved also with works. For this reason
Jesus said to the disciples: `If you love me, observe my commandments.' For he had first

enough to ask, he added: `If you love me'. `Only under such a condition—he says—will I
do it'” (Saint John Chrysostom, In Ioannem Homilia, 75, 1: PG 59, 403), our translation.

Chapter 6
do”;82 but it can never become good: “If acts are intrinsically evil, a good
intention or particular circumstances can diminish their evil, but they cannot
remove it. They remain 'irremediably' evil acts; per se and in themselves
they are not capable of being ordered to God and to the good of the person
[. . . ]. Consequently, circumstances or intentions can never transform an act
intrinsically evil by virtue of its object into an act 'subjectively' good or
defensible as a choice.”83
In reality, the person who knowingly chooses an action contrary to a virtue
never has—except in cases of invincible ignorance—a morally good intention:
in such cases the intention is only apparently good, and the reasons which are
given for acting have, at their base, more the character of self-justifications
than reasons for acting in that way.84
6.4.4
The Circumstances
Beyond the two principal elements of the moral act, there exist a set of sec-
ondary elements that influence its morality: the various personal and environ-
mental conditions, the appearance—attached to the principal intention—of
diverse secondary motives, the time or place in which the action is executed,
etc. All these elements constitute the moral circumstances, which are also
components of the human act but of a secondary moral value.
The Bible
takes account of this reality when, beyond the essential elements, it reaffirms
the importance of such concomitant factors: the value of the widow's mite, the
difference in fault between Pilate and the Pharisees, the greater responsibility
of the person who is placed in a position of authority.85 The consideration
of the moral circumstances allows us, furthermore, to adequately understand
man's behavior in concrete situations, the behavior of a being who acts in his
own environment and in continuity with his temporal existence.
Following S.Th. I-II, q. 7, a. 3, the moral circumstances can be grouped
into two categories:
82 Lk 23:34; cf. Mt 11:20–24.
83 Veritatis Splendor, 81.
Saint Paul said that one cannot do evil, even with a good
intention (Rom 3:8) and Saint Thomas writes: “No evil done with good intention can be
excused” (In Duo Praecepta Caritatis, 6, n. 1168; cf. S.Th. I-II, q. 88, a. 6, ad 3). In fact,
“A good intention (for example, that of helping one's neighbor) does not make behavior
that is intrinsically disordered, such as lying and calumny, good or just. the end does not
justify the means. Thus the condemnation of an innocent person cannot be justified as a
legitimate means of saving the nation.” (CCC, 1753).
84 “Quando aliquis vult malum propter bonum, illud bonum non est finis actus voluntatis,

85 Cf. Mk 12:41–44; Jn 19:11; Titus 1:5–9.


The Nature, Structure, and Evaluation of the Moral Act
1. 1) Circumstances which regard the moral object:
 time (quando): a late act of service loses some of its effectiveness;
 place (ubi): it is not the same to insult a person in public as in private;
 quantity of the object (quantum): economic value of the stolen goods;
 effects of the action (quid): the alms a person receives save him from
grave physical or moral danger.
2. Circumstances which regard the agent:
 condition of the subject who acts (quis): example of the widow's mite;86
“it is not the same when a person who has the advantage of the Holy
Spirit and is filled with His benefits incurs a fault [. . . ] than when the
same transgression is done by a person without such privileges”;87
 mode of acting (quomodo): e.g. the order and intensity of exercising
one's duties88, or else to act deliberately in contrast to acting with ob-
scured reason on account of a vehement passion;
 means employed (quibus auxiliis): for the employment of more effec-
tive means implies a greater voluntariness for doing good or evil; e.g.
the good Samaritan adopts extraordinary means for helping the injured
man;89
 circumstantial motives (cur): e.g. to perform a service out of courtesy,
but expecting a certain recognition or compensation is less meritorious
than doing it for charity and absolute benevolence.90
The morality of human action does not only depend on the object or the end,
but also on the moral circumstances. However, not all of the morally relevant
circumstances are in the physical order, but there are also circumstances of
the moral order: a physical circumstance can be morally irrelevant in certain
cases (if the thief is married) and relevant in other cases (if the person who
fornicates is married). Sometimes it happens that something which would
seem to be a circumstance in reality modifies the moral essence of the act and,
therefore, is no longer a moral circumstance in a strict sense (e.g. a theft in a
Church is a sacrilege: its own moral object). The Council of Trent recognized
this when it prescribed that grave sins should be confessed in the sacrament
86 Cf. Lk 21:1–4.
87 Saint John Chrysostom, In Matthaeum Homilia, 26, 7: PG 57, 341, our trans-
lation.
88 Cf. Lk 19:17,19.
89 Cf. Lk 10:34–35.
90 Cf. Mt 5:44–47.


Chapter 6
of penance along with circumstances capable of changing the species of the
acts.91
Strictly speaking, moral circumstances exist as accidents of the moral act,
whose substantial morality is provided by the object and end. Thus, they
increase or diminish the goodness or evil of the act, without however ever
rendering an evil act to be good, or a good act to be evil, and without changing
its moral or theological species.92
We just spoke of there being circumstances that cannot be considered acci-
dental elements of the moral act. These are aspects which change the moral
species of the action. Therefore, sins of theft do not all pertain to the same
moral species: there is simple theft, robbery (with violence), and sacrilegious
theft. In general terms it can be affirmed that a circumstance is that char-
acteristic which would have no relation with the moral order if it did not
accompany something which in itself already possesses a relation of confor-
mity or opposition with the virtues. For example, that there is much or little
money is morally significant only if it is stolen money, that is to say, the
amount stolen is morally significant and not the amount of money in itself.
In contrast, if a determinate quality is the primary reason for which an action
is opposed to the moral order, such a quality constitutes the moral object.
For example, if a person interrupts a religious ceremony by singing a popular
song (which he could freely sing at home when he likes), it would not be said
that the chosen action was that of singing, and that the presence of a religious
ceremony was a circumstance of place: the moral action (genus moris) that is
considered in contrast to the virtue of religion is the interruption of a religious
ceremony, and singing is a circumstance (the means employed for interrupting
the act). The circumstances which change the moral species of the action are
in truth elements of the very essence of the act's moral object.93

in Response to the Debate

consequentialism and proportionalism because they deny the existence of acts
which are intrinsically evil, as well as the absolute value of ethical norms
which forbid such acts.94 “[T]he opinion must be rejected as erroneous which

without taking into account the intention for which the choice was made
or the totality of the foreseeable consequences of that act for all persons

Without the rational determination of the morality of human

`objective moral order' and to establish any particular norm the content of
which would be binding without exception.”95 The encyclical seems to want
to put in relief the concrete doctrinal motivation of this expressed judgment,
and therefore explicitly affirms that these two ethical theories are not faithful
to the doctrine of the Church, inasmuch as their methodologies have justified,
as morally good, “deliberate choices of kinds of behaviour contrary to the

Starting from a simplistic conception of the problem raised by proportional-

Some authors have erroneously thought

cannot be willed as such and must be justified in relation to the entire action

“a moral judgment can be formulated only from a simultaneous considera-

The realization of the three elements (a. Taking money from another person,
b. Who is very poor, c. To please a friend) is not the combination of three
human actions, which can be evaluated separately, but constitutes a single
human action.”102 A moral norm, in order to be truly universal, must take
account of all three elements in all their breadth, but this is “theoretically
impossible,” and for this reason in the moment of the application of a norm

As diverse authors have noted,104in the reasoning of McCormick and Fuchs
there is an error regarding action theory, which perhaps was inherited from a
certain strand of moral casuistry. The error consists in the physicalist consid-
eration of the moral action (the killing in itself, which Fuchs speaks about),
deprived of the significance of its voluntariness, a void which they try to over-
come by adding elements taken from the person's intentionality (finis operan-
tis), the circumstances, and consequences of the act. McCormick and Fuchs
are right in stating that an action described in a purely physicalist way (with-
out voluntariness) could not be evaluated morally, because it is not a human
action, given that human action is an essentially voluntary reality. However,
instead of seeking to understand voluntariness (and therefore the morality) as
intrinsic to the action (which they took away in order to consider the action
as a pre-moral reality) they want to introduce voluntariness (and therefore,
morality) only on the basis of the agent's intention, on the circumstances, and
the foreseen consequences. As Rhonheimer wrote, for these authors human
action—as a voluntary and therefore moral reality—would be the sum of a
physical, or physically described, action (the killing in itself) plus the attitude
of the person toward an end (the finis operantis of the manualistic tradition,

Therefore, the clarification made by the above-cited editorial can be under-
stood perfectly: “Providing guidelines for understanding the moral object,
the encyclical cautions about consequentialism and proportionalism as the-

as to accept, first, an undue moral neutralization of the chosen action and,
then, its constant redefinition based on ulterior intentions and consequences.
In such a way, an argumentative context is constituted which certainly does
not deny the principle that the end does not justify the means, but renders
it practically inapplicable. It is this complex methodological operation which
is to be absolutely rejected.”106
6.5
The Morality of an Act's Effects
The voluntariness of an action carries with it, at least in a certain measure,
the voluntariness of the effects which come about because of such an action.
A moral evaluation of an action must keep in mind the morality of its conse-
quences. The problem that can be presented is very complex. Moral theology
has drawn some criteria that may help us solve these problems from the living
tradition of the Church and the many concrete experiences and reflections on
life contained therein.
6.5.1
The Moral Imputability of the Consequences
The problem we face is in knowing when one is morally responsible for good
or bad consequences of an action or omission of action. Even if this theme is
rather broad, here we shall limit ourselves to indicate five principles that may
help us to resolve the cases that are more frequently presented.107
1. We are responsible for the negative consequences of our evil actions,
even if these consequences were not foreseen: though having been fore-
seeable.108 We could have avoided them if we had done what is good or
if we had not done an evil action. When someone throws a person to
the ground to rob from him, and as a consequence the attacked person
105 Cf. M. Rhonheimer, Intentional Actions and the Meaning of Object (1995), 286–287.
106 “La ricezione della «Veritatis Splendor» nella letteratura teologica” (1995), 1.
107 We follow here the more essential aspects of the more broad study offered by M. Rhon-
heimer, The Perspective of Morality (2011), 385–389.
108 Cf. CCC 1736.


Chapter 6
dies from the fall, then the thief is responsible for his death, even if he
only intended to rob him: not intending to kill him.
2. The good consequences of evil actions cannot be ascribed as merit to
the agent. For example, a thief will not be praised or awarded who,
committing theft in a place where he does not expect anyone to be
present, collaterally prevents a terrorist from leaving an explosive device
there that could have hurt many people.
3. We are not responsible for the unforeseeable negative consequences of
our good actions.109 Such consequences are simply not intentional, as
long as we really could not predict them. The policemen that uncover a
crime and bring a criminal to justice are not responsible if the criminal,
once in prison, commits suicide.
4. We are not responsible for the foreseen negative consequences of the
omission of an evil or forbidden action. Whoever rejects someone else's
bribe is not responsible for the illicit actions which that other person
does in order to get what he desires, even if they are more immoral.
5. One is not culpable for the foreseen negative consequences of a good
action, so long as the action meets the conditions proposed in our dis-
cussion of the principle of double effect.
6.5.2
An Action of Double Effect
A recurrent reality of daily life is the existence of acts which, beyond their
desired effects, have also consequences which are not desired, but tolerated
for love of the good effect which is sought; this type of action can also be
called a “voluntarium indirectum” or “indirect voluntary act.” 110 The moral
problem is present when one of these effects which are not desired appears
as an ethical evil: for example, to sell a gun to someone who can use it to
steal something. The question which is posed is: when is it licit to perform
an action which beyond its good effects involves something which is morally
evil?
We can specify some summary conditions which must be fulfilled—all to-
gether—in order for it to be licit to perform an action (or to not act) when
this also provokes an evil effect.111 These are:

110 Cf. what was said above in subsection 6.2.2.

1. The performed act must be good in itself, or at least indifferent: the
morality of the action in itself has priority over the effects; for this
reason, before studying the goodness or evil of the effects the act itself
must be considered, otherwise any act could be licit which here and now

2. Good effects cannot be accomplished through an evil action: We should
not do evil that good may come of it.112
If good comes about from
evil, the evil is not “indirectly voluntary” but rather willed directly as a

3. The person must directly will the good effect (i.e. have a good intention),
and accept reluctantly and tolerate grudgingly the evil effect. There-
fore, the person must do whatever possible to avoid, or at least limit,
the evil effect. This is so because people do not will things in a general,
but rather a concrete manner: in a free agent “the intention is directed
