Therefore, if a particular good that is intended has attached to it, ei-
ther always or frequently, a privation of good according to reason [thus
voluntary or morally qualified], then the result is a moral evil; and not
by chance, but either invariably or for the most part.” 114
4. There must exist proportionality between what is intended and the evil
which is tolerated: it is not morally justified to risk one's own life to
earn a few dollars, nor to put pregnancy in danger in order to avoid

has many immoral publications than it is to invest it in a bank which
has partial ownership of that publishing company; c) the greater the
certainty of the evil effect: e.g. selling alcohol to a drunk person; d) the
sis, this would not always be possible if one ignored the role of the “indirect voluntary” act.

6.6
The Psychological Integrity
of Human Action
and Its Moral Imputability
Having exhausted our study of the evaluation of voluntary action regarding
its matter (object, end, circumstances), and its consequences, we now shall
move on to concern ourselves with the elements which guarantee or limit the
subjective imputability of an action.
6.6.1
Notion of Moral Imputability
To impute means to attribute an action to a person.
Imputability is the
quality which an action has of being attributed to someone or, more exactly,
the state of the person inasmuch as he is the source of the action, in virtue
of which this action is to be attributed to him as its author. If the action
can be attributed as merit or moral fault we have moral imputability, which
does not exactly coincide with juridical imputability.115
Only free actions
are morally imputable: man can answer for (give reasons), to himself and to
others, only for actions which he himself has planned or organized. That is
to say, he should only feel responsible for the actions which can be attributed
to him as their author, and in the measure in which he is their author. Now
it is of interest to us to study certain conditions and circumstances of the
agent which modify the freedom of an action and, consequently, its moral
imputability. These are conditions or circumstances of diverse origin which
directly or indirectly impact, at least partially, the essential elements of a free
act, i.e. formal knowledge of the end and voluntariness, diminishing or even
annulling the freedom to act or the act's imputability.
6.6.2
Circumstances Regarding Knowledge
that Modify Moral Imputability
Advertence and Its Different Types — Relating to the formal knowledge
of the end, we need to first consider the role of advertence (moral awareness-
knowledge) and ignorance. Advertence is the mental act through which the
115 Juridical imputability also depends on certain provisions of the civil law. A person can
be obligated, by civil law or the sentence of a judge, to pay restitutions for damages caused
by an action which was not voluntary, and therefore without having committed a moral
fault. In such a hypothesis there is juridical imputability but not moral imputability.


The Nature, Structure, and Evaluation of the Moral Act
person recognizes what he is going to do or what he is doing, as well as the
morality of his action. Regarding moral advertence it is fitting to keep in
mind the following distinctions:
1. Regarding its intensity, i.e. for the degree of the person's knowledge of
his act and its morality:
(a) full advertence: when the person clearly recognizes both what he
does and the morality of his act;
(b) partial advertence:
when there are obstacles which render full
moral awareness to be difficult, without annulling it; e.g. partial
drunkenness, a state of sleepiness or great agitation;
(c) inadvertence: when the obstacle totally impedes the person's aware-
ness.
2. Regarding its mode: this refers to the aspect of the human act grasped
by advertence; it is not the same thing, for example, to know the traffic
rules and nonetheless not see a stop signal; or to recognize a yellow
stripe, but not know that it means that parking is forbidden. For this
reason we can distinguish between:
(a) advertence (or inadvertence) of the law: to know (or not know) the
existence of a moral law; for example, to know that Sunday Mass
attendance is a serious obligation;
(b) advertence (or inadvertence) of the fact: to recognize (or not rec-
ognize) a concrete act, while knowing the law relating to it; for
example, to know (or not know) that today is Sunday.
3. Regarding its actuality:
(a) actual advertence: knowledge of the act and of its morality in the
moment in which the person performs it;
(b) virtual advertence: is present when there previously was an adver-
tence that still influences the act, however it is not present in the
moment of acting; for example, the advertence of one's destination
when he is traveling. Many of our actions are performed only with
virtual advertence.
4. Regarding its extension:
(a) distinct advertence (or clear): when there is a precise advertence of
the ethical particulars of an act; for example, to pay a debt while
aware of it being an obligation of justice;


Chapter 6
(b) generic advertence (or confused): when there is advertence only of
the goodness or evil of the act, without exactly distinguishing the
specific morality; for example, when it is understood that paying
taxes is good, without knowing that it is an obligation of justice.
Moral Principles Concerning Advertence —
1. An action is morally imputable if it is performed with at least virtual
advertence, for this is sufficient for guaranteeing the free nature of the
act. Moreover, it is not possible to always have actual advertence in
all our actions. Virtual advertence is also sufficient for committing a
mortal sin or performing a heroic virtuous act. Actual advertence is per
se a cause of greater voluntariness, but per accidens a virtual knowl-
edge can generate a more intense moral act; for example, the virtual
advertence of a father who works intensely for a long time for his family
involves a greater voluntariness than the actual advertence of a little act
of courtesy in social life.
2. Generic advertence of the morality of an action is sufficient for the moral
act: though it is not knowledge of the specific morality of an action, it
is a knowledge which nicely distinguishes good from evil.
3. Partial advertence diminishes freedom, and therefore diminishes the im-
putability of an act. In fact, for a sin to be mortal, there must be full
advertence, which is not to be confused with reflexive awareness of hav-
ing offended God: it is sufficient to be fully advertent—but perhaps in
confuso—that the action is evil, that it is not good to do it, that it is
not congruent with the teachings of the Lord, etc. Moreover, partial
advertence is not the same as inadvertence; the former, in fact, does not
completely take away freedom and, therefore, acts done with it are still
partially imputable; for example, a sin which is mortal in itself, if done
with partial advertence, becomes venial.
Ignorance — Another problem is that of ignorance. Here there does not
exist an obstacle which impedes the application of the act of knowledge which
one normally possesses, but, rather, an erroneous understanding of the cir-
cumstances of the action and, above all, its morality. That is, an action which
is in reality evil is considered good, or vice versa. Ignorance will be studied
in Chapter X, when we treat of moral conscience.


The Nature, Structure, and Evaluation of the Moral Act
6.6.3
Circumstances Pertaining to Voluntariness
that Modify Moral Imputability
Non-Voluntary, Involuntary, Mixed Voluntary Actions — At
this point we know what a voluntary action is. Right now it needs to be
added that an action is called non-voluntary in order to indicate the sim-
ple lack of voluntariness. The most frequent cause of non-voluntariness
is ignorance of the concrete circumstances of an action, principally of
its object. Whoever uses a tree as a shooting target and injures a dog,
whose presence in proximity of the tree was not recognized, does not
hurt the dog voluntarily, for such an effect was never the object of a
positive or deliberate act of his will. Such actions do not pertain to
the ambit of formal morality, though they can have a certain degree of
imputability insofar as non-voluntariness admits of diverse grades.
The concept of an involuntary action adds another element to that of a
non-voluntary action. This element is contrariety or opposition of the
involuntary action to the act or habitual disposition of the person's will.
One of the most frequent causes of involuntary action is violence, but
also ignorance of the concrete circumstances of an action. This happens,
for example, when a person feels great pain after having realized that
he has done, without knowing it, something which he never would have
wanted to do, as it was against his own sentiments, convictions, etc.
More frequently the actions are performed by a healthy person, in whom
the voluntariness and involuntariness are mixed together: these are
called mixed actions. Mixed actions are free actions that do not how-
ever respond to the free initiative of the person. They are actions done
on account of the difficult situation the person finds herself in, and
they are done only after having overcome a certain amount of repug-
nance, for they are opposed to the person's desires, and therefore would
not be performed outside of the particular situation in which they are
performed. Aristotle fully described this type of action.116 From the
116 It is helpful to include here what he has to say: “But with regard to the things
that are done from fear of greater evils or for some noble object (e.g. if a tyrant
were to order one to do something base, having one's parents and children in his
power, and if one did the action they were to be saved, but otherwise would be put
to death), it may be debated whether such actions are involuntary or voluntary.
Something of the sort happens also with regard to the throwing of goods overboard
in a storm; for in the abstract no one throws goods away voluntarily, but on condition
of its securing the safety of himself and his crew any sensible man does so. Such
actions, then, are mixed, but are more like voluntary actions; for they are worthy
of choice at the time when they are done, and the end of an action is relative to
the occasion. [ base or painful in return for great and noble objects gained; in the

end or for a trifling end is the mark of an inferior person. On some actions praise
indeed is not bestowed, but pardon is, when one does what he ought not under
pressure which overstrains human nature and which no one could withstand. But
some acts, perhaps, we cannot be forced to do, but ought rather to face death after
the most fearful sufferings; for the things that 'forced' Euripides Alcmaeon to slay


Chapter 6
moral point of view, it should be added that pressures of a situation
do not in themselves eliminate the moral imputability of an action, but
sometimes they can reduce or even eliminate it, if the terrors or other
passions caused by the proximate peril impede or diminish the use of
the reason.
Consent and Types of Consent — We mean by consent the essential
element of voluntariness: the free direction of the will (approval, acquiescence)
toward the good (real or apparent) presented by the reason. Consent is found
to be intimately connected with advertence: the latter being a condition of
the former. However consent is not a pure redundancy of advertence, for the
will can intend the known good more or less intensely, and choose from among
diverse goods. Consent pertains both to the intention of the end, and to the
choice of the directed actions (means). For practical purposes, the following
distinctions are important:
1. Regarding the degree of consent:
(a) perfect consent: the will adheres fully to the act, at least in its
essential aspects;
(b) imperfect consent: entails the partial adhesion of the will: either
because the will does not adhere fully to the object, or because it
follows a partial advertence.
2. Regarding the actuality of the consent: this is analogous to the divisions
for the actuality of advertence (see above), in reference to the will and
not to knowledge.
It is also to be remembered that consent can be in reference to the indirect
effects of the will, of which we spoke previously.
Moral Principles Concerning Consent —
1. Imperfect consent, which follows a partial advertence or full advertence,
but with an incomplete acquiescence of the will, is sufficient for the
morality of the act. This is so because the will has dominion over its
own act and, therefore, if there is advertence and there does not exist vi-
olence, the act is to be considered voluntary and imputable. Certainly
imperfect consent still diminishes the positive or negative morality of
the act.
2. For mortal sin, which involves a great evil with serious consequences,
there needs to be perfect consent; notwithstanding, as has been said, it
his mother seem absurd.” (Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics, III, 1: 1110 a 3 - 28; trans.
W.D. Ross, http://classics.mit.edu//Aristotle/nicomachaen.html).


The Nature, Structure, and Evaluation of the Moral Act
is compatible with a certain reluctance and mixed voluntariness. Within
the essential perfection of the consent there exist diverse accidental
grades: a sin of passion is not the same as a sin of malice; in these cases
the intensity of the will influences the degree of the morality, without
changing the species of the act.
3. The reality of our free nature implies that, with normal advertence and if
there does not exist external coercion, consent can be said to be perfect
when the act is accomplished externally.
In acts which do not have
an external manifestation it is more difficult to appreciate the level of
perfection of the consent; nonetheless there exist some signs, which can
help in cases of doubt (i.e. when the person, in good faith, is not sure
to have perfectly consented):
 a perfect consent which changes deep personal behavior is, appar-
ently, clear; in doubt, it is presumed that the person in a state of
grace did not sin gravely (perhaps he did so only venially), and the
person in a state of sin has committed a new sin; analogously if a
person who battles to be holy doubts if he has performed an act of
worship in a mindless habitual manner, it is probably not the case,
but is fully voluntary;
 with partial advertence, the consent is presumed to be imperfect,
even if the act is external; for example, in a state of sleepiness or
partial drunkenness;
 if it is easy to accomplish the exterior act, and it is not done so, it
must be supposed to be an imperfect consent.
We shall return to some of these concepts when sin is dealt with specifically
(Chapter XI).
6.6.4
Relation of the Passions to Moral Imputability
The Passions in General — It is possible to formulate some principles
regarding the influence of the passions on moral imputability that are useful
for casuistry.117 The principles are as follows:
1. The antecedent passions, in the measure in which they disturb the reason,
diminish the responsibility of the act; for example, an angry person says
and does things which he would not do if he were calm. If the passion
completely impedes the use of the reason, it annuls imputability, though
117 Here we use concepts and distinctions which were studied in Chapter IV subsection
4.4.4.


Chapter 6
this does not happen frequently; sins committed through antecedent
passions are called sins of weakness and, though still potentially mortal,
are less grave than those committed deliberately.
2. Concomitant passion, which spontaneously follows the voluntary act,
does not affect responsibility; nonetheless it is a sign of the intensity of
voluntariness.
3. Consequent passions increase imputability, for they were provoked freely
in order to act more easily; for example, to excite one's anger in or-
der to attack with more violence. Here can be included those passions
which seem to be antecedent, but in reality are voluntary in their cause,
as when a person does not want to reject the thought of a fault com-
mited against him immediately so when he finds the offender again, he
is immediately angry.
Special Study of Fear — Fear merits a special consideration, which can
have notable repercussions for the will, comparable to those of violence, di-
minishing and in some cases even annulling moral responsibility.118 Fear can
be serious or mild according to its intensity, which is, however, rather sub-
jective: what is serious for one person, is rather mild for another. It can be
just to cause fear in another (a police officer might justly frighten a thief), or
it can be unjust, when in itself or its intensity it is not caused by a just or
proportionate motive.
Regarding the relation between fear and moral imputability, the following
principles can be considered:
1. Fear diminishes voluntariness— though normally does not annul it—
according to its subjective or objective gravity; for example, to do good
through fear of punishment is less meritorious than to do it with full
voluntariness.119
2. Positive law does not oblige in cases of grave fear, for it does not oblige
cum grave incommodo; for example, a person does not sin who does not
go to Mass for fear of his life. However, such laws oblige with mild fear;
for example, when a person does not go to Mass for fear of getting a
chill.
118 Cf. CCC, 1735.
119 The good done only through fear is not meritorious for lack of a good intention; while
an evil done only for fear is less grave, but is not fully inculpable, for “the love of God
entails the obligation to respect his commandments, even in the most dire of circumstances,
and the refusal to betray those commandments, even for the sake of saving one's own life”
(Veritatis Splendor, 91).


The Nature, Structure, and Evaluation of the Moral Act
3. Negative moral laws (which regard intrinsically evil acts) oblige even
with grave fear; for example, it is not licit to apostatize even for fear of
death.
4. To overcome fear is a sign of greater voluntariness, as would be the case
of helping a person who is very sick, even while having fear of contracting
a contagious disease.
5. Fear can render null or at least rescindable certain acts which, for their
importance and consequences, require full freedom. So, for example, a
marriage contracted under the pressure of a grave fear that is unjustly
caused would be invalid.
As we have said, these principles exclusively regard the relation between the
passions and moral imputability. From other perspectives other considerations
would be possible. It may be enough to consider, for example, that the person
who does not succeed in overcoming fear, according to the demands of a
healthy realism and due trust in God, should often run into characterological
problems that are not of little importance: from anxiety to pusillanimity, from
mild neurotic forms to more profound personality disorders. Also from this
perspective the virtuous regulation of the passions always comes to coincide
with the balance and maturation of the person.120
6.7
Meritorious Moral Actions
6.7.1
Merit in Sacred Scriptures
The term merit indicates the due retribution for an action or conduct. Sacred
Scriptures rigorously emphasizes that the Creator owes nothing to the crea-
ture, but likewise clearly teaches that God rewards good human actions and
punishes evil ones.121 The Old Testament uses different terms which pertain,
with more or less exactness, to the idea of retribution: reward, chastisement,

place to the grace of God, then to the faithful.” 134 The grace of God is the
first spring of every human merit.135 The Saints have always had a living
awareness that their merits were pure grace.136
6.7.2
The Content of Merit
What is the content of merit? Man who, helped by grace, gives himself to
God in good actions, receives as recompense the gift of the same Lord, that is,
a more profound union with the Most Holy Trinity: “Whoever loves me will
keep my word, and my Father will love him, and we will come to him and
make our dwelling with him”;137 and this is exactly the grace which makes a
person “come to share in the divine nature.”138 To the increase in sanctifying
grace is added an increment of actual grace, which is a transient aid on the
path toward sanctity. On the other hand, because grace is the seed of blessed

Thus supernatural merit is the title given to supernatural good acts performed

Theology distinguishes between de condigno merit, i.e. due in justice, and de
congruo merit, which supposes a certain suitability, but still takes account of
the generosity of the giver. The supernatural order exceeds so greatly human
action that de condigno merit in a strict sense is proper only to Jesus Christ;
regarding the rest of us we can speak instead of de condigno merit founded
on the gratuitous divine promise, through which, if the person accomplishes
good works, and in virtue of the Redemption, he has a right to receive eternal
life and the increase of grace and of glory:140 “Filial adoption, in making us
partakers by grace in the divine nature, can bestow true merit on us as a
result of God's gratuitous justice.”141 De congruo merit is not born from a
proportionality—even in virtue of the promise— between action and reward,
but from pure divine generosity, inasmuch as it becomes suitable that good
works are rewarded. Included in this merit are the grace of conversion, the
grace of final perseverance, and the grace which one can merit for others.
Given that the grace of God is the first spring of every human merit, “no one
can merit the initial grace of forgiveness and justification, at the beginning
of conversion. Moved by the Holy Spirit and by charity, we can then merit
for ourselves and for others the graces needed for our sanctification, for the
increase of grace and charity, and for the attainment of eternal life. Even
temporal goods like health and friendship can be merited in accordance with
God's wisdom. These graces and goods are the object of Christian prayer.
Prayer attends to the grace we need for meritorious actions.” 142
6.7.3
Conditions for Merit
The conditions for human action to be susceptible of supernatural merit are:
1. That it is a human act: without freedom, there is no merit, because no
one merits a reward if he does not act with full freedom and responsi-
bility.
2. That it is a good act: only acts directed a God have the promise of
retribution; this does not entail that the action actually be directed
toward God, for, as was said, a virtual intention is sufficient; though

renewing a good intention so that it is as actual as possible is a great

3. That it is an act of the person as viator: “For we must all appear before
the judgment seat of Christ, so that each one may receive recompense,
according to what he did in the body, whether good or evil.” 143
4. That the action is performed by a person in a state of grace: as was
said, only charity accomplishes the union with God which is the root of
all merit. A person in a state of sin can only have de congruo merit.144
5. For the same reason, the measure of merit depends on the quality of the
person's love.145 A more arduous action does not entail greater merit
in itself, though the degree of difficulty can be a sign of the degree of
charity in the act.146
6. If the doctrine of merit is understood correctly, the Christian will never
become an egotistical “reward seeker”: the Christian does not love for
merit, but merits because he loves.147 Nonetheless, because the sought

to the Christian. Sacred Scripture, in praising Moses (and other righ-

why the thesis that it is a sin to desire merit was condemned.149 In the
depths of the believers soul there will always be a supreme aspiration as
sung by the psalmist: “your face, Lord, do I seek!” 150

## CHAPTER 7 {#colom-scelti.7}
The Moral Virtues and the
Gifts of the Holy Spirit
7.1
The Virtues in the Catholic Theological
and Moral Tradition
7.1.1
Origins in Greek Philosophy
Virtue (aretê) is one of the fundamental concepts of Greek philosophical
anthropology and ethics, where it means the moral excellence of a per-
son. Originally, the Greek language knew a more broad use of the term
virtue, which could express the excellent qualities of things, animals,
men, or divinities. Already with Socrates it was employed with a more
restricted meaning to refer particularly to moral excellence, understood
prevalently as knowledge of the good which could be communicated
through teaching. In this line, Plato develops the classification of the
four virtues: prudence, fortitude, temperance, and justice,1 which have
gone on to be celebrated in western philosophical thought. In a rather
critical dialogue with the Socratic-Platonic tradition, Aristotle carried
the doctrine of the virtues to their most complete classical expression.
For him, virtue is the habitual and stable (héxis) perfection of the hu-
man operative faculties: both the intellectual faculties (dianoetiche or
intellectual virtues) and the appetitive faculties (ethical virtues). Hu-
man life lived according to the virtues represents for Aristotle the best
mode of living for humans—the good life, or happiness. The stoic tradi-
tion would take up the doctrine of the virtues, particularly insisting on
the harmony between the life according to the virtues and life according
1 Cf. Plato, Republic, Bk. IV: 427 E, 433 B-C, 435 B, etc.


Chapter 7
to nature. In this direction, Cicero's work De Officiis was of notable
importance for its influence on some Christian writers.
7.1.2
Sacred Scriptures
The Hebrew language does not possess a correspondent term to the Greek
word aretê. The Greek version of the Old Testament, the Septuagint, uses
the word aretê to translate certain Hebrew expressions which almost always
mean the glorious action of God. In the books of the Maccabees, the term
aretê is often employed to mean the fidelity of God, as well as courage, virility,
and prudence. The Greek influence is rather evident in the book of Wisdom:
virtue is contrasted with vice,2 and put in relation with immortality,3 while
the four platonic virtues are also mentioned: “[I]f one loves justice [in a generic
sense to mean sanctity], the fruits of her works are virtues; For she teaches
moderation and prudence, justice and fortitude. . . ” 4 As far as the Old Testa-
ment is concerned, a virtuous man acts with the power and vigor (virtus) of
the divine Spirit, as is seen, for example, in the messianic oracle of Isa 11:2:
upon the Messiah will rest a spirit of wisdom and understanding, of counsel
and fortitude, of knowledge and fear of the Lord.
In the New Testament the term aretê is seldom used. In 1 Pet 2:9 and in 2
Pet 1:3 it is applied to God. In two other passages, Phil 4:8 and 2 Pet 1:5,
it refers to the good behavior of Christians. Nonetheless, there are numerous
catalogues both of virtues and vices, which summarize the moral attitudes
that are congruent, or not, with the Christian life: concretely, in the New
Testament there are found at least fourteen catalogues of virtues5 and twenty-
one catalogues of vices.6 Though the vices listed are many, and not always the
same, their common denominator can be recognized as an inordinate love of
self, which leads to the satisfaction of the desires of the “flesh”: lust and greed,
which become sorts of idolatry that produces envy, quarrels, dissensions, etc.
In general terms, it can be affirmed that the Scriptures underline that the
direct effort toward virtue does not begin with man himself, but with God: the
Christian virtues are explicitly connected with the action of the Holy Spirit;
they are the “fruits of the Spirit,”7 because under His influence we await the
hope of justification through faith working through charity.8 For a Christian,

The Moral Virtues and the Gifts of the Holy Spirit
not only the origin, but also the end of the principal virtues is God Himself;
these are the theological virtues, the soul of the Christian life: “[C]alling to
mind your work of faith and labor of love and endurance in hope of our Lord
Jesus Christ.”9
Many passages in the New Testament emphasize that through the virtues,
the Christian walks according to the example of Christ.10
The perspective
of the virtues can well constitute “the human and rational prerequisite for a
Christocentric morality of charity, which allows one to overcome a morality of
pure obligation and makes it possible to unite the natural and supernatural
dimension.”11
Within the study of the virtues in light of the Scriptures, a distinction
must be made between virtue as moral excellence and virtue in connec-
tion with the philosophical/anthropological doctrine of the habits
as
perfections proper to the human operative faculties. From the first point
of view, it cannot be denied that the Bible underlines more often ethical
excellence as a set of possessed and integrating qualities of the person's
moral being and, therefore, the concept of “righteousness” corresponds
to the person who practices the virtues and not so much to someone
who simply adheres to an external norm. The Old Testament is not
lacking in concrete descriptions of virtuous or vicious behavior and the
examples of virtuous persons are highlighted: Abraham, Moses, Ruth,
Judith, etc.; there is also praise and stigmatization of attitudes proper
to the virtues or vices, especially in the prophets and wisdom literature.
For example, Sirach speaks of fear of God (Ch. 1), patience (Ch. 2),
humility (Ch.3), mercy (Ch. 4), sins to avoid (Ch. 7), prudence (Ch.
8), avarice (Ch. 14), lying (Ch. 20), laziness (Ch. 22), lust (Ch. 23),
honesty (Ch. 27), temperance (Ch. 31), etc. The New Testament also
assigns the title of “righteous” (holy) to different persons: Abel, John
the Baptist, Joseph, Zachariah and Elizabeth, Simeon,12 etc. The Ser-
mon on the Mount appears as a summary of the moral attitudes proper
to Jesus's disciples, nonetheless taking account of the fact that Chris-
tian life is not an accumulation of disparate good acts, but a unitary
interior disposition which is made concrete in singular actions.13 Be-
tween the exalted moral and religious qualities of the Sacred Scriptures
and the moral qualities considered virtuous by ethical philosophy there
exists a notable convergence. It could not be otherwise, for the perfect-

of the saint.14
On the other hand, for what regards a habit as a category of philosophical
anthropology, there is not found an explicit treatment in the Bible. Revela-
tion intends, primarily, to transmit a moral and religious teaching, and not to
furnish the philosophical categories suitable for a systematic comprehension
of the moral life as a human and Christian phenomenon.
This is a prob-
lem that remains open to further theological elaboration, as we shall see in
what follows. Now we would like to point out that the concept of virtue is
more congruent with the moral message of the New Testament than the dis-
cussions about moral normative foundations (sometimes deontological, other
times teleological) which are so prevalent in contemporary ethics.
7.1.3
The Fathers, the Magisterium,
and the Theologians
The Fathers saw in the virtues the stairs to climb from the earth to Heaven
and dispositions for achieving identification with the Lord: “The end of a
virtuous life consists in becoming similar to God.” 15 The virtues are necessary
for reaching the goal to which God calls us16; and, in turn, they are already a
certain actualization of the divine call, inasmuch as they make man similar to
the unique and perfect model who is Jesus Christ; the human virtues do this as
well, because He is also “perfectus homo.” The cardinal virtues which, perhaps
under other names, are praised in other passage of the Scriptures,17 form a
part of the Christian tradition.
Among the Fathers of the Latin Church,
the contributions of Saint Ambrose18 and Saint Augustine were important.
The Augustinian definition of virtue was, in fact, the most used by Christian
writers in the Middle Ages: “Virtue is a good quality of the soul through
which we live rightly, which cannot be used for evil, and which God produces
in us without us.”19 Among the Fathers of the Church, moreover, it was very

poverty, patience, etc., would constitute a further and decisive confirmation of it.
15 Saint Gregory of Nyssa, Orationes de Beatitudinibus, 1: PG 44, 1199 D. Our transla-
tion.
16 “The certain road for reaching beatitude is virtue” (Saint Thomas, Compendium The-

19 This definition was formed by Peter Lombard (Liber Sententiarum, II, d. 27, c. 5) and

of the reflections of Saint Augustine in Chapter 19 of the second book of the De Libero
Arbitrio (NBA 3/2, 275). Saint Thomas Aquinas uses it for an example in S.Th. I-II, q.
55, a. 4 and in De Virtutibus in Communi, a. 2.


The Moral Virtues and the Gifts of the Holy Spirit
much debated whether or not the acquired human virtues, separated from
charity, could be considered true virtues.
The concept of virtue is frequently used by the Magisterium of the Church and
by Christian catechesis to refer both to the theological virtues—faith, hope,
and love—and to the ethical qualities which, in the Christian, are connected
to the former. “The human virtues are rooted in the theological virtues, which
adapt man's faculties for participation in the divine nature: for the theological
virtues relate directly to God. They dispose Christians to live in a relationship
with the Holy Trinity. They have the One and Triune God for their origin,
motive, and object.”20 There are many other documents that could be cited
which express the moral perfections of man in terms of the virtues.21 Leo
XIII, for example, speaking of Jesus Christ, affirms: “From contemplation
of this divine Model, it is more easy to understand that the true worth and
nobility of man lie in his moral qualities, that is, in virtue; that virtue is,
moreover, the common inheritance of men, equally within the reach of high
and low, rich and poor; and that virtue, and virtue alone, wherever found,
will be followed by the rewards of everlasting happiness.” 22
Regarding theology, it may be enough to remember that Saint Thomas consid-
ers the principles of Christian life (faith, hope, and love) as theological virtues
and, with this in mind, his most mature theological synthesis, the Summa
Theologiae, is structured according to the theological and moral virtues. He
not only takes up what was said concerning the virtues in his time period, but
also takes up and integrates into a theological context the specific originality
of Aristotelian ethics as an ethics of virtue, while introducing into it some
important modifications.23 From the time of Saint Thomas on, the treatment
of the virtues was an integrating part of moral theology, even if the specific
characteristics of virtue ethics were not always well understood and often were
lost along the road. This has created significant problems for moral theology,
and even biblical theology, as we have already seen.24
Today, there is no shortage of authors—and in some theological envi-
ronments it has become commonplace—who retain that the concept of
virtue is irreparably marked by a sense of a self-affirmation or purely
human ethical achievement which renders it unusable for moral theol-
ogy. In light of the preceding considerations—and primarily in light
of the use of this concept by the Fathers, by the Magisterium, and by
the Catholic theological tradition, wherein they have been inserted into

7.2
The Moral Virtues
7.2.1
Intellectual and Moral Virtues
We shall move now to an initial description of the virtues and their diverse
types, in order to deepen our understanding of the concept of moral virtue. In
general terms, virtue can be defined as a good operative habit.25 An operative
habit is a stable disposition of a human faculty (the intellect, the will, the
sensible appetites), through which it is well or poorly structured regarding
the actions proper to it. The habits which perfect the human faculties are
the virtues; the habits which, instead, denigrate them are the vices.
The
virtues perfect the operative powers so that they can accomplish good and
excellent actions with ease, readiness, pleasure, and naturalness in different
circumstances and before diverse objects. Understanding virtue in this sense,
Aristotle considers virtue as that which renders good its possessor and his
work.26 All of the virtues, inasmuch as they are operative habits, distinguish
themselves from entitative habits, which are qualities which well dispose (or
poorly dispose) the nature of man, and not the faculties directly; so, for
example, sanctifying grace is a supernatural entitative habit, infused by God,
which elevates human nature, rendering it a mediated principle of actions
proper to a child of God.
Among the operative habits (virtues) there need to be distinguished the su-
pernatural or infused virtues, which man receives from God as a gift linked
to grace, and the virtues which are human and acquired by man through his
own exercise and personal effort. We shall occupy ourselves with the infused
virtues in section 5 of this chapter. As regards to the human or acquired
virtues, they can be either intellectual or moral: the intellectual virtues per-
tain to the reason and perfect it both in its speculative aspect as well as its
practical aspect, whereas the moral virtues perfect the will and the tenden-
cies. Prudence,27 justice, fortitude, and temperance are the principal moral
virtues—referred to as the cardinal virtues.
The virtues of the speculative reason are: 1) the habits of the first
speculative (intellect) and moral (synderesis) principles; 2) the habit of
considering things in relation to the ultimate causes of all reality (wis-
25 Cf. S.Th. I-II, q. 55, a. 3.
26 Cf. Nicomachean Ethics, II, 6: 1106 a 15ff.
27 Even if prudence perfects the reason, for its object it is a moral virtue, as will be
explained in what follows.


The Moral Virtues and the Gifts of the Holy Spirit
dom); and 3) the habit of studying the ultimate causes of each genre of
things descending from them to conclusions (the diverse sciences). The
habits of the practical reason are: 4) prudence (recta ratio agibilium),
which determines and dictates what must be done in each concrete case
in order to act in a virtuous way, and 5) art (recta ratio factibilium –
techne), which teaches us how to produce determinate objects well. The
distinction between prudence and technical knowledge presupposes the
distinction between acting (agere) and making or producing (facere).
The intellectual habits provide the capacity for working well, but do
not ensure the right use of this capacity: for it is possible to utilize
science or technology to do evil. For this reason, such habits do not
fully exemplify the essence of virtues, which must be a quality which
renders its possessor morally good. The exception is the virtue of pru-
dence because, although it is an intellectual habit with reference to the
faculty to which it pertains (practical reason), it is a moral virtue for
its object and inasmuch as rectitude of the will is an essential prereq-
uisite of it. The task of prudence is not that of knowing what would
be necessary to do if one desired to do good, but rather to direct right
action; its principal act is not judgment, but command, through which
it guides the other powers in accordance with the demands of moral
virtue. Prudence cannot exist if the person does not first wish to be
virtuous, and in this sense it presupposes a good will and, as we shall
see, the other moral virtues.
7.2.2
Definition of Moral Virtue
We can now take on the study of what more directly interests moral
theology, the moral virtues. It will be a study of the philosophical foun-
dations held by Saint Thomas that will, nonetheless, take full account of
the data of Revelation, as well as Christian experience. Such a concept
of moral virtue is proper to Aristotle, and was easily taken up by Saint
Thomas, because it responds to the topic—so important in Christian
life—of the achievement of moral excellence, a theme which arises in
both ethical philosophy and moral theology.
Saint Thomas performed the study of the moral virtues on the basis of
his psychology of the faculties (the reason, the will, the irascible and
concupiscible appetites).
We can complete such a study—primarily
from a descriptive and phenomenological point of view—in the light of
what was said in Chapter 5 regarding the tendencies and sentiments.
Man possesses an innate desire to arrive at the fullness of the human condition.
The Christian, in virtue of faith, knows broadly what holiness is, union with
Christ: through hope and love he desires and loves such a union. However, a
problem immediately arises as to how to govern the tendencies, and regarding
which goods one should tend toward in order to accomplish union with Christ
on a daily basis, in the multiplicity of personal and social circumstances: in


Chapter 7
the situations in which one finds himself, oftentimes situations which are new
and truly unforeseeable that push him to make a choice often rendered more
difficult on account of the tendencies and sentiments involved. In this regard,
it is possible to point out some actions which should never be done (intrinsi-
cally evil actions, always incompatible with life in Christ). However, it is not
possible to determine in advance all that each man must choose in order to
accomplish, day by day, union with Christ,28 both on account of the complex-
ity and variability of the good to be performed in diverse circumstances, and
also on account of the unique “tendential” and characterological equilibrium of
each individual person. Individuality implies both richness and limits at the
same time: “The reason for the deficiency and inadequacy of man's operative
capacities to perform good acts is found in the disparity which individua-
tion introduces between man's operative capacity as such and the operative
capacity of this or that individual person.” 29
Definitively, the concretization in operative terms both of the human good
and of life in Christ requires that the individual is capable of deliberating and
judging correctly regarding circumstances, persons, things, affections, etc., in
order to identify and make the right choices.
In order to ensure the con-
crete accomplishment of moral excellence, teachings and general rules are not
enough.
A special perfection in the order of concrete choices and circum-
stances is necessary. Such a perfection is moral virtue, which therefore comes
to be rightly defined as “an elective habit which consists in a middle term
relative to us, and which comes to be regulated by right reason in the form
in which it would be regulated by the truly prudent man.” 30 This definition
