The Moral Virtues and the Gifts of the Holy Spirit
contains three elements which we shall study in the following three subsec-
tions.
7.2.3
Moral Virtue as a Habit of Good Choice
In the first place, we shall note that moral virtue is an “elective” habit (héxis
proairetichê). Elective means “pertaining to choice,” and choice is an act of the
will which we have already studied,31 which consists in the determination of
the action to perform in view of a further end. Elective habit means, therefore,
a habit of good choice, or rather, a habit of a good choice of action,32 a stable
disposition which permits the identification and making of right and excellent
choices in every moment and circumstance, a specific perfection of the human
capacity of choosing or preferring. In practical terms, this means three things:
1. Virtue cannot be conceived as a thoughtless habitual response or as an
addiction. It is not an automatism which mechanistically inclines the
person to always repeat the same actions. Ethical conduct as an ad-
diction would be completely insufficient for human and Christian moral
life, also for the reason indicated in the preceding subsection.
2. The proper and principal act of a virtue (even if it is not the only act,
as we shall see shortly) is the good choice.33 The acts of the intellectual
virtues—for example, the formulation of a scientific proposition—are ob-
jects of choice (I choose to take on the task of developing a mathematical
theorem), but do not in themselves regard choices. Here we mean by
choice both the choice of action and also the choice of a sentiment or
passion.
3. In order to be able to speak of virtuous actions there must not only be
an exterior act conforming to a norm, but also a determinate mode of
action. Concretely, it requires: a) knowledge of what one does; b) to
interiorly choose the action as such, i.e. inasmuch as it is good here and
now; c) to act with firmness and constancy, without shrinking before
obstacles.34 With regard to virtue or vice, voluntariness35 and interior
choice must be judged more than exterior action, although virtue de-
mands both; this is because an exteriorly correct action may proceed
from virtue, but also from ignorance, chance, or a distorted intention.
On the other hand, a virtuous choice might not come to effective fruition
31 Cf. Chapter VI, Section 6.3.
32 Cf. M. Rhonheimer, The Perspective of Morality (2011), 198.
33 Cf. S.Th. I-II, q. 58, a. 1, ad 2; q. 65, a. 1; In Decem Libros Ethicorum, lib. II, lect.
7, n. 322.
34 Cf. In Decem Libros Ethicorum, lib. II, lect. 4, no. 283.
35 Cf. Chapter VI, subsection 6.1.2.


Chapter 7
because the situation does not demand it or for motives that are extra-
neous to the will and to the foresight of the person who acts.
In light of these three characteristics, it can be said that moral virtue adapts
itself to the freedom proper to the action that perfects it. Indeed, moral virtues
are in themselves a principle of elective (choosing) action: each person finds
choosable the type of action to which he is inclined by his own habit, given that
this renders his object to be connatural and lovable to him.36 For this reason,
moral virtue does not bypass deliberation or choice, but rather guarantees
that both are good. Virtuous action is performed easily, but not instinctively
or automatically, but always in an “elective” way, because this is how the
virtues' respective faculties operate.
It remains to be explained how it is possible to perfect and guarantee
the rectitude of a capacity, such as the capacity of choosing, which by
nature remains open to diverse possibilities, and whose concrete content
cannot be fixed universally or in advance. This complicated problem
will be studied shortly (section 7.3 of this chapter), after the other
elements of the definition of a virtue have been studied.
7.2.4
The Medium Term or Mean of Moral Virtue
It is said that moral virtues consist in a medium term (in medio virtus) because
their elective act—primarily for what regards the affections—must conform
itself to the dictates of right reason, and the measure imposed by the reason
can be surpassed (in a negative way) or not reached (again in a negative way)
by the spontaneous movements of the powers lacking in virtue.
Regarding the cardinal virtues of fortitude and temperance we treat of
a “medium rationis” (a mean of reason), not because the reason is at-
tracted to a middle point at the moment of establishing what would
satisfy the tendencies in a suitable way here and now, but because the
judgment of the reason guides the sensible tendencies, whose acts come
to be directed toward a middle point. That is to say, it is discovered
that these tend toward their object with an impulse which is neither
greater or less than that indicated by the reason.
For example, the
mean of the human virtue of temperance with respect to nutrition con-
sists in the desire of necessary nourishment to preserve health, and this
requires both that one avoids gluttony as well as the opposite defect
of an unhealthy lack of appetite. The mean is not the same for each
person but it comes to be established by prudence in the particular case
according to the condition of each individual; therefore, in the definition
of a virtue it speaks of a “medium term relative to us.” In the virtue
of justice, whose object is a right (that which is due to another) the
36 Cf. S.Th. I-II, q. 78, a. 2.


The Moral Virtues and the Gifts of the Holy Spirit
medium rationis coincides with the medium rei, for here excess and de-
fect in the actuation of a tendency are not what is regulated, but rather
a thing (a right) is regulated and this right can be violated through
excess or defect: the just person is he who renders to each his own,
neither more nor less.
7.2.5
The Regulation of the Mean by Right Reason
According to the definition of moral virtue which we are now studying, the
medium term relative to us “comes to be regulated by right reason in the form
in which it would be regulated by a truly prudent man.” The act of the virtue
(that is to say, the execution of the tendency conformed to virtue) comes to
be identified and commanded by a judgment of the reason, and not just any
reason, but by right reason, i.e. by the practical reason perfected by the moral
virtue of prudence. We already knew that it is up to the reason to interpret,
evaluate, and direct affective phenomena.37
Prudence is the virtue which
perfects the practical reason in the accomplishment of this task. It comes to
be rightly called “auriga virtutum”, the guide of virtue; in a similar way the
Bible praises the prudent person38 and underlines that prudence pertains to
the Lord.39
We shall occupy ourselves with prudence several times. For now it is enough
to note that the moral virtues, considered all together as being like an organ-
ism, are the principle of excellent choice not only inasmuch as they guarantee
that such a choice will be made and taken to completion but, even more so,
inasmuch as they allow for the identification of the choice to be made here
and now. Moral virtues have an important cognitive aspect, and are not in
any way just a simple disposition that helps to accomplish a course of action
that has been identified without them. The anthropological foundation of the
cognitive dimension of ethical virtues is, as we know by now,40 the antic-
ipating character proper to the tendencies and the valuations contained in
the sentiments. Ethical virtues take advantage of this anticipation and pen-
etration of affectivity for a good purpose. On the other hand, even if it is
possible to achieve knowledge in the abstract of what should never be done
because it is opposed to the essential demands of virtue (adultery, for exam-
ple), and such knowledge can be transmitted through teaching (for instance,
catechesis), without the moral virtues it is not guaranteed that such universal
knowledge will become in the person a personal conviction, firm and practical,
to which he may always adapt himself with his own behavior. Practical moral
conscience presupposes a well-educated affectivity. The person in whom such
37 Cf. Chapter V, subsection 5.4.3.
38 Cf. Prov 3:13, 21; Sir 18:27–29; Mt 24:45–47; Titus 2:5.
39 Cf. Job 12:13; Prov 8:14; Isa 40:14.
40 Cf. Chapter V, subsection 5.4.1.


Chapter 7
a predisposition does not exist will not adapt himself to the aforementioned
moral knowledge in practice, and in the end will neither understand it even
in theory.
7.3
The Habitual Perfecting of Choice
through the Moral Virtues
7.3.1
The Two Dimensions of Moral Virtue
We shall now move on to explain how the moral virtues can habitually perfect
human choices. To put it simply, such a perfecting is only possible if, firstly,
the principles of excellent choice are guaranteed and, secondly, obstacles that
are opposed to it are removed. Keeping mind of what we studied in Chapters
V and VI, the habitual perfecting of human choices requires:
1. The habitual intention of a good end, and the removing of obstacles
which are opposed to such an intention.
This makes it so that the
tendencies and the will are rightly ordered in a stable manner.
2. The habitual capacity of identifying the action or actions through which
the right end can be performed here and now, and the neutralization of
the elements which get in the way of identifying the right choice. These
obstacles are in good part constituted by the influence of the preceding
passions on the practical judgment of the reason.41
3. The choice and performance of the action indicated by the prudential
judgment.
Consider, for example, a lawyer who works along with other colleagues
in a law firm, who is habitually overcome by the deformation of the
tendency to be esteemed by others which we have called the anxiety of
notoriety.42 The habitual deformation of the intentionality at the base
of that tendency is a principle of repeated concrete, mistaken choices:
each time that the lawyers must study together a strategy to follow in
order to resolve a case entrusted to the firm, this lawyer obstinately
holds onto his own opinion, and the desire that his opinion prevail and
become shared by the others frequently makes him lose his objectivity,
without him clearly being aware of it, and this often leads to not only
a few problems and failures. In a virtuous person, on the other hand,
the base intentionality of that tendency is habitually ordered, and this
means that she certainly desires that her own opinions be received by
41 Cf. Chapter V, subsection 5.4.4.
42 Cf. Chapter V, subsection 5.2.3.


The Moral Virtues and the Gifts of the Holy Spirit
others with respect, even when they are not shared by those same per-
sons, but primarily that they come to be appreciated and evaluated for
their real value. The tendency, then, remains dependent on the reality
of the things, on the value and reasonableness of the given opinion. This
attitude is in itself a principle of right choice, which at least avoids an
important cause of errors of judgment.
The habitual right ordering of the tendencies according to the measure of
truth and reasonableness (right reason) is the first task performed by virtue
ethics, and such a task we shall call the intentional dimension of virtue,
because it consists in rendering habitually right the base intentionality of the
tendencies.43 The right habitual intention generally cannot have as an object
a concrete behavior, because this depends on the circumstances.44 What is
proper to a virtuous person is his habitual search for, and subordination to,
truth, justice, and reasonableness (right reason). Nonetheless, this, though
being necessary for virtue, is not sufficient. Starting from right intention there
must yet be performed the second and more important dimension of virtue,
that is, the elective dimension.45
One can then say that moral virtue is the habitual desire of right ends (in-
tentional dimension) and choices of action which accomplish them (elective
dimension), because the ends of virtue are fixed and universal (justice, truth,
reasonableness, etc.), while the concrete actions necessary for accomplishing
them vary in diverse occasions and circumstances.46 We shall now see more
specifically way how the virtues act on both levels.
43 Cf. In Decem Libros Ethicorum, lib. VI, lect. 10, nos. 1269 & 1273. Thus writes a
famous commentator of Saint Thomas: “To render the intention of the ends of virtue right
pertains to the same virtue, not as their consummated and final act, which is the choice
(virtue, is in fact an elective habit), but as their first and undeveloped act, through which the
appetite is well disposed for the virtue with respect to its good” (John of Saint Thomas,
Cursus Theologicus, ed.
Solesmes, 1938, Isagoge, vol.
I, 171).
And in the same sense
Cajetan writes: “In electione ipsa clauditur intentio finis, quoniam electio est eorum quae
sunt ad finem propter finem [ quod in definitione, dum dicitur quae est habitus electivus,
implicite dictum est quod etiam intentivus finis est” (Cajetan, Commentary on the “Summa
Theologiae”, I-II, q. 58, a. 5, Comm. IX).
44 Thus, in the first cited example, it cannot be said that a virtuous person always re-
nounces her own opinion in order to adopt that of her colleagues. There will be cases in
which the person is certain that she is right and, for the good of all, must insist on defending
her own opinion. There will be other times in which insisting on one's own opinion would
be unreasonable obstinacy.
45 Once the virtuous lawyer of our example takes on the aforementioned problem with
righteous intentions, that is to say, seeking to resolve the problem in accord with truth and
justice (and not seeking other ends: for her own opinion to prevail, or to obtain at all costs
the most earnings possible, etc.), it must be, in the first place, that prudence determine
what is demanded by justice in this concrete occasion, and afterwards the choice recognized
by prudence must then come to be made and brought to completion, even if this carries
with it sacrifices and difficulties.
46 For the good of all, sometimes one must insistently defend his own opinion; sometimes
it would be unreasonable to do so.


Chapter 7
7.3.2
The Intentional Dimension of Virtue:
Prudence Presupposes the Moral Virtues
The moral habits perfect, in the first place, the basic intentionality of the ten-
dencies and the will in the measure in which each person has need of them.
The ethical virtues, as an interconnected whole, make it so that all of the ten-
dencies studied in Chapter V (tendency toward nourishment, sexual impulse,
tendency toward possession, desire to know, tendency toward work, etc.) be
turned toward their object (food, sexuality, useful goods, knowledge, work,
etc.) not in the absolute, i.e. for any cost or without any measure, but that
they habitually seek them within the limits of reasonableness, that is to say,
in the measure and mode in which right reason considers them proper for the
good of the person who acts and for other persons involved.
Saint Thomas refers to the intentional dimension of virtue when he affirms
that the moral virtues are the necessary prerequisites of prudence. He means
to say that if the tendencies and the will are not well ordered in a stable way,
not only will it not be possible to perform what is good, but neither will the
person successfully identify what would be good to do in a concrete case. A
person habitually overcome by thirst for power or profit, or else by the desire
of controlling others, etc., will act in a mistaken way with great naturalness,
without being able to understand that he should have acted differently.
The other intellectual virtues can still exist without the moral virtues
(one can be a good mathematician without being courageous or without
being moderate), but this is not the case with prudence. “The reason
for this is that prudence is the right reason about things to be done (and
this, not merely in general, but also in particular); about which things
actions are. Now right reason demands principles from which reason
proceeds to argue. And when reason argues about particular cases, it
needs not only universal but also particular principles.” 47 Saint Thomas
explains in what follows that with regard to universal principles we are
well disposed by moral knowledge, but the same thing cannot be said
with regard to particular principles, so that practical knowledge of the
good is subject to the influence of the personal dispositions. And so he
concludes: “so, in order that he be rightly disposed with regard to the
particular principles of action, viz. the ends, he needs to be perfected
by certain habits, whereby it becomes connatural, as it were, to man to
judge aright to the end. This is done by moral virtue: for the virtuous
man judges aright of the end of virtue, because 'such a man is, such
does the end seem to him' (Ethic. iii, 5). Consequently the right reason
47 By “universal principles” we mean here moral ideas of a general character; for
example, justice imposes that we respect the property of others. “Particular princi-
ples” are instead the virtuous desires which constitute the point of departure for the
concrete and circumstantial reasoning which each individual person performs here
and now, and which leads to action.


The Moral Virtues and the Gifts of the Holy Spirit
about things to be done, viz. prudence, requires man to have moral
virtue.”48
In the same sense, Saint Thomas affirms that the virtuous ends are the princi-
ples of prudence49, in an analogous way to how the first speculative principles
are the prerequisites of all scientific reasoning. The ends of the virtues are the
principles of the personal moral knowledge that directs conduct, or practical
knowledge in the strictest sense of the term. By “virtuous ends” we mean
here the modes of rational regulation of the tendencies, sentiments (passions),
and actions, required for the full success of human and Christian life, and
which generically (i.e. without departing from the concrete actions which here
and now are required) we call prudence, justice, humility, sincerity, fortitude,
generosity, temperance, etc.50
The virtuous end is not a principle of prudence if one considers it as a theoret-
ical proposition that forms the major premise of a syllogism or as an abstract
value. What is properly a principle of practical reasoning is a desire for an
end, insofar as the moral virtues—in their intentional aspect—consolidate
the desire for virtuous ends: it is said, then, without these there cannot be
prudence. The last practical judgment concerning what is here and now suit-
able, in fact, cannot avoid taking account of the person's actual desires. The
correctness of the final practical judgment can be guaranteed only if the per-
son's habitual rectitude of desire is guaranteed (the intentional dimension of
virtue).51 Nonetheless, the moral virtues are not sufficient alone for there to
be prudence. That is, the right habitual ordering of the tendencies of the will
is indeed a necessary, but not a sufficient, condition.
In summary, the intentional dimension of virtue produces a stable orientation
of the appetites and tendencies that allows one to deliberate without any ob-
stacles coming from the virtues' ends. In contrast, vice carries with it poor
judgment, not only of this or that act, but fixes in the soul a distorted pur-
pose, which can be translated in its extreme as, “all that is pleasurable should
be enjoyed,” “all difficult efforts should be avoided,” etc., taking as its point
of departure those things about which the reason imprudently deliberates in
an habitual way. The function of virtue is not therefore merely negative—to
48 S.Th. I-II, q. 58, a. 5.
49 Cf. In Decem Libros Ethicorum, lib. X, lect. 12, no. 2114; S.Th. I-II, q. 65, a. 1, ad
4.
50 Cf. the explanations furnished by G. Abbà, Felicità, vita buona e virtù (1995), 244–
250.
51 “From this it results that, in order to have the habit of forming such a judgment, a
good habitual inclination of the appetitive faculty is necessary; that is, moral virtue. This
is the reason for which prudence, as is called the habit relative to this judgment, even if it
is essentially an intellectual virtue, constitutes nonetheless, in a material and prerequisite
mode, a moral virtue, inasmuch as it supposes the rectitude of the appetite and has as an
object the morally good acts proper to it.” (A. Millán Puelles, Fundamentos de filosofía,
6th Ed., Madrid: Rialp, 1969, p. 654, our translation).


Chapter 7
impede the obstacle of the passion—but also positive: to establish a right
desire as a practical principle.
Something different happens with a person who does not possess either
virtue or vice: which is the case, for example, with those whom Aris-
totle and Saint Thomas call continent or incontinent persons. In these
two persons there are present a set of demands of right reason and of
concupiscence, and for this reason Aquinas says that they implicitly
utilize a practical syllogism that concludes in one way or another ac-
cording to what prevails on each particular occasion, the reason or the
passion. In both cases the reason commands: “You should not commit
any sin” and the concupiscence at the same time suggests: “Seek plea-
sure!” The incontinent man is overcome by the passion, assuming the
principle which it proposes, and so deliberates and concludes: “this is
pleasurable, therefore, it is suitable for me to do it.” The continent man
succeeds in resisting concupiscence, deliberates, and concludes accord-
ing to the demands of reason: “This is contrary to virtue, therefore I
shall avoid it.”52
The continent man does well, but not virtuously, because he lacks the
firm and peaceful possession of the principles of good deliberation and
action; and for this reason his action remains imperfect, full of bat-
tle and restlessness, not fully in harmony with the good life.53
The
incontinent man acts poorly, but with less immoral intent than the in-
temperate person (who possesses the vice of intemperance). Aquinas
affirms that the incontinent person acts eligens (choosing) and not ex
electione (from choice)54because his evil action is not the logical result
of a stable possession of the principles of evil work, but of a momen-
tary passion—to which he has certainly consented—which compels and
distorts the deliberative-elective genesis of the action. The intemperate
man, instead, peacefully makes decisions contrary to virtue out of a
possessed habit.
All of this is a consequence of the different dispositional influence the
passions and habit exercise on the practical reason. Antecedent passion
is per se an irrational element which, due to the disorder of sin, tends
to disturb the decisional process, being able to render it imperfect or
evil. Moral habit is, for its intentional aspect, a principle of the prac-
tical activity of the reason freely acquired or preserved, and therefore
the reason does not suffer violence from it as regards its psychological
normalcy. A good moral habit (virtue) is an imprint of the right rea-
son in the person's affectivity, which permits a peaceful and positive
integration of affectivity according to right reason. Vice is, in contrast,
the imprint of a reason given over to the attractions of the passions,
and so it gives rise to moral evil to whomever consciously and freely
52 Cf. De Malo, q. 3, a. 9, ad 7; In Decem Libros Ethicorum, lib. VII, lect. 3,
nos. 1328–1353.
53 Cf. S.Th. I-II, q. 58, a. 3, ad 2.
54 Cf. S.Th. I-II, q. 78, a. 4, ad 3.


The Moral Virtues and the Gifts of the Holy Spirit
brings together and organizes its powers in order to procure for himself
pleasure or fulfill his egoistic desires.
7.3.3
The Elective Dimension of Virtue:
The Moral Virtues Presuppose Prudence
Starting from the stable desire for virtuous ends, prudence can identify the
action which here and now accomplishes the virtuous end, in a way that
can be chosen and taken to completion (elective dimension of virtue).
If
the intentional dimension of moral virtue is a prerequisite of prudence, then
prudence is at the same time a prerequisite of the elective dimension of the
moral virtues.
On account of its dependence on the virtuous ends, truth reached by prudence,
called practical truth, possesses a particular nature. In a similar way to how
the speculative reason is right in the measure in which it conforms to its
own principles, practical reason is right when it adheres to its own, which
are the virtuous ends; from which it results that practical truth consists in
the conformity of the reason to right appetite, that is to say, to the desire
for the virtuous end.55 In his commentary on the Nicomachean Ethics, Saint
Thomas explains that the relationship between right appetite and practical
reason is the relationship between the moral virtues and prudence. To say
that practical truth consists in the conformity of the practical reason to right
appetite is the same as affirming prudence's dependence on the moral virtues.
This dependence seems to create a vicious circle, since prudence presupposes
the moral virtues and the moral virtues presuppose prudence. The circle is
resolved by taking into consideration the two aspects of virtue, the inten-
tional and elective aspects: “The rectitude of the appetite with respect to the
end [intentional aspect of virtue] is the measure of the truth of the practical
reason [prudence], which itself is measured according to its conformity with
right appetite. This truth of the practical reason is then the measure of the
appetite's rectitude with regard to the means [elective aspect of the virtues].
For this reason, we call right appetite that which pursues what is indicated
by right reason [vera ratio].”56 In one sense, the virtues are the measure of
right reason and, in another sense, right reason (prudence) is the measure of
the elective act of virtue. The apparent circle is resolved, but nevertheless
this opens the door to an important problem regarding to the formation of
the virtues in man, as we shall soon see.57
The concept of practical truth must be understood attentively. It ex-
55 Cf. S.Th. I-II, q. 57, a. 5, ad 3.
56 In Decem Libros Ethicorum, lib. VI, lect. 2, no. 1131. The clarifications within the
square brackets are ours.
57 Subsection 7.4.3 of this Chapter.


Chapter 7
cludes not only the idea that a subjectively right intention is enough
—with which the person wishes to do well or believes herself to be act-
ing well and is nonetheless found in error—but also the idea that an
objectively right intention is enough. The conception delineated up to
now, characterized by a strict relation between virtuous ends and pru-
dence, underlines the unity and coherence of the practical reason. The
same reason that has as its specific principles the virtuous ends is also
that which determines what here and now should be done (prudence).
In fact, it can determine what here and now must be done inasmuch as
practical reasoning has its point of departure in the desire for virtuous
ends and, through a process of always greater concretization, comes
to the point of determining the concrete action whereby here and now
justice, temperance, etc., are realized. The virtue of prudence renders
perfect the maximally concrete moment of the practical reason: the
judgment concerning the choice of what to do here and now. The fact
that right choice is the principal act of ethical virtue means that in
practical reasoning, directed toward action, the desire for the virtuous
end (therefore, the right intention) is the initial phase of a process that
culminates in the concrete and particular action. A good intention can
succumb or go astray before its first encountered obstacle, out of a lack
of either conviction or prudence.58
From these considerations we can draw two conclusions. The first is
that the determination of the action to be done not only is not an
ethically neutral activity, but it is the object of the specific virtue of
the practical reason as such, the crossroads of all moral action, since,
on the one hand, it presupposes the intentional dimension of ethical
virtue and, on the other hand, it is the condition of the possibility
of their concrete realization. The second conclusion is that the unity
and coherence between the intention and choice is the normal operating
condition of the practical reason. The reason which determines an end is
the same which determines the most suitable action for achieving that
end, and the same unity exists between the voluntas intendens and
the voluntas eligens. Practical reasoning starts from the virtuous end
(justice, temperance, etc.) and per se concludes in a just and temperate
choice.59 For this reason, according to the normal functioning of human
moral action, an erroneous choice presupposes a moral disorder of the
will,60 because the virtuous end (justice, temperance, etc.) is properly
affirmed or denied in the concrete choice. Imprudence—i.e. reasoning
and practical judgment which conclude in a choice contrary to virtue—is
a moral fault, and not a technical error of valuation.
Analogously,
habitual imprudence is a vice.
58 Remember what was said in Chapter VI, subsection 6.4.3.
59 Reason, per se, functions well, also with regard to morals. Saint Thomas affirms
that for this reason “perversitas enim rationis repugnat naturae rationis” (In decem
libros Ethicorum, lib. II, lect. 2, n. 257), and also that “corrupta ratio non est ratio,
sicut falsus syllogismus non est syllogismus” (Scriptum Super Sententiis, lib. II, d.
24, q. 3, a. 3, ad 3).
60 Cf. CCC, 1761 and Veritatis Splendor, 78.


The Moral Virtues and the Gifts of the Holy Spirit
It remains to be added that to the judgment and command of prudence follows
the elective act of virtue, the virtuous choice conformed to the dictates of
prudence. We treat of a choice of action which can imply also an actuation
of sensible affectivity, which will then be a consequent passion.61 It is to be
noted, then, that each appetite which can be reached by the control of the
command of prudence can as such participate in the virtuous choice. The
actuation of the virtuous habits of sensibility are identified, therefore, with a
deliberate appetite, that is to say, with a sensible aspiration (desire, joy, fear,
etc.) preceded by deliberation and by a commanding judgment of prudence,
and for this reason such an actuation is morally excellent.62
7.3.4
Virtuous Ends as Natural Principles
of Practical Reason
We must now highlight an important question. We know that virtuous choice
is regulated by prudence, and that the truth of the commanding judgment
of prudence consists in conformity with the virtuous ends. This brings us to
the question: How are the virtuous ends determined? What is the measure
of the intentional dimension of moral virtue? The response to this question
is that the knowledge of the virtuous ends pertains to the natural reason and
precedes prudence, as the understanding of speculative principles precedes sci-
ence.63 The human practical reason has, therefore, some natural principles
that constitute the cognitive point of departure for both practical reasoning
and the process of forming the virtues. In such a sense, Saint Thomas “affirms
that both prudence and the ethical virtues depend on reason inasmuch as it is
natural, i.e. inasmuch as it is naturally capable of conceiving and prescribing
general virtuous ends of the good life and certain types of actions, absolutely
required or excluded by such ends.”64 The natural conception of the virtuous
ends is an important part of the “practical nature” of man, and constitutes
the fundamental content of the natural moral law, a topic we shall have more
to say about in the third part of this book.
61 Cf. Chapter V, subsection 5.4.4.
62 Cf. De Virtutibus in Communi, a. 4, ad 1. John of Saint Thomas affirms that it is
the mission of moral virtues “reddere appetitum sensitivum promptiorem ad recipiendam
rectam electionem” (Cursus Theologicus, in I-II, d. 15, q. 2, n. 39). See also: Cajetan,
Commentary on the “Summa Theologiae”, I-II, q. 56, a. 4.
63 This thesis is sustained by Saint Thomas in S.Th., II-II, q. 47, a. 7; De Veritate, q.
5, a. 1 and in Scriptum Super Sententiis, lib. III, d. 33, q. 2, a. 3. Regarding these
texts, see A. Rodríguez Luño, La scelta Etica (1988), 50–55. This is one of the points in
which Saint Thomas adds important developments to the Aristotelian theory of the virtues:
cf. regarding this point G. Abbà, Quale impostazione per la filosofia morale? (1996), 66;
M. Rhonheimer, The perspective of Morality (2011), Ch. V, section 1.
64 G. Abbà, Quale impostazione per la filosofia morale? (1996), 66, our translation.


Chapter 7
7.4
The Organism of Moral Virtue
7.4.1
The Differentiation of the Virtues
The moral virtues, considered together, perfect in a stable way all of the human
tendential dynamism, and therefore all the tendencies we have studied up to
this point. The mode of differentiating and organizing the virtues depends in
good part on the instrument of analysis and classification employed in regard
to the tendencies.
The Sacred Scriptures contain references to a wide range of virtuous attitudes,
at the summit being the three theological virtues, but it also speaks of moral
virtues, such as audacity, purity, courage, fidelity, a good work ethic, humility,
sincerity, etc.65, without, however, employing a specific principle of classifica-
tion. Plato distinguished between four fundamental virtues: prudence, jus-
tice, fortitude, and temperance. Aristotle elaborated a phenomenology of the
ethical virtues, making recourse also to descriptive models.66 The Catholic
theological tradition structures the virtues around the four fundamental or
cardinal virtues.
The Thomistic classification of the virtues is based on his conception of the
soul's faculties (practical reason, will, irascible appetite, concupiscible ap-
petite) and also on the relation that the diverse passions, and the goods to-
ward which they are aimed, have with respect to the reason that must regulate
them.67 Prudence is the fundamental (cardinal) virtue of the practical reason;
justice is the cardinal virtue of the will and its operations; fortitude and tem-
perance correspond respectively to the irascible and concupiscible appetites.
In relation to the four cardinal virtues there are organized all the other moral
virtues as being subjective, integral, or potential parts.68 The subjective parts
65 Cf. Gen 13:8–9; 30:33; Ex 23:4; Deut 1:16–17; Prov 28:20; 31:10–31; Wis 3:13; Sir 2:4;
6:14–16; 7:15; Isa 35:3–4; Zech 8:16; Mk 15:43; Lk 6:36–38; Acts 20:33–35; 1 Cor 4:12–13;
Eph 4:25–32; Col 3:12–15; 2 Tim 2:22–25; Heb 10:33–36; Jas 3:2–12; 1 Pet 4:9–11; 5:8;
Rev 14:4–5.
66 Cf. for example Nicomachean Ethics, III, 5–11: 1113 b - 1119 a.
67 It could be useful to recall a noted explanation of Saint Thomas: “The good of the
appetitive powers is not performed in the same way in every type of human behavior.
Such a good is in reference to a three-fold subject-matter: a) to the irascible and aggressive
appetites, b) to the impulses toward pleasure, c) to the operations through which we occupy
ourselves with external things: such as with acquisitions, sales, renting and loaning. The
good of man with respect to the impulses stands in dealing with them in such a way as to
not allow oneself to be dragged far from the judgment of reason by them; and so, in relation
to the passions which push a person in a way contrary to reason, the good of virtue consists
in restraining them, as temperance does by moderating the impulse toward pleasure. In
relation to impulses that hold a person back from acting according to the indications of
reason, such as fear, the good of virtue will consist in resisting the impulse which holds a
person back from acting, as valor and fortitude do. “ (De Virtutibus in Communi, a. 12,
our translation).
68 Cf. S.Th. II-II, q. 48, a. 1.


The Moral Virtues and the Gifts of the Holy Spirit
pertain to distinctions of partial domains within a cardinal virtue: sobriety
and chastity are subjective parts of temperance. Integral parts are the habits
required for the full realization of a cardinal virtue: patience and perseverance
are integral parts of fortitude. The potential parts are virtues connected to
a cardinal virtue that do not fully fulfill the ratio of the cardinal virtue: the
virtues of religion and piety toward parents are potential parts of justice.
We shall give a brief overview of the Thomistic classification. The sub-
jective parts of prudence are personal prudence, with which a person
governs himself, and governing prudence, proper to those who are lead-
ers, parents, etc.
The integral parts are virtues like memory which
knows how to draw from experiences of the past, understanding of the
present situation, docility, diligence, foresight, caution, etc. Potential
parts are the capacity to deliberate rightly (eubulia), the capacity to
judge rightly in ordinary situations (synesis), and that of judging rightly
in extraordinary situations (gnome), which regulates epikeia.
The subjective parts of justice are general or legal justice, commutative
justice, and distributive justice.
The potential parts are the virtues
which either do not perfectly possess the aspect (ratio) of equality
proper to justice, like religion, piety toward one's parents, respect for
those in authority, and obedience; or which do not imply a duty in a
rigorous sense, such as veracity, gratitude, kindness, liberality, etc.
Magnanimity, magnificence, patience, and perseverance are integral
parts of fortitude if we consider them as prerequisites of the princi-
pal act of fortitude, which is to undertake action or resist attacks that
put one's life at risk. If we consider it instead as a virtue which regards
secondary objects of fortitude, those four virtues are potential parts.
The subjective parts of temperance are moderation of eating (absti-
nence), sobriety in drinking, and chastity—which regards the sex drive.
The integral parts are decency and honesty.
Its potential parts are
continence, gentleness, clemency, modesty, humility, moderation of the
desire to know and of curiosity (studiositas) and the moderation in
games, sports or, more generally, fun activities.
Every moral virtue has its own specific mode of regulating actions, tendencies,
and passions, and thus its own internal logic: a normative framework which,
if adequately developed, allows us to resolve the problems posed by normative
ethics.
7.4.2
The Connection of the Virtues
What is called the connection of the moral virtues is the fact that one cannot
find virtue in a perfect state without their being the other virtues present. The
reason for the connection of the moral virtues is that they all participate in


Chapter 7
prudence and, from the Christian point of view, because of their relation with
charity: the form and root of all the virtues.69
Saint Augustine speaks of the connection of the virtues as an idea which
was widely held: “The doctrine that the virtues are inseparable was
embraced by all of the philosophers who proclaimed the same virtues to
be necessary for a righteous life [ The reason for which they believe that,
if one possesses a virtue he possesses them all and if one is deprived of a
virtue he does not possess any of them, is without doubt the following:
prudence cannot be either lazy, or unjust, or intemperate; for, if it
had one of these defects, it would no longer be prudence. In reverse,
if prudence is present when it is courageous, just, and temperate, then
where it is there will undoubtedly also be the other virtues. In the same
way, neither can fortitude be imprudent, nor intemperate, nor unjust;
so also temperance must be naturally prudent, courageous, and just,
and so also justice is not justice if it is not at the same time prudent,
courageous, and temperate. In such a way, when there is one of those
virtues, there will also equally be the others; when, instead, these are
lacking, that virtue is not authentic, even if it can seem so in some
aspect.”70
Saint Thomas also uses a similar argument, perhaps with greater breadth.
He notes, as has already been said, that moral virtue is a certain partic-
ipation in the right reason of the appetitive powers.71 Such a participa-
tory relation existing between prudence and the moral virtues explains
at the same time the distinction of the virtues (an impossibility if there
existed a single ethical virtue) and the connection which exists between
them.
The moral virtues participate in a certain mode in the unity
which the good has in prudence, so that they are formed and developed
together and according to a certain harmonious proportion, in a similar
way to how the fingers of the hand grow proportionally.
This is even more apparent if one takes account of the fact that the passions
and actions regulated by the virtues are found to be in reciprocal relation: the
passions “have their rise in certain initial passions, viz. love and hatred, and
terminate in certain others, viz. pleasure and sorrow. In like manner all the
operations that are the matter of moral virtue are related to one another, and
to the passions.”72 Moral virtue, then, can only function as an elective habit
of the righteous mean under a prudence which is referred to all sectors of the
moral life.
Temperance, for example, is the elective habit of the right mean regard-
ing sexual pleasure and enjoyment, but not insofar as this mean can be
abandoned for the impulse of this or that passion, but in the absolute,
69 Cf. 1 Cor 13, 1–13; Col 3, 14; CCC, 1827–1828; Veritatis Splendor, 15.
70 Saint Augustine, Epistula 167, 2, 4–5: NBA 22, 763–765, our translation.
71 Cf. De Virtutibus in Communi, a. 12, ad 16.
72 S.Th. I-II, q. 65, a. 1, ad 3.


The Moral Virtues and the Gifts of the Holy Spirit
regardless of where the disordered impulse proceeds. Through the con-
nection of the operations and the passions it can happen that someone
may perform an intemperate action not out of a desire for pleasure, but
for avarice, revenge, etc. So, temperance must safeguard the right mean
between the extremes which oppose it per se and between those which
oppose it on account of the above-mentioned connection: temperance
renders man temperate in the absolute, and not only under a certain
aspect.
7.4.3
The Formation of the Virtues
Growth and Diminution of the Habits — The human virtues (and vices)
are acquired and perfected through repeated acts. Virtues pertain to the powers
not insofar as they are active powers, but only in the measure in which they
also have a certain passivity. These powers, being moved by a superior power,
are disposed by it in a certain way, for all that is moved by another receives
a disposition from that agent. If this movement is repeated, the disposition
is rendered stable and a habit is formed. Fortitude, for example, is formed
in the irascible appetite on account of acts commanded by the reason so that
this tendency may act according to the demands of virtue, overcoming its own
spontaneous passions when these do not coincide with the dictates of right
reason. Therefore, Aquinas affirms that virtue “is a disposition engraved or
impressed into the appetitive power by the reason”;73 and the Bible counsels:
“Learn to do good.”74
The virtues diminish and are lost through the performance of acts contrary to
them. In this way, a new habit is formed in the power, vice, which annuls
virtue, for two contrary forms (intemperance and temperance, injustice and
justice, etc.) cannot coexist in the same faculty. The prolonged absence of
virtuous acts can also occasion the debilitation or even the loss of virtue, for if
the effort to reorder the powers according to the dictates of right reason is not
constant, acts will necessarily arise which are opposed to them, on account of
the instinctive movements which the sensible tendencies preserve.
No human operative habit proceeds exclusively from nature; that is to say,
there are no innate operative habits. Nonetheless, some habits can be called
natural, because they proceed in part from nature and in part from acts per-
formed by the person.
There are two such “natural” habits: the habit of
the first principles of the speculative reason (intellectus) and those of the
first moral principles (sinderesi). In contrast with the other habits (which are
called acquired), these are constituted as natural dispositions in order to judge
infallibly, once the terms of judgment are known through ordinary experience.
73 De Virtutibus in Communi, a. 9.
74 Isa 1:17; cf. Ps 1:2; Lk 16:8; Rom 1:25–32.


Chapter 7
In a parallel mode to the intellectual habits of the first principles, there is in
the will a natural principle of moral rectitude: the natural inclination toward
good as known by the reason, which, however, is not a habit in an early stage
of development, but rather something which pertains constitutively to the will
itself.
The Formation of Prudence — The development of the moral virtues
presents an important problem from the practical point of view, one which
we have already mentioned.75 It is the problem of how it is possible to develop
prudence.76 For, in a perfect state, prudence presupposes the possession of
all the moral virtues, but these on their part can come about only through
the guidance of prudence.77 This circle, already resolved from the theoretical
perspective, creates practical difficulties. This is so both for those who are
young and are still in a stage of maturation, and for adults, who from the
standpoint of the virtues find themselves in a rather imperfect state while
nonetheless being confronted each day with problems and choices on which
they must, through effort, take positions, and all of this without counting on
the help of the habit of prudence.
Aristotle already put forth this problem, which he resolved with his ethics
of the polis: those who find themselves in the state we have just described
will be taken by the hand—and in a certain sense by force—toward virtue
by the law of the polis, which came about with such a goal mind.
This
solution is insufficient today, even if it still holds some validity. Indeed, the
State, the family, the mass media, language, commonly held models of society,
etc., exercise—whether one likes it or not—an important educative influence,
which can be positive or negative.78Moral theology, moreover, adds to this
another response: “There is a theological answer for the problem of incomplete
prudence: the `healing of nature' through grace and the revelation of the
fundamental moral principles as divine law.” 79 Only the law of Christ (lex
nova), which consists primarily in the grace of the Holy Spirit, can render
man perfectly virtuous.80
75 See above: subsection 7.3.3.
76 We take account here of what was said in M. Rhonheimer, The Perspective of Morality
(2011), 229.
77 Cf. Saint Ambrose, De Officiis Ministrorum, 1, 27, 126: Biblioteca Ambrogiana 13,
(Rome: Città Nuova, 1977), 101.
78 It is a problem which must be confronted in the study of human law in Chaper IX; see
also what was said regarding traditions of moral life in Chapter I, subsection 1.1.2.
79 M. Rhonheimer, The Perspective of Morality (2011), 229.
80 We shall occupy ourselves with the law of Christ in Chapter VIII.


The Moral Virtues and the Gifts of the Holy Spirit
7.5
Infused Virtues, Gifts of the Spirit,
and Charisms
7.5.1
The Existence of Infused Virtues
Revelation and the doctrine of the Church teach that God transforms re-
deemed man into a new creature and renders him able to act as a son of the
Father in Christ and through the Holy Spirit. This supernatural elevation em-
braces the person's entire humanity, including his operative faculties. Given
that the perfection of an operative faculty is called virtue, as we already know,
it is theologically legitimate to speak of supernatural virtues.
The immediate fundamental principles of supernatural life which the Spirit
establishes in man are the theological or “divine” virtues, i.e. faith, hope, and
charity.
Theology and ecclesial doctrine retain as a virtue the very “love of
God [that] has been poured out into our hearts through the holy Spirit that
has been given to us”81, and it considers hope and faith virtues as well. These
three divine virtues inform the moral virtues, adapting them to the demands
of life in Christ.82
Beyond the theological virtues, diverse passages of Scripture remind us that
the moral virtues are also gifts of God.83 Not a few Fathers and documents
of the magisterium, as well as the vast majority of theologians, affirm that
along with received grace, there also exist infused moral virtues.84 This would
be logical, because for the Christian life it is not enough to have qualities
which dispose a person to immediately act in a way directed toward God
(theological virtues), but also needed are those capacities which make it so
that actions that regard created things be rendered supernatural and merito-
rious of eternal life (infused moral virtues). These are parallel to the human
virtues, but in the supernatural order: infused prudence, justice, fortitude,
and temperance.
The following definition of virtue, of Augustinian origin and already cited
above, can only be applied to the infused virtues in a rigorous sense: “Virtue
is a good quality of the soul through which one lives rightly, which cannot be
81 Rom 5:5.
82 Cf. CCC, 1813.
83 Cf. Prov 2:6; Wis 9:10–11 & Lk 1:17 (prudence); Prov 8:16 & Isa 1:26 (justice); Ps
17:33 & 1 Tim 1:12 (fortitude); Mt 19:11 & 2 Tim 1:7 (temperance and other virtues).
84 Saint Gregory the Great considers the four virtues as being bestowed by the Holy Spirit:
cf. Moralia in Iob, 2, 49: CCL 143, 106. With regard to the Magisterium, see Innocent III,
Ep. Maiores Ecclesiae Causas: DS 780; Council of Vienna, Cost. Fidei Catholicae: DS
904; Roman Catechism, II, 2, 51. Regarding Saint Thomas Aquinas: cf. S.Th. I-II, q. 51,
a. 4; q. 63, a. 3. The Catechism does not directly speak about the infused moral virtues,
and their redaction could lead one to suppose that it may not consider them necessary;
nonetheless, such an omission does not automatically mean a denial of their existence.


Chapter 7
used for evil, and which God produces in us without us.” These are virtues
which are given to the Christian with sanctifying grace and which are distin-
guished from their corresponding acquired virtues not by the material that they
regulate (actions, tendencies, passions), but by the criteria that inspires this
regulation. Christian temperance, for example, regulates a person's consump-
tion of food or drink in order to progress in the spiritual life with a diverse
criterion from that whereby human temperance regulates eating in view of
the preservation of health, even if there are points of contact between the
two: e.g. drunkenness is equally opposed to human and Christian temper-
ance. Faith illuminates in a new way the meaning of human goods and their
privation (health and sickness, suffering, absence of economic means, profes-
sional failure, etc.), and, therefore, at least partially modifies the criteria for
man's attitude regarding them. So, for example, the attitude of the Lord,
who “for your sake [. . . ] became poor”85, illuminates the meaning of poverty
and sobriety in the use of goods, and opens the way toward virtuous behavior
which would have no meaning without faith in Christ.
On the other hand, theology retains that the infused virtues give to man
the radical capacity to make valid choices toward progress in the Christian
life and toward eternal life, but do not give the facility characteristic of an
acquired habit.86 Therefore, the acquired virtues are absolutely necessary for
the Christian.
It must certainly be conceded that the existence of the infused moral
virtues is not a dogmatic matter of the faith concerning which the
Church has set forth a definitive judgment. It is rather the more com-
mon doctrine among the great classical theologians.
The Christian
moral life could also be explained differently: grace renders merito-
rious the exercise of the acquired virtues, the theological virtues elevate
and partially modify the regulating criteria of human prudence, and
charity remains equally the “form” of all the virtues. However, from
our point of view it seems that to posit the existence of the infused
moral virtues facilitates our understanding of Christian moral action;
furthermore, we have not found in the theological literature any argu-
852 Cor 8:9.
86 Nevertheless, the infused virtues, in a remote way, also give a certain facility of acting

7.5.2
The Gifts of the Holy Spirit
Revelation shows another and more elevated mode of acting, which is verified
when God Himself acts in us: “For those who are led by the Spirit of God
are children of God [ In the same way, the Spirit too comes to the aid of our
weakness; for we do not know how to pray as we ought, but the Spirit itself in-
tercedes with inexpressible groanings.”87 In such a sense, the Christian's good
works are truly fruits of the Holy Spirit.88 The Spirit guides the life of the
Christian so that, through Christ, “we both have access in one Spirit to the
Father.”89 But because this happens, there needs to be a certain stable dis-
position, a certain “connaturality” in the depths of the person, which renders
him ready to accept divine guidance and inspirations. Such stable infused
qualities in the soul from God are the gifts of the Holy Spirit. “These are
permanent dispositions which make man docile in following the promptings of
the Holy Spirit.”90 Being based above all on the text of Isaiah, they come to
be listed as seven gifts through which the Spirit moves the faithful:91
 Wisdom: to promptly know and love divine things;
 Understanding: to understand in depth the truths of the faith;
 Knowledge: to evaluate human things in their relation to the final end;
 Counsel: to discern the things to be done;
 Piety: to act with diligence and a filial spirit regarding what pertains
to one's relationship with God and, secondarily, with other people;
 Fortitude: to be ready to reject negative suggestions in perilous situa-
tions;
 Fear of the Lord: to avoid the stimulations of disordered passions for
the purpose of not offending the Lord.

Chapter 7
The Church's tradition has spoken constantly of these gifts.92 The necessity of
the gifts is based on the overflow of the supernatural order, which has need not
only of the infused virtues, but also of the impulse of the Holy Spirit. So the
Fathers compare the practice of the virtues to navigation using oars, and the
gifts to navigation pushed by the wind (the breath of the Spirit); nonetheless,
like every example, it would not be ideal to take it to the extreme, for in the
Christian life infused virtues and gifts of the Holy Spirit are closely connected
and, from the beginning to the end of the walk toward sanctity, both are
necessary for responding to the divine call.
7.5.3
The Charisms
The Greek word charism means favor, gratuitous gift, or benefit; and in this
sense it is employed in the New Testament fourteen times in the Pauline
letters. Thus employed, one could say that grace, the virtues, the gifts of the
Holy Spirit, etc., are charisms. But in our modern languages the word charism
(and its cognates) has acquired a technical meaning, and as such is used in
the New Testament only a few times.93 In this sense charisms are various
gifts—a diversity of charisms94—that the Spirit distributes as He wishes “for
building up the Church.”95 Moreover, not all persons receive them,96, because
they are not necessary for each Christian in order to develop in holiness.
Both the etymology of the word, and the explicit indications of the Sa-
cred Scripture, show that the charisms are gratuitous gifts of God—at times
the Holy Spirit is explicitly mentioned—in relation to the supernatural end.
“Whether extraordinary or simple and humble, charisms are graces of the Holy
Spirit which directly or indirectly benefit the Church, ordered as they are to
her building up, to the good of men, and to the needs of the world.” 97 They
have, then, a very strict relationship with the life of the Church; in fact, Rom
12 and 1 Cor 12 use the example of the body in order to show the diversity,
unity, and utility of the charisms. On account of their ecclesial relevance, and

all of the Catholic catechisms and the Church's liturgy attest to their existence; and the
theologians so as well (cf. S.Th. I-II, q. 68). For a deeper look at this, see: M. M. Philippon,
I doni dello Spirito Santo, (Milan: Ancora, 1965).
93 In the Italian translation of 1 Cor 12:4 and 31 the word “carisma” is used, whereas in

Almost always the charisms are received for
the utility and the service of others. (gratiae gratis datae: 1 Cor 14:19), but sometimes

himself up” (1 Cor 14:4).
96 Cf. 1 Cor 12:28–30.

are mentioned, as well as the rules given by the Apostles for the use of the
charisms,99 it would appear that not only is there not opposition between
charism and hierarchy, but rather they are two strictly connected realities.
“Charisms are to be accepted with gratitude by the person who re-
ceives them and by all members of the Church as well.
They are a
wonderfully rich grace for the apostolic vitality and for the holiness of
the entire Body of Christ, provided they really are genuine gifts of the
Holy Spirit and are used in full conformity with authentic promptings
of this same Spirit, that is, in keeping with charity, the true measure
of all charisms.”100 Saint Paul's Letters provide diverse lists of them;
together they list twenty charisms: some are prodigious, like healing
through the Spirit or the power to work miracles;101 others involve only
a particular aptitude for a certain office, like that of the apostle for in-

for instructing them, etc. Many other passages of the Bible, both from
the Old and New Testaments, without using the term, speak of diverse
charisms: prophecy, from Moses to John the Baptist;102 speaking in
tongues;103 the power to work miracles;104 the power to cast out demons
and to heal the sick;105 the prudence for judging and governing;106 etc.
While the prodigious charisms became very rare with the establishment
of the Church, those which are ordinary and necessary for the develop-
ment of the life of the Church always exist in it. So writes the Second

Chapter 7
7.6
The Relationship between the Human
and Infused Virtues
The relationship between the human and the infused virtues (virtues and
gifts) depends on the mutual coordination between nature and grace, and it
can be summarized in the following points:
1. Even if there exists a distinction between natural and supernatural
moral action, in the Christian life there is found a reciprocal influence
between the human and infused virtues: both are found in the concrete
effort toward holiness.
2. On account of original sin, man cannot persevere in natural moral good,
considered in its completeness, without supernatural help; consequently,
natural virtues can arrive at their perfection only with the help of
grace.108 Along with the Second Vatican Council, it can be affirmed
that “[w]hoever follows after Christ, the perfect man, becomes himself
more of a man.”109
3. Infused supernatural virtues facilitate the attainment of their correspond-
ing human virtues because the Holy Spirit pushes and drives the person
in a state of grace in all of his being. Therefore, when such a person
puts into practice the virtues infused in him, he also develops elements
of the correlative natural virtues.
4. The complete dynamism of concrete action for the sake of holiness re-
quires both types of virtue: the acquired and the infused (including also
the supernatural gifts). Neither order is complete without the other, as
was said in the second point. For human virtue will never be complete
without supernatural help, while at the same time the infused virtues,
without the contribution of corresponding human virtues, will lack au-
thentic perfection: grace presupposes nature and, although divinization
is an act of God, humans must cooperate. The human virtues, in a cer-
tain sense, support and stimulate the exercise of the infused virtues.110
7.7
Growth of the Infused Virtues
The growth of the infused virtues, as is the case with their acquisition, does
not depend so much on human action, as it depends on the grace of God.
108 Cf. CCC, 1810.
109 Gaudium et Spes, 41.
110 In fact, we deal here with a natural quality of man, the habilitas ad gratiam, which
disposes him to receive, or receive more, of the supernatural life: cf. E. Colom, Dios y el
obrar humano (1976), 92–118.


The Moral Virtues and the Gifts of the Holy Spirit
Nevertheless, the acts of a supernatural virtue ensure its possession.111 This
happens, among other reasons, because they increase the corresponding ac-
quired virtue, which then successively facilitates the use of the infused virtue.
For this reason, man must be personally disposed to such a development, re-
sponding with generosity to the gifts already bestowed by the Lord, since the
good works of the person in a state of grace merit an increase in grace and
virtue.112
For the same reasons it must be said that the properly infused virtues cannot
diminish: neither lukewarmness nor venial sin can deprive a person of such
virtues or diminish them.113 Very different is the relationship between the
infused virtues and grave sin: with the latter, man loses the supernatural
elevation of his being (sanctifying grace) and of his faculties (infused virtues
and gifts of the Spirit) because he becomes closed to the source who is God;
nonetheless, except when one treats of a sin against faith or hope, these two
virtues persist in the person, though in a precarious condition.114
An increase in the infused virtues follows an increase of God's grace. Good
works, prayer, and the frequenting of the sacraments carry with them an in-
crease in the infused virtues. In fact, Sacred Scriptures teach to ask for the
virtues in prayer,115 while the sacraments nourish, strengthen, and express
the faith, while disposing the person to exercise charity.116
To summarize, the infused virtues are bestowed with grace to all those who
believe in Christ but they also require free human correspondence.
111 “Acts produced by an infused habit, do not cause a habit, but strengthen the already

112 Cf. Chapter VI, section 6.7.
113 This does not mean that, with regard to the virtues, it is a matter of indifference to act

Part III
The Path toward
Identification with Christ


Introduction
We saw that every person is called by God to be holy through identification
with Christ (Part I). We then studied the natural and supernatural operative
principles which allow a Christian to elaborate a program of life consistent
with this divine call (Part II). Now what needs to be studied are the norma-
tive points of reference whereby the believer disposes himself so that he may
effectively achieve his desired goal.
By now we know that the theological and moral virtues, insofar as they are
specific principles of the Christian life, are also the rules of the life lived in
Christ, present in every morally formed Christian.1 However, the formation
of the virtues in man marked by sin, beyond having natural prerequisites
(the natural moral law, participation in the eternal law), has need of divine
help (the divine law, especially the lex gratiae) to go along with human laws
(civil and ecclesiastical), and the teachings of moral knowledge which come
to be applied through the conscience.
This explains why moral theology,
on the foundation offered by Sacred Scriptures, has traditionally framed the
study of moral rules within the context of a theology of law (eternal law,
natural moral law, divine-positive law, etc.) and of conscience. The moral
law (Chapters VIII and IX) and conscience (Chapter X) are precisely the two
elements which make up the path toward the acquisition and consolidation
of the theological and moral virtues, through which man is united to Christ.
This perspective allows us to understand that if it is true that Christian ethics
takes due account of the law and conscience, it cannot be structured around
moral obligation as being in some way opposed to conscience.2
Finally, we shall take a deeper look at the act through which man can distance
himself from the path toward Christ, sin, and the returning path of conversion
(Chapter XI).
1 Cf. Chapter I, subsection 1.2.2 & 1.3.3; Chapter II, subsection 2.4.2 & 2.4.3; Chapter
VII, sections 7.2–7.4.
2 Cf. Chapter I, subsection 1.2.2 and the bibliography there cited. Furthermore, see
R. García de Haro, Legge, coscienza e libertà, 2nd ed., (Milan: Ares, 1990); S. Pinckaers,
Linee per un rinnovamento evangelico della morale. Una lettura della “Veritatis Splendor”,
Annales theologici 10 (1996) 3–68.


## CHAPTER 8 {#colom-scelti.8}
Law within the Context of
the Doctrine of the Virtues
8.1
The Salvific Design of God in Christ
and Man's Participation in It
The notion of law, especially moral law, finds ample biblical resonances. It
is true that a normativistic “hypertrophy” of the moral life and legislative
excess in socio-political life resulted in disaffection with the law. Nevertheless,
abuse does not dispense us of the necessity of this concept even in the field
of morality. For this reason, the existing relationship between virtue and the
doctrine of the moral law now needs to be considered in order to emphasize
that an ethics of virtue is not an ethics without a moral law. Rather, the
perspective which sees virtues as the foundation and reason for moral norms
constitutes, in our view, the most adequate way of interpreting the doctrine of
the moral law proper to Christian thought.
8.1.1
The Original Divine Salvific Plan
as the Eternal Law
In Greco-Roman thought there already existed an important reflection
regarding the eternal law, particularly in stoicism. There is no doubt
that Saint Augustine1 and other Christian theologians made use of the
1 Saint Augustine defines the eternal law as “the reason or the will of God which
commands to preserve the natural order and prohibits to disturb it” (Contra Faus-
tum, 22, 27: CSEL 25, 621).


Chapter 8
definition of it provided by Cicero.2
However, the stoic formulas do
not explain the important role attributed to the moral law by Christian
thought. It depends in a rather profound way on the biblical concept of
God's law, linked already in the Old Testament to the Covenant between
God and His people: we refer here to the “Law and the Prophets” which
Jesus claimed to not abolish, but to bring to completion.3
In the current state of Catholic moral theology it can be confidently affirmed
that the Christian concept of the eternal law cannot be adequately under-
stood if starting from stoic reflections on the cosmic order.
Consideration
of the universal salvific design of God as the eternal law constitutes the cor-
nerstone of Christian thought concerning this notion.
That is to say: the
decree through which God “chose us in him [Christ], before the foundation
of the world, to be holy and without blemish before him,” 4 can and must
be called the eternal law. Law because it is the ordinatio or plan accord-
ing to which the divine Wisdom, who “reaches from end to end mightily” 5,
created the universe and “governs all things well.” 6 Eternal because we are
dealing with “the mystery hidden from ages past in God who created all
things,”7 or the “manifold wisdom of God” which “might now be made known
according to the eternal purpose that he accomplished in Christ Jesus our
Lord”:8 this law is eternal as the wisdom of God is, with which it is identi-
fied.
When treating of the infinite creative wisdom of God, it is clear that it en-
compasses and measures all of created reality, and in particular the existence
and life of humans, reaching them in their singularity. Nothing escapes the
divine gaze.9 Saint Thomas Aquinas makes it more precise that the eternal
law is not only the plan of creation, but also the plan which is brought to
effect by God's providence. Thus he defines the eternal law as “the type of
Divine Wisdom, as moving all things to their due end.”10 Furthermore, eccle-
sial doctrine considers the eternal law as a supreme moral norm, archetype of
all goodness, justice, and righteousness. The Second Vatican Council, in fact,
affirms: “the highest norm of human life is the divine law-eternal, objective
and universal-whereby God orders, directs and governs the entire universe
and all the ways of the human community by a plan conceived in wisdom and

in the eternal law.”12
The theological concept of the eternal law is of extreme importance for
explaining the theonomic foundation of the moral order. However, from
the standpoint of our knowledge, one must take account of the fact that
we cannot know directly the ordinatio of divine Wisdom in itself . His
plan is “the mystery hidden from ages and from generations past.” 13
It becomes accessible to us only in a mediated way, through the ways
foreseen by God's providence in order to render us participants in moral
and salvific truth.14 We shall occupy ourselves in this chapter with the
diverse modes of man's participation in the eternal law, first offering a
comprehensive vision of the whole, and then focusing on each particular
mode of such participation.
8.1.2
The Communication of the Eternal Law:
From the Natural Moral Law
to the Christian Virtues
as the Most Perfect Human Participation
in the Plan of Divine Wisdom
Presupposing here the dogmatic doctrine concerning the gratuitousness
of the elevation of man to the supernatural order,15 we can affirm in
general terms that there are two paths which allow us to reach knowl-
edge of God.
One path is natural, to which Saint Paul refers when
he affirms that “[e]ver since the creation of the world, his invisible at-
tributes of eternal power and divinity have been able to be understood
and perceived in what he has made”;16 and the other is supernatural,
consisting of the divine Revelation which was revealed gradually and
historically.17 These are, substantially, also the paths to knowledge of
the eternal law as the supreme rule of moral conduct.
The first and fundamental participation of man in the eternal law comes to
be called in theology the “natural moral law”. It consists in the “light of the
understanding infused in us by God. Thanks to it we know what must be
done and what must be avoided. This light and this law God has provided in

DS 3973; Veritatis Splendor, 43.
12 CCC, 1951; see also numbers 1950 & 1952.

14 Cf. 1 Cor 2; Dignitatis Humanae, 3.

16 Rom 1:20.

Chapter 8
creation.”18 The natural moral law is none other than the incontestable fact
that man was created by God as a moral being, and that human reason is,
per se, a moral reason, capable of ordering our conduct in view of the human
good. In other terms, moral demand immediately arises from the interiority
of man, and finds in it a structure which nourishes and sustains it, without
which moral demands—and even the language which expresses them—would
not only be extraneous, but also completely unintelligible.
We said that the natural moral law is the first and fundamental participation
of man in the eternal law. First and fundamental in a logical sense, as it is
the original constitution of man as moral subject, which renders both intelligi-
bility and the reception of any other ethical-positive disposition to be possible,
whether it be divine or human. Furthermore, the natural moral law ensures,
as we shall soon see, the first principles of ethical virtue. At the same time,
however, the natural moral law is objectively insufficient and fragmentary. It
is insufficient for ordering the social life in common necessary for the attain-
ment of the human good, and for this reason it must be made explicit and
given determination by civil law. In practice it is also insufficient for guar-
anteeing the acquisition of the personal good: for though it may indicate in
principle all the demands of the human good, it does not possess the neces-
sary force to prevent certain ethical demands from being obscured due to the
disorder introduced by sin into the human operative faculties. On the other
hand, the totality of the salvific plan of God being considered, it is obvious
that the supernatural good of man—the achievement of union with Christ
through hope, faith, and love—completely exceeds the reach of the natural
moral law.
The totality of the salvific plan of God in Christ has been the object of a grad-
ual and historical divine revelation (the history of salvation), through which
man's progressive supernatural participation in the eternal law has been es-
tablished: something which commonly comes to be called the divine-positive
moral law. The law of the Old Testament possesses a provisional and imper-
fect character, while being pedagogically very important insofar as it confirms
the most essential aspects of the natural moral law and prepares for the work
of the Messiah. It is to be distinguished from the law of the New Testament,
also called the lex gratiae because it primarily consists in the grace of the Holy
Spirit given to those who believe in Christ, which finally makes possible the
knowledge and practical realization of our life as children of God in Christ.19
It needs to be added, for completeness, that the life of Christians within the
Church needs a further human regulation, which in good part renders explicit,

Law within the Context of the Doctrine of the Virtues
or is a determination of, the natural moral law and the divine law, and this
is called ecclesiastical, or canon, law.
From the normative standpoint it must be affirmed that the law of the New
Testament preserves and carries to completion the demands of the natural
moral law, even if it is not limited to this;20 it represents, for this reason,
the final fullness at which all of the law aims.
From a real point of view,
instead, it must be affirmed that the perfect participation in the salvific plan
of God is verified (is made a reality) in the virtuous Christian, that is to
say, in the person who is interiorly renewed by the grace which, through the
virtues and affected by the action of the gifts of the Holy Spirit, is capable
of identifying and accomplishing in each situation the right way of relating
to God, to himself, to others, and to the diverse goods which here and now
respect and promote his life in Christ.
Only in the virtuous Christian is
the plan of God's wisdom participated in to such a degree that he would
be able to accomplish and effectively evaluate the actions and situations in
their specific singularity; in other words, only then does the person reach by
his practical knowledge—always within the limits of human possibilities—the
characteristic reach of the plan of God's wisdom.21
This is put into relief
by the encyclical Veritatis Splendor: “[I]n order to 'prove what is the will
of God, what is good and acceptable and perfect' (Rom 12:2), knowledge of
God's law in general is certainly necessary, but it is not sufficient: what is
essential is a sort of 'connaturality' between man and the true good. Such a
connaturality is rooted in and develops through the virtuous attitudes of the
individual himself: prudence and the other cardinal virtues, and even before
these the theological virtues of faith, hope and charity.” 22

Chapter 8
8.1.3
The Analogy of the Law
and Its General Ordination toward Virtue
The comprehensive vision proposed in the preceding subsection is enough in
order for one to recognize that the concept of the moral law is an analogous
concept, that is, it is a concept that has different meanings depending on its
particular use, though always preserving a common semantic nucleus. This
renders difficult any sort of general discourse on law.
In the body of the
laws that have moral significance we have divine laws (the natural law, the
Old Law, and the New Law)23 and human laws (the civil and ecclesiastical
law) which, nonetheless, must remain connected with the former. Among the
divine laws, the natural law and the New Law are substantially internal laws,
not written laws, with the first consisting in the natural light of the reason,
and the second consisting in the grace that heals and elevates the human
person and operates fundamentally through the theological virtues.24
The
Old Law, on the other hand, is a written and external law which in its moral
parts responds in good part to the natural moral law, but which, however, is
not able to overcome the obstacles found within sinful man.
We shall not enter here into the debate regarding which law should be
considered the principle analogue. It seems opportune to us to observe
rather that, from the standpoint of our knowledge, the laws which in
themselves, and in their process of elaboration and promulgation, be-
come more known to us are the human laws (civil and ecclesastical
laws). This obliges us to be particularly cautious to not fall into the
grave error of wanting to conceive of the natural moral law and the New
Law along the same lines as civil laws.
While keeping in mind what has been said, it is possible to dedicate some
brief considerations to the law in general.25
The law, any law, is “aliquid
rationis”,26 it is an operative order elaborated by the reason. Moreover, law
is a rule and measure of action, and to order actions in view of the good is
23 “Even if moral-theological reflection usually distinguishes between the positive or re-
vealed law of God and the natural law, and, within the economy of salvation, between the
'old' and the 'new' law, it must not be forgotten that these and other useful distinctions
always refer to that law whose author is the one and the same God and which is always
meant for man. The different ways in which God, acting in history, cares for the world
and for mankind are not mutually exclusive; on the contrary, they support each other and
intersect. They have their origin and goal in the eternal, wise and loving counsel whereby
God predestines men and women 'to be conformed to the image of his Son' (Rom 8:29)”
(Veritatis Splendor, 45).
24 As we shall see further on, the New Law is secondarily also a “written” law, inasmuch

New Testament and apostolic Tradition.
25 Cf. S.Th. I-II, q. 90.
