Law within the Context of the Doctrine of the Virtues
a task that only the practical reason can accomplish.27
Therefore, without
excluding the intervention of the legislator's will,28 the formality of the law
is provided by the reason and not the will, which by itself could not be the
rule and measure of action. Secondly the law always aims in some way at the
common good,29 though this characteristic is a thesis that is subject to diverse
interpretations: interpretations that are not necessary for us to consider at the
present moment. It may be enough to say that the necessity of the law derives
in good part from the relational and social dimensions of man. “Therefore he,
in order to perform good acts, not only has need of the internal complement
of the virtues, but also of the external aid of society. Now, society furnishes
this external aid for the regulation of conduct by means of the law: hence
the necessity of a political approach to the concept of law. This necessity
remains also in the order of eternal beatitude: even with regard to this, the
individual depends on society, which for this reason must be ordered in a way
conducive to this end.”30 It should be said, finally, that the law is directed
toward virtue,31 so that—as has been said before—only thanks to the virtues
does man fully and actively participate in the plan of the divine wisdom, be-
coming himself capable of rightly ordering his own conduct. This thesis will
come to be further elaborated in this chapter and in the next and, for what
regards the political law, it will also be made more precise.
8.2
The Radical Constitution of Man
as a Moral Being: The Natural Moral Law
8.2.1
The Natural Moral Law in Catholic Doctrine
The Natural Moral Law in the Sacred Scriptures — The concept
of the natural moral law clearly has a sound basis in Scriptures, even if it
does not come to be explicitly utilized as a technical expression within them.
One of the classic examples is above all the Letter to the Romans. In the
first chapter, Saint Paul sees a direct connection between the more perverse
forms of immorality and the refusal of a God who can be known by human
reason. It is understood that the immorality of the pagans is worthy of blame,
inasmuch as they do not give ear to the human experience of good and evil,
an experience which is nonetheless common to all people, even to those who

do not know the law of Moses. In the second chapter, Saint Paul explicitly
confronts the question: “For when the Gentiles who do not have the law by
nature observe the prescriptions of the law, they are a law for themselves even
though they do not have the law. They show that the demands of the law
are written in their hearts, while their conscience also bears witness and their
conflicting thoughts accuse or even defend them.” 32 Those who do not know
the torah act in conformity to it through nature: it is written in their hearts
and it comes to be demonstrated by the testimony of their conscience.33
A complementary perspective emerges in the Lord's discussion with the Phar-

In confrontation with the
indulgence of the Mosaic law, probably made greater by the subtleties of the
pharisaic tradition, Jesus refers “to the beginning”, that is, to the truth of
Creation. “He said in reply, 'Have you not read that from the beginning the

God has joined together, no human being must separate.' They said to him,

this passage is not so much the testimony of one's conscience—which does not
come to be invoked regarding an ethical demand that was partially obscured–,
as is Jesus's recourse “to the beginning”, understood as an original truth of
matrimony according to the creative design of God, which the natural moral
law expresses and in which it participates.35

The Universality and Immutability of the Natural Moral Law —
Universality and immutability are two properties of the natural moral law
constantly recalled by ecclesiastical teaching. Here we limit ourselves to recall
the fundamental aspects of this doctrine. The natural moral law is universal
in the sense that “its precepts and its authority extends to all men.”61 Such
universality finds its foundation, in the final analysis, in the substantial unity
of the human reason and its participation in the eternal law. Without a sub-
stantially unitary moral reason, it would be impossible to have a true dialogue
between cultures, and for there to be a universal recognition of human rights
and international law. The universality of the natural moral law does not ren-
der illegitimate every differentiation in the more concrete applications. The
natural law “can demand reflection that takes account of various conditions
of life according to places, times, and circumstances.
Nevertheless, in the
diversity of cultures, the natural law remains as a rule that binds men among
themselves and imposes on them, beyond the inevitable differences, common
principles.”62
The natural moral law is also immutable in the sense that it is “permanent
throughout the variations of history; it subsists under the flux of ideas and
customs and supports their progress. The rules that express it remain sub-
stantially valid.”63 The immutability of the fundamental moral principles is
not opposed to the historical progress of man's moral conscience, which ac-
quires a more acute sensibility regarding certain values. There exists, in fact,
and it is good that it exists, also a progress in the linguistic formulation of
natural moral demands, in such a way as to “discover the most adequate for-
mulation for universal and permanent moral norms in the light of different
cultural contexts, a formulation most capable of ceaselessly expressing their
historical relevance, of making them understood and of authentically inter-
preting their truth.”64 In this case we are dealing with a positive progress in
moral science, and not properly with a change in the principles of the natural
moral law.

Chapter 8
The universality and immutability of the natural moral law does not
in fact mean that all people perceive in every moment all of the moral
principles with equal clarity.65 Soon we shall see that not all of the pre-
cepts of the natural moral law enjoy the same evident quality. One may
consider that the natural moral law is “natural” for the human person in
a very similar way to how language is natural to him: irrational animals
never succeed in speaking, while man has the natural capacity to do it,
but this requires, however, a long period of education. As the quality of
each person's ability to speak a language depends on education, so the
diversity of moral judgments concerning the same behavior sometimes
found between different people depends on defects in the moral edu-
cation each person receives, but this does not constitute an objection
against the existence of a natural moral law. What could constitute an
objection would be the existence of completely amoral humans, with-
out practical reason, who did not assume when confronted with their
own life or that of others a behavior which was evaluative or capable of
being judged, even if we were dealing with a behavior which was very
deformed on account of certain causes. From the fact that a natural
capacity could be developed and exercised in a defective way, it is not
licit to conclude that such a capacity does not exist or that it does not
exist for all peoples.
8.2.2
The Natural Principles of the Moral Virtues
The Natural Reason and Practical Principles — In the study of the
moral virtues we said that in order to overcome the apparent vicious circle
between the moral virtues and prudence, we need not only distinguish between
the intentional and elective dimensions of the moral virtues,66 but also to
presuppose natural knowledge of virtuous ends, knowledge which constitutes
a fundamental part of the natural moral law.67 Now is the moment to study
this point in depth.
Saint Thomas retains, in fact, that the virtuous ends are known by nature.68
Before explaining how and in what sense the ends of virtue are naturally
known, we must make an important clarification. The existence of a natural
knowledge of virtuous ends cannot be interpreted as a simple psychological
fact (in a naturalistic sense), without moral relevance. To speak of natural
knowledge of ends means that the practical reason has natural principles, on
which are founded all of its activity, so that in the practical order such ends
have the character of principles, that is, of points of departure for the practical
65 Cf. CCC, 1960.
66 Cf. Chapter VII, subsection 7.3.1.
67 Cf. Chapter VII, subsection 7.3.4.
68 Cf. In Decem Libros Ethicorum, lib. III, lect. 13, nos. 524–525; lib. VI, lect. 3,
no. 1131. The considerations which we espouse in what follows owe much to M. Rhon-
heimer, The Perspective of Morality (2011), 256ff.


Law within the Context of the Doctrine of the Virtues
reason that are concluded with choice. From this perspective, speaking of ends
known by nature is another way of saying ends that are necessarily criteria
for moral rectitude.69
What was said above allows us to understand that when it is affirmed that
some goods are known by nature as ends, this is simply speaking of the nat-
ural moral law. This is a natural ordinatio rationis toward the good, as a
participation in the eternal law. Man has the perception of what is reason-
able by nature, independently of any positive law. The natural moral law is
the law which reason possesses by nature, in virtue of which some ends are
naturally known by man as such, as principles of the practical activity of the
reason. We can speak in this sense of a ratio naturalis, an essential part of
man's practical nature,70 i.e. of the nature proper to man as a rational agent
or moral subject. If there did not exist a natural reason, if there did not exist
anything in the reason which was determined by nature and a principle of all
the rest, then there would not exist any reasonableness in action, but only
blind desire.
The First Principle of the Practical Reason — We can examine now
the contents of the “law” which the practical reason possesses by nature. The
practical reason has a first and fundamental principle, constituted by the prac-
tical perception of the good as that which must be done and of evil as that
which must be avoided.
The expression of this principle in the form of a
proposition or judgment—bonum est faciendum et prosequendum, et malum
vitandum”71—does not offer an adequate idea of its nature. It is not a sim-
ple judgment or proposition, but represents, at a much higher level than the
operation of judgment, the first and fundamental expression of the human
reason as practical reason, the light in which every practical object is ren-
dered visible inasmuch as it is practical. The fundamental perception of the
good, possessed by nature and not through the free choice of the individual,
explains why the human reason can conceive of an object not merely as an
object of knowledge (“A is A”), but as an object of execution (“I must do A”),
i.e. as a good, and it determines the way of approaching the world proper to
man as a moral being.
This first principle is presupposed in all practical reasoning as a point of
departure, and performs in the practical order an analogous role to that
69 This means that “an appetition or striving that is directed toward that which the
reason 'by nature' recognizes as good is necessarily also 'right'. The freedom that would
recognize such a striving only as a mere fact, in order to then question it for its rectitude,
would in this way be annihilated as a reason-guided freedom. It would be asking, that is to
say, whether the rational is rational, when otherwise the question about rightness has been
the same as the question about rationality” (M. Rhonheimer, The Perspective of Morality
(2011), 259).
70 Cf. G. Abbà, Felicità, vita buona e virtù (1995), 250–253.
71 S.Th. I-II, q. 94, a. 2.


Chapter 8
performed by the principle of non-contradiction in the speculative order.
We shall consider the following example. If I start from the premise:
“humans have need of food to live”, and I add: “I am a human”, logic
requires the conclusion: “I am one of those who has need of food to
live”. We treat here of speculative reasoning, which makes me know
something about myself. Practical reasoning is constituted instead in
light of the original perception of the good as something to do or of
evil as something to avoid, as well as the equally practical perception
of other goods (for example, life).
Thus one arrives logically at the
imperative conclusion: “I must eat food”.
From the epistemological point of view, it can be added that the first practical
principle is grasped by the intellectual habit called “synderesis”.72 We are deal-
ing with a habitual knowledge, a theme which possesses notable importance
for the theory of knowledge, and with which we cannot concern ourselves at
this moment. It interests us, rather, to explain that synderesis also grasps
the ends of the virtues with a certain universality, without identifying in a
particularized way the concrete demands of justice, temperance, etc.73 Let us
now see how this happens.
The Virtuous Ends as Practical Principles — The moral virtues are
types of rational regulation for actions, tendencies, and passions regarding
certain goods; for example: interpersonal relationships are regulated by jus-
tice, eating and drinking are regulated with temperance, etc. Therefore, the
perception of the virtuous ends is connected to the perception of certain fun-
damental human goods which are achieved in a certain way: all the things to
do and to avoid pertain to the natural law inasmuch as the practical reason
naturally knows them as human goods, and it knows as human goods all that
toward which humans are naturally inclined.74 Therefore the ends of the nat-
ural inclinations are goods for humans only inasmuch as they are known and
regulated by the reason.
As was said before,75 Aquinas identified three large groups of natural
inclinations. We know that the enumeration is exhaustive, and can be
usefully completed. Now what interests us is pointing out that those
tendencies do not yet allow us to know properly human goods or the
virtues. The reason must understand what is the right way (“reason-
able”, “conforming to reason”) of satisfying the tendencies and of achiev-
ing their ends, in such a way that they are integrated into the totality
of the person and contribute to her good. Not just any way of feeding
oneself is a good for man; not just any sexual union is good for man.
72 See Chapter VII, subsection 7.2.1.
73 Cf. S.Th. I, q. 79, a. 12; II-II, q. 47, a. 7; A. Rodríguez Luño, La scelta etica (1998),
50–55.
74 Cf. S.Th. I-II, q. 94, a. 2. On the natural inclinations see D. Composta, Natura e
ragione. Studio delle inclinazioni naturali in rapporto al diritto naturale (1971).
75 Cf. Chapter V, subsection 5.2.1.


Law within the Context of the Doctrine of the Virtues
Nutrition as a human good is not something which nature has taught
to all animals, so neither is sexuality as a human good something which
nature has taught to animals.
Only the reason teaches us what are
nutrition and sexuality as human goods. The natural inclinations offer
only the material or subject-matter which must be further directed by
the practical reason.
It is here that the virtues come to play their role. The virtues are the ra-
tional modes of regulation of the natural inclinations and of the goods toward
which they tend. Rational regulation as it refers to nutrition and sexuality is
temperance; the rational regulation of what pertains to human life in com-
mon is justice, and so forth. It is in this sense that the virtuous ends come
to be grasped naturally, that is, as the highest standards according to which
the goods that the human tendencies tend toward are desired, managed, and
realized so that they may effectively contribute to man's good. There exists,
therefore, a natural sense of justice, temperance, etc. which give rise to prac-
tical principles that follow the first principle of the practical reason, and that
are fundamentally rational modes of regulation both in relation to the natural
inclinations and within the natural inclinations. It can be affirmed that in
the natural perception of the virtuous ends, the reason and the inclinations
converge, relating to each other as form and matter. The inclinations furnish
the material, while reason gives the form: and without the latter there would
not exist a properly human good conformed to virtue. The necessary regulat-
ing intervention of the reason implies that the properly human (moral) good
is always an intelligible good.
The virtuous modes of regulating the tendencies' ends are not possessed by
the reason as innate ideas. But in their general terms they are easily known,
thanks to the natural disposition constituted by synderesis. However, coming
to be presupposed is a spontaneous understanding of the meaning of the
natural inclinations and of the relation that they have between themselves,
with the whole person, and other persons.76 In sum, moral good and evil can
only be determined, in the last analysis, in reference to virtue. Moral good
means conformity to virtue, with moral evil being contrary to it.
It would be valuable to specify, nevertheless, that the role of the natural in-
clinations and tendencies, though being material, is not purely material in
the sense that the reason may not find in them an anticipation of meaning.
For this reason it would not be exact to affirm that the only moral regu-
lation of the inclinations and tendencies is that established in each case by
76 For example, man tends toward sexual union, but also toward friendship, communi-
cation, justice understood as equality in giving and receiving, toward fidelity to promises,
etc., and all this has much to do with the mode of regulating the execution of the sexual
tendency, and therefore with what is honest and due in the ambit of this tendency, and
with what is contrary to honesty in the same ambit.


Chapter 8
prudence. The practical principles grasped by synderesis, which are in reality
the intellectual dimension of the moral virtues, have a normative content and
structure that already expresses in a general sense the role performed by each
good (nourishment, economic goods, friendship, sexuality) in human life con-
sidered as a whole. This normative structure is further developed by moral
knowledge, giving rise to more concrete ethical norms. Only then, in the third
“moment”, does prudence intervene, and it does so maintaining consistency
with synderesis and moral knowledge. The practical reason which formulates
the prudential judgment is the same reason which grasps the first practical
principles and develops them by formulating concrete operative norms. In this
process of realization, the reason is always consistent with itself. A concrete
moral judgment contrary to practical principles (if a person were to think,
for example, that in this concrete case adultery was justified) would not be
a rational or prudential judgment, but a judgment deformed by error or the
passions. The reason would not be able to recognize itself in it.
The First Principle of the Practical Reason and the First Principle
of the Natural Moral Law — What we have said concerning the first prin-
ciple of the practical reason and the virtuous ends as the subsequent practical
principles, explains the genesis of the natural moral law as a spontaneous
regulating activity of behavior that the human reason possesses and exercises
“by nature”. If we look at the full development of this activity, which can be
reached in connection with the intellectual virtues (knowledge, wisdom) and,
in the Christian, with faith, we must say then that the first principle of the
natural moral law, in the sense of being the most important and of being max-
imally “architectural”, is the love of God and neighbor.77 The virtues express,
then, the modes in which the tendency and the realization of human goods
must be regulated so that they are congruent with a will intent on perfection
in God both for its possessor and for every human person.78
8.2.3
The Precepts of the Natural Moral Law
In theological literature, and also in documents of the Church's magisterium,
there is often mention of precepts of the natural moral law.
This can be
legitimately discussed when one passes from the level of the direct exercise
of the practical reason (“ratio practica in actu esercito”), in which is placed
what we have said up to this moment, to the level of the reflective exercise
of the same reason (“ratio practica in actu signato”79), when one passes, that
is, to the systematic reflection of the practical activity of the human reason,
77 Cf. A. Rodríguez Luño, La scelta etica (1998), 52.
78 Cfr. G. Abbà, Felicità, vita buona e virtù (1995), 196.
79 Cf. Cajetan, Commentary on the “Summa Theologiae”, I-II, q. 58, a. 5, Comm. VIII.


Law within the Context of the Doctrine of the Virtues
a reflection which pertains to moral science.80 It is at this level of reflection
that moral science establishes normative statements, that is, propositions in
terms of “one must” or “one must not” which express the contents of the
principles of the practical reason or of judgments concerning these principles.
For example, the proposition “one must give to each his own” expresses the
principle of “justice” at a general level, while the proposition “one must restore
what was stolen” expresses a more concrete demand of the same principle.
These are the normative statements which are normally referred to when one
speaks of precepts of the natural moral law.
Following Saint Thomas, a distinction was established between the diverse
categories of precepts of the natural moral law, according to their degree of
evidentness or proximity to self-evident principles.81 These categories of the
precepts of the natural moral law are three: the first and common precepts; the
secondary precepts very close to the first precepts; and the secondary precepts
that can be derived from these other precepts only through reasoning which
is more or less difficult and complicated.82 The first precepts are those which
enjoy the most evidentness of all and regard diverse ambits of action, as for
example “one must not do evil to anyone”, the golden rule, etc. They respond
also to virtuous ends considered in their highest generality. Saint Thomas
retains that the first precepts were not promulgated in the Decalogue, since
their evidentness would render their promulgation superfluous. The secondary
precepts close to the first precepts refer already to specific ambits of action,
and can be known from the first precepts with simple reasoning, of which
all are capable; to this group pertain the precepts of the Decalogue.
The
precepts of the third category can be based logically on those of the second
category through more complicated reasoning, accessible only to the wise,
i.e. to the devotees of moral science; according to Saint Thomas “the people
receive these principles from God, through being taught by wise men.” 83 They
are not explicitly contained in the Decalogue, though they may find in the
Decalogue the premises from which they are derivable.
We must retain, therefore, that the natural light of the practical reason
reaches some knowledge with immediate evidentness: the first princi-
ples and the virtues considered in their more general content. Departing
from this first moral knowledge, it arrives discursively to other truths,
more or less distant from the first evident principles. But, on the re-

81 It is not entirely easy to get an exact idea of the thought of Saint Thomas on the

3; II-II, q. 122, a. 1. On the other hand, he did not furnish a list of precepts pertaining
to each of the categories, something which, moreover, there would not be much interest for
doing.

Chapter 8
flective level of the precepts of which we are speaking, what is decisive
for establishing if a moral assertion is an expression or not of the nat-
ural moral law, is not so much the immediate or mediate character of
the principles, as is the fact of having a necessary connection with the
first principles or the virtues. If the necessary connection exists, even if
people have discovered it only with the passing of time, we are dealing
with a precept of the natural moral law; if it does not exist, we will
certainly be before an ethical disposition established by an authority,
whether it be political, religious, etc.
8.3
The Moral Law of the Old Testament:
Covenant, Gift, and Promise
8.3.1
The Old Testament in the History of Salvation
It is frequent in theological literature to speak of the “Law” to refer (pars
pro toto) to the moral teachings of the Old Testament. Nonetheless, in
a rigorous sense, the “Law” is only part of it, concretely, the essential
content of the Pentateuch, which the New Testament often calls “The
Law of Moses”.84 Alongside the “Law” are mentioned “the Prophets”,85
or “the Prophets and Psalms”.86 In Old Testament biblical theology,
generally accepted is a distinction between an ethics of the law, an ethics
of the prophets, and a wisdom—or sapiential—ethics,87 a distinction
which, nonetheless, should not be conceived of as a separation, since
between the three sources of Old Testament ethics there exist evident
connections and points in common.
The entire economy of the Old Testament is primarily ordained to prepare,
announce, and signify the coming of the Savior.88 According to the Pauline
expression, the “Law” is good and holy,89 but considered as a whole it is
not definitive. “The law was our disciplinarian for Christ, that we might be
justified by faith.”90 It is, therefore, ordained toward Christ, who constitutes
its fulfillment: “Christ is the end of the law.”91 “An end not as a lapse into
discontinuance—comments Saint Ambrose–, but as the fullness of the Law:
this is fulfilled in Christ, from the moment He came not to abolish the Law,
84 Cf. Lk 2:22; Jn 1:17; 7:19; Heb 10:28.
85 Mt 5:17; Lk 24:25,27; Acts 28:23.
86 Lk 24:44.
87 Cf. E. Testa, La morale dell'Antico Testamento, (Brescia: Morcelliana, 1981);
W.H. Schmidt, Einführung in das Alte Testament, 2nd ed., (Berlin: 1982).
88 Cf. Dei Verbum, 8. For a synthetic vision cf. J.-D. Barthélemy, Dio e la sua immagine,
4th ed., (Milan: Jaca Book, 1980).
89 Cf. Rom 7:12.
90 Gal 3:24.
91 Rom 10:4.


Law within the Context of the Doctrine of the Virtues
but to bring it to completion.”92 The Pauline polemic does not mean that
the “Law” is opposed to grace, but it is directed against those for whom it,
“despite the coming of grace, persists in maintaining its own domain. If, in
fact, it locks up those who would need to turn themselves toward grace, then it
depraves our salvation. Like the lamp that shines in the night, if, at the dawn,
it were to impede the sight of the sun, not only would it not be something
pleasing but instead something harmful, thus the law would be if it were an
obstacle to the attainment of that which is best.” 93
Having made this necessary caveat, it should be noted that the Old Testament
is an essential part of the Word of God, and its books preserve perennial
elements.94 Along with some evidently imperfect things, these books contain
instructions and moral examples of permanent and even excellent value. For
this reason, the law—and primarily the Decalogue—will come to be widely
taken up again, executed, and deepened in the New Testament95 and in the
Christian theological and catechetical tradition. These books, “though they
also contain some things which are incomplete and temporary [ life, and a
wonderful treasury of prayers.”96 “The Church has always vigorously opposed
the idea of rejecting the Old Testament under the pretext that the New has
rendered it void.”97 The books of the Old Covenant, in fact, were always used
in the Church's teachings and liturgy, and the Decalogue, for example, still
serves as a basic structure for Christian moral catechesis.
The books of the Old Testament possess, furthermore, a characteristic of im-
mense interest.
They present moral and religious teachings making use of
rather diverse literary genres. Alongside texts of a more strictly legal nature,
there exist historical texts with a fundamentally narrative structure, poetic
texts, collections of prayers and wise maxims, recounts of the deeds of heroes
of the elect people, instructions regarding feasts which commemorate the di-
vine gifts, etc. Modes of expression that sometimes reveal the nature and
conditions of the moral life in a rather more exact manner than discourses
structured according to the canons of present-day normative morality.
It should not be forgotten that the study of the moral teachings of the
Old Testament present more than a few problems. There are studies of
the dating, the literary genre, of the history and redactional composition

of the texts, relationships with the literature of the surrounding peoples,
relationships between the social evolution of the people of Israel, divine
revelation and the reflection on the tradition of divine revelation. These
are questions for specialists which we do not intend to delve into here.
Lastly, there is the problem of the breadth of material available. Here
we shall limit ourselves to offering a comprehensive vision, attentive to
the more fundamental elements and, among these, to those which, for
their strictly moral nature, are permanent, and therefore absolutely not
to be disregarded by a Christian.98
8.3.2
The Ethics of the Law
In studies of the Pentateuch it is normal to distinguish between moral, cul-
tual, and judicial precepts. Judicial precepts comprise norms of penal, civil,
and procedural law, which are found principally in the “Covenant Code” 99
and in Deuteronomy. The cultual norms are contained principally in Leviti-
cus, but also in Exodus and in Numbers: among these we can cite the norms
concerning worship,100 legal purity,101 and those contained in the “Holiness
Code”.102 We find the moral norms scattered throughout Exodus, Leviticus,
and Deuteronomy, and they contain prescriptions regarding behavior to ob-
serve with one's neighbor, sexual behavior, and, above all, the Decalogue or
Ten Commandments, which has come down to us in two versions.103 Accord-
ing to the theological tradition, the cultual and judicial norms are to be consid-
ered repealed after the coming of Christ. We shall thus concern ourselves only
with the moral norms, which, for what regards their content, substantially
comply with the natural moral law,104 and therefore with the virtues.105

e G. Barbaglio, voce Decalogo, in Nuovo Dizionario di Teologia Morale (1990), 770–
786 and 204–218 respectively. Of notable interest, even if being more complex, is
the synthesis of the biblical morality of the Old Testament offered by G. Angelini,

Law within the Context of the Doctrine of the Virtues
From a general point of view, it should be noted first of all that the ethics of
the “torah” has a religious-theological character. Faith in YHWH as the only
God who has a particular relationship with Israel, understood as a covenant,
is the framework in which this ethos is inserted, in such a way that all of the
ethical prescriptions come to be seen as proceeding from God, and respect for
them is seen as the people's part to play within the covenant. Therefore, the
moral life does not come to be conceived as an autonomous earthy dimension.
It is rather permeated with religiosity understood in a dialogical sense, and
possesses an altogether secondary significance in relation to God's initiative
and loving election. The divine moral instruction is lived as a gift and as
grace, a sign of the closeness and the care of God toward His people. 106
The Law has a pronounced social character. It is firstly the law given to the
people of Israel, to ensure justice, peace, prosperity, and above all fidelity
to the covenant sealed with YHWH. The precepts of the Decalogue all aim
toward justice: toward justice with God and justice with one's neighbor. Af-
ter the precepts which refer to God, comes commanded the sanctification of
the Sabbath—which possesses a cultual aspect as well as a social aspect (rest
must be guaranteed for servants and foreigners)–respect for one's parents, for
innocent life, for matrimony, and the property of others; finally one's neigh-
bor comes to be protected from injustices which arise from false testimony
in judicial processes and from another's unjust covetousness of his wife or
property. The law takes into account the real weakness of the people, and
on some points concedes with the “hardness of your heart”.107 Even if the
precepts of the law oftentimes command or forbid certain actions (“you shall
do”, “you shall not do”), it is notable, however, that they intend to lead the
people toward virtuous dispositions: faith and love of God, justice and love
toward neighbor.108 That which stands behind the commandments given by
God to the elect people is a request for faith and trust. The people are re-
buked when, despite the powerful deeds done by the Lord in their favor, they
allow themselves to fall into fear or complaining which show a lack of faith
ordered. But this is effected by the acts of all the virtues” (S.Th. I-II, q. 100, a. 2).
106 Deuteronomy is perhaps the best testimony: “Therefore, I teach you the statutes and
decrees as the LORD, my God, has commanded me, that you may observe them in the land
you are entering to occupy. Observe them carefully, for thus will you give evidence of your
wisdom and intelligence to the nations, who will hear of all these statutes and say, 'This
great nation is truly a wise and intelligent people.' For what great nation is there that has
gods so close to it as the LORD, our God, is to us whenever we call upon him? Or what
great nation has statutes and decrees that are as just as this whole law which I am setting
before you today?”(Deut 4:5–8). The law is the intelligence and wisdom that will ensure
the coming of freedom and peace purchased with the exodus from Egypt.

and trust. In contrast, that which comes to be praised in the righteous and
the heroes of the elect people is their faith.109
8.3.3
The Ethics of the Prophets
The prophets energetically underline ethical demands, which are not satisfied—
and still less can one flee from them—by cult acts alone.110 “Their fundamen-
tal intuition is that the ethical demand is the primary demand of the true
God.”111 Obviously, the prophets are not opposed to cult, but to a cult with-
out soul which could coexist with injustice and a failure to listen to the divine
words. In this perspective there is found in the prophets a strong insistence
on social duties, that is, on justice and on the law: a commitment to the un-
derprivileged, the defense of the weak, and the overcoming of inequalities.112

the Letter to the Hebrews (11:2–38): through faith Abel offered to God a sacrifice that was
better than that offered by Cain; Enoch, before being transported away, was attested to as
being pleasing to God; Noah, divinely warned of things that were not yet seen, constructed
an ark to save his family; Abraham was obedient in departing for a place where he would
receive his inheritance, and departed without knowing where he was going; by faith he
sojourned into the promised land as in a foreign region, living in tents, as also did Isaac and
Jacob; Sarah was given the opportunity to become a mother because Abraham considered
faithful the one who gave the promise; Abraham, put to the test, offered his only son; Isaac
also blessed Jacob and Esau regarding future things, etc.

those who feast on the mountains; in your midst are those who do lewd things. In you are
those who uncover the nakedness of their fathers, and in you those who coerce women in
their menstrual period. There are those in you who do abominable things with the wives
of their neighbors, men who defile their daughters-in-law by incest, men who coerce their
sisters, the daughters of their own fathers. There are those in you who take bribes to shed
blood. You exact interest and usury; you despoil your neighbors violently; and me you have
forgotten, says the Lord GOD”(Ezek 22:3–12).


Law within the Context of the Doctrine of the Virtues
There is undoubtedly in the prophets a very lively sense of sin, which is seen as
an expression of human pride. Thematically speaking, there are not any sub-
stantial novelties in the prophetic ethos with respect to the Pentateuch: the
prophets evoke the torah in an historical and social context in which respect
for the law seems to have decreased.
The morality of the prophets should also be seen in a religious context. Behind
one's neighbor and social duties stands YHWH. In socially just behavior the
presence of the Lord becomes visible: “Did not your father eat and drink?
He did what was right and just, and it went well with him.
Because he
dispensed justice to the weak and the poor, it went well with him. Is this not
true knowledge of me?”.113 Above all, faith in God comes to be vigorously
emphasized, and from Him proceeds all salvation and security: “For I will
trust in the LORD, who is hiding his face from the house of Jacob; yes, I will
wait for him.”114
8.3.4
The Ethics of the Wisdom Books
General Characteristics — The Wisdom Books, with respect to the rest of
the Old Testament, present entirely unique characteristics.115 Their connec-
tion with extra-biblical literature (Egyptian, Mesopotamic Babylonian and,
for the more recent layers, also Hellenistic literature) is particularly relevant,
and their ethical-rational content is prevalent.116 As evidence for the speci-
ficity of the “sapiential ethics” it is normal to refer to Jer 18:18: “It will not
mean the loss of instruction from the priests, nor of counsel from the wise,
nor of messages from the prophets.” The sapiential ethics of the Wisdom
Books contain the counsel of the wise ones of Israel.
In the more ancient
layers (Proverbs 10–31), affirmations of an ethical type are quite distant from
113 Jer 22:15–16.
114 Isa 8:17.
An expression which is quite telling of the prophetic attitude is that of
Jeremiah; “Cursed is the man who trusts in human beings, who seeks his strength in flesh,
whose heart turns away from the LORD. He is like a barren bush in the desert that enjoys
no change of season, But stands in a lava waste, a salt and empty earth. Blessed is the
man who trusts in the LORD, whose hope is the LORD. He is like a tree planted beside
the waters that stretches out its roots to the stream: It fears not the heat when it comes,
its leaves stay green; In the year of drought it shows no distress, but still bears fruit” (Jer
17:5–8).

(1981), 211–283; G. von Rad, La sapienza in Israele, (Casale Monferrato: Marietti,1982).
For an initial, but good, introduction: A. Minissale, Siracide. Le radici nella tradizione,
(Brescia: Queriniana, 1988); A. Bonora, Proverbi e Sapienza, (Brescia: Queriniana, 1990);
J. Rybolt, Sapienza, (Brescia: Queriniana, 1997) and Siracide, (Brescia: Queriniana, 1997).
116 The biblical wisdom literature comes from a period of time comprising almost a millen-
nium. A more ancient layer can be distinguished—represented fundamentally by Proverbs
10–31, Job, and Ecclesiastes—which before certain paradoxical facts (the suffering of the
just and death) seems to put into crisis the “why” of traditional morality, and a more modern
layer to which pertains Proverbs 1–9 and the books of Sirach and Wisdom.


Chapter 8
abstraction and deduction. They proceed rather from the experiential obser-
vation of real connections, which oftentimes offer a basis for the induction of a
general principle. “The wise one transmits, first of all, a culture from which he
derives his motivations for behavior. The principal criterion is the success of
man in the society of his time. In this sense it can be said that the foundation
of sapiential ethics is anthropological, because it is based on experience, and
makes use of rationality, it emancipates freedom and tends to guarantee to
the person a more balanced and gratifying integration into the world.” 117
In Proverbs 1–9 and in the books of Sirach and Wisdom the fundamental value
is represented by wisdom, of which an undoubtedly more theological concept
is proposed. The wisdom of which it speaks is divine wisdom. In Proverbs
1–9 one arrives at wisdom through listening to the ancient masters, and the
ethical contents are the fruit of a centuries long search, “with the difference
that they now acquire an almost dogmatic value and they approach, even if
still implicitly, toward becoming a type of revelation.” 118 For Sirach wisdom
is the property of God, it is identified with the revelation at Sinai119 and
must be sought with a disposition referred to as “fear of God”; the correlation
between wisdom, law, and fear of God is central to this book.120 The beautiful
hymn of Chapter 24 speaks of a personified wisdom who takes His dwelling
place in Israel in order to then be spread throughout all the earth. Although
it is made concrete in the torah, it is present in all the works of God and
reaches every people and nation.121 Finally, the book of Wisdom adds the
conviction of life after death. And, on such a conviction are the theological
and anthropological conceptions of the righteous and the unrighteous put in
contrast to each other.
For what regards the properly ethical themes, the Wisdom Books dedicate a
very large space. Practically all of the sectors of existence of that time come to
be contemplated, even if not in a systematic way. However, what is especially
surprising is the mode in which ethical themes are treated. The typically nor-
mative language is almost absent. Instead experiences, intuitions, maxims,
counsels, and rational arguments come to be communicated. Their aphoris-
tic presentation stimulates reflection. Their motivation is the correspondence

is nationalized and limited, it is also true that it is seen at the same time in the universal
perspective of the rationality of all men, who are invited to approach it.
This position
of Sirach constitutes the principal merit of his book in relation to the legacy of the Old
Testament” (Ibid., 31), our translation.


Law within the Context of the Doctrine of the Virtues
of what is stated with reality, with the experience of conduct in view of the
success of human life. Furthermore, the results of the actions are opportunely
emphasized, sometimes as expressions of immediate or mediate compensation;
nonetheless, one cannot truly speak of it being a utilitarian approach.122 It
also needs to be noted that great attention is given to virtuous and vicious
forms of human life, to attitudes, to ways of feeling and valuating, to ways of
relating oneself to reality and to the situations which take place in it. Addi-
tionally, moral teaching comes to be transmitted through the examples of the
great protagonists and through the principal events of the history of Israel.123
However, its religious horizon remains. For everything takes place on the ba-
sis of faith in God the Creator, who has ordered all aspects of existence.124
Fear of God is “the beginning”, the “fullness”, the “crown”, and the “root” of
wisdom,125 and life conforming to the law of YHWH constitutes its greatest
expression. Such a life comes to be seen mostly as a virtuous life: i.e. pru-
dent, balanced, serene, prescient, temperate, far from excesses, but above all
founded on faith and fear of God.
Virtues and Vices in Sapiential Ethics — In our study of the
moral virtues we already noted, on the mere level of vocabulary used,
the presence of the virtues in the Wisdom Books.126 Now, considering
the reality itself of the virtues, we must acknowledge that they are ubiq-
uitous, at least in the books of Proverbs, Wisdom, and Sirach. Moral
discourse is developed in them according to the approach characteristic
of an ethics of virtue. Without the pretense of being exhaustive, we
want to offer at least an idea of their principal contents.
Sir 3:17–28 contains a beautiful instruction concerning humility and
pride, a virtue and vice which are seen in this passage as regarding the
way one relates to knowledge. It is not fitting to seek things that are
overly difficult or inquire into things that are too grand; the sense of
mystery should not be lost (vv. 21–23). “Humble yourself the more,
the greater you are” (v. 18), because a humble man is loved by men
and pleasing to God; the humble person finds grace before God and “by
the humble He is glorified” (v. 19). Disastrous are the consequences of
pride: “Their own opinion has misled many, and false reasoning unbal-
anced their judgment. Where the pupil of the eye is missing, there is no
light, and where there is no knowledge, there is no wisdom. A stubborn
man will fare badly in the end, and he who loves danger will perish in
it. A stubborn man will be burdened with sorrow; a sinner will heap

Chapter 8

the offshoot of an evil plant. The mind of a sage appreciates proverbs,
and an attentive ear is the wise man's joy” (vv. 23–28).
Numerous are the reflections dedicated to the use of the tongue. Great
is the power of the tongue that it can be used for good and for evil:
there is a word which helps and another which harms and kills.127 Both
in speech or in the choice to remain silent128 are manifested wisdom
and foolishness, virtue and vice, love and hate, friendship and envy.
He makes good use of the word whoever knows to be silent when it
is fitting to do so,129 who reflects before speaking,130 who chooses the
opportune moment to say what he must say, who safeguards confidential
information,131 who does not confide himself with a fool,132 who does
not scold another person while in the grips of anger.133 Making poor
use of the word is he who speaks at the inopportune time,134 who
speaks too much and tells lies and calumnies,135 the hypocrite and
the flatterer,136 who is quick to judgment137 or who abandons himself
to obscene speech.138 For what regards the consequences of evil speech,
these words of Sirach are emblematic: “A meddlesome tongue subverts
many, and makes them refugees among the peoples; It destroys walled
cities, and overthrows powerful dynasties. A meddlesome tongue can
drive virtuous women from their homes and rob them of the fruit of
their toil; Whoever heeds it has no rest, nor can he dwell in peace. A
blow from a whip raises a welt, but a blow from the tongue smashes
bones; Many have fallen by the edge of the sword, but not as many as by
the tongue. Happy he who is sheltered from it, and has not endured its
wrath; Who has not borne its yoke nor been fettered with its chain.” 139
Moderation should govern all dimensions of life. In eating and in drink-
ing140 and, more in general, in all of the passions: “Fall not into the grip
of desire, lest, like fire, it consume your strength; Your leaves it will eat,
your fruits destroy, and you will be left a dry tree, For contumacious
desire destroys its owner and makes him the sport of his enemies.” 141

Law within the Context of the Doctrine of the Virtues
There are exhortations to monogamy,142 to conjugal fidelity, 143 and to
chastity,144 as well as warnings against lust: “For burning passion is a
blazing fire, not to be quenched till it burns itself out: A man given to
sins of the flesh, who never stops until the fire breaks forth. The rake to
whom all bread is sweet and who is never through till he dies.” 145 In or-
der to live chastely, prudence in social relations are also recommended:
“Avert your eyes from a comely woman; gaze not upon the beauty of
another's wife - Through woman's beauty many perish, for lust for it
burns like fire. With a married woman dine not, recline not at table to
drink by her side, Lest your heart be drawn to her and you go down in
blood to the grave.”146
Work should be done with effort and perseverance: “hold fast to your
duty, busy yourself with it, grow old while doing your task,” 147 while
avoiding the will to embrace too many things with one's own activ-
ity.148 One must flee from laziness, enjoy with moderation of one's own
prosperity, while not trusting too much in it.149 Greed does no good:
“Keeping watch over riches wastes the flesh, and the care of wealth
drives away rest [. . . ] The lover of gold will not be free from sin, for he
who pursues wealth is led astray by it.” 150 The miser loses serenity and
misunderstands the true value of wealth.151 Coming to be illustrated,
furthermore, are the maxims and conditions of prudence,152 justice,153
meekness,154 docility,155 true friendship,156 solidarity,157 etc.
Effec-
tively it puts into relief the cognitive dimensions of virtue and vice,
that is to say, their influence on judgment: “Speak not to a woman
about her rival, nor to a coward about war, to a merchant about busi-
ness, to a buyer about value, to a miser about generosity, to a cruel man
about mercy, to a lazy man about work, to a seasonal laborer about
the harvest, to an idle slave about a great task: pay no attention to any
advice they give. Instead, associate with a religious man, who you are
sure keeps the commandments; Who is like-minded with yourself and
will feel for you if you fall.”158

Chapter 8
We can say in summary that, despite its limitations, the ethics of the
Wisdom Books offers a fairly comprehensive vision of virtue and vice.
On the basis of an acute and realistic empirical observation and of
fidelity to divine instruction, sapiential ethics succeed in tracing an
image far from negligible of the righteous attitudes of man with regard
to personal and material goods, as well as the criteria which inspire
right choice.
8.3.5
The Positive Promulgation
of the Natural Moral Law in the Old Testament
Classical theology considers that in the Old Testament there occurred a pos-
itive promulgation of the natural moral law, at least in its fundamental con-
tents.159 Saint Thomas retained that the moral precepts of the Old Testament
are related to virtue,160 and therefore to the regulation of actions according
to their conformity to reason. One deals, then, with the precepts of the nat-
ural moral law.161 Now at this point it is logical to ask ourselves why it was
necessary to positively promulgate something which in reality is written in
the hearts of all people.162
Basing itself on the teachings of the First Vatican Council,163 the encyclical
Humani Generis responds thus: “For though, absolutely speaking, human
reason by its own natural force and light can arrive at a true and certain
knowledge of the one personal God, Who by His providence watches over and
governs the world, and also of the natural law, which the Creator has written
in our hearts, still there are not a few obstacles to prevent reason from making
efficient and fruitful use of its natural ability [ of such truths is hampered both
by the activity of the senses and the imagination, and by evil passions arising
from original sin. Hence men easily persuade themselves in such matters that
what they do not wish to believe is false or at least doubtful. It is for this
159 On some points, as for example the indissolubility of matrimony, the law of the Old
Testament adapts itself to the weakness man had in that state, and does not completely
express the ethical demands of the natural moral law. This will be fully restored by Christ.
160 “Therefore it was necessary for the Old Law to include precepts about acts of virtue:
and these are the moral precepts of the Law” (S.Th. I-II, q. 99, a. 2).
161 Cf. S.Th. I-II, q. 100, a. 1. In the preceding subsection 8.2.3, we considered more
specifically the relationship between the precepts of the natural moral law and the Deca-
logue.
162 In his response, Saint Thomas considers four motives. “First, because many tumbled
into sin because of a contrary custum. And then, with many, the natural reason wherein
they were written [the precepts of the natural law] was darkened. Second, because, even if
reason prevailed, these persons nonetheless lacked love of the good; and therefore they had
to be induced to do good through a compulsion of the obligatory law. Third, so that it
would not only be nature which pushed towards the works of virtue, but also respect for the
divine commands. Fourth, so that they might be better memorized and often meditated
upon in thought.” (Scriptum Super Sententiis, lib. III, d. 37, q. 1, a. 1).
163 Cf. I Vatican Council, Cost. Dei Filius, Ch. 2: DS 3005.


Law within the Context of the Doctrine of the Virtues
reason that divine revelation must be considered morally necessary so that
those religious and moral truths which are not of their nature beyond the
reach of reason in the present condition of the human race, may be known by
all men readily with a firm certainty and with freedom from all error.” 164 The
same doctrine was re-proposed by the Catechism of the Catholic Church165
and by the encyclical Veritatis Splendor.166 Both in the dogmatic ambit, as
in the moral ambit, the object of revelation comprises also truths which are
not, per se, unreachable for human reason. Revealed truth is not synonymous
with mystery or truth that is not accessible for man. Revealed truth can also
be confirmation of truth that is accessible, in principle, to the reason.
8.4
The Law of Christ
8.4.1
The Law of Christ as “Lex Gratiae”
The messianic prophecies of the Old Testament announce the coming of the
kingdom based on a just and complete law,167 consisting in an infused interior
principle in the hearts of men: “I will place my law within them, and write
it upon their hearts; I will be their God, and they shall be my people. No
longer will they have need to teach their friends and kinsmen how to know the
LORD. All, from least to greatest, shall know me, says the LORD, for I will
forgive their evildoing and remember their sin no more.” 168 All this happens
with the redemptive work of Christ, who justifies men with a righteousness
that overcomes that of the scribes and Pharisees,169 though not wanting to
abolish the law, he changes their heart giving them His Spirit,170 and renders
them to be children of God.171 Saint Paul speaks of the “law of the spirit of
life in Christ Jesus,”172 with which the economy of the Old Testament comes
to be surpassed and abandoned.173 And so the way toward Christian holiness

as the fullness of divine filiation is opened, something of which we already

The encyclical Veritatis Splendor synthetically expresses the ecclesial doctrine
concerning this law of Christ: “Going to the heart of the moral message of
Jesus and the preaching of the Apostles, and summing up in a remarkable
way the great tradition of the Fathers of the East and West, and of Saint
Augustine in particular,175–Saint Thomas was able to write that the New Law
is the grace of the Holy Spirit given through faith in Christ.176 The external
precepts also mentioned in the Gospel dispose one for this grace or produce
its effects in one's life.”177
Therefore, two elements in the law of Christ are distinguished. The first and
principal element is the grace of the Holy Spirit, which heals the entire per-
son and elevates his operative faculties through the theological and the infused
moral virtues. The new law is truly the lex gratiae, because the grace of the
Holy Spirit is not simply an aid for observing the law, but it is the essential
element of the law itself, “consisting in faith that worketh through love.” 178
For this reason the new law is fundamentally an interior law, and not a writ-
ten law, because the Holy Spirit interiorly instructs the faithful;179 it is also
a “law of freedom”, as we know by now.180 In the second place, the new law
is also a written law; as such it is constituted by the Lord's teachings (the
Sermon on the mount, the Beatitudes, etc.) and by the moral catechesis of
the Apostles,181 which can be summarized in the double commandment of
love.182 These teachings regard the things which dispose one for the acquisi-
tion or recovery of grace, and the dispositions and works through which grace
expresses itself and grows. Saint Thomas, in fact, speaks of the sacraments
and the virtues synthetically.183
In order to understand the meaning of this doctrine, a possible misunderstand-
ing should first of all be avoided: the written moral precepts are not secondary
in the sense of being less important or not essential; for the grace of the Holy
Spirit infused in the heart of the believer necessarily implies to “walk accord-

8.4.2
The Theological Virtues and the Infused
Moral Virtues as Principles of Christian Life
“Love and life according to the Gospel cannot be thought of first and foremost
as kinds of precept, because what they demand is beyond man's abilities.
They are possible only as the result of a gift of God who heals, restores and
transforms the human heart by His grace.”187 In its work of rehabilitation and
transformation, grace adapts itself to the fundamental structure of human
morality. In this, as we already know, the precepts, in the sense of normative
statements, are not a primary reality; they are rather reflected normative
expressions of the law constituted of the practical reason.188 In the law of
Christ something analogous happens: the law of Christ is essentially the grace
of the Holy Spirit, which carries with itself new principles (the virtues) which
assume, complete and elevate the natural principles of the human reason,
giving rise to a new interior law of man.
In the lex gratiae the diverse supernatural gifts189 accomplish specific
functions; therefore, the roles of the theological virtues and those of
the infused moral virtues need to be distinguished.
Faith enlightens
the intellect, and hope and charity elevate and incline the will, so that
man can adhere to God with a supernatural love, a participation in
the love with which the Son loves the Father in the Holy Spirit. Un-
der the influence of charity, the form of all the Christian virtues190,
the infused moral virtues elevate and modify the regulating criterion
(medium rationis) of the human ethical virtues, allowing them to regu-
late the relationship of man with his neighbor, with himself, and with
the diverse human goods in such a way as to realize in a practical way
the life which is proper to a child of God in Christ. Divine filiation can

be known, desired, possessed, and translated into a practical conduct
only because man has received, as a divine gift, grace and the virtues:
the operative principles of this life. Without the real possession of such
principles even the evangelical and apostolic teachings would be a dead
letter that kills.191 On the other hand, relying on the possession of the
vital principles, these teachings are the divine light which teaches us
concerning the dispositions, desires, and works which express, consoli-
date, and increase the divine life infused in our hearts.
It is worthwhile to quote from a significant page of Saint John Chrysostom.
“Our life should be so pure as to have no need of any writing: the grace of
the Holy Spirit should substitute books, and as these are written with ink,
so our hearts should be written with the Holy Spirit. Only because we lost
this grace must we make use of writings: but how much better the first way
was, God Himself clearly showed us [. . . ] To His disciples, in fact, God did
not leave anything in writing, but promised them the grace of the Holy Spirit:
'He—[Jesus] told them—will suggest to you all things' [ from Heaven when
the new law was promulgated, and the tablets on which He etched in this
occasion are well superior to the first ones: for the Apostles did not descend
from the mountain carrying, like Moses, tablets of stone in their hands; but
they came down carrying the Holy Spirit in their hearts, by grace becoming
a living law and book.”192
This reflection of Chrysostom is rich in implications for moral theology. Re-
calling to our attention man's weakness, also the Christian's weakness while
living in this world, he underlines the practical importance of the external ele-
ment of the law of Christ,193 which, preserved and transmitted by the Church,
constitutes the necessary normative aid for the formation of the Christian
virtues in the faithful and also for resolving the problems which, already on
the level of natural morality, the formation of prudence presents.194 For this
reason, to insist on the importance of the interior element of the law of Christ
with the purpose of obscuring or relativizing the normative value of its exterior
element would be theologically incorrect 195 and pastorally devastating.
However, it would be equally harmful to lose sight of the importance for moral
theology of the prevalently interior character of the law of Christ. A similar
error would lead—as it has in fact led—to putting in practice a defective
theological methodology and to approaching the moral teachings of the New
Testament in an inadequate way. In fact, the theological value of the inte-

Law within the Context of the Doctrine of the Virtues
rior element of the law of Christ comes to be misunderstood from the moment
that the cognitive dimension of the Christian virtues are not sufficiently rec-
ognized, being demoted to a simple aid for the execution of moral demands
which are knowable and known independently of them. A perspective proper
to an ethics of obligation then emerges,196 as well as the “normativistic pre-
understanding” which negatively conditions the understanding of the specific
identity of Christian morality already at the level of biblical theology.197
In fact, from the moment that one fails to see the moral-theological rel-
evance of the virtuous vital regulation that develops (in actu exercito)
within the Christian community under the guidance of its pastors, the
New Testament comes to be confronted in a reductive and isolated way
as a text, and one proceeds to the study it with the only tools—which
are nonetheless always necessary—furnished by literary hermeneutics.
Problems inevitably emerge regarding the relationship between reason
and Revelation, and between absolute validity and historical applica-
tive development, which without the proper moral epistemology of the
virtues are not easy to adequately confront, and even more so if one
takes as a starting point the baseless theological presupposition that
considers as revealed by God only what is not accessible to human rea-
son.198 But it is especially noteworthy that the “normativistic preun-
derstanding” that we have discussed finishes by impeding the awareness
of the full correspondence between the interior and exterior elements of
the new law, given that the first consists in grace, charity, and in the
other virtues, while the second is interpreted in a forced way under the
perspective proper to an ethics of obligation.
8.4.3
The New Law as the Fullness of the Moral Law
The new law “is the perfection here on earth of the divine law, natural and
revealed.”199 It brings to fulfillment both the natural moral law and the moral
law of the Old Testament. Regarding the latter, the new law “releases their
hidden potential and has new demands arise from them [. . . ]
proceeds to
reform the heart, the root of human acts, where man chooses between the pure
and the impure, where faith, hope, and charity are formed and with them the
other virtues. The Gospel thus brings the Law to its fullness through imitation
of the perfection of the heavenly Father, through forgiveness of enemies and
prayer for persecutors, in emulation of the divine generosity.” 200 With the
new law, the free and eternal decree of God through which we were chosen in
196 Cf. Chapter I, subsection 1.2.2.
197 Cf. Chapter II, subsection 2.4.3.
198 Cf. what was said above in subsection 8.3.5.
199 CCC, 1965.
200 CCC, 1968.


Chapter 8
Christ to be children of God arrives at fulfillment and with the help of grace
perfect virtue is rendered possible.
Deeper theological study of this doctrine opens up diverse questions.
Concretely, it raises three questions regarding: the status of the natural
moral law once it has been assumed by the new law; the relationship be-
tween charity and the moral virtues; and the existence or non-existence
of specific moral precepts of the new law.
The Christocentric Character and Autonomous Epistemology
of the Natural Moral Law — Regarding this problem it is important
to find a balance, insofar as two equally important needs must be settled
despite seeming to be opposed to one another.
We come to the first term of the problem. By now we know that all
the expressions of the moral law have a common origin and a common
end.
All “have their origin and goal in the eternal, wise and loving
counsel whereby God predestines men and women 'to be conformed to
the image of his Son' (Rom 8:29).”201 If the call to live in Christ is, by
the free choice of God, the center of the eternal law, then the natural
law and also the law of the Old Testament are elements or fragments
ordered toward the whole, which is the law of the New Testament or
lex gratiae.202
From this it follows that, factually and gratuitously, creation and the
subsequent natural moral law are as the first passage of the carrying out
of the predestination of man in Christ. With the words of John Paul
II, “all the work of creation pertains to the plan of salvation, the mys-
terious project 'hidden from ages past in God who created all things'
(Eph 3:9). Through the act of the creation of the world, and in partic-
ular of humanity, the plan of salvation begins to be realized.”203 In fact,
it must be added that “predestination” 204 precedes “the foundation of
the world”, that is, it preceeds Creation, since this is realized from the
standpoint of the predestination of humanity. Applying to the divine
life the temporal analogies of human language, we can say that God
wants “first” to communicate Himself in His divinity to the humanity
called to be in the world, created in His image and likeness; “first” He

202 Cf. on the subject-matter A. Scola, La competenza del magistero a definire “in
re morum”. Elementi per una fondazione teologica, in Various Authors., “Humanae
vitae”: 20 anni dopo (1988), 530; I. Biffi, La prospettiva biblico-cristologica della
“Veritatis Splendor” (1995)
203 John Paul II, Discorso 5-III-1986, n. 3: Insegnamenti, IX-1 (1986) 614–615,
our translation.
204 It is helpful to note that John Paul II clarifies that “predestination” has here
the meaning of “choice”. It deals with the fact that we were chosen in Christ before
the creation of the world, as was said in the Letter to the Ephesians and to the
Colossians.


Law within the Context of the Doctrine of the Virtues
elects humanity, in the eternal and consubstantial Son, to participate
in His sonship (through grace), and only “after” (“in its turn”) does He
will creation: the world to which humanity pertains. In this way the
mystery of predestination enters “organically”, in a certain sense, into
the entire plan of Divine Providence.”205
On this basis it can be affirmed then that the diverse forms of the moral
law are “translations” of our predestination in Christ. The natural law
does not lose its consistency and its essential rationality, but it is still
not extraneous to the Christocentric perspective, rather, it is included
in it. Christ, the new Adam, assumes all of the demands of the first
Adam, and the natural moral law and the old law are thus recapitulated
in Christ. The entire Christ becomes the regulating structure of all the
fragmentary forms of ethics. The lex nova cannot be reinterpreted in
light of the natural law, but instead the contrary should be done. The
natural law is included in the law of Christ. This does not imply limit-
ing the validity of the natural moral law to a single religious confession,
because what is assumed (the natural moral law) is not abolished nor
essentially altered. In being assumed within Christian morality, the nat-
ural moral law not only remains in all of its validity, but is furthermore
brought to completion and acquires a salvific value.206 Moreover, there
is a perfect correspondence between the universality of the moral law
and the universality and immutability of our being chosen in Christ.207
We shall now examine the second term of the problem. From the epis-
temological point of view, i.e. from the point of view of the acquisition
of knowledge, the natural moral law continues to possess its own intelli-
gibility in terms of moral reasonableness (recta ratio). Even if from the
ontological point of view there exists the aforementioned relationship,
even if existentially a “human morality” and “Christian morality” form
in the Christian an organic unity, from the cognitive point of view the
two levels always remain differentiated and relatively “autonomous” in
such a way that one can and must speak of a “rightful autonomy of the
practical reason”208. This means that there exists a level formed by the
natural ethical virtues regulated by prudence, and that knowledge of
such a level is found within a specific rational methodology that in prin-
ciple does not have need of a theological methodology.209 Therefore, the
ambit of the natural moral law is par excellence the ambit wherein a
dialogue with non-believers is always possible, and it is also the ambit
205John Paul II, Discorso 28-V-1986, n. 4: Insegnamenti, IX-1 (1986) 1699, our
translation.
206 Cf. Chapter I, subsection 1.1.3.
207 Cf. A. Scola, La competenza del magistero a definire “in re morum” (1998),
534–535.
208 Cf. Veritatis Splendor, 40; see Chapter I, subsection 1.3.2.
209 Cf. regarding this aspect of the problem M. Rhonheimer, Morale cristiana e
ragionevolezza morale: di che cosa è il compimento la legge del Vangelo?, in G. Bor-
gonovo (ed.), Gesù Cristo, legge vivente e personale della Santa Chiesa, (Casale
Monferrato: Piemme, 1996), 147–168.


Chapter 8
in which it is crucial—also for theological motives—to use reason with
rigor, making the highest effort to adapt interpretive schemes to what
is truly human moral activity. For this purpose, it was rightly observed
that, “in order to bring together the natural and supernatural levels and
this means to overcome a morality of pure obligation [. . . ], it needs to
be rediscovered at the human-natural level that moral rationality that
is the necessary and indispensable prerequisite of any morality of char-
ity and of the beatitudes. This rationality is that which is peculiar to
the moral virtues.”210
It remains to be clarified why we said that the epistemological auton-
omy of the natural moral law is relative. We intended merely to recall
that, in fact, the perception of some ethical demands of the natural
moral law can be obscured or rendered difficult, and for this reason—as
we know—the revelation of some natural ethical demands is “morally
necessary.” To this it can be added that Revelation permits of a deeper
understanding of certain aspects of the natural moral law; for example,
the perspective delineated in Chapter 5 of the Letter to the Ephesians
further reveals the value and reasons for the indissolubility of marriage.
We retain, furthermore, that the cognitive dimension of the theological
virtues renders easier the right evaluation of certain human situations.
Hope, for example, permits prudence to judge rightly if it is worth it to
sustain certain efforts or to undertake certain projects.
Charity as the Form of the Virtues — As we know, charity is
considered by theology as the form of all the virtues.
There exist,
however, diverse opinions concerning the exact meaning of this thesis.
For some, charity is the supreme motive of moral behavior, it is like
the motor and the end, but the good that it pushes one to do is not
constituted in any way by it. That is to say, charity compels one to
do the good and to order toward God the realized good, but it does
not enter in to form a part of the constitution of the good action. The
moral good is then an autonomous ambit which can be extrinsically
(at the level of the finis operantis) ordained to the supernatural end by
charity.211 For others, charity not only motivates, moves, and finalizes
the good work from the outside, but it enters in to objectively form a
part of the good moral quality of all other virtues or virtuous actions,
even if together with other elements. That is to say, every virtue or
virtuous action is seen also as a way of expressing love of God and
neighbor, as the realization of love in every ambit of human life.212
The first opinion responds to the truth in the sense that, even in the new
210 Ibid., 161.
211 For this position, cf. C.A.J. Van Ouwerkerk, Caritas et ratio. Etude sur le
double principe de la vie morale chrétienne, (Nimega: 1956).
212 Concerning this position, cf. G. Gilleman, Il primato della carità in teologia
morale (1959) Concerning the entire issue, cf. A. Günthör, Chiamata e risposta
(1998), vol. II, nos. 307–310.


Law within the Context of the Doctrine of the Virtues
law, the reason is always a principle of morality insofar as any virtuous
act, including charity, requires rational discernment. It is also true that
charity is not identified with the other virtues; otherwise there would
exist only a single virtue and a single sin, something which is evidently
false. However, all things considered, it seems to us that the second
opinion is preferable, so long as it is not taken to the extreme. The
life of the Christian is unitary, it is not integrated by two autonomous
spheres of value, one exclusively human and another entirely deter-
mined by charity. Charity exercises a manifold influence that cannot
be limited to a motivation or an extrinsic efficient influence. Charity
certainly acts as a motivation but, if it is solidly rooted in the heart,
begins to determine actions, carrying them well beyond what is strictly
due. “This applies above all regarding the knowledge of the particular
virtues and commandments. Whoever loves God is united to the source
and absolute fullness of moral good. In such a way he understands that
he must give himself to Him in every moral decision and become capa-
ble of discerning the partial values in whose implementation he gives
himself to God. Whoever loves God discovers with fine sensibility the
beauty of the particular moral values, in which the holiness of God are
reflected, the value of various virtues, and the meaning of the particular
commandments.”213 It also seems true to us that there exists an objec-
tive connection between the virtues and charity, and that each virtue
can be seen as a direct consequence of the love of God and neighbor.214
The Existence of Specific Ethical Demands in the New Law — In
general terms it seems clear that the law of the Gospel contains new moral
demands both with respect to the natural moral law and the law of the Old
Testament. The novelty can either regard the contents or at least the mode
in which the demands are to be satisfied. In this last sense Leo XIII explained
that the commandment of love was called by the Lord a “new commandment”
not because it was not contained in the Old Testament, but for the new way
in which people must love each other:215 “As I have loved you, so you also
should love one another.”216
The “novelty” of the Gospel Law does not consist in the fact that all of its
teachings are something which never crossed the mind of man. The novelty
sits, on one hand, in the transformation of the regulating criteria of the use of
human goods (infused moral virtues) and, on the other, in the comprehensive
form of the moral life which results of it when it comes to be considered
in its deep dynamism animated by the theological virtues, on account of the
particular connections that each virtue has with the others (justice with mercy
213 A. Günthör, Chiamata e risposta (1998), vol. II, no. 308.
214 Cf. Saint Augustine, De Moribus Ecclesiae Catholicae, 1, 15, 25: NBA 13/1,
53; Saint Gregory the Great, Moralia in Iob, 10, 6, 7–10: CCL 143, 539–544.
215 Cf. Leo XIII, Enc. Sapientiae Christianae, 10-I-1890: ASS 22 (1889–90) 402.
216Jn 13:34.


Chapter 8
and forgiveness; fortitude with charity and fraternal affection; poverty with
magnanimity and liberality, etc.).
All this becomes clearer if the radical dependence of the Christian moral life
on faith that works through charity is considered.217
Faith constitutes the
fundamental act and at the same time the original force that informs the
Christian moral life.218 Through faith man opens himself freely to the salvific
action of God in Christ, remaining encompassed in His paternal goodness,
truth, holiness, and justice. Faith is a gift, as it is also the gratuitous salvific
initiative of God, while at the same time being a free human act, even the
first ethical-religious act of man. Furthermore, faith forms a vital whole with
hope and charity. Standing together with charity, faith is living, like a divine
force which enlightens and compels one toward the communion with God that
constitutes the supreme good of man and, at the same time, transforms and
molds the daily life of the believer in all its dimensions: the righteous one lives
by faith.219 The daily duties of life acquire a new sense when they come to be
performed in a spirit of faith, as difficulties, suffering, sickness, and failures
find a positive meaning in the perspective of the cross of Christ.220 Duties
and difficulties come to be lived in a spirit of obedience to the will of God and
so they become a means of identification with Christ, whose nourishment is
to do in everything the will of the Father.221
Faith is also an unwavering trust. The believer, like Abraham, believes against
all hope,222 even when all signs from the empirical world seem to be in contrast
to the convictions of faith. The book of Job and, in a different way, that of
Ecclesiastes, illustrate the behavior of the righteous in the face of trials and
the apparent denials of ordinary experience.223
The believer remains firm
in the expectations that motivate his own behavior even when all seems to
deny them. In such situations it is well understood that faith is accredited as
righteousness,224 because then it becomes clear that the first and fundamental
form of loving God is to believe in Him, to have a firm trust in Him. Faith
appears as the most basic and deepest openness of man toward the supreme
Good.
Faith brings with it some precise moral duties, for example the duty to profess
it and to not renounce it.225 However, for the understanding of the structure
