Morcelliana, 1953), 120.
219 Cf. Rom 1:17.

Law within the Context of the Doctrine of the Virtues
of the Christian moral life, it interests us to show how faith inserts itself
into the dynamism of the practical reason, enlightening and transforming its
principles. By its very nature, the saving action of God, received in faith, is
aimed at someone who already knows something: faith is not received in a
vacant human scenario. Faith is not, nor does it give to man, all that man is,
that man knows, or that man does; but in the person who receives it, faith
becomes the supreme criterion of life, and so it comes to constitute a filter
or criterion of judgment according to which what was already good in the
person will remain, what was in need of transformation will be transformed,
and what should be abandoned is abandoned. In this sense Saint Paul says to
the believers of the city of Rome: “Do not conform yourselves to this age but
be transformed by the renewal of your mind, that you may discern what is the
will of God, what is good and pleasing and perfect.” 226 From a formal point
of view, just as all the Christian's life is transformed, so also the capacity
of moral discernment is transformed by faith. But this does not mean that
all the criteria of behavior inspired by faith are also, from the material point
of view (relating to content), completely new.
Saint Paul shows himself
open to recalling the moral precepts of the Old Testament which pass the
test put to them by faith in Christ, just as he also makes reference to the
fundamental sense of right and wrong present in the human race: “Finally,
brothers, whatever is true, whatever is honorable, whatever is just, whatever
is pure, whatever is lovely, whatever is gracious, if there is any excellence and
if there is anything worthy of praise, think about these things.” 227
How does the renewal of the capacity for moral discernment through faith
happen?
How is faith inserted into the structure of the practical reason?
Keeping in mind that the fundamental elements for explaining the activity of
the practical reason are the goods toward which the natural inclinations aim,
the practical principles (moral virtues) that regulate the use of goods, and the
ethical norms or precepts, it seems to us that the principles of the Christian
life (faith, hope, and love) illuminate the value and meaning of the goods
with which man is confronted each day: health and sickness, pleasure and
pain, life and death, wealth and poverty, freedom and slavery, marriage and
celibacy, etc. This new dimension of value and meaning implies a renewal
of the practical principles (the new normative criteria of the infused moral
virtues). If the value and meaning of the goods change, the disposition of man
regarding their possession or privation must also change. The New Testament
shows this reality.
We shall look at some examples. In light of the relationship with mate-
rial and economic goods that went along with the life that Christ chose
226 Rom 12:2.
227 Phil 4:8.


Chapter 8
for Himself, the Christian virtue of poverty is understood: “For you
know the gracious act of our Lord Jesus Christ, that for your sake he
became poor although he was rich, so that by his poverty you might
become rich.”228 The eschatological tension imposes a certain reserva-
tion and a certain attitude with regard to earthly goods and situations,
as Saint Paul shows to the faithful at Corinth: “I tell you, brothers, the
time is running out. From now on, let those having wives act as not
having them, those weeping as not weeping, those rejoicing as not re-
joicing, those buying as not owning, those using the world as not using
it fully. For the world in its present form is passing away.” 229 Also with
regard to common situations in those times, like freedom and slavery,
one can take on a new attitude: “Everyone should remain in the state
in which he was called. Were you a slave when you were called? Do not
be concerned but, even if you can gain your freedom, make the most
of it. For the slave called in the Lord is a freed person in the Lord,
just as the free person who has been called is a slave of Christ. You
have been purchased at a price. Do not become slaves to human beings.
Brothers, everyone should continue before God in the state in which he
was called.”230
Even if we made a complete list of all that is found in the New Testament
regarding this, it would never be a closed list. By its very nature the renewal
of the mind is an open reality. The Christian possesses a new measure of
evaluation to apply not only to the human goods existing in Apostolic times,
but to all the good which will appear in human life alongside the historical,
cultural, and technological development of humanity.
It is helpful to emphasize that the demands of Christian morality are
based in faith and baptism, and involve equally all of the baptized, even
in the diversity of their circumstances and vocations. Certain ways of
understanding the distinction between commandments and evangelical
counsels offer a rather reductive vision of Gospel morality. As Pinckaers
writes, the impression can be given that there exists a double morality:
one for the people caught in the battle against sin, and another for a
reduced group of the “perfect” structured on the basis of the evangel-
ical counsels.231
On the wake of the Second Vatican Council, which
announced the universal call to holiness, the Catechism of the Catholic
Church232 and the encyclical Veritatis Splendor sought delicately to
correct such a vision: “This vocation to perfect love is not restricted
to a small group of individuals. The invitation, 'go, sell your posses-
sions and give the money to the poor', and the promise 'you will have
treasure in heaven', are meant for everyone, because they bring out the

Law within the Context of the Doctrine of the Virtues
full meaning of the commandment of love for neighbour, just as the
invitation which follows, 'Come, follow me', is the new, specific form
of the commandment of love of God.
Both the commandments and
Jesus' invitation to the rich young man stand at the service of a single
and indivisible charity, which spontaneously tends towards that perfec-
tion whose measure is God alone: 'You, therefore, must be perfect, as
your heavenly Father is perfect' (Mt 5:48).”233 From the standpoint of
a morality of the virtues, like the one we have proposed, the distinction
between commandments and counsels would be abandoned and, with it,
the rigid distinction between moral and spiritual theology.

## CHAPTER 9 {#colom-scelti.9}
Civil Law
and Ecclesiastical Law
9.1
The Civil Law
The Christian lives her life, as a child of God in Christ, together with other
Christians and other persons within civil society, and today the latter is po-
litically organized as a State. Life in common within the State possesses a
relevant moral value and presents specific demands that—according to the law
of the Incarnation, though with a completely particular modality—enter in to
form a part of the following of Christ. Therefore, moral theology must treat
of it.
The political dimension of the Christian moral life is a matter of great
complexity, for which there exists an endless bibliography.
It is the
object of a part of moral theology known as the “social doctrine of the
Church.”1 Fundamental moral theology can limit itself to examining a
few general aspects of this doctrine, which nonetheless are the necessary
basis for further in-depth study.
9.1.1
The Attitude toward Authority and the Civil Law
in the New Testament
The Gospels — The message and activity of the Lord were essentially re-
ligious. He did not participate in, nor did He let Himself get involved in,
the political activities of His contemporaries. It is not possible to find in His
preaching anything like a properly political alignment, nor what today would
1 Cf. John Paul II, Enc. Sollicitudo Rei Socialis, 30-XII-1987, 41.


Chapter 9
be considered a theory of the State. Nevertheless, it is possible to discover
at least a significant indication. Jesus is insidiously interrogated by his ad-
versaries regarding the licitness of the payment of taxes due to the Roman
rulers. “'Teacher, we know that you are a truthful man and that you are not
concerned with anyone's opinion. You do not regard a person's status but
teach the way of God in accordance with the truth. Is it lawful to pay the
census tax to Caesar or not? Should we pay or should we not pay?' Know-
ing their hypocrisy he said to them, 'Why are you testing me? Bring me a
denarius to look at.' They brought one to him and he said to them, 'Whose
image and inscription is this?' They replied to him, 'Caesar's.' So Jesus said
to them, 'Repay to Caesar what belongs to Caesar and to God what belongs
to God.' They were utterly amazed at him.”2 Jesus's response seems to put a
greater emphasis on the necessity of giving “to God what belongs to God,” but
without doubt it also contains a general indication regarding the demeanor
to assume before political authority. Duties toward God are not opposed to
duties with respect to the State: whoever gives to God what is God's can be
without contradiction in giving to Caesar what is Caesar's, with the latter
certainly excluding idolatry.
Schnackenburg summarizes the passage in four points: “a) Jesus does
not confer to the emperor (or to the State) the aura of divine gratifica-
tion, but recognizes his (or its) rights and invites his (or its) subjects
to obedience; b) In its own ambit, the State has its meaning as a power
capable of guaranteeing order: the ordering that it accomplishes works
for the advantage of all (economic advantage, advantage of security); c)
Calling the duty toward God as something higher, Jesus creates a reser-
vation with respect to state power: it must not violate God's honor, nor
contradict His commandments; d) Jesus does not emphasize that the
State is limited and ephemeral, but knows that it is subordinated to
the will and power of God.”3
Apostolic Writings — The Acts of the Apostles present diverse examples
of that reservation regarding human authority: “We must obey God rather
than men.”4 In the Catholic theological tradition, the Pauline instructions
found in the Letter to the Romans have had great importance, and they seem
to go a step beyond what was said in the Gospel: one cannot render to God
what is God's without rendering to Caesar what is Caesar's.5
Saint Paul,
who more than once had unpleasant incidents with the representatives of the
2 Mk 12:14–17; cf. Mt 22:15–22; Lk 20:22–26.
3 R. Schnackenburg, Il messaggio morale del Nuovo Testamento (1989), vol. I,

the response of Jesus to Pilate: cf. Jn 19:11.
4 Acts 5:29; cf. also 4:19.
5 “Let every person be subordinate to the higher authorities, for there is no authority
except from God, and those that exist have been established by God. Therefore, whoever
resists authority opposes what God has appointed, and those who oppose it will bring


Civil Law and Ecclesiastical Law
Roman authorities, intends to instruct the readers of the letter regarding
the correct attitude to have with regard to the State. We are not dealing
with merely pragmatic recommendations or those dictated by the opportunity
of the moment, because what is given is a precise theological foundation.
Political authority is traced back to God: it is “established by God” and is
“a servant of God for your good”; whoever is opposed to authority “opposes
what God has appointed.” For this reason, the purpose of civil obedience is
not simply the avoidance of punishment, but is done “because of conscience.”
In the Pastoral Letters obedience to the magistrates and authorities comes
to be equally recommended,6 and these authorities are to be remembered in
prayer, so that we may enjoy a calm and tranquil life with complete piety and
dignity.7
An analogous instruction is given by the First Letter of Saint Peter.8 Without
canonizing the political system, obedience to civil authority also comes to be
traced back to the will of God here as well. Out of love for God, an attitude of
submission and collaboration with the legitimate authorities must be main-
tained, even if at the same time one's own moral identity should be preserved
with freedom. The framework is then completed in the book of Revelation.
This book reflects on the persecutions against the Christians of Asia Minor
who refused to give divine worship to the emperor Domitian.9 The origin of
the State that abuses its power in this sacrilegious way comes to be attributed
to Satan.10 The angel of God makes exhortations to give glory to God and
announces the fall of “Babylon the great.”11 “We have here the other side of
the coin regarding the recognition of the State on the part of the Christians:
judgment upon themselves. For rulers are not a cause of fear to good conduct, but to evil.
Do you wish to have no fear of authority?
Then do what is good and you will receive
approval from it, for it is a servant of God for your good. But if you do evil, be afraid, for
it does not bear the sword without purpose; it is the servant of God to inflict wrath on the
evildoer. Therefore, it is necessary to be subject not only because of the wrath but also
because of conscience. This is why you also pay taxes, for the authorities are ministers of
God, devoting themselves to this very thing. Pay to all their dues, taxes to whom taxes
are due, toll to whom toll is due, respect to whom respect is due, honor to whom honor is
due” (Rom 13:1–7).
6 Cf. Titus 3:1.
7 Cf. 1 Tim 2:1–2.
8 “Be subject to every human institution for the Lord's sake, whether it be to the king
as supreme or to governors as sent by him for the punishment of evildoers and the approval
of those who do good. For it is the will of God that by doing good you may silence the
ignorance of foolish people. Be free, yet without using freedom as a pretext for evil, but
as slaves of God. Give honor to all, love the community, fear God, honor the king” (1 Pet
2:13–17).
9 Cf. Rev 13:16–17.

Chapter 9
to a power which scorns the glory and commandments of God, one must offer
extreme resistance.”12
The teachings of the Letter to the Romans, and those of the Acts of the Apos-
tles and Revelation, are not incompatible.
They represent two consistent
applications of the same principle (“Repay to Caesar what belongs to Caesar
and to God what belongs to God”), which in its concision is clear and pro-
found, but whose particularized application to situations of each time remains
open to further theological understanding.
9.1.2
Personal and Political Morality
Before passing to an exposition of the ecclesial doctrine and to theological
reflections on the civil law, it seems helpful to propose an initial clarification
of a systematic type. Regarding the attitude of the Christian with respect
to the civil law—for example, to the tax law—two kinds of question can be
evoked. The first regards the attitude of the individual: whether Tom must
pay taxes; whether it is a moral fault to entirely or partially evade paying
them; whether there are reasons that could justify a partial evasion of paying
taxes on Tom's part, etc. The second regards the morality of the law itself:
whether the tax law of this or that country is right; whether those imposed
directly or indirectly are more fair; whether taxes must be equal for all or if
they must be proportionate to the person's income, etc. Now it seems to us
that we are dealing with two types of formally diverse questions, even if being
connected, that must be studied with specific methodologies. The diversity
consists in the fact that the first type of questions pertains to personal morality
(it pertains to the honesty of Tom, his duties toward the state, the possibility
that he commits a moral fault or not), while the second type pertains to
political morality (it pertains not to the personal honesty of the citizen, but
the correctness or incorrectness of a legal arrangement).
Therefore, there
needs to be established a distinction between personal and political morality.13
Such a distinction can be based in the consideration of the particular way in
which political society comprises a whole:14 the individuals and the groups
who compose it always preserve a sphere of action and of their own ends,
something which does not happen in other types of wholes, but at the same
time there exist actions proper to the political whole as such, resulting from
collaboration of the parts in view of the good proper to political society, which
12 R. Schnackenburg, Il messaggio morale del Nuovo Testamento (1989), vol. I, 335, our
translation.
13 For a wider study of the problem, see A. Rodríguez Luño, “Le ragioni del liberalismo”,
in J. Joblin - R. Tremblay (eds.), I cattolici e la società pluralista.
Il caso delle “leggi
imperfette”, (Bologna: ESD, 1996), 225–238.
14 It is the way followed by Saint Thomas Aquinas: cf. In Decem Libros Ethicorum, lib.
I, lect. 1.


Civil Law and Ecclesiastical Law
is the common good. On this basis, it can be affirmed that personal morality
is occupied with all the actions of the individual, even those which are referred
to political society, directing them to the final good of the person (holiness).
Political morality is occupied instead with actions performed by political society
insofar as they are directed toward the common good, that is to say, it evaluates
from the standpoint of the common good the rectitude (or lack thereof) of acts
through which political society gives itself a form and organization, whether
it be political, juridical, fiscal, administrative, economic, etc.15
A complete elaboration of the formal distinction between personal morality
and political morality cannot be proposed here. We shall limit ourselves to
saying that such a distinction does not imply a separation between morality
and politics, just as the concept of an “information ethics” does not respond
to an intention of separating informative activity from morality. On the con-
trary, we intend here to underline that political praxis is an intrinsically moral
praxis, and that the common political good is always an expression of the truth
of man and concerns his essential sociality, and therefore political activity is
an object of the study of morals. At the same time it needs to be affirmed
that politics is not an all-encompassing dimension, and moral rectitude can-
not be, as we shall see in what follows, reduced to simple legal rectitude. In
fact, political morality aims directly at achieving the political common good,
which is not identified with the final good of the person, and this is a rea-
son why the moral logic that immediately and directly regulates the political
world is formally diverse from the logic of personal morality.16 However, this
formal diversity does not impede the fact that political and personal morality
are parts of a unitary moral knowledge, since in the end the common politi-
cal good stands in function to the good of the person. In summary, political
morality is a part of morality for the evident fact that political activity is not
the entire moral activity of the Christian, but a sector of it. It could not be
otherwise, since life in Christ is a reality which has notable implications for
political activity, while at the same time transcending it.
9.1.3
Value and Purpose of the Civil Law
Morality and Legality — The moral value at the basis of the civil law
pertains to the fact that it promulgates, renders explicit, and determines those
demands of the natural moral law that are necessary for making the life in
15 Cf. In Decem Libros Ethicorum, lib. I, lect. 1, nos. 4–6. Political ethics are occupied
also with some actions of the individual person, but not to establish their morality, which
is determined by personal morality, but rather to be able to identify their punishability, if
this is required for the common good.
16 “Bonum commune civitatis et bonum singulare unius personae non differunt solum
secundum multum et paucum, sed secundum formalem differentiam: alia est enim ratio
boni communis et boni singularis” (S.Th. II-II, q. 58, a. 7, ad 2).


Chapter 9
common we share in a politically organized society possible and adequately
regulated.17
First, we shall look at the meaning of promulgation, rendering explicit, and
determination, which are three modes in which the civil law connects with the
natural moral law. To promulgate the natural moral law means to render some
of the precepts of the natural moral law public in a legal text and impose their
observance, for example, when the civil law considers intentional homicide
or theft as being against the law and determines a penalty for them. The
natural moral law is rendered explicit when the civil law formulates certain
conclusions taking as its starting point some of the precepts of the natural
moral law, for example, when the civil law recognizes in parents all the duties
and rights derived from parental authority. Finally, there is a determination of
the natural moral law when the civil law chooses one of the different modes of
realizing a natural ethical demand, for example, the necessity of guaranteeing
safety in traffic can be realized by driving on the right side of the road, as it
is done in the United States, or by driving on the left side of the road, as it
is done in England.
It is the task of the civil authority to promulgate, render explicit, and deter-
mine the natural moral law not because the political authorities are directly
the guarantors or the ones responsible for the personal morality of the people,
but insofar as this is necessary or helpful for rendering possible the free, just,
and peaceful life of people in society. In other terms, “human law is ordained
for one kind of community, and the Divine law for another kind. Because
human law is ordained for the civil community [ for which the Divine law is
ordained, is that of men in relation to God, either in this life or in the life to
come. ”18 From this it follows that the ambit of the civil law is more limited
than that of the natural moral law,19 since the competence of the former is
limited by its end: the common political good. No morally evil act can be
commanded by the civil law, and no morally necessary act can be prohibited;
however not all which is good from the moral point of view can be required
coercively nor can all which is morally evil be coercively prohibited, but only
that which is in some way relevant to the common good of society.
Purpose of the Human Law — The ecclesial doctrine concerning the com-
mon good can be summarized in affirming that it implies the recognition and
defense of the fundamental rights of the person, as well as the promotion of
peace and public morality.20 “Certainly the purpose of civil law is different
and more limited in scope than that of the moral law. But 'in no sphere of
life can the civil law take the place of conscience or dictate norms concerning
17 Cf. S.Th. I-II, q. 95, a. 2.
18 S.Th. I-II, q. 100, a. 2.
19 Cf. Evangelium Vitae, 71.
20 Cf. Dignitatis Humanae, 7.


Civil Law and Ecclesiastical Law
things which are outside its competence', which is that of ensuring the com-
mon good of people through the recognition and defense of their fundamental
rights, and the promotion of peace and of public morality. The real purpose of
civil law is to guarantee an ordered social coexistence in true justice, so that
all may 'lead a quiet and peaceable life, godly and respectful in every way' (1
Tim 2:2). Precisely for this reason, civil law must ensure that all members
of society enjoy respect for certain fundamental rights which innately belong
to the person, rights which every positive law must recognize and guarantee.
First and fundamental among these is the inviolable right to life of every inno-
cent human being. While public authority can sometimes choose not to put a
stop to something which-were it prohibited-would cause more serious harm,21
it can never presume to legitimize as a right of individuals-even if they are the
majority of the members of society-an offense against other persons caused
by the disregard of so fundamental a right as the right to life.” 22 “Thus any
government which refused to recognize human rights or acted in violation of
them, would not only fail in its duty; its decrees would be wholly lacking in
binding force.”23
In virtue of its specific task, ordinarily the civil law shall regulate external
acts pertaining in some way to justice, and with a view to the future (prin-
ciple of the non-retroactivity of the law). We know, however, that the civil
law possesses indirectly a very wide educative and cultural influence.24 For
this reason the civil law should be evaluated not only for what it directly
commands, prohibits, or permits, but also for the conception of the person
and of life that it expresses. This educative dimension of the civil law con-
stitutes a challenge for Christians, and not only for them, and also needs
to be adequately interpreted. If the political systems considered as a whole
are not unjust, widespread opposition to them is not beneficial. Instead, an
attentive discernment should be exercised, in a way that Christians manage
to strengthen and make prevalent the humanistic and Christian roots of the
modern State. This requires a generous and incisive cultural intervention,
capable of bringing back a Christian soul to the current political culture.
In this perspective, a Christian cannot but sense that in reality cer-
tain parts of the legislative body express a conception that does not
respond to the culture of the rights of the person, and therefore exer-
cises a heavy negative influence on personal and social behavior. Such
laws, in fact, contribute to weakening the natural, cultural, political,
moral, and religious conditions of personal identity, as well as the loss
of the recognition of the ethical significance of politics, culture, and
21 Cf. S.Th. I-II, q. 96, a. 2.
22 Evangelium Vitae, 71.
23 Blessed John XXIII, Encyclical. Pacem in Terris, 11-IV-1963, part II: AAS 55 (1963)
274.
24 Cf. Chapter VII, subsection 7.4.3.


Chapter 9
communication. Political society easily becomes a simple instrument
at the service of the satisfaction of individual interests, and comes to
be regulated only by consensus concerning economic and vital values;
or else it happens that in legislative and juridical practice the human
rights are subordinated to the purposes of a particular side, and through
imperfect and unjust laws such rights come to be denied or emptied,
losing their function of structuring social life.25
9.1.4
The Christian Citizen and the Civil Law
The Obligatoriness of the Civil Law — In general terms, the Christian
attitude regarding the civil law is that which is expressed in the Letter to the
Romans: that is, the civil law is morally obligatory.26 In principle, Christian
morality retains that the civil and political order is “established by God” and
“a servant of God” for the good of humanity. Whoever opposes it “opposes
what God has appointed.” For this reason, obedience to the law is done “be-
cause of conscience”; more concretely, obedience to the civil law is a demand
of the virtue of justice (legal justice).
Notwithstanding its possible deficiencies, human law is absolutely necessary
for safeguarding the common good, which is its raison d'être. In many cases
prudence and each person's individual initiative would be sufficient for guar-
anteeing an ordered life in common; however, growing interdependence helps
us to see the necessity, in many areas, of a more or less meticulous regula-
tion of diverse matters: it may be enough to think of the economic provisions
necessary for civil society, that require a complex tax system, in order to rec-
ognize that it is impossible to leave them up to the “good will” of each citizen,
who lack a vision of the whole. On the other hand, man has need of a precise
framework of reference in which to insert his own relationship—whether it
be economic, political, cultural, etc.—with others. It is unimaginable that
in each occasion one might think up from scratch a set of behavioral rules
that would take account of all the possible implications of such a relationship.
Furthermore, it would be naïve simply to count on the natural goodness and
25 Some valid thoughts concerning the social function of fundamental rights are
offered by P. Häberle, Le libertà fondamentali nello Stato costituzionale, (Rome: La
Nuova Italia Scientifica, 1993). Many theorists of liberalism have difficulty recogniz-
ing the “expressive” dimension of the political order, probably under the influence
of their polemic with the political romanticism of Herder and Hegel, in which the
expressivist principle plays a primary role. They retain that the State must be neu-
tral, while leaving it to the individual, the families, and to other groups to transmit
values and ideals. Before any ethical-political evaluation, it needs to be said that
experience demonstrates that the State, laws, the social environment, etc. always
express some conception, and always exercise an important educational influence,
whether it be positive or negative.
26 Cf. above, subsection 9.1.1.


Civil Law and Ecclesiastical Law
maturity of persons to leave up to their will the right behavior to adopt in all
social relations.
Though there may exist unjust laws, as we shall immediately discuss, we
must not forget that the overwhelming majority of the human legal corpus is
composed of just norms, more or less connected with the moral law, which
therefore oblige in conscience.27 However, it needs to be underlined—in order
to not fall into useless rigorisms—that the obligation of conscience of the legal
order “is not a mechanical effect of juridical norms. Moral obligatoriness is in
direct relation with the value and importance of the social goods safeguarded
by such norms, both when one treats of the protection of such goods, and
when one deals with the goods that must be obtained. In other words, moral
obligatoriness is not a dimension of juridical norms considered in an isolated
way, but is an effect of human responsibility in relationship with the social
reality, in what refers to both the person's relationship with authority, to
reality, and to the social ends of each particular case.” 28 There exists a certain
gradualism of obligation that depends on the varying degrees of connection each
law has with the common good.
Unjust Laws — We now shall continue on to the study of the problem
presented by unjust laws. Civil laws which are opposed to the common good
are unjust. So, for example, clearly and gravely unjust are those laws which
attack or render legal attacks against the fundamental rights of the person
(right to life, political or religious freedom) or against fundamental institutions
or social relationships (matrimony and family, parental rights, the exercise of
justice, etc.). Unjust laws do not oblige in conscience, rather, there is moral
obligation to not follow their provisions, to not accept them, to manifest one's
disagreement with them, and to seek to change them as soon as possible and,
if that is not possible, to seek to reduce their negative effects.
A different problem is that of the tolerance of evil.
Civil authority has the
duty of punitively sanctioning those immoral actions that are harmful to the
common good; nonetheless, keeping in mind human weakness, the State can
tolerate, as a lesser evil, certain immoral actions whose absolute prohibition
could have negative repercussions for the common good, as is the case in
certain situations with prostitution:29 if this is done, it must be ascertained
with certainty that such a concession is the only way of effectively avoiding
a greater evil for all of society. Logically, “political tolerance of evil” should
27 Cf. Gaudium et Spes, 30 and 74.
28 A. Del Portillo,”Morale e diritto,” Seminarium 23 (1971), 736, our translation.
29 It is this example that Saint Thomas indicates (S.Th., II-II, q.
10, a.
11), citing
Saint Augustine (De ordine 2, 4, 12: NBA 3/1, 304). However, it should be kept in mind
that the common good does not tolerate the infringement of its essential components. For
example, attacks against fundamental rights of the person, such as abortion, euthanasia,
racial discrimination, etc. cannot be legally tolerated.


Chapter 9
not be confused with “legalization” (to consider that which is contrary to the
common good as a reality not contrary to the law) and even less so with
“moral justification.” Therefore, political tolerance of evil does not justify the
performance of the evil act on the part of the individual. Even if the law did
not punish a lesser evil, it is never licit for any person to commit a sin in order
to avoid a greater sin. According to what was said before, if from a situation
of tolerance there is a passage to the legalization of what is contrary to the
common good or even an imposition of it, the Christian is obliged to disobey,
to invoke an objection of conscience and, in limited cases, to passively or even
actively resist, according to the principle that one “must obey God rather
than men.”30
The Catechism thus summarizes this doctrine: “Public authority is obliged
to respect the fundamental rights of the human person and the conditions
for the exercise of his freedom.” “It is the duty of citizens to work with civil
authority for the building up of society in a spirit of truth, justice, solidarity,
and freedom.” “Citizens are obliged in conscience not to follow the directives of
civil authorities when they are contrary to the demands of the moral order.” 31
Finally, it should be considered that beyond the laws which are clearly and
gravely unjust, there can also exist laws that for their content, or for the
procedure by which they were passed, are slightly unjust, or sometimes sim-
ply imperfect. It can happen, for example, that a tax law may penalize in
a small but relevant measure a category of worker, or does not sufficiently
protect numerous families, or may inadequately distribute public resources,
or was promulgated without entirely following the procedure set down in the
constitution. In this case, we are presented with difficult problems for which
it is difficult to give general rules. On one hand, if they are unjust laws ac-
cording to common sentiment, they do not oblige in conscience; on the other
hand, the law is always a principle of order necessary for social life, and dis-
obedience, even when it is not completely unjustified, can easily become a
principle of anarchy, of injustice, and sometimes even violence. Therefore, an
attentive and responsible evaluation of the situation is necessary—of the pros
and cons—before making a decision.
9.1.5
Christians and Politics
The Perspective of Political Morality — According to the distinctions
previously proposed,32 obedience to the civil law is a problem of personal
morality; we treat concretely of a duty derived from the virtue of justice.
The following of Christ entails a duty of obedience, within the terms indi-
30Acts 5:29.
31 CCC, 2254, 2255 and 2256.
32 See above subsection 9.1.2.


Civil Law and Ecclesiastical Law
cated above. When one must judge if a law is just or not, we are instead
in the camp of political ethics, because here the judgment is not regarding
what the person should do or not do, but rather the justice of the law that
political society has given itself. In modern political systems, in which the
citizen participates through voting and in other modes of electing governors
and legislators, and contributes in diverse ways to the formation of political
orientations and legislative choices, Christians, like other citizens, see them-
selves continually confronted with problems of political morality: they must
continuously reflect, express their opinions and act with regard to the po-
litical, administrative, educational, health-care, economic, etc. structures of
society. For this reason moral theology has had to occupy itself also with
problems of political morality and, in the last two centuries, the ecclesias-
tical magisterium extensively developed the teachings known as the “social
doctrine of the Church.”33 It is the object of a specific theological treatment
that, for obvious reasons of space, cannot be presented here.34 Therefore, we
shall limit ourselves to a few general considerations.
In the first place, the roles of the pastors and of the lay faithful regarding
political activity need to be distinguished.35 The pastors have the right and
duty of pronouncing moral judgments regarding temporal realities when this
is required by faith and Christian morality, “nevertheless, active participation
in political parties is reserved to the lay faithful.” 36 That is, when we deal with
the discussion of different concrete political options, which represent diverse
legitimate possibilities of concretely realizing the same base value, the lay
faithful act freely according to their conscience.37
What can be said in general is that “in order to achieve their task directed
to the Christian animation of the temporal order, in the sense of serving per-
sons and society, the lay faithful are never to relinquish their participation in
'public life', that is, in the many different economic, social, legislative, admin-
istrative and cultural areas, which are intended to promote organically and
institutionally the common good. The Synod Fathers have repeatedly affirmed
that every person has a right and duty to participate in public life, albeit in a
diversity and complementarity of forms, levels, tasks and responsibilities.” 38

Doctrine of the Faith, Doctrinal Note on Some Questions Regarding the Participation of

Chapter 9
The effective exercise of this right and duty of participation requires forma-
tion and competence “for the lay faithful who have responsibilities in various
fields of society and public life. Above all, it is indispensable that they have
a more exact knowledge—and this demands a more widespread and precise
presentation—of the Church's social doctrine.” 39
Principles of Political Morality — The attitudes with which the social
and political activities of the Christians—especially of the lay faithful—should
be addressed, that is, the practice of the ethical-political virtues, depends on
their life in Christ. In this regard, the reflections of Saint Josemaría Escrivá
are enlightening.40 The logic of the Incarnation is the perennially relevant
and working foundation of the Christian transformation of humanity and the
world: “The apostolic task that Christ entrusted to all his disciples leads to
specific results in social matters.”41 From this Christological principle flows
the vision of what for a Christian means being situated in and living in the
world or, to say it in other words, the concept of secularity. This is translated
into what we shall call the principle of responsibility and participation: to live
in the world means to feel oneself responsible for the world, assuming the task
of participating in human activities to give them a Christian configuration. In
the accomplishment of this task the autonomy and value of temporal realities
need to be emphasized, as well as the demand of knowing and respecting their
intrinsic dynamic, a fruit of the rationality that the Wisdom of the Creator has
impressed in His works.42Therefore, it comes to be required of persons to have
an adequate understanding of the nature and intrinsic value of social relations,
as well as the practical character of social and political activity. It is not
the simple enunciation of perennial principles, but a concrete achievement of
human and social goods in a determined historical, geographical, and cultural
context, characterized by an at least partially unsurpassable contingency.43
The autonomy of temporal realities also calls for a marked sensibility for
human freedom, conceived as a substantial value, indissolubly united to the
principle of responsibility and, therefore, to the principles of participation and
solidarity.44 To freedom should always be united the principle of responsibil-
ity, in virtue of which freedom cannot be either a merely formal value or a
method, and even less the expression of an atomic-individualist conception of
man; the fact that responsibility is seen as inseparably united to the principle
of freedom leads to the refutation of any type of social provision that dam-
39 Christifideles Laici, 60; cf. Gaudium et Spes, 75.
40 We borrow some ideas from A. Rodríguez Luño, “La formazione della coscienza in
materia sociale e politica secondo gli insegnamenti del Beato Josemaría Escrivá,” Romana
13 (1997) 162–181.
41 Saint Josemaría Escrivá, Christ is Passing By (1974), no. 125.
42 Cf. Gaudium et Spes, 36.
43 Cf. John Paul II, Enc. Centesimus Annus, 1-V-1991, 57.
44 Cf. Paul VI, Lett. Ap. Octogesima Adveniens, 14-V-1971, n. 50; CIC, can. 227.


Civil Law and Ecclesiastical Law
ages or suppresses the “subjectivity” of social formations, namely, one which
negates freedom or in some way causes irresponsibility.
The Obligation and Mode of Political Participation — To the prin-
ciples of freedom and responsibility is linked the principle of participation:45
passivity, laziness, the “leave it for someone else” attitude, represent a contin-
ually lurking temptation, because work for the common good requires effort
and sacrifice. The principle of participation is not just directed towards a few
citizens who are professionally employed in politics. It is directed toward all
citizens who perform their duties and exercise their rights, and in all cases
live consistently with their own conception of the world, of man, and of the
common political good, and who associate freely with those who—Christian
or not—share their same ideas and are disposed to put them into practice.
To the principles cited above—freedom, responsibility, pluralism, solidarity,
participation—there also needs to be added the principle of truth in charity.46
The problems historically linked to religious and moral differences, along with
factors of an ideological type, brought origin to the mentality, in some very
widespread environments, for which the conviction that there exists a truth
concerning the good of the person and of the human community can cause
unjust relations of domination and violence between people. From this idea,
which we shall not analyze in particular, diverse attitudes can be derived:
some consider that it is a good, or at least a necessary lesser evil, for demo-
cratic coexistence to have a certain dose of agnosticism or relativism,47 and
for this reason they think that in a public environment it is better to not
speak of absolute truth, leading them to require, as a condition for any form
of dialogue, the openness of the interlocutor to give up or, at least, mute, his
existential convictions constitutive of his own identity. Whoever is not dis-
posed to do so is accused of being a bad citizen, or an enemy of coexistence.
In the face of this perspective, some close themselves off to dialogue, because
they do not want, or do not know how, to give certain explanations, either out
of fear or because they feel themselves subjected to blackmail; others think
that the dialogue is a good for which it is worth it to give in, that is, to give
up—at least externally and tactically—their own identities, even if it is an
attitude which brings with it a certain duplicity, not very true to their own
convictions or to those with whom they are having dialogue.
Confronted with these alternatives, the Christian is called to show with his
public behavior the compatibility between the highest degree of charity and
steadfastness in the truth of faith or morals. “Loving souls for God's sake will
make us love everyone: understanding, excusing, forgiving We should have a
45 “The Christian who neglects his temporal duties, neglects his duties toward his neigh-
bor and even God, and jeopardizes his eternal salvation” (Gaudium et Spes, no. 43).
46 Cf. Eph 4:15.

Chapter 9
love that can cover the multitude of failings contrived by human wretchedness.
We have to have a wonderful charity, veritatem facientes in caritate, defending
the truth, without hurting anyone.”48 Dialogue, collaboration, and charity
with those who think differently is always possible. What we deal with here is
distinguishing between the intimate relationship of personal conscience with
the truth, and the relations between persons. The first relationship is resided
over by the normative power of the truth; the second by justice, charity, and
the inalienable demands of the dignity of the person. As the firm adhesion to a
truth of faith is not fully Christian if it is not united to loyal and loving respect
toward those who do not share the same faith, so respect of others is not
an authentic ethical virtue if it comes to be exchanged with “confusionism,”
duplicity, or the giving up of one's identity for tactical motives. The practical
and concrete achievement of this equilibrium is an important part of the
Christian animation of social life.
9.2
Ecclesiastical Law
In baptism we were generated in the Church's womb as children of God;
through baptismal grace we become members of Christ and members of His
body, which is the Church.49 The Church on its part safeguards and dispenses
the necessary means for developing in the Christian moral life leading up to
the achievement of holiness, and the Church's laws, or ecclesiastical laws,
should be counted among these means.
From apostolic times up until our time the Apostles and their successors
promulgated laws and decrees regarding the moral life and ecclesial activities
(sacraments, the liturgy, the apostolate, etc.) of those baptized in the Catholic
Church or received into it.50 The exercise of such legislative power has a clear
dogmatic foundation, attested to by the Sacred Scriptures,51 the apostolic
Tradition, and the constant teaching of the magisterium of the Church.52
The laws of the Church are general normative instructions promulgated by
the ecclesiastical authority, having legislative power (principally, the Roman

Civil Law and Ecclesiastical Law
Pontiff for all the Church and the diocesan Bishop for his own diocese53), and
which aim at the promotion and safeguarding of the Church's mission, the just
regulation of the activity of believers and ecclesiastical institutions and, in the
last analysis, to the salvation and sanctification of people. The special study
of ecclesiastical laws is the task of a specific discipline called canon law.54
Here we shall limit ourselves to some considerations of a general character
that may be of help in understanding the role of ecclesiastical laws in the
Christian moral life.
9.2.1
Nature and Scope of Ecclesiastical Law
For an adequate theological understanding of ecclesiastical law and its role
in the Christian moral life it is helpful to take as a starting point a consid-
eration of the nature and mission of the Church in the context of the divine
salvific plan.55 More concretely, we shall consider two points of special in-
terest: the divine constitution of the Church as a visible and hierarchically
ordered society, and its sacramental dimension.
The Divine Constitution of the Church as a Visible Society — “God,
however, does not make men holy and save them merely as individuals, with-
out bond or link between one another. Rather has it pleased Him to bring
men together as one people, a people which acknowledges Him in truth and
serves Him in holiness.”56 For this reason, the fullness of time having arrived,
“Christ, the one Mediator, established and continually sustains here on earth
His holy Church, the community of faith, hope and charity, as an entity with
visible delineation,”57 and as a society “hierarchically ordered,”58 in which the
ministers “are endowed with sacred power”,59 a power that must be conceived
as a service for edifying and not for destroying.60 In order to accomplish the
mission of the Church, Christ sent the Apostles, as well as their successors:
“As the Father has sent me, so I send you,”61 and conferred on them the office

Chapter 9
of teaching, sanctifying, and governing,62 being a part of this last office the
power of legislating,63 just as he promised them the assistance of the Holy
Spirit in the exercise of such functions.
The mission of the Church is principally of a spiritual and supernatural char-
acter, 64 and for this reason ecclesiastical law “is in no way intended as a
substitute for faith, grace and the charisms in the life of the Church and of
the faithful. On the contrary, its purpose is rather to create such an order
in the ecclesial society that, while assigning the primacy to faith, grace and
the charisms, it at the same time renders easier their organic development in
the life both of the ecclesial society and of the individual persons who belong
to it.”65 Already this consideration allows us to understand that, even within
the limits proper to human law, ecclesiastical law reaches a more interior di-
mension of man and is ordered toward the virtues more directly than what
can be done by the civil law.
With the Church being a society made up of people, the achievement
of the common spiritual good requires numerous activities and exter-
nal means: the teaching of the faith, the administration and reception
of the sacraments, the organization of divine worship, missionary ac-
tivities, etc., which presuppose the interaction of different persons and
structures, as well as a material basis. We deal here with external and
visible realities that must be socially organized according to justice and
charity in terms of their purposes, and which permit us to further un-
derstand the role of ecclesiastical law. “Since, indeed, it [the Church]
is organized as a social and visible structure, it must also have norms:
in order that its hierarchical and organic structure be visible; in order
that the exercise of the functions divinely entrusted to her, especially
that of sacred power and of the administration of the sacraments, may
be adequately organized; in order that the mutual relations of the faith-
ful may be regulated according to justice based upon charity, with the
rights of individuals guaranteed and well defined; in order, finally, that
common initiatives, undertaken for a Christian life ever more perfect
may be sustained, strengthened and fostered by canonical norms.” 66
The Divine Constitution of the Church as Universal Sacrament of
Salvation — For a complete theological understanding of ecclesiastical law
and its role in the Christian moral life it needs to be remembered that, accord-
ing to the divine plan, the Church is the “universal sacrament of salvation”:67

Enc. Immortale Dei, 1-XI-1885: DS 3167).

Civil Law and Ecclesiastical Law
“like a sacrament or as a sign and instrument [ union with God.” 68 Through
the Church, as a visible and hierarchically ordered society, Christ is present
and continues to work in the world, spreading “truth and grace to all” 69 to
unite people more closely to Himself.70 The perspective of the sacramental
economy, which illuminates the nature and mission of the Church, is indis-
pensable for the theological understanding of ecclesiastical law and its role in
the moral life. Christ lives in the Church and acts through it in “its sacra-
ments, its liturgy, its preaching—in all that it does.” 71
The path of believers toward imitating and identifying with Christ
passes through the “ecclesial mediation” assumed and established by
Christ Himself. Saint Cyprian affirms it concisely: “He cannot have
God for his Father who does not have the Church for a Mother.” 72 In
other terms, if Christ said, “whoever listens to you listens to me. Who-
ever rejects you rejects me. And whoever rejects me rejects the one
who sent me,”73 then the ecclesial dimension is an essential character-
istic of Christian moral life, and not simply the sociological space in
which it takes place.74 To “have the Church for a Mother” means that
the Christian life includes the formation of “a true filial spirit toward
the Church,”75 the docile acceptance of the preaching of the Gospel and
of the teachings of the ecclesiastical magisterium, the reception of the
sacraments and participation in liturgical worship, and also the obser-
vance of ecclesiastical laws. These are all equally authentic expressions
of the “ecclesial mediation” willed by Christ.
The Moral Value of Ecclesiastical Law — In comparison to civil law—
which orders the life of men within political society according to justice
and therefore constitutes a substantially juridical order even if obligatory in
conscience—ecclesiastical law has a wider scope.
On the one hand, ecclesiastical law orders the life of believers within the
Church according to justice, and therefore many ecclesiastical laws regard true
duties and true rights, that is, dispositions that are due or guaranteed ac-

from a divine and a human element. For this reason, by no weak analogy, it is compared

serves the divine Word as a living organ of salvation, so, in a similar way, does the visible
social structure of the Church serve the Spirit of Christ, who vivifies it, in the building up
of the body” (Lumen Gentium, 8).

Chapter 9
cording to justice and which constitute juridical relations in a proper sense of
the word. “There will be a diversity of opinions regarding what is the specific
character of the juridical nature of canonical norms, but there is no doubt
that one is dealing with a true law. And this, not only because the canonical
ordering in obedience to the will of Christ applies the fundamental principle
of justice of recognizing and attributing “to each his own” (“unicuique suum”)
in the ecclesial community, but also because it does so with norms which fulfill
the triple technical demand of generality, stability, and obligatoriness.” 76 With
this affirmation an excessively juridical reduction is not performed, because
we are always dealing with the juridical dimension of salvific and ecclesial
goods.77
For just a few illustrative examples: a parish priest has the duty of
justice of applying the Mass for the people entrusted to him every Sun-
day and holy day of obligation in his diocese;78 for his own diocese, it
is the right of the Ordinary to nominate and approve the teachers of
religion or, if it is the case, to demand that they are removed;79 once a
priest has accepted a stipend for celebrating the Mass, he has a duty of
justice to apply it for the intention of the person offering the stipend;80
all of those who through their office have care of souls are held to the
obligation of providing that the confessions of the faithful entrusted to
them be heard, when it is reasonably requested of them;81 in case of
urgent necessity, all confessors have the same duty, and in the case of
the danger of death all priests do;82 it is the right of all the faithful to
freely choose the confessors they prefer;83 the faithful have the right of
manifesting to the pastors of the Church their own needs, above all spir-
itual ones, along with their desires.84 Moreover, even procedural laws
oftentimes satisfy the fundamental demands of fairness. And finally, it
is to be noted that the hierarchical constitution given by Christ to the
Church confers to it a basic juridical structure, out of which proceed
diverse duties and rights: the necessity of pontifical mandate for the
ordination of a bishop; the necessity that the decrees of the ecumenical
council are approved by the Roman Pontiff; etc.
On the other hand, the ecclesiastical legislator is aware that the Church car-

Civil Law and Ecclesiastical Law
and so promulgates laws regarding moral matters that are diverse from jus-
tice, regarding acts of the theological virtues or moral virtues such as religion,
repentance, etc. These laws can be both the simple positive promulgation of
ethical or religious demands of the law of Christ, an act of rendering these de-
mands explicit, or of their determination. These latter two have as an end “to
guarantee to the faithful the indispensable minimum in the spirit of prayer and
moral effort, in the growth in love of God and neighbor.” 85 The normative
instructions can simply be recommendations, they can oblige in conscience
sub gravi or, in more grave cases, they can sanction certain behaviors with
a canonical penalty: something which always has a pastoral, medicinal, or
preventative purpose, complying with the mission of the Church.
We shall also propose here some further examples for illustrative pur-
poses. As recommendations, which are not intended to create a precise
moral duty added to that which the matter possesses per se, are the
exhortation directed toward the faithful to receive the Eucharist with
frequency86 or the earnest recommendation to priests to celebrate the
Mass daily.87 As precepts of a principally moral nature, which per se
oblige sub gravi, the obligation to participate at the Mass on Sunday
and days of obligation;88 the obligation for all the faithful, once they
have reached the age of discretion, to confess their grave sins at least
once a year,89 that of receiving the Eucharist at least once a year in
the Easter season,90 and that of observing fast and abstinence days.91
As examples of penal laws we can cite the excommunication latae sen-
tentiae for the apostate, heretic or schismatic,92 or else for those who
procure an abortion, obtaining the effect.93
What we have said explains and exemplifies how the ecclesiastical law is not
limited to regulating communal relationships within the Church, since it also
regards the Christian personal life.94 Therefore, while respecting the distinc-
tion between moral laws and juridical norms, “ecclesial discipline responds
to a demand that is not entirely exterior and functional; its meaning is not
exhausted in ensuring a perfect organization and an efficient functionality of
the Christian community. We deal, more in depth, of an interior and essen-

sively disciplinary purpose, is always an expression of the salvific mission of
the Church that pertains to the believer as such, that is, insofar as he is a
person who seeks union with Christ, and not only as a “citizen” of the ecclesial
community. Ecclesiastical law aims also, and in a rather direct way, at the
spiritual good of the believer, at the life of grace and of virtue through which
the believer carries out the following of Christ.
9.2.2
The Moral Obligatoriness of Ecclesiastical Law
Ecclesiastical laws bring about a true moral obligation.
We deal here with
a doctrine of faith96 that, after the preceding clarifications, does not have
need of further proofs for what regard its general terms. Descending more
into the concrete, it must be affirmed that not all ecclesiastical norms have
the same value “either in themselves or in relation to the changing historical
conditions: consequently, their obligatoriness also has a diversity of grades.
However, when one treats of laws of the universal and particular Church
(norms of the Code of Canon Law, liturgical and sacramental norms, norms
promulgated by the bishop for his own diocese), they oblige in conscience, and
their infraction can even become a grave moral fault, relative to the greater
or lesser importance of what is commanded.”97
For what regards the nature of what is commanded, there exist fundamental
differences. Some ecclesiastical norms promulgate or render explicit demands
of the natural moral law, the Gospel law, or both: for example, the laws that
declare null the marriage between parents and their children98 or the marriage
of a person linked by a bond of a preceding marriage;99 one deals here with
laws that not only oblige sub gravi, but that truly do not admit of exceptions
or any kind of dispensation, not even from the Roman Pontiff. There are,
instead, merely ecclesiastical laws, or determinations in an affirmative form
of Gospel law that, though obliging sub gravi, admit of exceptions and dispen-
sations: for example, a person is not obliged to participate at Sunday Mass
when he is prevented from doing so by a grave cause (danger to his health,
having to walk a notable distance, a need to care for someone who is seriously
ill, etc.). It can be said in general terms that, treating of merely ecclesiastical

Civil Law and Ecclesiastical Law
laws, the legislator does not intend to oblige if there exists a grave inconve-
nience. There exist, furthermore, laws that regard something that is light
material per se, which do not then oblige “sub gravi.” 100
Finally, we shall point out some general characteristics of ecclesiastical laws.
Normally, according to the general law of the Church, the general laws enter
into force after three months have elapsed from the date of their publication
in the Acta Apostolicae Sedis, so long as they do not state the contrary, or the
nature of their matter does not imply an immediate obligation.101 Compliance
with purely ecclesiastical laws is required only for those who are baptized in
the Catholic Church or received into it, and who enjoy sufficient use of the
reason and, if they are not told otherwise, have completed seven years of
age.102 Nonetheless, he is not liable to any penalty who, when he violated
the penal law he had not yet completed 16 years of age, and who without
fault was ignorant of having violated a law.103 Contrary to what happens in
many civil ordinances, to be considered invalidating or disqualifying are only
those laws with which it is expressly established that the act is null or the
person is unable,104 and so it can happen that an act (for example, reception
or administration of a sacrament) is carried out illicitly but validly. Ignorance
or error concerning the invalidating and disqualifying laws “does not impede
their effect unless it is expressively established otherwise.” 105
100 Nonetheless, it seems important to us to insist on the fundamental principle. “One
would have a false conception of canon law and the conscience of the faithful would not be
formed rightly if the obligatoriness, even moral obbligatoriness, of the juridical norms of the
Church were denied: 'the canonical laws—reminds the Legislator in the Constitution Sacrae
disciplinae leges—by their very nature must be observed.' And this is the case not only for
those norms which translate in terms of direct positive provisions that are of the divine Law
(here is reached the highest level of obligatoriness) but also regarding those other norms of
human law—perhaps of secondary and technical content—which not without reason come
to be equally qualified as “sacrae”: “sacri canones,” “sacrae disciplinae leges.” In fact, also
these norms—and we know to not make an exaggerated statement of an overly juridical
nature—involve the conscience of the believer by recalling the divine Authority, from which
the sacred power of the legislator derives its foundation, which is ultimately connected with
every ecclesiastical norm, since—natura sua—every canonical norm aspires for the defense
of the Ordo Ecclesiae, for congruence with the design of Christ regarding the community
of believers” (J. Herranz, Crisi e rinnovamento del Diritto nella Chiesa (1994), 50, our
translation).

## CHAPTER 10 {#colom-scelti.10}
Moral Conscience
The theological study of conscience presents at least two difficulties that have
need of being clarified. The first is constituted by the wide range of meanings
which come to be attributed to it.1
The second consists in the fact that,
concerning the role of conscience and the mode in which it must be inserted
into the study of fundamental moral theology, there exist within Catholic
theology rather diverse opinions. These problems will be studied in sections
10.1 and 10.3.
10.1
Terminological Clarification
In order to introduce order between the different uses with which the con-
cept of conscience is employed in the Sacred Scriptures, in the documents of
the ecclesiastical magisterium, and in theological literature, a distinction is
useful—at this point classic in Catholic theology—between moral conscience
in a comprehensive sense, called habitual conscience,2 and moral conscience in
a strict sense, understood as a precise judgment regarding a singular action,
called actual conscience.3 In the first case moral conscience is spoken of in
a very wide sense, which comprehensively designates the moral awareness of
1 See the comprehensive visions offered by E. Kaczynski, “La coscienza morale nella teolo-

tempo, (Bologna: ESD, 1989), 47–80; M. Cassani, “La coscienza morale nella riflessione
teologica contemporanea”, in Various Authors, La coscienza morale e l'evangelizzazione
oggi. Tra valori obiettivi e tecniche di persuasione, (Bologna: ESD, 1992), 78–112.
2 Cf. R. García de Haro, “¿Qué es la conciencia habitual?”, Sapientia 35 (1980) 435–454.
3 For a study of these and other meanings of the term conscience, cf. F. Delhaye, La
coscienza morale del cristiano, (Rome: Desclée, 1968).


Chapter 10
man. In this use the conscience includes rather diverse cognitive principles,
such as synderesis or the habit of the first moral principles, the natural moral
law, the cognitive dimension of the acquired and infused moral virtues, pru-
dence, the actual conscience itself, etc., elements which in good part we have
already studied. Sacred Scriptures and the Fathers of the Church often utilize
this comprehensive concept of conscience.4 In contrast, in its restricted sense
conscience is a precise act of the practical reason; concretely a judgment re-
garding the moral goodness or badness of a singular act that we are about to
perform or have already performed, which is distinguished from synderesis,
the natural moral law, moral knowledge, prudence, and the cognitive dimen-
sion of the ethical virtues, even if there remains a strict relationship between
it and all of these realities.5
10.2
The Christian Doctrine Concerning
Moral Conscience
10.2.1
Moral Conscience in the Sacred Scriptures
Old Testament — The Old Testament does not use any specific term to
refer to what we call conscience. In the Greek version of the LXX the word
syneídêsis only appears in three late passages.6 This does not mean that its
content is absent, that is, as the voice of divine judgment which praises good
behavior and rebukes bad behavior. Most of the time the Hebrew term lêb
(“heart”) comes to be used instead. And so “David regretted having numbered
the people, and said to the LORD: 'I have sinned grievously in what I have
done”7 or it is requested to the Lord: “Create in me a clean heart, O God,
And renew a steadfast spirit within me,”8 where “pure heart” comes to mean

Moral Conscience
something very similar to what we call “good conscience”. In an opposing
sense, the Old Testament speaks of a “hardened” or “obstinate” heart: “Hard
of face and obstinate of heart are they to whom I am sending you.” 9
It seems important to us to point out, along with Günthör, that in the Old
Testament (but also in the New) moral conscience is always a “conscience
before God”:
“Man stands before the face of God, who is holy, and in this
light acquires the awareness of having acted well and rightly, or incorrectly and
poorly”;10 this is a known characteristic of the biblical notion of conscience.
Furthermore, it should be noted that the phenomenon of conscience comes
to be referred to with expressions that indicate the entire man, and not a
particular faculty considered in isolation. From this comes the preference for
the term lêb, which designates the most intimate center of the person, where
he enters into relationship with the Lord,11 accepting or refusing the divine
word. Man's attitude in relation to God comes about within the heart, which
can be “new”, “contrite”, “humble,” or in contrast “hollow”, “darkened”, etc.
New Testament — None of the Gospels use a specific term to indicate moral
conscience.12 This phenomenon is referred to especially by the term “heart”
(kardía) and “spirit” (pnéuma), in an analogous sense to that found in the
Old Testament, even if the interiority of behavior and moral judgment come
to be emphasized with greater vigor.13 In the hidden depths of the heart are
found the genesis of good and evil, and so the human heart is seen in all its
ambivalence: “For from the fullness of the heart the mouth speaks. A good
person brings forth good out of a store of goodness, but an evil person brings
forth evil out of a store of evil.”14
It is with the Pauline Corpus that the concept of conscience (syneídêsis),
widely used in the popular hellenistic environment, makes its entrance into
Christian doctrine. A certain attention is required in order to understand
the sense in which it comes to be used in the Apostolic Letters. It seems
beyond doubt that conscience is always invoked by Saint Paul as a witness.
In the Letter to the Romans the Apostle, wanting to render more credible the
suffering he has endured on account of his people's attitude, affirms: “I speak
the truth in Christ, I do not lie; my conscience joins with the holy Spirit in
bearing me witness.”15 In 2 Cor 1:12 he equally appeals to the “testimony

of our conscience” and subsequently to the testimony of the conscience of
others: “We have renounced shameful, hidden things; not acting deceitfully
or falsifying the word of God, but by the open declaration of the truth we
commend ourselves to everyone's conscience in the sight of God.” 16 Saint Paul
makes appeal to the capacity of judgment that is in him and in those he is
addressing, because it is present in every person. It is a reliable witness, but
it is not up to it to give the last word: “It does not concern me in the least
that I be judged by you or any human tribunal; I do not even pass judgment
on myself; I am not conscious (synoida) of anything against me, but I do not
thereby stand acquitted; the one who judges me is the Lord.” 17 Conscience,
as a human demand, comes to be given, in a certain sense, new dimensions
by Saint Paul: the ultimate demand is the judgment of God.18
In this passage of the First Letter to the Corinthians the universality of the
conscience is also seen; even among the different interpretive hypotheses, it
is beyond doubt that what Saint Paul said regarding himself in 1 Cor 4:3–
4 also pertains to pagans: “Syneídêsis appears as an immanent demand to
man, that presents to the conscience his behavior with a positive or negative
judgment. The knowledge of good and evil is presupposed here. Its foundation
is not however explained; nonetheless it is obvious that, as for the “natural
knowledge of God” (Rom 1:19ff), Paul is thinking of human reason.” 19 Similar
is the teaching of Rom 2:14–15—which we already studied in its relation to
the natural moral law20—where conscience appears as a witness of a strictly
moral nature.
A new problematic nucleus of extreme interest emerges in the same letters, in
the passages in which the delicate relationships between knowledge, conscience,
and charity toward the brothers of weaker conscience comes to light.
The
solution given by Saint Paul to the questions which were posited to him bring
to light that conscience presupposes knowledge, and it judges according to
knowledge; if knowledge comes to be lacking, conscience judges erroneously.
He recalls, furthermore, that the conscience of the Christian judges also in
light of the faith;21 and that charity wishes to avoid scandal even to those
who have a weak conscience.

Moral Conscience
The problem to resolve in 1 Cor is that of the possibility of eating meat
sacrificed to idols, a problem that acquires a social dimension in the
Christian community insofar as it could block the road to participation
at the table itself, an expression of ecclesial communion. Knowledge
teaches us that the idols are nothing, “but not all have this knowledge.
There are some who have been so used to idolatry up until now that,
when they eat meat sacrificed to idols, their conscience, which is weak,
is defiled [on, the brother for whom Christ died. When you sin in this
way against your brothers and wound their consciences, weak as they
are, you are sinning against Christ.” 22 Something similar happens with
pagans: “If an unbeliever invites you and you want to go, eat whatever
is placed before you, without raising questions on grounds of conscience.
But if someone says to you, 'This was offered in sacrifice,' do not eat it
on account of the one who called attention to it and on account of con-
science; I mean not your own conscience, but the other's.” 23 Analogous,
though perhaps more far-reaching, is the question clarified in Rom 14.
This refers here to the “strong” and “weak” in the faith. Neither must
the “strong” despise the “weak, nor should the latter judge the former.
The former may bear in mind the duty of not scandalizing their broth-
ers; the latter may not judge the former: we shall all be judged equally
by God.24 For what regards food: “Everything is indeed clean, but it
is wrong for anyone to become a stumbling block by eating [ this is not
from faith; for whatever is not from faith is sin.” 25
In the Pastoral Letters conscience expresses the position taken by man with
regard to God, which can be either positive or negative. Conscience can be
right or wrong, and then it is not possible “to always and absolutely identify
the voice of conscience with the voice of God. Conscience and the heart of
man are, yes, the voice of moral duty, but they are also personal realities,
proper to each individual, an immediate and profound expression of his own
will and moral personality.”26 This explains how predicates such as “pure”,27
“good,28 “contaminated”,29 etc. come to be attributed to conscience. With
a greater Christological emphasis, the Letter to the Hebrews bases the liber-
ation from an evil conscience on the blood of Christ: “How much more will
the blood of Christ, who through the eternal spirit offered himself unblem-
ished to God, cleanse our consciences from dead works to worship the living
God.”30 In summary, moral conscience, in its function as judge and witness,

10.2.2
Recent Teachings of the Ecclesiastical Magisterium
on Moral Conscience
The most important teachings of the recent magisterium on moral conscience
are found in the Constitution Gaudium et Spes (no. 16), in the Catechism
(nos. 1776–1802) and in the encyclical Veritatis Splendor (nos. 54–64).31 We
shall occupy ourselves with the latter, which contains a brief, but substantially
complete, exposition of the ecclesial doctrine concerning moral conscience.
The approach chosen by the encyclical responds to its purpose, that is, to
perform a doctrinal discernment concerning certain “'issues regarding the very
foundations of moral theology,' foundations which are being undermined by
certain present day tendencies.”32 The exposition is clearly divided into three
parts, dedicated to the examination of some contemporary doctrinal problems
(nos. 54–56), to the exposition of the notion of conscience (nos. 57–61), and to
the study of the problems concerning erroneous conscience and the formation
of conscience (nos. 62–64).
Contemporary Problems Regarding Conscience — Recalling explicitly
the teachings of Gaudium et Spes 16, the discourse is inspired by a just vindi-
cation of the interiority of the moral demand, with the purpose of clarifying
that this vindication does not pose any problem. In fact, it is most important
to remember that the “heart”, or the moral conscience is “the sanctuary of
man, where he is alone with God whose voice echoes within him.” 33 What
instead comes to be problematic are the tendencies which, opposing human
freedom to the law of God, propose “a 'creative' understanding of moral con-
science, which diverges from the teaching of the Church's tradition and her
Magisterium.”34
31 Among the literature, in the Italian language, regarding conscience in the encyclical

Various Authors, Lettera enciclica “Veritatis Splendor”. Testo e commenti (1994), 196–202;
I. Fucek, La coscienza morale, in R. Lucas Lucas (ed.), “Veritatis Splendor”. Testo integrale
e commento filosofico-teologico (1994), 299–316; R. Frattallone, La coscienza “scintilla di
verità”: dottrina della “Veritatis Splendor” e problematica odierna, in G. Russo (Compiler),
Veritatis Splendor. Genesi, elaborazione, significato (1995), 97–128.
