Moral Conscience
Making appeal to the existing difference between the consideration of universal
doctrine and the existential singularity of each action and situation, as well as
to the creative and responsible character of the tasks that God presents each
person, and to the complexity that the phenomenon of conscience acquires
on the psychological, affective, cultural, and social plane,35 the “creative”
interpretation of conscience retains that it would be possible “to do in practice
and in good conscience what is qualified as intrinsically evil by the moral law.
A separation, or even an opposition, is thus established in some cases between
the teaching of the precept, which is valid in general, and the norm of the
individual conscience, which would in fact make the final decision about what
is good and what is evil.”36
The Nature of Moral Conscience — On the basis of the teaching of Saint
Paul in Rom 2:14–15, “the biblical understanding of conscience, especially in
its specific connection with the law”37 comes to be made precise: conscience is
the unique witness of what happens in the intimate center of man, “a witness
of his own faithfulness or unfaithfulness with regard to the law, of his essential
moral rectitude or iniquity.”38 The conscience establishes an intimate dialogue
within man himself, but more profoundly there is found in it “a dialogue of
man with God, the author of the law.”39 It is therefore “the witness of God
himself, whose voice and judgment penetrate the depths of man's soul.” 40 The
dignity of conscience consists in its being the holy space wherein God speaks
to man.
Basing itself on the same Pauline teaching, this encyclical continues on to
explain the nature of moral conscience in a strict sense, that is to say, what
we called actual conscience. Three characteristics of it are mentioned, it is
1) a practical judgment, 2) that ultimately renders present a moral obligation
and that therefore 3) constitutes the proximate norm of personal morality.
1. Conscience is a “practical judgment, a judgment which makes known
what man must do or not do, or which assesses an act already performed
by him.”41 Through such a judgment, “the application of the law to a
particular case”42is performed.
The emphasis whereby it is affirmed
that conscience is a practical judgment intends to highlight that it is
not a choice or an option, but an affirmation regarding the morality of

science, with particular reference to psychoanalysis, cf.
A. Lambertino, Psicoanalisi e
morale in Freud (1987).

Chapter 10
a particular action (“to now do action 'x' is morally good'; “ to now
do action 'x' is morally evil”) that is situated in the order of practical
knowledge, and that as such is situated in the order of being true or
false. In the practical judgment of conscience “the link between freedom
and truth is made manifest.”43
2. Conscience formulates “moral obligation in the light of the natural law:
it is the obligation to do what the individual, through the workings of
his conscience, knows to be a good he is called to do here and now.” 44
Thus a theologically important claim is furnished, which will permit
us to better understand how the concept of moral obligation is to be
inserted into fundamental moral theology. We shall return to this point
in subsection 8.4.5.
3. Finally, moral conscience is “the proximate norm of personal moral-
ity”,45 in such a way that if one acts against it he commits a moral evil.
The value of the proximate norm, which it is never licit to act against,
pertains to conscience not because it is a supreme norm,46 a norma
normans, but because, while being a norma normata, it is an ultimate
(or final) norm, it is inescapable: “The judgment of conscience states
'in an ultimate way' whether a certain particular kind of behaviour is
in conformity with the law.”47 When conscience judges with certainty,
in the moment in which one acts there is not available a conscience for
the conscience, a judgment of the judgment, because then it would go
on to infinity: it is the “ultimate norm”.
Erroneous Conscience and the Formation of Conscience — Recalling
again the Pauline teachings and that of Gaudium et Spes 16, the encyclical
Veritatis Splendor warns that conscience is not an infallible judge, it can
err.48 The error of conscience “can be the result of an invincible ignorance,
an ignorance of which the subject is not aware and which he is unable to
overcome by himself”,49 and in that case the conscience does not lose its
dignity. In contrast, its dignity is compromised when it is “culpably erroneous,
that is to say, 'when man shows little concern for seeking what is true and
good, and conscience gradually becomes almost blind from being accustomed
to sin.' ”50

Moral Conscience
It is important to understand well the foundation of the classical thesis re-
garding the obligatoriness of an invincibly erroneous conscience. In each case
conscience derives its dignity and its obliging power from the truth: from the
truth known by man or by what is subjectively and inculpably retained to be
true.51 Nonetheless, inculpable subjective error, even if it is not formally im-
putable, cannot replace the truth: it “does not cease to be an evil, a disorder
in relation to the truth about the good. Furthermore, a good act which is
not recognized as such does not contribute to the moral growth of the person
who performs it.”52 In this regard it is helpful to “reflect on the words of the
Psalm: 'Who can discern his errors? Clear me from hidden faults' (Ps 19:12).
There are faults which we fail to see but which nevertheless remain faults,
because we have refused to walk towards the light (cf. Jn 9:39–41).”53
From here springs the necessity of the effort to form one's conscience well. To
do so, knowledge of God's law is indispensable, but not sufficient: a connatu-
rality of the person with the good is also needed; it “is rooted in and develops
through the virtuous attitudes of the individual himself: prudence and the
other cardinal virtues, and, even before these, the theological virtues.” 54 A
further aid for the formation of conscience comes from the Church, from its
life and above all from its magisterium, which is always placed at the service
of the conscience.55
10.3
The Placement of the Treatment
of Conscience
in Fundamental Moral Theology
10.3.1
The Two Traditions of Catholic Moral Teaching
It seems to us that the following observation can be widely agreed upon: “It is
important to keep in mind the insertion of conscience within a well determined
organization of the whole of morality, for its role and its very conception
depends on the relations that it entertains with the other elements of the
system.”56 Conscience is one of the themes on which the scientific positions
we have taken from the beginning of this book57 have major repercussions, a
reason why we consider it helpful to recall the essential terms of the problem.

Chapter 10
The study of the origin and historical development of the two scientific ap-
proaches at the base of moral theology, to which we referred in chapter I,
highlight in a rather clear way that “the Catholic teaching in the moral ambit
is constituted by two traditions which have given rise to two diverse systemati-
zations”:58 the post-Tridentine moral tradition, and an older tradition which
found its greatest systematic expression in Saint Thomas.
Post-Tridentine morality (casuistic morality) is in some way conditioned
by the voluntarism of Ockham: morality is born from the encounter of
divine freedom, which is expressed in the obliging law, with human free-
dom. Even if human freedom should be expressed in obedience, freedom
and the law finish by being opposed to one another “as two landowners
who dispute over the field of human actions [ What is attributed to
the one is necessarily taken from the other.” 59 In this approach, con-
science acquires an always greater importance. It is not a virtue like
prudence that is formed with its exercise, but an intermediate instance
between the law and freedom. With respect to the law, conscience is
passive: it limits itself to receiving the law, presenting it to freedom,
and applying it to its acts, signaling in each concrete situation the limit
between what is and what is not licit. The law, while being superior
to conscience, cannot “be applied without the conscience nor exercise
its force without it, because a law is not valid if it is not known and
promulgated before the conscience. Even freedom must pass through
the conscience in order to define its limits and those of the law.” 60 One
can then understand why the study of conscience and of the cases of
conscience becomes the most important and far-reaching problem of
fundamental moral theology.
It must be added that in this approach the law easily comes to be
seen in a rather reductive and negative way.
The law is an act of
God's will, positively understood, without a direct relationship with
the nature of things, for which there is little to be understood.61 The
norm is what it is, but it could be differently; consequently, the law is
presented as a limit to freedom. Within the practical ambits that are

extensive treatment see, from the same author, Le fonti della morale cristiana (1992), Chs.
X and XI. G. Abbà speaks in this regard of “figures of ethics”; see the extensive study con-
cerning their distinction, origin, and historical development contained in G. Abbà, Quale
impostazione per la filosofia morale?
(1996): according to Abbà, the morality of Saint
Thomas is understood as a search for the best life to live; the post-Tridentine casuistic
morality is understood instead as a search for the moral law to observe. Regarding the
entire theme, see, beyond the bibliography cited in Chapter I, the synthesis proposed by
A. Rodríguez Luño, “El primado de la persona en la moral fundamental”, in A. Sarmiento
(ed.), Moral de la persona y renovación de la teología moral, (Madrid: Ediciones Universi-
tarias Internacionales,1998), 41–51.
59 S. Pinckaers, Le fonti della morale cristiana (1992), 317.
60 Ibid., 322, our translation.

Moral Conscience
covered by the law one must obey, while the areas not covered by the
law are instead free. Conscience tends, through a thousand interpretive
tricks, to continually broaden the ambit of freedom and, therefore, to
continually restrict the scope of the law. This establishes an antithetical
relationship between law and freedom, tending toward minimalism. In
any case, the treatment of the final end, of virtues and prudence, as
well as the deepened study of Christian freedom, either disappear or
come to be reduced to a formality without great importance.
In the Thomistic approach, which we follow in this book, morality is based
on the theological and moral virtues, perfected by the gifts of the Holy Spirit.
“The practical virtue par excellence, the guide of the moral judgment toward
its own fulfillment, is prudence, and not conscience, as is instead the case in the
modern tradition.”62 Grace, and the theological and moral virtues, are both
the content of the moral law and the principles from which the practical reason
comes to identify the concrete modes of regulating the goods and human
activities in such a way as to render possible in each concrete situation the
following of Christ. These directive activities of the practical reason give rise,
on the reflective level, to formulations under the form of normative statements
(moral norms), but originally the activity of the practical reason consists in the
regulation of action and not in the production of norms or in the application
of norms to particular cases. In any case, there is no interest in “liberating”
practical ambits from the rule of the virtues or from the moral law. In fact,
it does not make sense to speak of operative ambits “not covered” by the law,
because this would mean that there exist realms of human action that are not
regulated by the reason illuminated by faith and therefore not relevant to the
Christian vocation.
This does not mean, however, that in the Thomistic approach there is no place
for moral conscience: “In Saint Thomas we still find a connection between the
virtue of prudence—analyzed with the instruments of the Aristotelian tradi-
tion and with the aid of the discernment provided by the monastic tradition—
and the doctrine of conscience, derived from Saint Paul and the Church Fa-
thers, in particular Saint Jerome.”63 It is just that the role of conscience is
seen in a diverse way, as we shall see in what follows.
But first, two clarifications are made necessary.
Our critique of casuistic
morality is a critique regarding the basic scientific approach, which does not
undermine the Christian doctrinal positions contained in it and transmitted
by it, and which furthermore recognizes the positive role played by it in a
given historical moment and for the sake of very specific pastoral demands.64
62 S. Pinckaers, Coscienza, verità e prudenza (1996), 127.
63 Ibid.
64 Cf. S. Pinckaers, Le fonti della morale cristiana (1992), 328–330. Even if in general
casuistic morality left the study of the virtues to another theological discipline, asceticism,


Chapter 10
It should also be clarified that there exist today critiques of casuistic moral-
ity that, far from succeeding in reformulating the basic scientific approach,
continue to construct themselves on the more or less antithetical relationship
between law and freedom, while however balancing such a relationship in favor
of a freedom that tends to be understood in a subjectivist way. The scientific
problems remain unresolved in this perspective, and doctrinal problems arise
that are mentioned in the encyclical Veritatis Splendor.
10.3.2
The Role of Moral Conscience
in Theological Virtue Ethics
For what regards the insertion of the treatment of conscience into a morality
of the virtues, the interpretation proposed by Abbà seems right to us,65 ac-
cording to which the distinction between the direct exercise and the reflective
(or reflexive) exercise of the practical reason (“ratio practica in actu esercito”
and “ratio practica in actu signato”66) must be recalled. On the level of its di-
rect exercise, the activity of the practical reason aims at identifying the choice
of action which would permit the regulation of the human goods involved in a
way conforming to the rule of the virtues (to justice, temperance, etc.). The
habitual perfecting of this activity of the practical reason is the virtue of pru-
dence which, as we know, presupposes not only the knowledge of the virtuous
ends, but above all the desire for them.67
The judgment of conscience should be placed, rather, on the level of the reflec-
tive activity of the practical reason, on the same level, that is, on which the
practical principles come to be formulated under the form of the normative
statements (precepts) of moral science.68
Actual conscience is a judgment
regarding the concrete action to be carried out or regarding one already car-
ried out based on such reflexive normative statements.
The connection of
the judgment of conscience with the actual and habitual dispositions of the
appetites is less strict than that of prudence, therefore the conscience pos-
Pinckaers rightly points out that in this period “many famous moralists were at the same
time also authentic spiritual persons, like Saint Alphonsus” (Ibid., 329).
65 Cf. G. Abbà, Felicità, vita buona e virtù (1995), 276–281.
66 See Chapter I, subsection 1.2.2.
67 Cf. Chapter VII, subsection 7.3.2. The direct activity of the practical reason finishes
with action, and “to act well it is not sufficient to elaborate a specific norm and to judge
that it is sufficiently reflected upon. It is yet necessary that one pass from the consideration
in universali, typical of conscience, to the consideration in particulari, that is, to that
consideration in which the premises of reasoning are not simply norms, even if being specific
and circumstantial, but are principally the right intentions of the individual agent, actual
inclinations of his will and of his passional appetities toward virtuous ends” (G. Abbà,
Felicità, vita buona e virtù, 1995, 277–278).
68 Cf. Chapter VIII, subsection 8.2.3.


Moral Conscience
sesses a prevalently, if not exclusively, cognitive character.69 The activity of
conscience aims at judging rightly on the basis of moral knowledge; prudence,
on the other hand, “consists not in thought merely, but in its application to
action, which is the end of the practical reason. Wherefore if any defect occur
in this, it is most contrary to prudence.”70 In other terms: the immediate end
of conscience, as a reflexive activity, is to judge the proposed action accord-
ing to the truth; the end of prudence, as a direct regulating activity of the
practical reason, is to identify, command, and to carry out the right choice.
If the latter is not carried out, there is a lack of prudence, but not necessarily
an error of conscience, since it is possible that the judgment which guides the
choice71 is opposed to conscience, “as when the desire of a dishonest action
clouds the reason so much as to impede it from deciding to reject the action.
Therefore, someone makes a mistake in a choice, but not in conscience, given
that he acts against his own conscience. It is said that he acts in bad con-
science because the deed does not agree with his moral knowledge.” 72 Moral
evil means precisely that the judgment of choice is not congruent with the
judgment of conscience.
It is not infrequent that someone may call a “judgment of conscience”
that which is properly a judgment of choice. This misunderstanding
needs to be corrected, for such an identification entails the admission
that any human decision could be identified with a judgment of con-
science; said otherwise, a generic “good will” would be sufficient for
acting “in conscience”: this conception is very close to that of creative
conscience.
Regarding the distinction between conscience and prudence, we need to con-
sider, secondly, the insistence of many authors, including Thomas Aquinas,
on the thesis that moral conscience is an act and not a habit, a thesis which
cannot be understood—if we do not want to fall into a banality—as the dif-
ference between a habit and its own act: this means, rather, that conscience
is not the proper and specific act of a single habit, but an evaluative act of the
practical reason that can be carried out at diverse levels, which is influenced
by diverse habits.73 The reason carries out such a moral valuation in diverse
moments: before acting, after the action, but also prior to the intention and
voluntary consent, for prior to each act of the will (whether it be desire, inten-
tion, consent, or choice) the reason grasps in it goodness or evil. We recognize
that one must not act or that it would be a duty to not act in such a way,

ad 4.
70 S.Th. II-II, q. 47, a. 1, ad 3.

Chapter 10
but also that it is not licit to desire such an end or to deliberate about means
for achieving it, etc. Conscience is therefore a broader phenomenon than pru-
dence, but for what regards the identification and carrying out of the concrete
choice, prudence extends itself to more things and manages more functions
than conscience: the latter judges solely the morality of the operative project;
prudence, on the other hand, aids in deliberating, judging, choosing, and car-
rying out, while bringing into play the annexed virtues for such a purpose, all
the while making use of judgments of conscience.
10.4
Systematic Theological Study
of the Problems of Moral Judgment
The concept of moral conscience in the strict sense (actual conscience) pro-
posed by the encyclical Veritatis Splendor is in line with the traditional doc-
trine inspired by Saint Thomas, for whom conscience is the judgment resulting
from the application of moral knowledge to an action to be done or already
done.74 At a superficial glance, the concept of application could seem to be
a mechanical, passive, and given deductive operation, that would finish by
banalizing the concept of conscience itself. This is not really the case. The
judgment of conscience is an extremely complex act of discernment, in which
diverse elements, such as moral knowledge, knowledge of the action and sit-
uation, the sense of moral obligation, and the affective components of choice
must adequately relate to each other in order to reach moral truth. We ded-
icate this section to a deeper look at these elements and of their reciprocal
interaction, limiting ourselves, for the sake of brevity, to only their essential
aspects.
10.4.1
Conscience and Moral Knowledge
Conscience judges on the basis of a preexistent moral knowledge. This means
that it presupposes not only the habit of the first moral principles (syndere-
sis), and therefore natural irreflective knowledge of the virtuous criteria for
the regulation of actions and of human goods, but also their reflective formula-
tion under the form of precepts or norms.75 The habitus of moral knowledge,
therefore, comes to be presupposed. Naturally, this is not intended to state
that only professional philosophers or moral theologians are capable of for-
mulating judgments of conscience, but rather that it presupposes a reflective
moral knowledge, even if this is normally possessed in a non-scientific way,
acquired through reflection, education, social customs, etc. Moral norms are
74 Cf. De Veritate, q. 17, aa. 1–2; S.Th. I, q. 79, a. 13.
75 See what was said in Chapter VIII, subsection 8.2.2 and 8.2.3.


Moral Conscience
one of the principal means for communicating and receiving reflective moral
knowledge. Broadly speaking, norms are logically universal propositions that
have as a subject an action or the description of an action, and for its predi-
cate expressions such as “morally good”, “morally evil”, “morally obligatory”,
or other analogous ideas. Norms are not only commandments or prohibitions,
but also instructions or teachings: by means of more or less simple formu-
las they transmit knowledge of the principal demands of personal and social
virtues.
We shall propose some examples. The virtue of justice imposes respect
for the rights and goods of others. For what regards the goods of a
material character, all can be said synthetically by stating: “do not
steal”; or by formulating moral norms in a more specific way like the
following: theft is morally evil; in case of extreme necessity it is morally
licit to take the necessary goods of another—but only those that are
strictly necessary—in order to depart from such a state, since in normal
conditions no one can reasonably deny to another what is necessary to
avoid dying of hunger or thirst; robbery is morally illicit and more grave
than theft, because to the material damage is added a threat or violence
against the legitimate owner; he who has stolen is obliged to restore to
the legitimate owner the stolen good or, if the good was consumed, its
economic value, etc. And in such a manner could all the demands of
justice be verbalized. These and other norms allow us to rightly judge
particular actions. If we deal with simple actions, synthetic formulae
suffice; in order to judge complex actions, for example, the moral licit-
ness of certain commercial or financial operations, more specific norms
would be necessary.
The application of moral knowledge is a thing that is far from simple and
obvious.
Norms are not the mere expression of a superior will that must
be followed even if the world crumbles, but are linguistic expressions of a
regulation (ordinatio rationis) that above all must be adequately understood in
its terms and in its true meaning. What comes to be required is an exact
understanding of the specific case and of the meaning of the norm itself, in
order to be able to overcome possible defects of the normative statement,
both because its linguistic expression is not completely exact and because in
a concrete case it enters into conflict with other likewise important demands
and because the person finds himself in a situation that the norm did not
intend nor could it contemplate.76 We must, nonetheless, point out that for
76 In this regard, there emerge a set of problems, with which we shall occupy ourselves in
the following subsections, which pertain to the theory of the reflexive judgment of an action.
Like all problems regarding reflexive knowledge, such a theory is principally of interest to
moralists and to those who must take on the study of very complex situations. Regarding
reflexive knowledge, the theory of the judgment of action presupposes the direct exercise of
the practical reason, which with the help of grace and of the Christian virtues manages to
identify for each problem its congruent solution. Nonetheless, it is good to remember that


Chapter 10
an adequate understanding of the specific moral case the doctrine concerning
the sources of morality which were studied in Chapter VI should be kept in
mind.
We shall take up again an example already proposed in that chapter.
It could happen that a married woman is directed, as the only possible
therapy for a disease, to consume a medicine that could cause as a collat-
eral effect temporary infertility. Reading the package leaflet, the woman
understands that it is an anovulatory pill, and thinks that consuming it
is morally illicit, since contraception is an action that no circumstance
can render legitimate.
In this case, it is clear that the woman does
not know the moral specifics of “contraception” well.
Contraception
is “any action which either before, at the moment of, or after sexual
intercourse, is specifically intended to prevent procreation—whether as
an end or as a means.”77 This definition permits us to understand as
morally licit “the use of those therapeutic means necessary to cure bod-
ily diseases, even if a foreseeable impediment to procreation should
result there from—provided such impediment is not directly intended
for any motive whatsoever,”78 and this is so not because an exception is
admitted, but simply because the judged action is not proposed, neither
as an end or as a means, to impede procreation, and therefore it does
not enter into the moral specifics of the act of “contraception.”
10.4.2
Moral Conscience, Norms of Behavior,
Exceptions
The application of norms of behavior on the part of personal moral con-
science must take into account the distinction between “legal norms” and
“moral norms”.79 Both have moral importance, but their relationship with
action and their type of obligatoriness is completely different.
We call “legal norms” those rules of behavior that are constituted of the moral
licitness or illicitness—or at least juridical licitness or illicitness—of actions
in order to promote or defend a good or an advantageous state of affairs.
Examples of “legal norms” are some civil and ecclesiastical laws, as well as
some norms established by moral science that do not have their own positiv-
ity or negativity independently of such norms: the necessity of safeguarding
important personal and social goods justifies a set of rules, according to which
actions which do not possess an intrinsic moral value become good or evil. As
we explained in Chapter IX, even positive human norms oblige in conscience,
but they are norms that generally leave open the possibility of exceptions
this part of moral theology is, after all, of secondary importance.
77 Paul VI, Enc. Humanae Vitae, 25-VII-1968, no. 14.
78 Ibid., no. 15.
79 We take this distinction from M. Rhonheimer, The Perspective of Morality (2011),
328–336.


Moral Conscience
or corrections according to epikeia,80 so long as one finds herself in concrete
situations in which the observance of such a norm is not necessary or would
even be harmful.81
A good example would be traffic laws. The orderly movement of auto-
mobiles, necessary for defending the good constituted by the mobility
and safety of citizens, compels the latter, for example, to keep to the
right side of the road and to stop before a red light, and to avoid the
contrary. But there can be exceptions and also epikeia: on a Sunday in
August in Rome, when the city is deserted, it is not a moral fault to not
wait at a red light, if visibility is good and there is complete certainty
that there exists no danger to oneself or others; in the same conditions
it is morally possible to keep to the left side of the road for a few yards
in such a way as to avoid an irregularity in the street, etc. All this is
possible because there is no intrinsic disorder in these actions, which
are good or evil only for their relationship to a rule that is generally
functional to obtain an advantageous, or even necessary, state of affairs.
“Moral norms” are, instead, normative statements whose ontological founda-
tion is the ethical positivity or negativity intrinsic to the action that is com-
manded or prohibited. Serving as examples are the norms that prohibit adul-
tery, abortion, rape, etc. These norms do not make up the moral licitness or
illicitness of the action, but, on the contrary, it is the licitness or illicitness of
the commanded or prohibited action that establishes the validity of the norm.
The moral norm is valid insofar as it truly expresses the real conformity or
opposition of a mode of acting with the principles of the reason enlightened
by faith, that is to say, with the theological and moral virtues. When a moral
norm is observed, we do not limit ourselves to respecting a rule that is gen-
erally useful or advantageous for the defense of certain goods, but we rather
perform an act of virtue (faith, charity, justice, etc.) or else we omit per-
forming an act that is opposed to it. In a rigorous sense, exceptions are not
possible in relation to these norms, because their good or evil is not based in
the observance of the norm so as to preserve a value or state of affairs; the
good or evil is based in the action itself, which in its intrinsic voluntariness
is an act of virtue or an act opposed to it. If in some case it seems that in
a properly moral matter an exception should be made, this happens because
the action does not in fact fall within the norm (as happened in the former
example of the assumption of an anovulatory medicine for truly therapeutic
reasons), and in such a case we do not deal with an exception, but a false clas-
80 We treat of epikeia in subsection d.
81 It is to be kept in mind what was said regarding the obligatoriness of the civil law
(Chapter IX, subsection 9.1.4): it obliges conscience, but its moral obligation is in direct
relation with the value and importance of the social goods protected by the norm. In other
words, the moral obligatoriness is not a dimension of the juridical norm considered in an
isolated way, but is an effect of human responsibility in relation to the social reality.


Chapter 10
sification or a defective understanding of the moral category. In the properly
moral ambit, the concept of an exception should be abandoned, because it—if
understood properly and rigorously—would imply admitting that from time
to time “a little injustice”, “a little violence”, or “a little unchastity” would be
morally acceptable, and therefore congruent with following Christ: something
which obviously cannot be admitted.
We still need to distinguish between “positive moral norms”, or norms which
command to do something (honor your father and mother), and “negative
moral norms”, or norms which prohibit one from doing something (do not
commit adultery). We affirm that negative moral norms oblige semper et pro
semper, in every possible circumstance or situation, because such a choice of
behavior prohibited by them “is in no case compatible with the goodness of the
will of the acting person, with his vocation to life with God and to communion
with his neighbour.”82 Postive norms, on the other hand, oblige semper sed
non pro semper, in the sense that, while conserving their substantial validity,
it is not always possible to carry out commanded positive works. “What must
be done in any given situation depends on the circumstances, not all of which
can be foreseen [ result of coercion or other circumstances, can be hindered
from doing certain good actions; but he can never be hindered from not doing
certain actions, especially if he is prepared to die rather than to do evil.” 83
What has been said allows us to understand that the application of moral
knowledge in order to formulate a judgment of conscience requires an active
and attentive understanding of the nature, foundation, and meaning of diverse
normative statements.
10.4.3
Moral Conscience and the Situation
The judgment of conscience also requires the right understanding and valu-
ation of the situation. The concept of a moral situation was sometimes in-
terpreted and utilized as an expedient for relativizing the absolute validity of
“negative moral norms”, and therefore to negate the existence of intrinsically
evil actions. While containing some positive instances, the Situational Ethics
which ensued created some important doctrinal problems, which motivated
diverse interventions on the part of the ecclesiastical magisterium.84 However,
82 Veritatis Splendor, 52.
83 Ibid.
84 Cf. Pius XII, Addresses of March 23 and April 18, 1952: AAS 44 (1952) 270–278 &
413–419; Congregation of the Holy Office, Istr. Contra Doctrinam, 2-II-1956: DS 3918–
3921.
For the sake of brevity, we shall not be able to address the epistemological and
theological problems of a Situation Ethics. It reflects some foundational limitations of an
ethics of obligation, which it seeks to overcome by moving the axis of the balance toward the
singular act. A right conception of prudence allows for greater satisfaction of the demands of
the unrepeatable singularity of the moral subject while still not relativizing the constitutive


Moral Conscience
the situation of the moral subject can and must be interpreted positively. It
expresses the embodiment, vocation, and sociality of the human moral subject
which, far from being a limitation, opens the personal path of each person
toward the one truth and one Lord.
There is no doubt that the state of life (single, married, priest, etc), the
profession (doctor, judge, soldier) and other characteristics of the person are
sources of particular duties and rights. The diverse ethical demands are struc-
tured, in practice, like the different levels of a house. The higher levels are
added to the lower levels and to the foundation, while the latter sustain the
former. Particular duties linked to civil, professional, etc., states presuppose
the ethical demands common to the human and Christian conditions. These
conditions can sometimes acquire some specific modes (charity, for example,
has some specific demands for a doctor, for a priest, etc.), but they cannot
be annulled or relativized in their substance by the particular condition of a
concrete person.
It should also be noted that every true moral demand is potentially universal;
this means that such a demand is incumbent upon whoever finds himself in
that concrete situation.
If a person were to find herself in a situation so
exceptional as to truly be the only of its kind in the world, it would still be
true that the valid ethical demands for her would be equally valid for any other
person who found herself in an identical situation. The quality of being purely
unique itself does not change the fact that the ethical demands pertaining to
the situation are potentially universal.
10.4.4
The Virtue of Epikeia
The Catholic theological-moral tradition has conceded ample space to epikeia,
which perfects moral judgment, allowing for the achievement of truth even in
exceptional situations. The study of the classical sources does not leave any
doubt regarding the fact that epikeia was seen, in all respects and in the
strictest sense, as a moral virtue,85 that is to say, as a quality pertaining
to the perfected moral formation of man.
This means that epikeia is the
principle of choices which are not only good, but truly excellent and optimal:
for Aristotle “the equitable (epieikés) is just, even better than a certain type
of just”;86 for Saint Albert the Great epikeia is “superiustitia”.87 It is not,
principles of the moral reason.
85 Cf. S.Th. II-II, q. 120, a. 1. For a detailed analysis of the classical sources, and
of modern proposals we refer the reader to A. Rodríguez Luño, “La virtù dell'epicheia.
Teoria, storia e applicazione,” Acta Philosophica 6 (1997) 197–236 & 7 (1998) 65–88 (with
bibliography).
86 Nicomachean Ethics, V, 10: 1137 b 24, our translation.
87 Cf. Albert the Great, Super Ethica Commentum et Quaestiones: Opera Omnia, Com-
piled by W. Kübel, (Münster: 1968–1972), vol. XIV, pars I, 384.


Chapter 10
therefore, something worse, a “discount” that should be tolerated. The original
placement of epikeia was in the area of behaviors regulated by the civil law,
to which the scholastics added behaviors regulated by canon law; in any case,
it pertains to perfectible human laws (we called them “legal norms” before).
Faithfully adopting the thought of Aristotle and Saint Thomas, Cajetan syn-
thetically explains the nature of epikeia with the following words: “Directio
legis ubi deficit propter universale”,88 a correction of the law where it is defec-
tive on account of its universality. The person who is well-formed morally not
only knows which behaviors are commanded or prohibited, but understands
also why they are so. However, as the law speaks in universal terms, something
may happen that, in spite of appearances, does not pertain to the universal
norm, and the virtuous person recognizes this, for she understands that in
such a case the literal observance of the law would give place to a behavior
that is harmful to justice and the common good, which are the supreme in-
spiring principles of each law and legislator. It then becomes a duty, where the
human legislator has overlooked some circumstance and missed the mark—for
the sake of speaking in general terms—to correct the application of the law
and to consider prescribed what the legislator himself would say if he were
present and would have included in the law if he could have known the case
in question (surely, we are assuming that the legislator is seeking the common
good with the legislation). And all this is done not because one cannot do
better, but because otherwise it would be an unjust behavior and injurious
to the common good. Epikeia is not something that can be benevolently in-
voked, and it has nothing to do with the principle of tolerance, rather, when
it is applicable it becomes a rule to follow necessarily.89
All are in agreement (from Saint Thomas to Saint Alphonsus) that a law
should not be observed when, for a particular case, it is defective aliquo modo
contrarie and not merely negative. That is to say, the law should not be lit-
erally observed if its observance gives rise to a behavior that is in some way
contrary to justice or the common good; epikeia cannot be invoked, on the
other hand, only because the ratio legis does not seem to be particularly per-
tinent or pressing in a concrete case (a simply negative cessation of the ratio

89 Saint Thomas even retains that justice is predicated per prius of epikeia, and per
posterius of legal justice, since the latter is directed by the former; in fact—he adds–,
epikeia is “a higher rule of human actions” (S.Th. II-II, q. 120, a. 2). This obviously does
not mean that epikeia stands above all good and evil, but simply that when the common
criteria of judgment are not present on account of the prior mentioned reasons, the act
to perform must be identified by a directive judgment, called by Saint Thomas “gnome”,
which must be directly inspired by higher principles (“altiora principia”): the same “ratio
iustitiae” and the common good, skipping the mediation of the precept that here and now is
defective. Epikeia is a “higher rule” insofar as one must directly appeal to moral principles
of a higher level in order judge of exceptional cases.


Moral Conscience
legis). In this regard, Saint Thomas retains that when the literal compliance
with the law is damaging to the common good, if the peril is not immanent,
recourse should be made to the legislator.90 In more concrete terms, when
can one consider that a law is defective aliquo modo contrarie? On the ex-
act meaning of aliquo modo there is not a complete agreement. For Saint
Thomas and for Cajetan there needs to be a true and proper opposition in
the observance of the law to justice or the common good. For Suárez such
an opinion is “nimis rigida et limitata”.91He retains that a human law comes
to be aliquo modo contrarie also in the three following hypotheses: 1) when
complying with it, while not being unjust, is very difficult and burdensome:
for example, if it implies a serious risk to one's life; 2) when it is certain that
the human legislator, while being able to oblige also in such a case, did not
and does not have the intention of doing so; 3) when the observance of the
law, even if it would not be in any way injurious to the common good, would
be detrimental to the good of the person in question, provided that—Suárez
clarifies—“the damage is severe and no demand of the common good forces
one to cause or permit such damage.” Suárez clarifies, moreover, that neither
irritating laws nor the divine-positive law can be corrected by epikeia.
We come now to the problem of the natural moral law, that is, to the possibil-
ity of correcting with epikeia also “moral norms” and not only “legal norms”.
Cajetan, the Carmelite theologians of Salamanca, and Saint Alphonsus re-
sponded yes; Suárez, on the other hand, responded no. But if studied accu-
rately it is seen that the first and the second sustain in reality a substantially
identical thesis, that the precepts of the natural moral law as such cannot be
corrected by epikeia in any way. It must therefore be concluded, despite some
recent interpretations to the contrary, that epikeia cannot be invoked to deny
the universal value of “negative moral norms”. Such interpretations not only
do not find a basis in the adopted classical texts, but they transfer epikeia
from its original context (an ethics of virtue) to a problem of contemporary
normativistic ethics that is completely extraneous to it. Epikeia finds itself in
the context of the prudent identification of the desired end made possible by
a virtuous habit. When an ethical demand, which is originally a demand of

would threaten, like the sword of Damocles, all legal certainty, and societal coexistence
would become a little less than impossible.

Chapter 10
virtue, comes to be expressed through a human linguistic-normative formu-
lation, which in its generality cannot foresee the exceptional circumstances
in which the agent comes to find himself, epikeia permits of a perfect con-
formity of the concrete behavior with the ratio virtutis. For example, a loan
should be restituted insofar as restituting it is an act of the virtue of justice.
In exceptional cases in which restituting a loan is no longer an act of justice
(to return a weapon to a person who manifests the will to commit a crime),
where in fact to restitute it would be an act contrary to justice, the virtue of
epikeia allows one to arrive at a prudential judgment that here and now she
should not restitute the lent item. The just person (who possesses the virtue
of justice) cannot but recognize this. Epikeia is necessary precisely because—
whatever a literal reading of the normative statement would be—justice and
the other ethical virtues do not admit of exceptions.
10.4.5
Conscience and Moral Obligation
Up until now we have spoken little of the meaning of moral duty. While in
the philosophical and theological ethics of obligation it is an ethical concept
of extreme importance (one thinks of Kant), in an ethics of virtue it plays an
important role, but nonetheless a derivative one.92 For a philosophical ethics
of virtue, the moral rule of virtue is a duty, and the same must be said in
theological ethics for what regards the rule of the Christian, theological, and
moral virtues. However, duty does not constitute the only, nor the principal,
motivation in ethics: which is instead the role of Charity; neither does it
necessarily presuppose the existence of a contrary inclination: rather, duty
orients itself in the same line as the person's sensible and spiritual inclinations,
as well as that of the dynamism of the grace of the Holy Spirit.
For theology, moral obligation contains a reference to the divine call to ho-
liness, and for this reason it is something more than a sense of duty. Moral
conscience is the privileged seat where the theonomous character of moral
obligation comes to be perceived in a clear and reflected way. The moral rule
of the virtues “is a duty insofar as it has for its normative end God who is the
perfect Good; it is also obliging, inasmuch as it is a rule that is in us, while
coming from God: through it God makes us aware of the obliging moral order,
and for this reason our will is obliged with respect to His will. If a moral rule
were only a rule and not also a law, the moral fault would only be a culpable
error, the failure of achieving the true end, but not also the violation of an
obligation. Instead, we have the awareness that in violating the moral rule
we violate an obligation. In Christian thought this awareness that the moral

literature, was achieved by G. Abbà, Felicità, vita buona e virtù (1995) To this work we
direct the reader who wishes to find a deeper study of this topic.


Moral Conscience
rule is also an obliging law that comes from God takes the name of moral
conscience.”93
10.5
Modes of Moral Conscience
10.5.1
Classification of the States of Conscience
We can now classify the diverse modes that the judgment of conscience can
take on, considering three criteria.94
1. For its relation to judged action we speak of antecedent conscience,
which judges of the act that is about to be carried out, commanding it,
permitting it, prohibiting it, etc., and of consequent conscience, which
approves or disapproves an action that is already carried out.
2. By reason of its conformity with the truth, there is a distinction between
right or true conscience, which judges with truth the moral quality of
an act, and erroneous conscience, which does not reach the truth with
regard to the moral quality of an act, esteeming as good an act that in
reality is evil or vice versa.
The cause of the error of conscience is ignorance. Ignorance can regard the
norm (ignorantia iuris), as in the case of the person who does not know that
there exists a law which commands that one report to the authorities those
who are responsible for certain crimes; or it can regard the fact (ignorantia
facti), as in the case of the person who does not understand that the action
under review is a crime of this type.
In order to evaluate the way in which ignorance can modify moral imputability,
it is necessary to distinguish between the diverse kinds of ignorance. Invincible
ignorance is that which dominates conscience to such a point so as to leave
no possibility of recognizing the ignorance and distancing oneself from it.
Vincible ignorance is that which, considering the circumstances of the agent,
can be recognized and removed, but remains because the person does not will
to overcome it or because what could be done to overcome it is not done.
Ignorance is invincible: a) when the person does not even suspect that his
opinion is wrong and that it, therefore, must be abandoned; b) when, despite
reflection, study, and asking questions to prudent and experienced persons
regarding a certain problem, one sincerely arrives at an objectively erroneous
93 G. Abbà, Felicità, vita buona e virtù (1995), 253, our translation. The reference of
moral conscience to God is emphasized both by the Sacred Scriptures and the teaching
of the Church, as we have already explained. This is all very important for the Christian
notion of sin, as we shall see in Chapter XI.
94 We take back up, with some modifications, what was written in A. Rodríguez Luño,
Etica (1992), nos. 133, 237–244.


Chapter 10
solution, even if the person is not at all aware of this. Ignorance is vincible
when doubts arise regarding the truth of one's opinion (either out of a certain
insecurity of conscience or on account of the contrast between our opinions
with those of persons in authority), and, making use of suitable means to
discover the truth, one does not act with due diligence on account of laziness,
malice, etc. It can also be said that ignorance is invincible in the measure
in which it is not caused either directly or indirectly by our own will; and
that it is vincible in the measure in which it proceeds from one or diverse acts
of the will: to not have willed to understand a certain question, perpetual
disregard for the moral aspects of one's professional work, closing oneself to
ethical demands, etc.
Invincible ignorance eliminates freedom and the moral imputability of action
in the same measure in which this ignorance is extended: it is, therefore, in-
culpable (whoever shoots at a person whom he did not recognize as his own
father is culpable of homicide, but not patricide). The action caused by this
type of ignorance is non-voluntary or even involuntary.95 Vincible ignorance,
however, does not take away the freedom or moral imputability of the action
(in the end, the person does not will the action because he is ignorant, he is
ignorant because he wills to be so), even if at times it can reduce it; conse-
quently it is culpable, because it presupposes a voluntary moral disorder, at
least through negligence. It needs to be evaluated whether this ignorance pre-
supposes in the person a grave or a slight fault, if it responds to an expressed
will to ignorance in order to satisfy one's own desires without obstacles (crass
or supine ignorance), or if it responds to a negligence that, without taking it
away, reduces moral responsibility (simply vincible ignorance).
3) According to the kind of assent, that is, according to the level of certainty
whereby the judgment is made, one speaks of certain conscience, if it judges
with certitude that an act is good or evil; of probable conscience, if the judg-
ment is not so certain so as to exclude the opposite possibility; and of dubious
conscience, if one does not know which side to take, and therefore is not able
to make a judgment.96
10.5.2
Principles for Following One's Conscience
1. Only certain conscience is a moral rule and must be followed. Whoever
acts against it certainly performs evil, for he contradicts a known moral
demand. It is not decisive in this regard that the conscience is true or

96 Because doubtful conscience is a suspension of judgment, diverse authors do not use

Moral Conscience
false: whoever wills an action judged with certitude as evil, even if it is
objectively good, wills what he sees with certitude as evil, and formally
commits sin.
2. Beyond certitude, the conscience must be true or invincibly erroneous
in order to be a rule of morality. In a strict sense, only true conscience
is such a rule. Nonetheless, imperfection and human fallibility render it
possible that in certain cases man, while exercising due diligence, may
without fault esteem as right a conscience that is in reality erroneous.
For this reason, even an invincibly erroneous yet certain conscience must
be followed. Such a conscience, however, is not a rule in an absolute
way, for it obliges only as long as the error remains; furthermore, it
obliges per accidens, not for itself, inasmuch as it must be followed in the
measure in which man invincibly retains it as true. Moreover, as we said
before,97 invincible subjective error, while not being morally imputable,
is nonetheless harmful and cannot in any case be a substitute for the
truth. The fallibility of human conscience underlines that its formation
is one of the most important and urgent moral tasks of the human
person.
3. The vincibly erroneous conscience is not a moral norm. It is not licit
to follow it, for the action consequent to a culpable error is culpable in
cause, that is, in the same measure in which the error that precedes it is
culpable. One cannot, however, act against it, for that would be what
here and now appears as evil. There is, then, an obligation to escape
from error before acting. It may then be kept in mind that whoever finds
himself in vincible error does not have a certain conscience: perhaps
such a person does not recognize the right solution to the problem,
nevertheless he understands that what he thinks is something that is
not certain, that he must do further research or continue seeking the
right solution, etc.
4. It is not licit to act with a probable conscience. Whoever acts with a
positive uncertainty (grounded on reasons and serious suspicions) re-
garding the evil of an act, voluntarily exposes himself to do evil, and for
this reason this person must confirm his judgment of conscience (reach
certain conscience) before passing on to action.
5. Neither can a doubtful conscience, which suspends judgment, be a moral
rule; to be so the conscience must judge with certainty.
The same
principles should be applied to doubtful conscience as were applied to a
probable one.
97 Cf. subsection 10.2.2.


Chapter 10
10.6
Conscience and Holiness
The analysis we have done regarding the notion of conscience has brought to
light, in the first place, that it can be identified with the most profound and
basic nucleus of the person: it is his heart, the intimate sanctuary where man
hears the voice of God; in this sense conscience occupies an important role
in the moral life and in the path of identification with Christ.98 A further
examination of the concept of conscience has led to identifying it with the
judgment of the practical reason concerning the moral act, which is config-
ured as the ultimate subjective norm regarding moral good and evil; such
a meaning would seem to devalue the importance of conscience in Christian
life, and it seems to reduce it to the simple ascertainment of the practical
truth. This apparent dichotomy is, nevertheless, that proper to a normativis-
tic moral viewpoint that, willingly or not, leads to the contraposition between
law/truth and the conscience.99 In a “first person” morality there is no space
for such a dichotomy, it is the person herself in all her truth who performs
the judgment of conscience:100 it is founded on the person and reaches her
concrete situation.
In this regard, conscience constitutes and institutes the “personalization” of
moral action and renders possible to the human person his own realization,
in its unrepeatable singularity and situation congruently with his profound
truth as man and as Christian.101 Therefore, this conception does not reduce
the moral value of conscience, but rather situates it in its proper role in the
structure of Christian life: carrying out the judgment of conscience, with the
help of moral knowledge and of personal dispositions, man in his integrity is
found in dialogue with God; and this voice of the Lord, which resounds in his
intimate center, indicates to him how he must act, here and now, for the end
of identifying himself with Christ. In other words, the purpose of conscience is
not simply that of achieving a practical judgment (to know the moral truth),
but that of facilitating through such a judgment (made in dialogue with God)
the achievement of the human good, the perfection of the person as such.
Through conscience, man finds himself capable of knowing in each concrete
situation what facilitates his life in Christ and what opposes it; since to follow
the voice of conscience is the sure path—in a certain sense, the only path—for
98 Conscience is a “sort of moral sense which leads us to discern what is good and what
is evil an inner eye, a visual capacity of the spirit, able to guide our steps along the path
of good” (Reconciliatio et Paenitentia, 26).
99 See subsection 10.3.1.
100 The full truth about the person has as a foundation and principal component her full
relationship with God, although it includes (in a secondary and derivative way) all the set
of relationships and qualities that determine the truth of this person, here and now.
101 Cf. C. Caffarra, Viventi in Cristo (1986), 97.


Moral Conscience
increasing in holiness:102 moral holiness is developed when the judgment of
choice coincides with the judgment of conscience, and sin is nothing other
than the disagreement between these two judgments.
The judgment of conscience could be summarized as such: man dialogues with
God, in the intimate center of his being, in order to discern the congruence
of a concrete action with life in Christ. Such a succinct statement includes
very diverse and complex situations. It may involve a bygone act and, in this
case, the dialogue approves of it, or perhaps it contests it while at the same
time motivating the person to rectify it. It can be a very simple act (to do a
small service) and thus the dialogue is brief, almost inexistent.103 In certain
circumstances, before situations of great personal relevance (recognizing one's
own vocation, etc.), the dialogue must be more reflective. In any case, the
conscience requires a sincere dialogue with the Lord in order to discover,
here and now, what He expects from each of us: for this reason conscience
calls for a life of prayer, in which “His gaze purifies our heart; the light of
the countenance of Jesus illumines the eyes of our heart and teaches us to see
everything in the light of his truth [. . . ]. Thus it learns the 'interior knowledge
of our Lord,' the more to love him and follow him.” 104
The moral importance of conscience is thus clear, the need of duly forming it
and the right of not being forced to act against it. Through conscience, the
person constructs—in dialogue with God—the path of his personal vocation,
of his own and unique way of living in Christ: the universal call to holiness
receives its personal specification from moral conscience.105 Conscience elicits
“in man a sense of responsibility and personality, the awareness of existential
principles and their logical development.
This logical development in the
Christian, that evokes his own baptismal character, generates the fundamental
concepts of the theology of man, who knows himself and feels himself to be
a child of God, a member of Christ, incorporated into the Church, bestowed
with the common priesthood of the faithful, whose fecund doctrine the Council
recalled and whereby the Christian's effort for holiness is born, toward the
fullness of the Christian life, to the perfection of charity.” 106 Consequently, it
should not be forgotten that the judgment of conscience, as an echo of the
102 “Moral conscience does not close man within an insurmountable and impenetrable
solitude, but opens him to the call, to the voice of God.
In this, and not in anything
else, lies the entire mystery and the dignity of the moral conscience: in being the place,
the sacred place where God speaks to man” (John Paul II, Address 17-VIII-1983, n. 2:
Insegnamenti, VI-2, 1983, 256). This passage is also cited by Veritatis Splendor, 58.
103 Among persons who love each other, the small deed of one is easily interpretable on
the part of another. If a person has an intimate relationship with God, he does need to
think for long in order to discern His will.
104 CCC, 2715.
105 Cf. C. Caffarra, Viventi in Cristo (1986), 105.
106 Paul VI, Address 26-IX-1970: Insegnamenti, VIII (1970) 937.


Chapter 10
voice of God, is always a call to holiness, which demands an authentic docility
to the movements the Holy Spirit elicits in each person.
What has been said can be summarized in two maxims: “Never make a deci-
sion without stopping to consider the matter in the presence of God.” “Seek
God within you and listen to him.”107
107 Saint Josemaría Escrivá, The Way, 36th ed., (Milan: Ares, 1993), 266 and 319.


## CHAPTER 11 {#colom-scelti.11}
Sin and Conversion
The themes studied up to this moment have given us the ability to understand
that voluntary action can be morally good or evil, and that such a character
depends upon the object, end, and circumstances seen in their relation to
the theological and moral virtues: the latter constituting the moral rules of
Christian life.1
Nevertheless, the theological study of sin continues to be
necessary because sin is something more than an ethically negative action.2
Sin is the negative response of man to the gift and call of the love of God,
which then reveals itself as an unrequited, betrayed, and offended love. As a
“no” of the human child to the divine Father, sin is the mysterium iniquitatis
without which salvation history would not have been what it was.
It can
be well understood that a reflection on sin is an essential part of Christian
doctrine and moral theology, and that it is only with the understanding that
comes with faith that the nature of sin can be fully grasped.3
1 Cf. Chapter VI, section 6.4, Chapter VII and above-all Chapter VIII, sections 8.2 &

Chapter 11
11.1
Sin and Conversion
in the Sacred Scriptures
11.1.1
Old Testament
The notion of sin, along with all the moral thought of the Old Testament,
is comprehensible after recognizing the free and gratuitous nature of God's
salvific plan. Humankind originally found itself in a state of justice and divine
friendship, from which the first parents excluded themselves with the first sin.4
The nature and background of this sin are illuminated well by Barthélemy:
Man, “having doubted the goodness of the Father, then sealed that
doubt with a deed which confirmed it like a seal at the bottom of an
official act. When man performed this deed of eating the fruit, this
meant: At its root, I recognized that God is the One who wants to hold
me in subjection, and that I must free myself from Him at all costs in
order to be a god myself. Eating the fruit implied this interpretation
of God's motives. With this deed, the climate of confidence was bro-
ken, the climate of filial abandonment into the hands of the Father, he
whose love would be our only treasure. Having broken all of this, man
knows he broke from the source of life. In fact, a person cannot receive
from God a continually renewed life if he does not face Him and become
open to Him with all of his being. Now, man, wishing to become a god,
deprived himself above all of that relationship of total and confident
openness which alone would have ensured him life.” 5
After the first disobedience, sin rose up in the heart of man as a pervasive
and destructive power,6 to the point that “when the LORD saw how great
was man's wickedness on earth, and how no desire that his heart conceived
was ever anything but evil, he regretted that he had made man on the earth,
and his heart was grieved.”7
However, the Lord did not abandon His plan of salvation and chose the people
of Israel to implement it.
The Covenant became, then, the new indicator
of humanity's fidelity or infidelity.8 The Lord established a Covenant with
Israel, and non-compliance with such a pact was not merely considered a
legal shortcoming: since it was not so much opposition to a norm, as to God
Himself.9 For with sin man refuses the love offered to him by his Creator
and becomes closed in himself, disrupting the familial relationship that God
established with him. The prophetic literature makes clear this fact that sin
4 Cf. Gen 3:1–13; see also the study of J.-D. Barthélemy, Dio e la sua immagine (1980),
66ff.
5 J.-D. Barthélemy, Dio e la sua immagine (1980), 77.
6 Cf. Gen 4:8, 23–24; 6:11–12; Jer 26:3.
7 Gen 6:5–6.
8 Cf. Deut 4:23–31; Josh 7:11; Judg 2:1–3; Jer 11:1–8; etc.
9 Cf. Hos 8:1–2.


Sin and Conversion
is an act of infidelity to divine love: referring to it as an act of adultery.10 In
a derivative way it is also a rupture with the people, insofar as it is an offense
against the divine plans concerning it; and for this reason, even injustices
against one's neighbor are truly offenses against God.11
11.1.2
Synoptic Gospels
The person of Jesus and His message are the New Covenant's point of ref-
erence.12 He makes evident that sin carries with it a distancing of oneself
from God and the will to find one's happiness elsewhere, something which in
fact leads to the most abject misery;13 and thus he brings to light the interior
nature of sin, bypassing the exterior formalism of many of his contemporaries.
The Incarnation was designed for the salvation of men, and so an essential
part of Christ's mission is to liberate from sin;14 therefore, the Lord does not
reject proximity to sinners, in fact He came precisely to call them, receive
them with mercy, and to forgive them.15 Man, on his part, is asked to have
a penitent attitude and not one of self-forgiveness.16
The Gospels show as well that there does not exist merely one kind of fault.
Rather, Jesus renounces a grand variety of sins: hypocrisy, vainglory, injustice,
homicide, adultery, covetousness and pride;17 nonetheless, it is emphasized
that sin is not so much the mere external action, as the perverse interior
attitude of the will that is its origin.18 Such a disordered attitude, nonetheless,
does not always have the same gravity: sins which are forgiven with prayer
are less serious than blasphemy against the Holy Spirit or the scandalizing of
the youth.19 This distinction, already mentioned in the Old Testament,20 is
also found in the Apostolic Letters.21
11.1.3
Pauline Corpus
The Pauline writings are permeated with the doctrine of sin, inserted into the
salvific perspective of Christ the Redeemer. Since we have already discussed

Chapter 11
the typically Pauline conception of sin,22 we now have the opportunity to be
concise as we move forward. Characteristic of Saint Paul is the use of the
term sin (hamartía) in the singular, as a personified power that operates in
man and through him.23
The evil of men made it possible that sin could
have a universal scope and could reign over the entire world, however, this
does not excuse the sin of each individual, whether he be Gentile or Jew.24
The universality of sin springs forth from the disobedience of Adam: “Just as
through one person sin entered the world, and through sin, death, and thus
death came to all, inasmuch as all sinned.”25 Thus, sin and death are the
destiny of those alienated from Christ.
Jesus, in order to destroy the dominion of sin and to liberate men from the
“law”, defeated sin on the Cross in order that righteousness would be fulfilled
in us.26 In such a way the new life of Christians, sharing in the resurrection of
Christ, began.27 Such a life is applied to persons through Baptism, wherein
man dies with Christ to sin and is reborn to a new life in such a real way
that we can truly speak of a “new creation”.28 The “new creation”, however,
is not fully free from the fomes peccati 29 and will be, so long as one finds
himself in this world, in danger inasmuch as one can still distance himself
from God again. For this reason, the Apostle continually exhorts an ascetic
commitment in order to resist the pitfalls of sin.30
In light of the redeeming work, sin represents the “non-acceptance” of Christ,
that is, “non-faith”.31 This does not mean that there exists a single sin, since
Saint Paul explicitly affirms the contrary when he lists off the vices which
exclude man from the Kingdom of God.32 What he means to say is that the
more profound reality of sin, of any sin, consists in the non-acceptance of the
salvific action of God in Christ and, for believers, it consists in the distancing
of oneself from Christ in order to follow the works of the flesh.33 Whoever
sins re-crucifies the Lord.34
In the last analysis, for Saint Paul sin is the
non-acceptance or distancing of oneself from the merciful God who came to
meet us in Christ.

Sin and Conversion
11.1.4
Johannine Corpus
The use of the term sin in the singular is also characteristic of John. There
exists a quintessential sin: the refusal to accept Christ as light, Truth, etc.35
God sent His Son not to judge the world, but to save it: Jesus is the Good
Shepherd who offers His life for His sheep, who receives sinners and forgives
them, while asking them to sin no more, to reject evil works, to believe in the
Son, and to walk in the truth.36 Therefore the failure to recognize Christ as
Savior, unbelief, is presented as the sin for which the Spirit will reprove the
world, and Jesus continuously forewarns of this danger.37 In the first letter of
John, sin is seen as opposition to love. This letter is marked throughout by the
tension between being generated by God, and therefore being free from sin,
and the possibility and reality of committing sin, something that if recognized
will be remitted by Christ.38 Moreover, this letter speaks of sin that leads to
death, making reference to apostasy and idolatry.39
11.1.5
The Remission of Sins
The Revelation of sin is not limited to showing the reality and evil of it, but also
highlights the superabundant mercy of the Lord: “Where sin increased, grace
overflowed all the more, so that, as sin reigned in death, grace also might
reign through justification for eternal life through Jesus Christ our Lord.” 40
In this way, sin is a reality that can and must be overcome and conquered,
since Christ died so that men might not live according to the flesh: all of this
does not come from one's own strength, but from God who, in Christ, forgives
men of their faults, that is, if the latter allow themselves to be reconciled with
God.41
The formula “remission of sins” is frequent in the New Testament writ-
ings: to proclaim it is part of the mission of John the Baptist who shows
Jesus to be the Lamb who takes away the sins of the world.42 It is also
the motive for which Jesus made Himself equal in all things to us, which
justifies His name and all of his actions up to the culminating moment
of the Cross.43 This forgiveness forms an important part of the mission
of the Church44 and of the kérygma of the Apostles;45 for this reason it

Chapter 11
is found in the symbols of the faith from the beginning. Man responds
to the remission of sins through a conversion that, beyond accepting
the grace of Jesus, entails the recognition of one's own faults and the
beginning of a new life, a life that is verified in its fruits.46
11.2
Principal Moments in the Development
of the Ecclesial Doctrine Regarding Sin
Since in the successive paragraphs we must take a deeper look at the diverse
aspects of the doctrine of sin, now we shall limit ourselves to offering a syn-
thetic vision of the most significant moments in the formation and exposition
of the doctrine of it on the part of the Church Fathers and the ecclesiastical
magisterium.
11.2.1
The Fathers
The sacrament of penance is testimony of the knowledge that the Church has
always had of sin as enmity with God and a rupture with the ecclesial commu-
nity. The Apostolic Fathers re-propose the biblical teachings regarding sin,
underlining the existence of two ways (that of good and that of evil), com-
posing catalogues of virtues and vices in consonance with the two ways, and
openly expressing their conviction that sin constitutes the greatest evil. The
Apologetic Fathers insist on the religious peculiarity of sin, in the face of a
paganism which conceives it as a simple external action meritorious of punish-
ment; in contrast with Gnosticism they reveal its character as a free personal
act, even if being connected with original sin; they propose, moreover, diverse
lists of vices and virtues. Finally, Tertullian recalls the sinfulness of internal
acts as well, and considers all sin as idolatry and contempt for God.
Saint Augustine elaborates a body of doctrine that in its fundamental features
remains with us to this day.
Delving further into the teachings of Sacred
Scripture and the practice of the Church, and taking account of his own sinful
experience and of his battle against the Manichees, Augustine brings to light
the psychology of the fault, distinguishing between suggestion, enjoyment,
and consent; and affirms that sin comes from a disordered free will when it is
deprived of the good and of due moral rectitude.47 He develops the doctrine
of sin as aversio a Deo (seperation from God) and conversio ad creaturas
(disordered tendency toward earthly goods): man is ordained toward the
absolute Good, which he reaches also through creatures. When pushed by
an inordinate self-love, he seeks satisfaction in finite goods against the will of
46 Cf. Mt 12:33; Mk 1:5; Acts 19:18; 1 Jn 1:8–9.
47 Cf. De Civitate Dei, 11, 13–20 & 19, 13, 2: NBA 5/2, 91–103 & 5/3, 51–53.


Sin and Conversion
God, he contradicts the divine law, and separates himself from God;48 this
also has a negative influence on ecclesial and social life.49 In harmony with
the Bible, Augustine joins to the doctrine of sin the trust in the redemption
carried out by Jesus, the possibility of receiving forgiveness, and the necessity
of personal conversion.
The patristic legacy lasts throughout the High Middle Ages, a time
period that does not register any significant doctrinal or theological
development.
This is the epoch of the conversion of the barbarian
people and of the grand diffusion of private confession.
Penitential
books were published as catalogues—sometimes quite chaotic—of sins
and penances that the confessors must impose for each of them. From
the 12th Century on, intellectual activity of great importance resumes—
the scholastic renaissance– of which Saint Thomas represents one of the
culminating moments of synthesis. In continuity with the Augustinian
reflection, Aquinas offered some theological contributions of decisive im-
portance that from that point forward were always in some way present
in Catholic theology and in the documents of the ecclesiastical magis-
terium.
11.2.2
The Council of Trent
The Council of Trent elaborated on the development of the doctrine of sin as
a reaction to the protestant doctrine.
Protestantism points out, in agreement with the Gospel teaching, that
the essence of sin consists in opposition to God for the sake of full au-
tonomy; it is born from a lack of trust in the Lord and is reflected in
pride, rebellion, and disobedience. This doctrine underlines some cen-
tral points of Christian harmatology, like the anti-divine character of
sin, its gravity, and the heavy influence of sin on the person's moral
action and on social life. Nonetheless, in contrast with the Catholic
faith, the distinction between original sin and individual actual sins is
not very clear in this line of thought: the former would be the corrup-
tion of nature that perverts all persons without a possibility of being
overcome. This deprivation is then made concrete in the acts of persons
as individual sins, and in this specific way it more obviously highlights
its character as being subjective and situated in time. Consequently,
man would be born and would always remain a sinner: he is not a sin-
ner because he sins, but precisely on account of his “natural” condition
as a sinner. And this would also be true for the person in a state of
grace, on whom God would simply not impute sin, thanks to the for-
mer's trusting faith: he would remain a sinner for the moral quality of
his action and, at the same time, righteous on account of the mercy of
48 Cf. De Libero Arbitrio, 2, 19, 52–53: NBA 3/2, 277; Contra Faustum, 22, 27: CSEL
25, 621.
49 Cf. De Civitate Dei, 22, 22: NBA 5/3, 379–381.


Chapter 11
God due to the merits of Jesus Christ; the person with trusting faith
would be simul peccator et iustus. It remains to be seen how redeemed
man could be truly a “new creation”, or in what sense the works of the
justified could be called fruits of the Holy Spirit.
The Council of Trent concerned itself with sin primarily on three occasions. In
session V it expounded the doctrine of original sin. In session VI, covering the
stages of justification, it reiterated some fundamental points of the Catholic
doctrine concerning sin: not only lack of faith, but every mortal sin, deprives
one from the grace of Christ; the distinction between mortal and venial sin
needs to be maintained; and that sin does not completely destroy human
freedom. In session XIV, regarding the sacrament of penance, the necessity
of confessing each and every mortal sin was pronounced.
11.2.3
The Second Vatican Council
The most recent Council dealt repeatedly with sin, though systematically it
principally did so in Gaudium et Spes, nos. 13 and 37. Sin has existed in the
world since the beginning of history and, as a possibility, always continues
to exist; therefore man is prone to evil, and human activities are “constantly
imperiled by man's pride and deranged self-love.” 50 This is, at the same time,
both a fact of experience and a revealed fact: “What divine revelation makes
known to us agrees with experience. Examining his heart, man finds that he
has inclinations toward evil too, and is engulfed by manifold ills which cannot
come from his good Creator.”51 In the face of the secularization of the concept
of sin, the Council affirms that sin always stands in opposition to God, and
from this opposition arise its other effects: the sinner destroys the due order
toward himself, toward other people, and toward the whole of creation.52
The last word of the Council regarding sin is not, however, its power, but the
announcement of the reconciliation carried out by Jesus: certainly “man finds
that by himself he is incapable of battling the assaults of evil successfully, so
that everyone feels as though he is bound by chains. But the Lord Himself
came to free and strengthen man, renewing him inwardly and casting out that
'prince of this world' (John 12:31) who held him in the bondage of sin.” 53
Meanwhile, man must commit himself to the effort against sin, because “all
of human life, whether individual or collective, shows itself to be a dramatic
struggle between good and evil, between light and darkness.” 54
