11.2.4
Other Documents of the Magisterium
The apostolic exhortation Reconciliatio et Paenitentia, focuses on three fun-
damental points: conversion, sin, and the ministry of reconciliation. Here we
shall explain, in broad terms, the second part. Man must recognize his own
sin not in abstract, but concretely, and evaluate its consequences with the eyes
of faith. Sin is the attempt to be powerful without God, if not specifically
to be against God; its deepest and darkest essence is disobedience to God
and to His law and, consequently, it is also a rupture with one's neighbor.
Furthermore, sin, in a true and proper sense, is always an act of the person
that, although it can be conditioned, is never determined by external realities.
Nonetheless, one can also speak of social sin, in virtue of human solidarity,
in three senses: 1) every sin has negative repercussions on the entire ecclesial
body and on the whole of humanity; 2) there are certain sins that are more
directly opposed to one's neighbor that constitute an offense to God precisely
because they offend one's brother or sister; 3) one can speak in an analogous
sense of social sin for certain collective situations or behaviors, while knowing
that these are the fruit or concentration of many personal sins. With texts of
Sacred Scripture and from the living tradition of the Church, the Exhortation
recalls of the division of sin into mortal and venial sins and, as a matter of
principle, excludes the tripartition of venial, grave, and mortal sins, because
between life and death there is no middle way. Similarly to be avoided is the
reduction of mortal sin to an act of a fundamental option directly opposing
God.55
The Catechism grants notable attention to the theme of sin, always in re-
lation to the mercy of God, to the redemption executed by Christ, and to
the sanctification worked by the Holy Spirit. In fact, sin is spoken of in dif-
ferent sections, concretely when the following are discussed: a) original sin
(nos. 385–421); b) faith in Jesus our Redeemer (nos. 422–682); c) faith in the
forgiveness of sins (nos. 976–987); d) the sacrament of baptism (nos. 1213–
1284) and of confession (nos. 1422–1498); e) sin as an obstacle to the human
vocation (nos. 1846–1876); f) the Ten Commandments (nos. 2083–2557): in-
cluded in this section are sins and vices opposed to each commandment; and
g) the final three petitions of the “Our Father” (nos. 2838–2854).
The Encyclical Veritatis Splendor also treats of sin, both original and actual.
It concretely recalls that only the Gospel can reveal the entire truth about sin:
that is, that sin is an offense against God that obscures the human conscience.
Furthermore, sins can be avoided with the grace of the Lord, but it is necessary
for the person to recognize himself as a sinner and ask divine help.56

Chapter 11
11.3
The Essence of Sin
11.3.1
Definition
Without any indications to the contrary, what is said subsequently is applied
in a proper sense to mortal sin, being that which completely fulfills the ratio
of sin: see subsection 11.4.1 The Augustinian definition of sin is traditional
in theology: it is “an act, a word, or a desire contrary to the eternal law.”57
The two aspects of sinful action are highlighted in this definition. The first
is that sin is a human act, that is, a free act carried out with sufficient
advertence and consent: for all that diminishes freedom also diminishes the
ratio of sin.58 The second consists in the fact that sin is a human act contrary
to God's law.59 In more general terms, it can be affirmed that any human
act opposed to the moral law—and therefore also opposed to right reason
or to a human, civil, or ecclesiastical law—is a sin. Saint Augustine, in the
definition that we are studying, puts it in relation to God's eternal law, that
is, the first and supreme moral rule,60 for two reasons: a) because it is the
ultimate foundation of all other laws and therefore virtually contains them
all; b) to highlight that, in transgressing any real moral demand, man puts
himself in a negative relation with God. If we consider that God's eternal
salvific design aims at the holiness of people, that it must be reached through
the practice of the theological and moral virtues, we can then also define sin
as an act contrary to the ethical virtues (natural or supernatural), that breaks
the communion of man with God in Christ and, consequently, impedes one's
definitive arrival at divine filiation.
such as to diminish his responsibility. But his prayer does not dwell on such justifications,
but rather on his own unworthiness before God's infinite holiness: 'God, be merciful to me a
sinner! ' (Lk 18:13). The Pharisee, on the other hand, is self-justified, finding some excuse
for each of his failings. Here we encounter two different attitudes of the moral conscience
of man in every age.
The tax collector represents a 'repentant' conscience, fully aware
of the frailty of its own nature and seeing in its own failings, whatever their subjective
justifications, a confirmation of its need for redemption. The Pharisee represents a 'self-
satisfied' conscience, under the illusion that it is able to observe the law without the help
of grace and convinced that it does not need mercy” (Veritatis Splendor, 104).
57 Saint Augustine, Contra Faustum, 22, 27: CSEL 25, 621; cf. Saint Thomas's comment
in S. Th. I-II, q. 71, a. 6, and CCC, 1849.
58 The definition speaks explicitly of an “act”, a “word”, or a “desire” in order to exclude
two possible misunderstandings, that of thinking that sins are only internal acts, or that of
retaining that they are only external acts: the sinful act can be internal or external, and it
can also consist in an omission.

Sin and Conversion
11.3.2
“Aversio a Deo” and “Conversio ad Creaturas”
At least since Saint Augustine, it has been traditional to distinguish two
elements in sin, one formal and another that is quasi material. The element
that formally constitutes sin as such is the aversio a Deo. The quasi material
element of sin is the conversio ad creaturas.61
The Latin word aversio entails separation, detachment, and not properly
adversion or hate. It is good to remember this because even if grave sin implies
an aversio a Deo, not every grave sin carries in the person who commits it
an explicit intention of distancing oneself from God. One does not sin out of
a will to be opposed to the good or, normally, to trample the Divine law; a
person commits sin out of a desire for a finite good not ordered according to
the rule of virtue (justice, temperance, etc.). Therefore, sin carries with it a
paradoxical and harmful exchange: the sinner wants the limited good that a
creature can offer him and, in order to possess it, distances himself from God
who is the infinite Good and our true and definitive good, as well as from the
source out of which flows the partial goodness that is found in things.62
Generally the psychological point of departure of a sinful action is not oppo-
sition to God. It happens, rather, that the person is left seduced by a limited
good that is contrary to his integral good and, thus, to the divine will, and
does not care that to obtain it means opposing a moral rule. Nonetheless,
from a theological point of view in agreement with biblical and Christian doc-
trine concerning sin,63 the root of it is found in the doubting of God, in not
recognizing Him as Lord, Love, and absolute Good. Therefore, at the base of
every sin is discovered a disordered love of self and lack of trust with respect
to God, for which man seeks his own satisfaction in the disordered use of
earthly goods. Beyond sinning, man enters into contradiction with his deepest
tendency, since “the love of God does not derive from an external discipline,
but is found in the very natural constitution of man, as a seed and a force of
nature itself.”64
11.3.3
The Only Real Evil in an Absolute Sense
Every evil is the privation of a good. Evils of a non-moral character (sick-
ness, poverty, etc.) are privations of finite, limited goods. Sin, any mortal

Chapter 11
sin, deprives man of the infinite Good, that is, moreover, the complete and
definitive good of the human being. It is in this sense that it is affirmed that
sin is the only evil in an absolute sense.65 It needs to be remembered that
the dignity of God, offended with sin, is infinite; therefore the damage of sin
and the corresponding liability are in a certain sense infinite. The gravity of
sin can be observed when one considers the gravity of its punishment (hell),
and the seriousness of the Passion of Jesus as a just satisfaction for it.66
11.3.4
Why is Sin always a Distancing
of Oneself from God?
What has been said allows us to understand that, from the perspective of
positive theology, it is an incontestable fact that Sacred Scripture and the
doctrine of the Church consider that mortal sin is a distancing of oneself from
and rupture with God. However, our current object of investigation does not
regard the what of sin, but the why. Why is every sin a distancing of oneself
from God? The problem must be confronted at different levels, and there are
at least two things to consider.
In the first place, it must be said that for persons disposed to a good level
of moral awareness, the response is not difficult to understand. In our study
regarding the natural moral law,67 we noted that when the moral conscience
is fully developed, in connection with the intellectual virtues (knowledge, wis-
dom) and, in the Christian, with faith, one arrives at an understanding, on
the one hand, that the natural moral law is a divine law and, on the other
hand and primarily, that its first principle—its most important and “archi-
tectonic” principle—is the love of God. The moral virtues then express the
modes in which the tendencies, and the exercising and obtainment of human
goods must be regulated in order that they be congruent with a will intent on
perfection in God both for oneself and for every human person.68 The acts
opposed to the virtues are objectively incompatible with the tendency of the
will toward God, in such a way that to perform such an act and to voluntarily
separate oneself from God are truly the same thing.
65 Cf. John Paul II, Allocuzione 20-VII-1983, n. 4: Insegnamenti, VI-2 (1983) 95; CCC,
1488.
66 The Letter to the Hebrews, speaking of those who “have once been enlightened and

having recalled the chastisements of the Old Testament, he affirms: “Do you not think that
a much worse punishment is due the one who has contempt for the Son of God, considers
unclean the covenant-blood by which he was consecrated, and insults the spirit of grace?”

Sin and Conversion
Before passing to the second consideration, another dimension of the problem
still needs to be highlighted. In our study of the law of Christ, or lex gratiae,
it was explained that “the law of Christ is essentially the grace of the Holy
Spirit, which carries with itself new principles (the virtues) which assume,
complete, and elevate the natural principles of the human reason, giving rise
to a new interior law of man,”69 accompanied by the moral teachings of the
New Testament. The Holy Spirit present in the Christian impresses on the
soul a real interior dynamism toward virtuous works, and thus a sinful action
(opposed to the virtues, even the moral virtues) is not objectively possible to
do without resisting or truly opposing oneself to the divine dynamism (grace)
present in our hearts, which even in its content becomes known to us both
by the interior inspirations of the Holy Spirit, and at very least from the
moral teachings of Sacred Scripture. In any case, sin is a real opposition and
resistance to the grace of the Holy Spirit.
We shall now move on to the second consideration. What happens with non-
believers, or with believers that out of lack of moral and religious formation
are not aware, or at least aware to a rather small degree, of what we have just
said? Would it not be possible for them to have a fault that, while being a
true ethical error, is not subjectively a sin, that is, an offense against God?
On the level of positive theology it should be said that the Church retains that
there exists no moral fault that is not at the same time a sin: the so-called
“philosophical sin” does not exist.70 However, it also interests us here to un-
derstand why. It needs to be noted, in the first place, that free action is always
projected into the horizon of the complete good of the human person, which
objectively consists in life in God. This objective fact has some phenomeno-
logical manifestations in common moral experience, even in the experience of
those who are disposed to minimal moral awareness. Moral demands present
themselves, in fact, with an absolute and unconditioned character that is not
fitting, in the proper sense, if not toward God; therefore, they present a “di-
vine character” that perhaps is not seen as divine, but certainly as absolute.
Through this absolute and unconditioned character of ethical demands, God
is present in a certain way in each human act (being present is not always the
same as there being a clear and explicit knowledge of it); so whoever infringes
upon an ethical demand is in some sense aware, according to varying degrees,
of infringing upon an order that is not just immanent, precisely because it
is also presented as something absolute and unconditioned. A person who is
aware of having violated a grave moral demand, may not be explicitly aware
of having distanced himself from God, but knows that he has infringed upon
69 Chapter VIII, subsection 8.4.2.
70 Cf.
Decree of the Holy Office, 24-VIII-1690: DS 2290–2292.
In an analogous way,
Veritatis Splendor, 37 denies the possibility of separating the ethical order from the order
of salvation: see Chapter I, subsection 1.3.2.


Chapter 11
something absolute and very important present in him: and in acting in such
a way one puts himself in negative relation with God. His distancing from
the Absolute could never be, for the guilty person, a complete surprise.71
Caffarra puts it well when he writes that “the identity between a morally
dishonest act and sin should not be understood in the superficial sense
that because the moral value is founded ultimately on God then to
act contrarily to it entails opposing oneself to God. But that identity
should be understood in the sense that the moral value has in itself
and through itself a character that allows it to be representative, to our
eyes, of God, and it is for this, its character, that each violation of it is
an offense to God Himself. It is not therefore necessary that whoever
performs this violation explicitly thinks of God and explicitly intends
to disobey His will as such. In the free decision to violate a moral value,
already implicit and present is the decision to disobey His will.” 72
In the final analysis, that the moral good and evil contained within a human
action, with the latter being a finite reality, have an absolute and uncondi-
tioned character, responds to the fact that the value of the human act which
affirms what is good for man is constituted as a participation and imitation
of the absolute good of God, that is to say, as a participation in the holy
will whereby God affirms the infinite good that He is in Himself and freely
wills man's good as well.
This transcendent dimension of the moral good
is confirmed by Sacred Scripture: “you shall make and keep yourselves holy,
because I am holy,”73 and stands also at the base of the natural moral law,
which considers the moral perception of the human reason as the kind of par-
ticipation in divine Wisdom proper to man. This explains why the voluntary
distancing of oneself from the moral good is always a distancing of oneself
from God, a profound reality that can only be fully understood in philosoph-
ical and theological reflection, but for which sufficient evidence can be found
in moral experience, though this is not always the same as a clear and explicit
knowledge of God, as we have just said.
11.4
Division of Sins
Although the essence of each sin is the denial of God, not all sins are of the
same gravity, have the same proximate subject, the same object, an identical
origin, etc. Sacred Scripture, the tradition of the Church, and human reason
itself demonstrate a diversity of sins, which is to be explained in what follows,

no. 265; J. De Finance, Etica Generale (1984), 230–231.

beginning with the most important, which is the distinction between mortal
and venial sin.
11.4.1
Mortal and Venial Sin
On the basis of Sacred Scripture (as already indicated), the tradition of the
Church74, Catholic theology,75 and human reason itself, the magisterium of
the Church has taught the existence of mortal and venial sins:76 “the dis-
tinction between mortal and venial sin, already evident in Scripture (cf. Jn
16–17), became part of the tradition of the Church. It is corroborated by
human experience.”77
Analogous Meaning of Sin — When the term “sin” is employed in reference
to mortal and venial sin, it needs to be noted that the term “sin” is used in
an analogous sense. Between mortal and venial sin exists some similitude,
but at the same time an enormous difference is manifest, properly for what
regards their condition as sin: this difference is not reduced to greater or less
gravity, to a difference of degree, but rather that they are sins in an essentially
diverse manner, and for this reason we speak in their regard of there being a
theological distinction between the sins.78
The “ratio” of sin is found fully only in mortal sin and, in an imperfect way, in
venial sin: mortal sin is completely incompatible with grace and charity, and
therefore implies separation from God, while venial sin is not incompatible
with charity, even if it weakens it:79 mortal sin leads one to lose divine life in
his soul, and venial sin merely weakens it and renders difficult the exercise of
the infused virtues; as a consequence, only mortal sin precludes entrance into
the Kingdom of heaven.80 It is affirmed “that by a conscious and free act of
his [man's] will he can [. . .] go in a direction opposed to God's will, separating

that God offers, preferring to turn in on himself or to some created and finite

Not all mortal sins have, however, the same gravity;82 Jesus said to Pilate:
“the one who handed me over to you has the greater sin,” 83 and Jeremiah
said of his contemporaries: “they have stiffened their necks and done worse
than their fathers.”84 Any grave sin deprives one of friendship with God,
nonetheless the disorder generated can be more or less grave: in fact, sin acts
as if it inserted an obstacle between the person and divine love, an obstacle
that can be more or less great and that, however great, can always continue
to increase. The gravity of the sin, per se, depends on the intensity of the will
in accepting the disorder. Nonetheless, the material of the immoral act has
a decisive significance, since a more grave object requires, normally, greater
voluntariness. In this sense, the objective importance of certain immoral acts
carries with it that, in order to choose them, there must be, per se, a full
intensity of the will.
Conditions for Grave Sin — For a sin to be grave, it requires three con-
ditions: grave matter,85 full advertence, and perfect consent; this constitutes
a constant teaching of the magisterium of the Church.86 All three conditions
must be present simultaneously: “The statement of the Council of Trent does
not only consider the 'grave matter' of mortal sin; it also recalls that its nec-
essary condition is 'full awareness and deliberate consent.' In any event, both
in moral theology and in pastoral practice one is familiar with cases in which
an act which is grave by reason of its matter does not constitute a mortal sin
because of a lack of full awareness or deliberate consent on the part of the
person performing it.”87
The matter of a sinful action is grave when the moral act is incompatible per
se with charity, something which happens in any act opposed to an essential
demand of a moral or theological virtue.88 For the gravity of their matter, sins

can be: mortal ex toto genere suo, mortal ex genere suo and light ex genere
suo. The matter that is grave ex toto genere suo is that which, while being
important (i.e. opposed to an essential demand of a virtue), is never divisible,
for, when it is performed, the person is always dealing with a undivided whole,
for example, the honor of God and human life; in this sense, blasphemy, hatred
for God, and the taking of innocent life constitute matter that is grave ex toto
genere suo. Matter that is grave ex genere suo is an important matter, but
divisible, and that therefore admits of parvitas materiae; for example theft
and abuse. Matter that is light ex genere suo is a matter that per se entails
a modest subject-matter: for example, an unhurtful white lie. The nature of
full advertence and of perfect consent was studied in section 6 of Chapter VI.
Recent Problems Regarding Mortal Sin — Sin, especially grave sin,
raises a number of different questions that do not always have easy solutions:
it is not without reason that one speaks here of the mysterium iniquitatis.
It should not be surprising if diverse critiques of the traditional doctrine
have been raised recently. As, for example, the theories which affirm:
1) that the theological division of sins was proposed by the scholastics
unduly exaggerating the biblical and patristic distinction, for the sake
of distinguishing sins that must be confessed from those which did not
have to be confessed; 2) that some rigorist theologians mixed up grave
and mortal sin; 3) that, furthermore, the theological position is thus
mistaken that hastily admits of the possibility of mortal sin, and of
passing from a state of grace to that of sin, and vice versa;89 4) that,
finally, no categorical error, not even in grave matter, is mortal, and
neither are those sins which are of weakness or performed in adolescence.
In expressing the nature of sin, the ecclesiastical magisterium, basing itself on
solid reasons, warns of those authors who reject “the traditional distinction
between mortal sins and venial sins. They insist that the opposition to God's
law which causes the loss of sanctifying grace—and eternal damnation, when
one dies in such a state of sin—could only be the result of an act which engages
the person in his totality: in other words, an act of fundamental option.” 90
Those who defend such ideas seem to accept two important misconceptions:
1) a secularization, which implies a decrease in knowledge of God and His
love for the human race, and this leads to a decrease in the sense of sin: these
authors think of an overly distant God, without recognizing that grace entails
entrance of the person into the divine intimacy, and that “nothing unclean
constitute grave matter.

impossibility.

Some complementary observations can then be added. 1) The distinc-
tion of sins is not an invention of the theologians, but was proclaimed
by the Church: “This doctrine, based on the Decalogue and on the
preaching of the Old Testament, and assimilated into the kerygma of

of the theological division does not depend on a rigorist approach, but
rather on the teaching of Sacred Scripture; for example Saint Paul,
speaking of the sins of the flesh, writes with great clarity: “Shall I then
take Christ's members and make them the members of a prostitute? Of
course not!”;94 and it is frequent in the catalogues of vices to indicate
which are the sins that exclude one from the Kingdom of heaven. 3)
The Church teaches that even isolated sins and those of weakness can

she is not surprised by sins, but wishes that men would repent and fre-
quently approach the sacrament of penance, because it knows that the
human heart would otherwise be hardened: as has been said, Jesus does

it misunderstands deep psychology; far from it: the Church, precisely
out of its knowledge of human nature, recognizes the diverse gravity
of sins, and that there are some which in themselves are incompatible
with charity.
Diverse authors have proposed a tripartition of sins, with various names,
but which we can identify as: venial, grave, and mortal (or lethal). The
second would certainly be a grave disorder of the moral life, but, fol-
lowing from the weakness of freedom, would not carry the imprint of
irrevocability; in fact, some think that only a conscious resolution to
offend God could be qualified as a mortal sin, and furthermore some
maintain yet that such a decision that is so lucid can only be made,
in fact, at the point of death. The Church rejects this possibility of
identifying mortal sin with an explicit decision against God; rather, re-
garding the threefold division of sins, it says: “This threefold distinction
might illustrate the fact that there is a scale of seriousness among grave
sins. But it still remains true that the essential and decisive distinction
is between sin which destroys charity and sin which does not kill the
supernatural life: There is no middle way between life and death.” 98
Ultimately, it seems to us that the Church bases itself on solid reasons when
it affirms that “mortal sin is a radical possibility of human freedom, as is love
itself. It results in the loss of charity and the privation of sanctifying grace,
that is, of the state of grace. If it is not redeemed by repentance and God's
forgiveness, it causes exclusion from Christ's kingdom and the eternal death of
hell, for our freedom has the power to make choices for ever, with no turning
back.”99 For what regards the distinction between sins, some wise observations
of Saint Augustine should be taken into consideration: “There are then some
sins that would be retained as being most light, if in the Scriptures they were
not presented as more grave than one might imagine”.100 And furthermore:
“We do not get to use deceptive scales, on which to weigh what we want and
how we want it, and then say: 'This is heavy, this is light.' No, we use the
divine scale taken from Holy Scriptures, as from the treasures of the Lord,
and with it we measure to see what is heavier. In fact, we do not weigh it,
but we recognize the weights established by the Lord.” 101 The Church intends
primarily to maintain fidelity to the teachings of Sacred Scripture, without
however denying the complexity of the subtle nuances that can be hidden in
the depth of the individual consciences. For this reason it affirms: “However,

Chapter 11
although we can judge that an act is in itself a grave offense, we must entrust
judgment of persons to the justice and mercy of God.” 102
The paths are not closed to further developments regarding the doctrine
of sin, provided that they are well founded theologically and pastorally
useful.
The theories that we dealt with above, despite praiseworthy
intentions of clarifying a very delicate and important matter, create
more problems than they succeed in resolving, especially when they
utilize categories and divisions which escape all attempts at objective
verification or control, with the result of introducing further causes of
uncertainty in a matter that in itself is already rather difficult.
11.4.2
Internal and External Sins
External sins are those which are committed with an action that can be ob-
served exteriorly (theft, adultery, etc.). Internal sins remain within the per-
son: in thought, the will, or in the internal senses (imagination, etc.), without
being expressed in external actions. The existence of merely internal sins is
indicated by Jesus when He teaches: “everyone who looks at a woman with
lust has already committed adultery with her in his heart.” 103 In fact, the
moral act is properly an internal act of the will, therefore purely interior
acts can be sins and even grave sins: the final two commandments of the
Decalogue indeed prohibit such sins.104 The Old Testament teaches about
the wickedness of internal sins,105 Jesus frequently rebukes the Pharisees who
care for exterior honesty and forget interior rectitude,106 and the doctrine of
the Apostles is similar.107 Moreover, the Church reminds of the necessity of
confessing the sins that are more hidden and which are related to the final
two commandments in the Decalogue, precisely because it is not uncommon
for them to be more dangerous than external sins.108 Certainly internal sins,
even of the mortal kind, are in principle less grave than their corresponding
external sins, for their degree of voluntariness is normally less; nonetheless,
they are highly dangerous on account of the ease with which they come to be
carried out, and for which they can also easily degenerate into vices.
Traditionally, three types of internal sins have been distinguished: consented
thought, desire, and satisfaction for a performed act.
1. Consented thought (delectatio morosa) is not merely a thought, or
merely something imagined, but a will to think or imagine a determi-

103 Mt 5:28.

nate immoral act in its formality as evil; in such a sense, it is different
to think about an injurious sin studying moral theology than to con-
sent to a thought that is configured as a concrete injury to Tom. Evil
thoughts—pride and vanity, impurity, envy for wealth, etc.–morally poi-
son man, corrupting him in an always growing measure.109
2. Desire (desiderium): we do not deal here so much with a decision to
perform an action, as with an interior and generic desire which the
person welcomes with pleasure.110 Evil desire, e.g. a disordered desire
for wealth and a thirst for power, distances a person from God and
neighbor and puts the person on a dangerous slide toward evil.
3. Satisfaction (gaudium) for a performed act: this means enjoying some-
thing carried out in the past without necessarily assuming the decision
to carry it out again. The sin resides properly in the particular satis-
faction originated by an evil desire: “He who gloats over evil will meet
with evil.”111 The gaudium peccaminosum can be the satisfaction in the
face of an evil that is carried out or the sadness before an action that
has not been carried out, for example, to grieve over having missed the
opportunity to have stolen something easily and without risk.
11.4.3
Social Sin
and the Problem of Collective Responsibility
Revelation teaches of the existence of a “sin of the world” and of a certain social
responsibility for sins.112 As we know, social sin can be spoken of in a threefold
sense: each sin, even the more hidden ones, regards all of society; there are
sins that affect social life more directly; there exist collective situations that
induce persons toward sin.113
We shall look closer now at these last two
aspects114 and at the problem of collective responsibility linked to them.
Sacred Scripture, like the rest of human experience, attests to the fact
that humans are not isolated beings; for this reason—as was typical in

of the media, which increase the intentional tendency toward evil; it is good to remember
the counsel of Jesus: “if your eye causes you to sin, pluck it out” (Mk 9:47), if this show, if
this newspaper . . . scandalizes you. . . etc.

Chapter 11
the law of ancient Semitic peoples—the infraction of the law causing
damage to someone, even if done without awareness, produced an ob-
jective situation of disequilibrium that had to be corrected in some way,
because the carrying out of certain rules was vital for the ordered devel-
opment of society. Nonetheless, it does not seem proven that their exists
in the Old Testament an exclusive—or, at least, prevalent—collective
retribution, in which the righteous and sinners would have had to re-
ceive together the same sanction. This does not exclude the fact that,
from the moral standpoint, all may have a certain responsibility toward
others: the Lord assumed our moral condition in order to redeem us,115
and we are all morally united to grow according to the will of God.116
For this reason each person has some moral responsibility with respect
to the conduct of others117 and sometimes will have to pray: “Ab alienis
[peccatis] parce servo tuo,”118 since a person's own action, perhaps with
a good will but lacking in prudence, could render him complicit in the
sins of others.119 Later in this chapter, we shall study the problem of
cooperation with evil.
Morality depends on the awareness and, above all, free volition of each person.
A person does not have to be considered responsible for the good or evil
carried out by others or by the majority of the group to which he pertains.
Strictly speaking, moral responsibility in the end always leads back to the
individual responsibility of one or more persons. When one speaks of collective
responsibility, normally one does so in an improper sense, and such a way of
speaking can run the risk of confusing the concepts, rather than clarifying
them.
Nonetheless, the recognition of the personal character of responsibility should
not render us insensible before the cultural and social dimension of certain
moral phenomena. Man, for the simple fact of being man, possesses moral
principles only in a germinal state. Their full development requires the equi-
librium of the “tendential” system120. From an abstract point of view, there
exists a true circle between the practical reason and affective equilibrium, be-
cause each of these two elements presupposes the other.121 From the concrete
point of view, however, the circle is overcome by the education received in
the environment of the community to which the person pertains: the family,
civil and economic society, the Church, the State, etc. The customs, laws,
and models that are in force in these not only shape our life in common, but

117 Cf. Num 16:19–22; Josh 7:1–12; 2 Cor 11:28–29; Gal 6:1–2.
118 Ps 18:14 (Vulg).
119 Cf. 1 Tim 5:22.
120 Cf. footnote 11 of section 5.2 of Chapter V.

Sin and Conversion
they also express, and forge into new generations, certain modes of perceiving
and evaluating, since individuals tend to recognize themselves in the legal and
institutional environment in which they are born, and cannot do any less in
order to live, and this furnishes for them the categories for interpreting their
experience and for reinforcing their identity. To go against the current is per-
fectly possible, and oftentimes a duty, but will not be the majority tendency in
contemporary democratic societies en masse. In any case, it is true that per-
sonal moral formation possesses social, economic, and political preconditions,
and that without an adequate familial and social initiation, the development
of personal morality is rendered extremely slow and difficult.122
Certainly, moral conscience always preserves the capacity for judging and de-
ciding freely, but in order to do so it must first be formed, and such a formation
occurs in a concrete context, and not in some hypothetical other-worldly space.
As we know by now, the natural moral law is a natural capacity, but it is natu-
ral just as the capacity to speak is natural: their development and the quality
of their results depend in good part on the communicative context wherein
the education occurs.123 The achievement of personal moral awareness is not
independent from the immanent and objective logic found within the ethos of
the social group, an ethos that presupposes the sharing of certain ends and
modes of achieving them, of certain models and of modes of imitating them,
and which are expressed in the laws, customs, stories, celebrations of events,
and characters that best respond to the moral identity of the group.124
These reflections do not intend to put into question personal freedom
and responsibility; they intend rather to bring to light what is properly
cultural in certain positive or negative moral phenomena (for example,
what today is called a “culture of life” and a “culture of death”). We
treat of dynamics that, once formed, are relatively autonomous with
regard to the choices of individuals, and that insofar as they are hu-
man are prevalently communicative. For this reason, in cases of unjust
situations, structures, laws, etc. the individual must examine his own
responsibility for what he does or, more commonly, what he fails to do,
that is, for having remained silent or for having neglected due resistance
or contrasting action, for example, for what regards public morality. It
needs to be remembered, furthermore, that in the exercise of public re-
sponsibility for goods of a public nature, oftentimes individual action is
not enough, also necessary is a certain organization, like, for example,
the pro life movements, consumer groups, etc.

Chapter 11
11.4.4
Other Divisions of Sins
There are other divisions of sins, of less importance in the study of moral
theology, that nonetheless help us to have a more complete idea of the senses
in which the notion of sin is employed in this discipline.
1. Original and actual: Original sin is that committed by our first par-
ents and transmitted through generation to all people; it is a disorder
present in each person from the instant of conception.
Actual sin is
that committed by the person himself and that for which he is fully
responsible.
2. Formal and material: The first is a voluntary—and therefore culpable—
transgression of the divine law. Material sin is an objectively disordered
act in which due voluntariness is lacking, on account of invincible igno-
rance, external violence, or a failed use of the reason. Material sin does
not render the person culpable, but insofar as a disordered act produces
objective damage, it must be avoided.125
3. A sinful act and a state of sin (habitual sin): A sinful act is an act of the
will that chooses against the human good and the moral law. Such an
act procures in the person a state (macula peccati) that is the disorder
left in the sinner, as the guilt and the penalty and, in mortal sin, the
privation of grace.
4. Of ignorance, weakness, and malice: This refers to the internal factor
that induces one to sin. In principle it can be said that ignorance and
weakness, usually, diminish voluntariness; while sins of malice are those
born out of one's own evil will.
5. Carnal and spiritual: Based on whether they tend in a disordered way
toward a sensible good (for example, lust) or a spiritual good (pride).
Per se, the second are more grave; nonetheless carnal sins are, usually,
more vehement, and immediately enticing.
6. Of commission and of omission: Each sin brings with it the execution of
a disordered voluntary act: if it is translated into an action, it is called
a sin of commission; if instead the voluntary act is translated into the
omission of something due, it is called a sin of omission.126
125 Cf. CCC, 1793; Veritatis Splendor, 63.
126 “So for one who knows the right thing to do and does not do it, it is a sin” (Jas 4:17).


Sin and Conversion
11.5
Specific and Numeric Distinction of Sins
Sins are specified according to the virtues or precepts to which they are con-
trary; for example, homicide is a sin that is specifically diverse from theft.
The numeric distinction indicates the quantity of sins of a certain type which
were committed. Both distinctions are important, because in the sacrament
of penance one must be repentant and make manifest the sins in their species
and number127 in the measure in which that is morally possible.
Also for what regards the conversion from sins, which is authentic only if it
does not remain as a vague abstraction, the specific and numeric distinction of
sins is important. Nonetheless, if a person does not succeed in remembering
all of the sins committed since the last valid confession, or is not capable of
accurately making all of the specific distinctions explained by moral theology,
this should not be a reason for anxiety or scruples. The formal integrity of
the confession, necessary for the validity of the sacrament, requires the confes-
sion of all mortal sins remembered after a diligent examination of conscience,
specifying the number in the most exact way possible here and now, while
briefly and with simplicity mentioning only the circumstances which are re-
tained to be morally important. The consideration of the commandments of
the Decalogue and the precepts of the Church can help a person to make a
deep examination of conscience and, therefore, to prepare for the sacrament
of penance.
The numeric distinction of sins does not usually present great difficulty.
For some more difficult cases the following principles can be kept in
mind. 1) There are diverse acts when the moral unity of the decision is
interrupted: a) in the interior acts a temporary interruption is enough:
for example, diverse acts of hatred toward a person throughout the day;
b) in the exterior acts the actions are numerically distinct in a moral
sense when they are understood as diverse: for example, small thefts
which are deprived of any connection to one another; c) if, on the other
hand, all flow together for the same end, they constitute a moral unity:
as an example, whoever follows a strategy of stealing bit by bit ten
thousand Euro has committed a grave sin of theft, and not many small
venial sins. 2) Regarding indivisible material there are as many moral
actions as concrete acts which are performed: as examples of this are
acts of unchastity.
127 Cf. Council of Trent, De Sacramento Paenitentiae, cann. 7–8: DS 1707–1708; these
canons are recalled by Ordo Paenitentiae, 2-VII-1973, Praenotanda, no. 7. See also the
Catechism, nos. 1456 and 1497. The Council of Trent made it clear that this necessity is
a divine right, that is, men cannot change it; and this explains why a generic confession
of sins with a general absolution can be performed only in very exceptional cases, and also
why this does not take away the obligation of successively manifesting in confession the
mortal sins which were pardoned in the general absolution.


Chapter 11
11.6
The Cause of Sin
11.6.1
Remote and Proximate Cause
The concept itself of sin, as a moral evil, implies that it has proceeded from a
free cause. Given that God cannot be considered in any way the origin of the
sin,128 the cause of sin should be sought in the free creature who committed
it. In man it is possible to distinguish between a remote and a proximate
cause of sin. The remote cause is the natural defectibility of man and the
concupiscence that is subsequent to sin; the proximate cause is the wickedness
of the will. The remote cause does not explain every single sin, though it can
explain the presence of sin in general. It must then be concluded that “the
root of sin is in the heart of man, in his free will.”129
11.6.2
Sins and Capital Vices
Coming to be called vices are morally evil operative habits, which are thus
opposed to the virtues. The vices play on the intellectual, affective, and dis-
positional level an analogous role, though in an opposing sense, to that played
by the virtues. The vices consolidate mistaken modes of perceiving, judging,
and appreciating persons and things, which give rise to morally evil choices.
The vices are freely acquired qualities that have in themselves a negative
moral value, insofar as they constitute strong obstacles for man's success in
identifying, desiring, and effectively carrying out conduct that is congruent
with the following of Christ. They are, moreover, principles for further sins.
Since the beginning of the Fifth Century, Christian writers, as some pagan
writers had already done, have spoken of vices and capital sins, making diverse
lists of them. With Saint Gregory the Great, the list was established with
seven capital sins.130 Capital comes from caput (head), which is as the guiding
part of the entire body; for this reason, the habits and acts that characteristi-
cally act as the source and guiding principle of other sins are metaphorically
called capital vices and sins. The expression is utilized, therefore, both for
concrete disordered acts, and for their corresponding vices, wherein the origin
of other sins is properly found. These vices are: 1) vainglory or disordered
love of one's own excellence; 2) avarice or disordered love of exterior goods; 3)
lust and 4) gluttony, which derive from a disordered love for sensible pleasure;
5) sloth (and laziness), which is the refusal of and flight from the necessary
effort for obtaining the moral and spiritual good; 6) envy, that is, the sadness
128 Cf. Sir 15:11–13; Jas 1:13; Second Council of Orange: DS 397; Clement VI, Errori
di Nicola di Autrecourt, no. 58: DS 1409; Council of Trent, De Iustificatione, can. 6: DS
1556.
129 CCC, 1853.
130 Cf. CCC, 1866.


Sin and Conversion
over the good of others considered as one's own evil and delight for the evil
suffered by others; 7) wrath or violent impatience in the face of opposition.
Pride, or the disordered love of one self, more than being a capital sin, is the
root of all sin ex parte aversionis, insofar as the distancing of oneself from
God comes about from a disordered love of oneself. Complete pride is a grave
sin per se, because with it one sets himself against God and, as the root of the
sins, it is very detrimental to the spiritual life, since it refuses submission to
God and His law. Avarice is the root of all sin ex parte conversionis, insofar
as each sin presupposes a disordered love for a relative good: “For the love of
money is the root of all evils.”131
11.6.3
Temptation
The Nature of Temptation — To tempt, in a primary sense, means to try
the strength of someone and, more concretely, his readiness to do good;132
nonetheless, here we speak of temptation as the incitement to do evil.133 The
cause of sin, as was said, is the will itself; it, however, can be influenced
and lured, though not dominated, by the presentation of apparent goods:
temptation is precisely the instigation to do a moral evil that is masquerading
as a good to deceive the will.
Temptations, if they are not sought and if they are taken advantage of as a
motive for moral effort, have a positive significance for the Christian life; the
most clear argument is that Jesus Himself “was led by the Spirit into the desert
to be tempted by the devil.”134 Temptations, taken on with a supernatural
spirit, aid in one's growth in grace, in virtue, and in merit: “Blessed is the man
who perseveres in temptation, for when he has been proved he will receive the
crown of life that he promised to those who love him.” 135
Types of Temptation — Traditionally, it has been said that temptations
come about from the world, the devil, and the flesh. We shall now see more
concretely what these mean.
1. The world: We are not dealing here with the world as God's creation,
which is good,136 but rather of the world perverted by sin, which behaves
as an enemy of God and incites men to be separated from Him.137
131 1 Tim 6:10; cf. Mt 6:24; S.Th. I-II, q. 84, a. 1.

22:1 it speaks of the trial of Abraham, which is the temptation par excellence of the Old

2. The devil: The devil is the tempter without equal;138 his task, so to

Nevertheless, the instigations toward sin should be combated keeping in mind

occupying one's mind on other things, and it is counseled for one to do this
with temptations of sensuality, for otherwise they can become more violent.

Sin and Conversion
4) To experience temptation is not a sin, only consenting to them is: the
fomes peccati makes it so that all people can experience the attractiveness of
moral evil; the latter being left ad agonem, to be fought, but cannot harm
those who do not consent to it.147 5) It is not permissible to voluntarily put
oneself into temptation: if it is not lawful to risk one's corporal life without
a proportionate cause, still more is it unlawful to be reckless with one's su-
pernatural life. If there exists a proportionate cause, then one must use all
necessary means in order that the danger become remote; moreover, since no
one is a good judge regarding his own situation, if it is possible such a person
should follow the counsel of a prudent person.
Occasion of Sin — An occasion of sin is the technical term for those external
circumstances that occur more or less voluntarily and feature a temptation to
sin. The occasion may be: a) proximate, when the danger is serious; remote,
when the danger is slight; b) absolute, when any normal person feels such a
danger; relative, when it is dangerous only for some persons; c) continuous
or discontinuous, if it is habitually present or only in intervals; d) free, when
putting oneself in such an occasion depends on one's personal will; necessary,
when it depends only on a certain state of life; e) grave or light, according to
the theological species of the sin to which the danger pertains.
The same duty of avoiding sin carries with it a duty of avoiding the occasion
of sin. Nonetheless, one cannot avoid every such occasion, for, as Saint Paul
says, “you would then have to leave the world.”148 The moral obligations
regarding this topic can be summarized as such: 1) It is gravely obligatory
to avoid grave occasions of sin, proximate and free; otherwise one would not
have a serious will to avoid sin, something which constitutes per se an offense
to God. 2) One must do all possible so that the proximate and necessary
occasion becomes remote. 3) Also to be avoided are remote, continuous, and
free occasions of sin that corrode the spiritual life and predispose one to grave
sin: for example, to watch frivolous shows, to read books of dubious doctrine
without necessity, etc.
Whoever does not want to distance himself from a grave, proximate, and free
occasion of sin manifests that he does not repent of his own sins, nor does he
intend to do all that is possible to avoid them. With such a disposition, one
cannot validly receive sacramental absolution.149
147 Cf. Council of Trent, De Peccato Originali, can. 5: DS 1515; Saint Pius V, Bull Ex
Omnibus Afflictionibus, 1-X-1567, n. 50: DS 1950; CCC, 2847.
148 1 Cor 5:10.
149 Innocent XI condemned the following lax proposition: “Sometimes one can be absolved
who is found in a proximate occasion of sin that he can leave but does not want to leave,
but which he directly and purposefully seeks or exposes himself to” (Decree of the Holy
Office, 2-III-1679, n. 61: DS 2161, our translation.). This is based on the words of Jesus:
“If your right eye causes you to sin, tear it out and throw it away” (Mt 5:29).


Chapter 11
11.7
The Effects of Sin
The effects of sin are intimately connected with its essence and are intercon-
nected with one another; they principally derive from the aversio a Deo and
secondarily from the conversio ad creaturas.150
The first effect of mortal sin is exclusion from the divine friendship—the
aversio a Deo–: grave sin deprives one of the inhabitation of the three divine
Persons and therefore from supernatural life, sanctifying grace, and charity.
Along with grace, one also loses the infused virtues and the gifts of the Holy
Spirit, not to mention that faith and hope can remain in an amorphous state,
i.e one not vivified by charity. Lost as well are the supernatural merits that
had been obtained: “And if the virtuous man turns from the path of virtue to
do evil, the same kind of abominable things that the wicked man does, can he
do this and still live? None of his virtuous deeds shall be remembered”; 151
nonetheless, these merits can be recovered when the sinner repents and returns
to friendship with God.152 Mortal sin, moreover, merits eternal punishment.
With mortal sin, man, created in order to live in communion with God, also
contradicts the deepest truth of his being and his true good. In the recount
of the sin of the first parents there is manifested the intimate conflict that
sin introduces into the person:153 man hides himself from God, he becomes
aware of being naked, the land produces for him thorns and thistles, and a re-
lationship of distrust is established between persons. Sin, therefore, negatively
influences various human dimensions: theocentric, personal, social, and ma-
terial dimensions.154 These conflicts within the person produce a sentiment
of discomfort, that is called a remorse of conscience; such a remorse can help
one to repent and to atone for the punishment that is due on account of the
sin.155
150 Cf. Wis 11:16; 12:23,27; Ezek 23:35.
151 Ezek 18:24.
152 Cf. Pius XI, Apostolic Letter Infinita Dei Misericordia, 29-V-1924: DS 3670.
153 Cf. Gen 3:7–19. Regarding the vulnera of sin, see E. Colom, Dios y el obrar humano
(1976), 125–181.
154Sin generates in the person a set of divisions, “between man and the nature created by
God.” (Reconciliatio et Paenitentia, 23). “For sin has diminished man, blocking his path
to fulfillment” (Gaudium et Spes, n. 13), and therefore renders him unhappy: the sinner
seeks joy, but because he seeks in in a mistaken way, what he finds instead is unhappiness,
as Judas' fate demonstrates. In the final analysis, he finds the profound unhappiness of
one who is in contrast to himself; the Old Testament emphasizes it as so: “those habitually
guilty of sin are their own worst enemies” (Tob 12:10), and “he who strays after them [sinful
activities] sins against his own life” (Sir 19:4). Cf. De Malo, q. 2, a. 11.
155 “If man does evil, the just judgment of his conscience remains within him as a witness
to the universal truth of the good, as well as to the malice of his particular choice. But
the verdict of conscience remains in him also as a pledge of hope and mercy: while bearing
witness to the evil he has done, it also reminds him of his need, with the help of God's
grace, to ask forgiveness, to do good and to cultivate virtue constantly” (Veritatis Splendor,
61). Cf. CCC, 1781.


Sin and Conversion
The sin of an individual does not only harm the sinner, but also has negative
consequences in the ecclesial and civil community.156 The bond of charity,
which unites the members of the mystical body to Christ and to each other,
is weakened on account of personal sins: the moral fault distances the sinner
from the Church, and this introduces a disorder into the body of Christ. The
dogma of the communion of saints entails a communitary influence of the
moral action of the individual both when it is good and when it is bad:157
sinners refuse to collaborate in the edification of the Church and hinder the
accomplishment of the divine plan of holiness not only for what concerns them-
selves, but also for what regards the entire Church, “which they have wounded
by their sins.”158 This is also the case with internal sins and for those which
are committed directly against God and against themselves. Nevertheless,
the antisocial effects of sin are greater when their public repercussion is more
direct, as we said regarding social sin and collective responsibility.
11.8
Cooperation with Evil
Notion of Cooperation with Evil — In a technical sense we mean by
cooperation with evil (or with sin) the execution of an act that in some way
helps another person to accomplish an immoral action of which the latter
person remains the principal author. Growing social interdependence creates a
multitude of relations wherein this moral form is found: judges, businessmen,
educators, politicians, but also relatives, friends, etc.
On the other hand,
as has been said, morality cannot only be measured on an individual basis,
because the social dimension is an intrinsic characteristic of the human person;
in this sense, it is not enough to “act well” in the individual sphere, but it is
also necessary that one's actions have a positive repercussion in society. The
problem that now presents itself is that of knowing how far it is possible to
collaborate in an effective way, even if involuntarily or at least only indirectly
voluntarily, in the execution of what is morally illicit.
In the first place, cooperation with evil needs to be distinguished from scandal.
“Scandal is an attitude or behavior which leads another to do evil.” 159 Scandal
supposes a direct influence on the will of another. The one who scandalizes is
in some way the cause of the evil will of another person, while cooperation,
on the other hand, is an action that facilitates the execution of an evil design
that another person has on his own.
156 Cf. Heb 12:15.
157 “If (one) part suffers, all the parts suffer with it; if one part is honored, all the parts
share its joy” (1 Cor 12, 26).
158 Lumen Gentium, 11.
159 CCC 2284; cf. also nos. 2285–2287.


Chapter 11
Cooperation with another's sin can be willed directly or through free initia-
tive, and as such implies an approval of the other's action (formal cooperation
with evil); or it can be tolerated or endured, without this implying an approval
of the other's behavior, inasmuch as cooperation derives inevitably from an
action that must be done for whatever reason (material cooperation with evil).
What often happens, in this second case, is that determinate social circum-
stances or those relating to work put a person in the condition of making use
of another's behavior in order to carry out his own designs with greater ease.
Material cooperation with evil can be either immediate (direct) or mediated
(indirect); furthermore, it can be either proximate or remote.
1. Immediate or direct material cooperation with evil occurs when a person
helps another to execute an evil action; e.g. to help a thief to steal, even
while not approving of the theft.
2. Mediated or indirect material cooperation with evil occurs when one
provides another with an instrument which the other person will use
to do evil; e.g.
selling wine to a person who will use it to become
intoxicated.
3. The distinction between proximate material cooperation and remote
material cooperation depends on the physical or moral connection be-
tween the action of the person who cooperates and that of the principal
author. The manager of a bank who grants loans to a magazine that
fosters immoral behavior cooperates in a proximate way; a person who
holds his savings in a bank that grants such loans cooperate only re-
motely. Immediate material cooperation is always proximate; mediate
material cooperation can be either proximate or remote.
Moral Principles Regarding Cooperation with Evil — Formal coop-
eration with evil is always illicit.160 Material cooperation with evil, in general
terms, is also illicit, because the good of the human person, considered also
in its social dimensions, does not only demand that each person act according
to right reason, but that he do so in such a way insofar as it is in his con-
trol, that favorable conditions come about for the good of others, helping and
contributing to the best of his own abilities. Sociality has, and must have, an
eminently positive sense: it represents an aid of which each person has need
in order to grow as a person and to live, day to day, an honest life.
Nonetheless, there are some circumstances that can render licit certain actions
through which one materially cooperates with evil.
In the case of material
cooperation with evil, it is not the result of a free initiative to cooperate,
but of a certain necessity of achieving a good or avoiding an evil through
160 Cf. Evangelium Vitae 74; CCC 1868, 2272, 2282 and 2291.


Sin and Conversion
an action that another uses to accomplish his own immoral plan. The first
condition to be met for an action of this type to be potentially licit is that there
really is a need to execute it; i.e. there does not exist another possibility for
accomplishing the necessary good or avoiding the evil that must be avoided.
If there is the possibility of acting without cooperating with evil, even if this
carries with it a certain effort or presents the person with some discomfort,
cooperation with evil will not be morally admissible.
If there exists no other possibility, then the problem can be resolved with the
the same criteria studied in Chapter VI concerning the principle of double
effect, because this is its true nature. The action that is performed cannot
entail an injury per se to a virtue; the intention must be right; the evil action
of another person cannot be the cause (on the intentional level, the means)
for which the necessary good is obtained; and there must exist a proportion
between the importance and necessity of the good effect to be achieved and
the negativity represented by the cooperation (the gravity of the evil with
which the person cooperates, the proximity of the cooperation, etc.). There
exist actions that are very grave (homicide, abortion, etc.) with which it is
never licit to materially cooperate in an immediate way.161
In cases in which, following what has been said to this point, it were licit to
carry out an action wherein—without wanting to—one cooperates with evil, it
remains morally necessary to take opportune precautions to avoid the danger
of a moral fall for oneself or for others (scandal).
The problems of cooperation with evil are very frequent today. If they are
confronted with a weak moral attitude, the previously mentioned criteria can
give rise to a minimalistic casuistry in which, through the able application of a
rule, the person could avoid his own moral responsibility. Therefore, we need
to be aware of the ethical need of cooperating with good, as well as the moral
necessity of preventing and avoiding, in the measure in which it is possible,
difficult situations—for oneself, or for others—in which cooperation with evil
would become a little less than inevitable.
11.9
Conversion from Sin
The great novelty of the biblical announcement is that the reality of sin is
not definitive, that one can obtain the pardon of a God who is “a merciful and
gracious God, slow to anger and rich in kindness and fidelity.” 162 In fact, “God
161 Cf. Evangelium Vitae, 74. The principle applied there to abortion cannot be univer-
sally applied to all moral actions. The material cooperation with the onanism of one'se
spouse is immediate, but if there exists a grave cause it is morally licit: cf. Pius XI, Enc.
Casti Connubii, 31-XII-1930: DS 3718.
162 Ex 34:6–7; cf. Ps 101:14; 129:4.7,8; Isa 30:18–19; Mt 9:13; 1 Tim 1:13–15.


Chapter 11
rejoices in nothing as He does the conversion and salvation of man.” 163 The
consciousness of sin does not entail, for the Christian, a passive or negative
disposition; on the contrary, the reality of this fault emphasizes, by contrast,
four convictions solidly rooted in Revelation: the profundity of divine mercy,
the necessity of accepting human weakness, the overabundance of grace, and
the indispensability of human collaboration.164
11.9.1
The Mercy of God
The mysterium pietatis is greater than the mysterium iniquitatis: no sin can
extinguish the divine mercy; rather, it is precisely the pardoning of sin that
marks with precision the love of the Father, through the sacrifice of the Son
and the gift of the Spirit.165 For this reason, mercy is one of the most recalled
attributes of God in the Scriptures.166 In fact, the Lord calls sinners (all men)
to repentance, mercifully facilitates its actualization, and shows its path: “The
process of conversion and repentance was described by Jesus in the parable
of the prodigal son, the center of which is the merciful father (Lk 15:11–24):
The fascination of illusory freedom, the abandonment of the father's house; the
extreme misery in which the son finds himself after squandering his fortune;
his deep humiliation at finding himself obliged to feed swine, and still worse,
at wanting to feed on the husks the pigs ate; his reflection on all he has lost;
his repentance and decision to declare himself guilty before his father; the
journey back; the father's generous welcome; the father's joy - all these are
characteristic of the process of conversion. the beautiful robe, the ring, and
the festive banquet are symbols of that new life - pure worthy, and joyful -
of anyone who returns to God and to the bosom of his family, which is the
Church. Only the heart of Christ Who knows the depths of his Father's love
could reveal to us the abyss of his mercy in so simple and beautiful a way.” 167
11.9.2
“Metánoia”
The mercy and grace of God cancel sin and confer the strength to sin no more.
Nonetheless, He asks of the Christian a penitent disposition: “To acknowledge
one's sin, indeed-penetrating still more deeply into the consideration of one's
own personhood-to recognize oneself as being a sinner, capable of sin and
163 Saint Gregory of Nazianzus, Oratio 39, 20: SC 358, 194, our translation.; cf.
Lk
15:7,10,32.
164 Cf. Reconciliatio et Paenitentia, nos. 19–22.
165 Cf. Veritatis Splendor, 118.
166 Cf. Num 14:19; Tob 3:2; Ps 102:3–4; 117:1–4,29; Sir 2:9,18; Lk 1:50,54,78; 6:36; Rom
9:16; 2 Cor 1:3; Titus 3:5; Heb 4:16; Jas 5:11; 1 Pet 1:3.
167 CCC, 1439; cf. Reconciliatio et Paenitentia, 5.


Sin and Conversion
inclined to commit sin, is the essential first step in returning to God.” 168 The
most employed Greek word in the Bible for this human disposition is that of
metánoia.
The image contained within the Semitic word that corresponds to metánoia
makes one think of a person who recognizes his mistaken path and then
turns away, taking a new and diverse direction. Thus, metánoia means:
a) repentance and sorrow for the sin committed; b) conversion of mind
and transformation in one's mode of thinking, that entails trust in God
and a firm decision to carry out His will; c) a positive response to divine
grace wherein the possibility of being saved is found; and d) a commit-
ment to a new moral attitude, with regard to God and other men, that
involves all one's personal energy.
Speaking of the conversion of the sinner, Sacred Scripture emphasizes
five ideas: 1) sins distance one from God and make it so that the Lord
may abandon His people;169 2) the initiative in the work of reconcil-
iation is divine: one cannot arrive at an authentic repentance—and
therefore at friendship with the Lord and, definitively, at an integral
liberation and salvation—without the grace that comes from God;170 3)
conversion, more than an external rite, demands a change “of heart”;171
4) the sinner must recognize and confess his sins;172 5) and, furthermore,
he must change his life, distancing himself from perverse paths.173
Metánoia is not a disposition proper only to the beginning of the Christian
life: it must be permanent throughout one's entire existence in order that
one may continually convert each time closer to the Lord.174 Even those who
consider themselves to be “righteous” have need of conversion.175
11.9.3
The Sacraments of Forgiveness
In the actual economy of salvation reconciliation with God is possible only in
Christ and through Christ, “who overthrows the devil's domain and wards off

Chapter 11
the manifold malice of vice.”176 This is a reconciliation that is made concrete
through the Church, the universal sacrament of salvation.177
Jesus Christ,
with His Paschal Mystery, is the meritorious and efficient cause of conversion
and salvation; and for the purpose of perpetuating in time this salvific action
He instituted the sacraments, which justify and transform the person: they
presuppose, nourish, strengthen, and express faith.
Furthermore, they do
not act merely as an exhortation or occasion to do good, but work with a
more intimate efficacy, unparalleled in nature, that directs man toward God,
and imprints and perfects the image of the Holy Trinity in his soul. Thus,
Christian morality cannot but be a sacramental morality:178 indeed, the first
grace received is always through a sacrament, Baptism, at least by desire.
Furthermore, the ordinary path for the remission of sins committed after
Baptism is the Sacrament of Penance.179
11.10
Conversion, the Moral Life,
and the Ascetic Effort
Conversion entails a radical reorientation of one's entire life: a return to God
with all one's heart, a rupture with sin and repentance for disordered acts
that were committed; at the same time, it requires a desire and a resolution
to change one's life with the hope of God's mercy and trust in the help of
His grace.180 In fact, the Lord always concedes grace to those who do what
they can, though we should not forget that it is also Him who moves human
freedom in its dispositions to convert.181
The consideration of conversion as a moral and ascetic effort allows us to re-
view the principal themes of fundamental moral theology, even if in an inverse
order to that which we have followed up to this point. The full understanding
and acceptance without reservation of the divine call to holiness happens with
difficulty when there is no previous experience of sin and conversion. On one
hand, only for those who feel the necessity of being saved, and understand in
a sufficiently clear way from what it is that they have need of being liberated,
176Ad Gentes, 9.
177 Cf. Lumen Gentium, nos. 9 & 48; Gaudium et Spes, 45; etc.; for this reason, speaking
of the Sacrament of Penance, John Paul II indicates: while “nothing is more personal
and intimate that this sacrament, in which the sinner stands alone before God with his
sin, repentance and trust [. . . ], But at the same time one cannot deny the social nature
of this sacrament, in which the whole church-militant, suffering and glorious in heaven-
comes to the aid of the penitent and welcomes him again into her bosom” (Reconciliatio et
Paenitentia, 31, IV).
178 Cf. Chapter I, subsection 1.1.2.
179 Cf. Reconciliatio et Paenitentia, 31, I.
180 Cf. CCC, 1431.

Sin and Conversion
is it possible to have an authentic encounter with Christ Jesus, “who became
for us wisdom from God, as well as righteousness, sanctification, and redemp-
tion”;182 on the other hand, the encounter with the Lord and the verification
of our spiritual regeneration are one and the same thing.183 Regeneration in
Christ is a profound event, of an ontological character, that manifests itself
morally as a passage from vice to Christian virtue.184
Such a passage is not, however, immediate. It is true that Christ becomes
the principle of new life,185 which would not be possible without some initial
possession of the theological and infused moral virtues, however the life in-
formed by it begins to be expressed as a battle against sin and concupiscence;
a progressive clarification of conscience; an effort to interiorize the normative
directions of the moral law; an education of the capacity of judgment, of the
will, and of the sentiments; a correction of our attitude in the face of earthly
goods; constant recourse to the means of sanctification; an acceptance of the
demands of fraternal charity; and an effort to not be led away by discour-
agement. The normative statements of the moral law constitute in this first
phase of the Christian life an indispensable aid. They indicate the limits that
the believer must not exceed in the use of goods and in the execution of the
various activities that make up one's life, so that it may be effectively lived
in the Lord.
The intrinsic dynamism of the grace of the Holy Spirit goes much further. If
one is docile in his cooperation with it, he shall experience successive con-
versions, each of which represents Christ's growth within us. The moral and
ascetic effort aims at giving always greater space to the Lord in our existence,
in order to arrive at a point in which like Saint Paul we can say “yet I live,
no longer I, but Christ lives in me.”186 One passes, then, to the free and full
development of the Christian virtues and the gifts of the Holy Spirit, which, as
true vital principles, regulate our choices from within so that all the goods and
all the activities which perfect our existence might become, with spontaneity
and naturalness, effective means to union with Christ.
The path toward union with the Lord is not easy.
There are resistances,
hesitations, and moments of darkness and crisis that are sometimes also mo-
ments of purification and growth.
Only after the General Resurrection in
Jesus Christ will our transformation into the image of the Son be complete
and definitive.
Nonetheless, with the help of grace, the call to holiness is
already something concretely implementable and to be implemented in this
world, because God “chose us in him [Christ], before the foundation of the
